21 Linked Art API Endpoints: https://linked.art/api/1.0/endpoint/. 

Analysis of the Usability of Automatically Enriched Cultural Heritage Data 83
shedding light on its potential to shape perceptions, and importantly, its role in 
potentially fostering increased adoption of portals implementing standards that 
adhere to the LOUD design principles. 
4 LUX: Yale Collections Discovery 
LUX22 is an implementation of Linked Art and IIIF as a discovery and research 
platform for the combined collections of Yale University. This encompasses the Yale 
Center for British Art (YCBA), the Yale University Art Gallery (YUAG), the Yale 
Peabody Museum (YPM), and the Yale University Library (YUL). These collections 
encompass art, natural history, bibliographic and archival collections, and all of the 
related people, organisations, places, concepts, and events, totaling some 41 million 
records at the time of writing (Fig. 3). 
Beyond just using the Linked Art metadata application proﬁle, the development 
of LUX also tried to apply the same principles to other decisions that were needed 
when mapping data and use cases from the systems of record into Linked Art and 
which functionality was important to implement. 
The system consists of several interconnected components, namely data harvest-
ing, data pipeline, back-end database, middle tier, and front-end. These components 
have been integrated according to established standards including both IIIF and 
Fig. 3 LUX homepage
22 LUX, Yale Collections Discovery: https://lux.collections.yale.edu/. 

84 J. A. Raemy and R. Sanderson
Linked Art, so that any individual component can be replaced without requiring 
a complete rewrite of the system. 
4.1 Developing a LOUD-Driven Discovery Platform 
The usability of the data was extremely important to the development process as 
it meant that a relatively junior front-end software engineer was able to build the 
application without signiﬁcant assistance. The data format being easy to understand 
and work with meant she could dive in and get started and stakeholders could 
immediately see results. The consistency of the structure meant that components 
could be built that leveraged the repeated patterns and then could be reused 
whenever that pattern was encountered. By following the design principles adopted 
from IIIF, the implementation architecture meant that the resulting system is 
performant, scalable, relatively modular, and easy to adopt and adapt. 
Discussions around data mapping decisions were easier given the design princi-
ples and speciﬁcations. Rather than having discussions about competing viewpoints, 
which has often led to frustration and lack of commitment, they could instead 
be structured around working cooperatively to identify which possibilities best 
aligned with the principles and which were outside them. Examples of requested 
modelling that was determined through this process to be outside of the usability 
guidelines, and therefore out of the scope of the work, was a desire to align the 
parallel structures of textual description and structured data around dimensions 
and materials of an object, the inclusion of data about the metadata such as the 
provenance of where individual assertions came from in the merged records, and 
structured data around uncertainty of assertions. Cases that would have led to 
inconsistency and more exceptions in the mapping included that animals referenced 
as subjects or actors could be treated as people, and fossils in the natural history 
museum could be treated as human made objects. Without the structures to help 
focus the attention on usability rather than correctness and completeness, these 
situations all would have led to either long and fraught discussions or aggravated 
developers needing to deal with more and more complex data structures. 
This paradigm also helped with determining the correct approach for systems 
architecture and functionality. The hardest challenge of using a knowledge graph 
was the need to have a traditional record style interface with keyword search, facets, 
and views of the individual entities. A triplestore or native graph-based system 
does not easily enable any of these and requires multiple systems to be used in 
conjunction, which increases the complexity of development and maintenance of 
the platform. Instead after several months of research, a multi-modal platform was 
licensed which can treat the records as records and extract the relevant parts of the 
graph and allow a single query to use the features of both worlds simultaneously. 
Again following the principles such as “simple as possible but no simpler”, 
the graph parts of the queries were analysed against the search requirements and 
the resulting relationships simpliﬁed to only what was necessary. As the record

Analysis of the Usability of Automatically Enriched Cultural Heritage Data 85
maintains the full data, no information is lost; however the performance and ease 
of development was increased by collapsing complex chains of relationships down 
to only one artiﬁcial predicate. For example, in order to capture the role of each 
artist in the production of an artwork, the object is produced by a Production 
event, which then has parts to represent the roles, and each part is carried out by a 
Person or Organisation. To simplify the common query of objects produced 
by a given artist, that was reduced to the equivalent of the Dublin Core relationship 
of creator in the graph. This pattern was then applied across all of the record types 
and requirements such that only relationships between records were materialised, 
resulting in a 40% reduction in the size of the data and a much more performant 
system. 
One of the principles of Linked Art is that each relationship should only be 
present in the dataset in one record, including inverse relations. For example, if 
there are two Place records and one place is part of the other such as a county 
within a state, then the part of the relationship is only expressed in the county, 
and the state does not list all of the counties, cities, or other localities which are 
part of it. This direction is intentional to keep the size of each record down and 
relatively consistent. However, it leads to the inevitable and obvious question of 
how do you determine, in this case, the places which are part of the state? As the 
solution requires looking up many records, the implementation is a search on that 
property. To avoid technology dependence on a particular query language or search 
engine, the Linked Art API makes use of the Hypertext Application Language 
(HAL) speciﬁcation (Kelly, 2023), which allows the record to include links to search 
URIs and give each a name. The front-end needs only follow the link to receive a 
paginated list of all of the results, in the same format as for any other set of search 
results. This layer of indirection avoids technology dependence and increases the 
usability for the front-end developer, who no longer needs to understand the data 
model and query language in order to retrieve the list of child places, but instead is 
provided a named link in the record to follow, and a standard response with all of 
the functionality needed to produce different user interfaces for different situations. 
Several other practical choices were facilitated through the LOUD principles 
and practices. In the LOD world, there is a fascination with federated queries— 
distributing the query among multiple, potentially heterogeneous systems, and then 
bringing the results back together before presenting them to the user. This paradigm 
is unreliable as the speed of the search is dependent on the speed of the slowest 
participating system, and if any system is ofﬂine for some reason, then the results 
will necessarily be incomplete. The alternative is to harvest all of the data from 
every participating system and combine it in advance into a single infrastructure. 
The trade-off is between the extent to which the results are out of date with the 
source system and the speed at which searches can be accomplished by end users. 
Given the relatively infrequent change of the majority of the records and that the 
users’ information needs can likely still be satisﬁed by information that is a day 
out of date, the harvest approach was selected. The records are made available for 
synchronisation leveraging the IIIF Change Discovery API 1.0 (Appleby et al., 
2021), with the Linked Art data taking the place of the IIIF resources. This

86 J. A. Raemy and R. Sanderson
was signiﬁcantly easier to implement by the participating libraries, archives, and 
museums than every unit maintaining their own query endpoint. 
4.2 Automatically Enriched Cultural Heritage Data 
The LUX platform is distinguished by its extensive connections, not only within 
various Yale units but also outside, as it incorporates external data sources during 
data processing. These sources encompass a wide range of subject areas and 
perspectives. This enriches the data accessible to users by matching records within 
LUX. For instance, one of the key procedures employed to harmonise works 
and objects involves incorporating reconciled Wikidata records, 23 allowing for 
meaningful connections between items, for instance, in the YCBA collection 
and related works. Additionally, these sources incorporate additional names and 
terms from authority records and subject headings, such as those from the French 
National Library (BnF).24 the Library of Congress (LoC),25 or the German-speaking 
Integrated Authority File (GND).26 In addition, LUX integrates Wikimedia images 
that are in the public domain, as illustrated by Fig. 4.27 
This integration signiﬁcantly enhances the record by combining knowledge 
from different Yale units, Getty vocabulary terms, national libraries, and other 
external sources as shown in Fig. 5. This is an example of the positive impact and 
improvement that can be achieved by linking disparate data sources. The linking 
process is automated within the data processing code, using equivalent URI and 
intelligent matching of names associated with people, places, and things. However, 
matching and merging data into a single LUX record can be a complex task. Data 
quality is affected by human imperfections, as all data are derived from human input. 
Figure 6 depicts the overall data transformation, reconciliation, enrichment, and 
publication workﬂow for LUX. The base records come from both internal and 
external sources. 
The process (diamonds) named Harvest runs nightly, triggered by an operating 
system level scheduler to poll each stream to ﬁnd and retrieve records that have 
changed since the previous harvest. For external datasets that do not have associated 
Activity Streams, these records are either retrieved en masse via downloadable 
dump ﬁles or as needed when another record refers to them. The initial state, and 
all subsequent states after transformations have occurred, is stored in the “Record 
Caches” store. All records are passed through source-speciﬁc transformation rou-

Either external sources are collected record by record over the network as needed, 
or if a dump ﬁle of entire dataset is available, that is downloaded and ingested into 
the local cache on a regular basis. The transformations are implemented in Python 
using the Cromulent library 28 on a source by source basis; however, much of the 
heavy lifting is taken care of by the library code and these transformation routines 
are easy and fast to write. The validation is performed using a series of JSON 
Schemas for Linked Art at the syntax level 29 and however could be done using 
Shapes Constraint Language (SHACL) (Knublauch & Kontokostas, 2017) or other 
technologies to validate semantically as well. 
Once the records are connected, they have their internal identiﬁers rewritten to a 
central set of unique identiﬁers by means of “Identiﬁer Map”, a very fast in-memory 
database, that maps the original URIs to the internal identiﬁers ( Re-Identify). 
The result is a transformation of the records where the data remains the same, but 
the identiﬁers are now consistent. The records from multiple sources that have been 
mapped to the same identiﬁer are then merged together (Merge) to form the single 
record for the entity. The resulting dataset is then annotated with some additional
28 Cromulent: https://github.com/linked-art/crom. 
29 JSON Validator for Linked Art: https://github.com/linked-art/json-validator. 

Analysis of the Usability of Automatically Enriched Cultural Heritage Data 89
features for indexing and exported to Load into the back-end query engine, a 
product called MarkLogic,30 a licensed system by a company called Progress.31 
In order to interact with the data, a user connects to the LUX portal in their web 
browser and performs a search. That search is sent through a middle tier gateway that 
allows for seamless transition between MarkLogic installations (a process known as 
blue/green switching) and through an internal web cache built with Varnish to ensure 
that repeated queries are only evaluated once. Additional web caches are in place 
between the user and the LUX front-end, including CloudFront, 32 react cache, and 
the browser’s native web cache, to ensure performance is as fast as possible. 
After the public launch of LUX in May 2023, the focus for LUX involves 
developing various services. Among the requested services is direct access to the 
identiﬁer map of equivalencies, as well as the associated indexes for reconciliation. 
The open documentation of these services will be of signiﬁcant value to individuals 
and institutions within the cultural heritage sector. By providing open access to 
these resources, LUX facilitates streamlined data reconciliation processes and the 
creation of meaningful connections between diverse cultural heritage datasets. 
This accessibility will enable a wider community to make effective use of LUX’s 
capabilities, thereby promoting enriched data and interconnected cultural heritage 
resources across the sector. 
5 Discussion 
This discussion is divided into two parts reﬂecting on the IIIF and Linked Art 
communities as well as the development of LUX. 
First, we discuss the dimension of community engagement required to create 
open and interoperable standards, emphasising the collective effort required to 
create speciﬁcations that can be seamlessly integrated into different systems. 
The effectiveness of the second dimension, which focuses on how LOUD 
standards can facilitate data enrichment, is greatly enhanced by the successful 
implementation of the ﬁrst dimension. The collaborative approach to standards 
development lays the foundation for comprehensive data enrichment processes and 
highlights the need for standardised approaches to improve data enrichment in 
different domains.
30 MarkLogic: https://www.marklogic.com/. 
31 Progress: https://progress.com/. 
32 Amazon CloudFront: https://aws.amazon.com/cloudfront/. 

90 J. A. Raemy and R. Sanderson
5.1 Community Engagement Fosters Open Standards and 
Interoperability 
The openness of a standard, while critical, is arguably not sufﬁcient for widespread 
adoption. Achieving successful interoperability often depends on having a sig-
niﬁcant platform, either through commercial inﬂuence or through community 
involvement as articulated by Nelson and Van de Sompel (2022): 
Because of the growing global adoption of open standards by GLAM institutions, especially 
IIIF speciﬁcations stand as a testimony that rich interoperability for distributed resource 
collections is effectively achievable. But other promising speciﬁcations that aim for 
the same holy grail are struggling for adoption, and, many times, lack of resources is 
mentioned as a reason. While that undoubtedly plays a role, it did not stand in the way 
of rapid adoption of protocols that have emerged from large corporations, such as the 
Google-dominated schema.org. This consideration re-emphasises that a core ingredient of 
a successful interoperability speciﬁcation, and hence of achieving an interoperable global 
information web, is a large megaphone, either in the guise of commercial power or active 
community engagement. 
For community-driven initiatives like IIIF and Linked Art, they require transpar-
ent practices that facilitate on-boarding of new members and governance, such as 
the establishment of a consortium, to steer the initial vision. However, it is essential 
to recognise that ﬂexibility is equally paramount, particularly in the early stages of 
an initiative. Embracing adaptability allows these initiatives to respond to evolving 
needs and emerging insights from new members, ensuring that the initial vision 
remains dynamic and responsive to the changing landscape. 
Channeling the perspective of the World Wide Web Consortium (W3C) to 
accomplish a demonstration of (interoperable) implementations (Etemad & Rivoal, 
2023), here is how we deﬁne interoperability within a LOUD lens: 
Interoperability is a state in which two or more tested, independently devel-
oped technological systems can interact successfully according to their scope 
through the implementation of agreed-upon standards. 
This necessitates the development and availability of several compliant tools 
and software that adhere to these standards, forming an ecosystem of interoperable 
solutions. In striving for interoperability, it is essential to recognise the formation of 
sub-communities or satellite groups, often existing within or adjacent to communi-
ties. They play a critical role in the creation and maintenance of tools that align with 
the speciﬁed standards. Heavy reliance on a particular tool, if left without dedicated 
care and maintenance, can pose signiﬁcant challenges. In such cases, communities 
need to rally and take collective action to ensure the tool’s sustainability and 
continued functionality. These instances underscore the necessity for a shared 
commitment to support and collectively manage critical tools, demonstrating the

Analysis of the Usability of Automatically Enriched Cultural Heritage Data 91
communal responsibility and collaborative ethos that should deﬁne community-
driven initiatives. 
On a different level, the success of collaboration for developing LUX can be 
attributed to a shared vision that recognises the value of highlighting the connections 
between diverse collections across different domains. This shared vision has enabled 
the resources of all participating units to contribute signiﬁcantly over a number of 
years through active participation in committees, working groups, and unit-level 
development efforts. 
5.2 LOUD Standard F acilitates Data Enrichment 
Interoperability and openness stand as essential cornerstones in the facilitation of 
robust data enrichment processes. The principle of interoperability engenders a 
collaborative environment wherein disparate data sources and formats converge 
to augment the quality and completeness of data. This convergence is pivotal in 
data enrichment, allowing for a seamless ﬂow of data across a spectrum of tools 
and platforms. Concurrently, openness advocates for unhindered accessibility and 
availability of data, often epitomised by adherence to open standards. Through the 
lens of data enrichment, these principles synergistically operate to accommodate 
a diverse array of sources and perspectives, cultivating a more comprehensive and 
accurate enrichment process. 
The LOUD paradigm embodies the harmonisation of interoperability and open-
ness within data enrichment efforts. By harmonising data enrichment with speciﬁ-
cations compliant with the LOUD design principles, data connections are strength-
ened, ultimately improving both scholarly understanding and user experience by 
providing enriched, accessible, and contextually interwoven data. 
Many cultural heritage institutions have yet to embrace open APIs at scale, which 
hinders data accessibility and interoperability. Factors such as resource constraints, 
lack of awareness of the beneﬁts, and complexity of implementation contribute 
to this slow adoption. Yet despite these challenges, LOUD speciﬁcations, such as 
Linked Art, offer a promising opportunity to address these issues and improve 
interoperability and data sharing in the cultural heritage domain. As such, Yale’s 
LUX serves as an exemplary model of how combining these speciﬁcations, namely 
IIIF and Linked Art APIs, can provide pathways for robust data pipelines, data 
reconciliation, and subsequent data enrichment, thereby helping the cultural heritage 
ﬁeld to progress. 
6 Conclusion 
Both IIIF and Linked Art, supported by their dedicated and collaborative commu-
nities, are strongly committed to advancing the accessibility and interoperability 
of cultural heritage resources and their associated metadata. These communities

92 J. A. Raemy and R. Sanderson
actively contribute to the development and maintenance of shared APIs that are 
critical to promoting the seamless discovery and use of cultural heritage. 
LUX serves as a compelling case study for the use of linked data at scale, 
demonstrating the real-world application of automated enrichment in the cultural 
heritage sector. By leveraging linked data technologies, LUX enables users to 
seamlessly access and explore vast collections of cultural heritage data across 
Yale’s museums, libraries, and archives in a single environment. The platform 
demonstrates how automatically enriched data can improve accessibility, usability, 
and interoperability, ultimately transforming the way users engage with and discover 
cultural heritage resources. 
Achieving semantic interoperability requires the establishment of sound LOUD-
compliant ecosystems and workﬂows (Manz et al., 2023). More speciﬁcally, the 
use of standards such as Linked Art is essential to enable effective data sharing 
across different domains. In addition, the use of IIIF APIs plays a key role in 
the seamless delivery and annotation of image-based resources. Importantly, it is 
possible for institutions of limited resources and size, not necessarily of the scale of 
larger institutions such as Yale, to achieve this type of interoperability. Collaboration 
and engagement with the wider IIIF and Linked Art communities becomes critical, 
providing vital support and expertise, particularly in the absence of human resources 
or skills. 
This combination of collaborative standards and real-world application under-
scores the potential and need for initiatives such as IIIF and Linked Art to drive 
transformative progress in the cultural heritage sector and beyond.

work. We also extend our thanks to our colleagues at the University of Basel and Yale University 
for their unwavering support and expertise.

Cultural Relic Image Retrieval Based 
on Artiﬁcial Intelligence 
Yuan Zhou, QiQi Jiang, and Bingrui Wang 
1 Introduction 
Cultural heritage embodies the history and cultural progression of humankind, 
acting as a bridge linking the past, present, and future (Blake, 2000;F r e y , 1997; 
Silverman & Ruggles, 2007). As witnesses of history, they serve as cherished 
memories of the advancement and evolution of human society. As a signiﬁcant 
component of cultural heritage, cultural relics reﬂect cultural characteristics and 
human wisdom of different historical periods in their unique forms, styles, and 
techniques. Cultural relics possess both high artistic and historical value, as well 
as cultural signiﬁcance. These properties make cultural relics an important part of 
individuals’ spiritual and cultural identities. Due to the irreplaceable and unique 
nature as a kind of material cultural heritage, it is necessary that we appreciate and 
safeguard cultural relics for future generations. 
The circulation of cultural relics is a crucial part of its preservation (Geary, 1986). 
In recent years, with the increasingly active private collection activities and the 
continuous growth of the cultural relics trading market, the balance between the 
protection of cultural relics and rational use has become an important issue. How 
to meet people’s demand for collection and appreciation of cultural relics while 
blocking the illegal sales channels, effectively regulating the circulation market, 
and preventing the loss and destruction of cultural relics has become one of the 
important issues to be solved in the ﬁeld of cultural heritage protection.

95

96 Y . Zhou et al.
In this context, the advancement and utilization of cultural relic image retrieval 
technology plays a critical role. This technology is primarily employed to ensure 
the authenticity of traded cultural relics by analyzing their images and conducting a 
search against a database of culturally signiﬁcant objects that have undergone trade 
restrictions or historical transactions (Newell, 2008). At the same time, comparing 
the consistency of information between the inventory of cultural relics and the 
auction catalogue can also prevent the seller from stealing false items and other 
unethical behaviors. Therefore, cultural relic image retrieval technology can offer 
important basic support for protecting cultural relics and facilitating research, 
trading, and related activities. 
The majority of the existing cultural relic image retrieval techniques (Wei 
et al., 2005a, b; Wen et al., 2011; Ren & Wu, 2006) use traditional image 
processing and feature extraction methods. These methods present issues such 
as low processing efﬁciency, vulnerability to subjective inﬂuence, and inadequate 
retrieval performance. In order to solve these problems, researchers have attempted 
to introduce deep learning methods to leverage its potent feature comprehension 
and categorization abilities, with the aim of augmenting the effectiveness of cultural 
relic image retrieval. However, the large number and variety of cultural relics 
owned by different regions and individuals and the existence of a large number 
of tiny and complicated discriminative information in cultural relic images make 
it extremely challenging for generic deep image algorithms to deal with such 
problems. Speciﬁcally, on the one hand, key and small attribute features in cultural 
relic images, such as the design of curling tendrils and twisted ﬂowers, are difﬁcult 
to detect by the generic network. On the other hand, similar shape and structure 
features between different categories of artefacts confuse the discriminative ability 
of the generic network. For example, when extracting features from porcelain, 
generic networks tend to extract shape features and ignore designs and glaze 
patterns. 
Therefore, we propose a semantic a priori induced cultural relic image retrieval 
algorithm, which employs manually labeled semantic information as a priori 
knowledge to guide the deep model in learning and extracting crucial information 
from the images. By enhancing the deep model’s (He et al., 2016; Krizhevsky et 
al., 2012) ability to extract semantic information from images of cultural relic, the 
performance of cultural relic image retrieval can be improved, and the supervision 
of civil circulation of cultural relics can be achieved more efﬁciently. Numerous 
experimental results conﬁrm that the proposed algorithm demonstrates excellent 
performance advantages in the task of cultural relic image retrieval. 
Meanwhile, the current cultural relic image retrieval techniques mainly belong 
to two categories: text-based and content-based methods (Wei et al., 2005a, b; 
Wen et al., 2011; Ren & Wu, 2006). Text-based methods require a lot of manual 
annotation and are prone to introduce cognitive errors. Content-based methods often 
require users to have high-quality colored images of cultural relic as input, which 
are scarce. These problems are not conducive to the popularization of artifact image 
databases. Thus, we propose sketch-based cultural relic retrieval, which is a typical 
cross-domain retrieval task. It can synthesize information from multiple domains

Cultural Relic Image Retrieval Based on Artiﬁcial Intelligence 97
for ﬂexible and convenient retrieval and satisfy the retrieval needs of different users 
in a more intuitive way. A large number of experimental results demonstrate the 
superior performance of the proposed algorithm on this cross-domain retrieval task. 
We believe that the sketch-based cross-domain retrieval technique will bring new 
opportunities to the ﬁeld of cultural relic image retrieval. 
Cultural heritage holds a signiﬁcant place in the spiritual life and cultural identity 
of individuals. Our goal is to offer a fresh impetus and support for the preservation 
of cultural heritage, through our research and introduction of cultural relic image 
retrieval technology. By doing so, we hope to engage a broader audience and 
encourage wider participation in this crucial cause. 
2 Semantic a Priori Induced Cultural Relic Image Retrieval 
Algorithm 
2.1 Challenges in Cultural Relic Image Retrieval 
Cultural relic image retrieval is one of the key technologies for monitoring the 
circulation of cultural relics, which can help personnel to search and identify 
cultural relics quickly and accurately, improve efﬁciency and accuracy, and play 
an important role in many aspects of cultural heritage protection work. 
Traditional cultural relic image retrieval methods (Wei et al., 2005a, b; Wen et 
al., 2011; Ren & Wu, 2006) usually require hand-craft features, which are retrieved 
by extracting low-level visual features such as color, texture, and shape of the 
image. This type of method is inefﬁcient, easily affected by subjective factors, and 
it is difﬁcult to represent high-level semantic information that cultural relic images 
contain, making the retrieval results unsatisfactory. At the same time, traditional 
cultural relic image retrieval methods usually require an independent index structure 
or a lot of time to build the index, further increasing the technical cost. 
At present, deep learning is developing rapidly and has achieved breakthroughs in 
many ﬁelds, such as image processing, natural language processing, the Go game, 
and molecular structure calculation. In particular, deep learning algorithms have 
surpassed human performance in general image recognition tasks (He et al., 2016; 
Krizhevsky et al., 2012). Its end-to-end architecture can also further reduce human 
overhead. All this brings new opportunities and possibilities for the cultural relic 
image retrieval task. 
However, cultural relic image retrieval faces greater challenges. The large 
number and variety of cultural relics from different regions and individuals have 
their own unique characteristics and discriminative features, which may include 
many aspects such as color, shape, texture, etc., and contain subtle variations and 
rich details. Figure 1 shows examples of complicated and confusing cultural relic 
patterns, twisted ﬂowers, curling tendrils, and honeysuckle. These tiny discrim-

98 Y . Zhou et al.
Fig. 1 Examples of complicated and confusing cultural relic patterns 
inative information are difﬁcult to be effectively extracted and distinguished by 
common deep image algorithms. 
To address these challenges, we propose a semantic a priori induced cultural relic 
image retrieval algorithm to enhance the feature extraction capability of cultural 
relic images and improve the performance of cultural relic image retrieval by using 
the manually labeled semantic information of cultural relics as a priori knowledge 
to guide the deep model to learn and extract the key information in cultural relic 
images. A large number of experimental results conﬁrm that the proposed algorithm 
has outstanding performance advantages in the cultural relic image retrieval task. 
2.2 Methodology 
In this section, we introduce the proposed semantic a priori induced cultural relic 
image retrieval algorithm, the main framework of which is shown in Fig. 2.I t 
mainly consists of two units: (1) the artifact attribute matching unit, which is used 
to enhance the ability of the image encoder in extracting the semantic information 
from cultural relic images, and (2) the confusion perception unit, which is used to 
enhance the ability of extracting the cultural relic visually discriminative features. 
At the end of this section, we describe the training and testing process of the cultural 
relic image encoder. 
2.2.1 Artifact Attribute Matching Unit 
Cultural relics contain a variety of semantic information, such as texture, pattern, 
vessel type, material, local pieces, color, etc., which is key to identifying and 
retrieving cultural relic images. However, many subtle and complicated semantic 
information are difﬁcult to capture and distinguish by common image encoders 
(such as resnet-101 (He et al., 2016) used in our experiments). Therefore, we 
propose the artifact attribute matching unit to guide the feature extractor to obtain 
the rich semantic information contained in cultural relics.

Cultural Relic Image Retrieval Based on Artiﬁcial Intelligence 99
Fig. 2 The framework of semantic a priori induced cultural relic image retrieval algorithm, which 
mainly consists of an artifact attribute matching unit and a confusion perception unit 
As shown in Fig. 3, the artifact attribute matching unit essentially computes 
semantic matching scores between the manually labeled semantic attribute vectors 
and the visual feature vectors extracted from the image encoder for subsequent 
matching loss computation, thus realizing semantically induced feature extraction 
of cultural relic images. Speciﬁcally, the cultural relic images are output from 
the image encoder as I-dimensional feature vectors, which are mapped onto the 
visual-spatial hypersphere after L2 normalization. At the same time, we reclassify 
the manually labeled semantic information in the cultural relic image dataset 
according to the expert knowledge, such as classifying the cultural relic “open-lit 
openwork pastel vase on sky-blue ground” into the attributes of “vase,” “open-lit,” 
“openwork,” “sky-blue glaze,” “blue-glazed celadon,” “folded branch,” “openwork 
carving,” “ear,” and so on (Farhadi et al., 2009; He & Peng, 2019), and then 
construct the S-dimensional feature vector of cultural relics based on the attributes 
obtained from the classiﬁcation of cultural relics and after L2 normalization and 
mapping to the semantic attribute-spatial hypersphere. Next, we design a multilayer 
perceptron network with I-dimensional input and S-dimensional output as the 
semantic extraction module of the cultural relic image to realize the mapping

In the process of minimizing L c(g), the image encoder will be induced by the

2.2.2 Confusion Perception Unit 
We also propose the confusion perception unit, as shown in Fig. 4, to enhance the 
ability to extract discriminative features of cultural relic images. Speciﬁcally, after 
the cultural relic images are input to the image encoder, an output I-dimensional 
visual feature vector is obtained, and this result is mapped onto the visual-spatial 
hypersphere after L2 normalization. 
Meanwhile, in order to strengthen the visual discriminative features of each 
cultural relic category and improve the intra-class consistency of the visual features 
extracted by the image encoder, we separately set up I-dimensional agent vectors for 
each cultural relic category in the dataset, the parameters of which can be involved 
in the model training and are also located on the visual-spatial hypersphere. Next, 
we calculate the matching scores between the extracted visual feature vectors and 
the agent vectors for each category as 
.Si =cos (Fi,f ) (3)

2.2.3 Training and Testing of Cultural Relic Image Encoders 
The entire algorithm obeys an end-to-end training process. Only after L c and L s 
have been computed does the model update the gradient and optimize the model. 
The overall loss function used in the training process is represented as 
.Ltotal =L C +L S (6) 
In the process of minimizing L total, the model takes into account the discrimina-
tive features used to distinguish the types of artifacts and the semantic information 
of artifacts that are manually labeled to jointly optimize the representation capability 
of the image encoder. 
In the testing stage, the trained encoder can be directly used for feature extraction 
of cultural relic images, and its output is an I-dimensional feature vector. The images 
in the test set are used as input, to retrieve in the set-up database. 
2.3 Summary 
There exists a large amount of tiny and complicated discriminative information in 
culture relic images, which is difﬁcult to be effectively extracted and distinguished 
by generalized deep image algorithms. We address these challenges by proposing a 
semantic a priori induced artifact image retrieval algorithm, which mainly consists 
of two units: an artifact attribute matching unit to enhance the ability of the image 
encoder to extract semantic information from artifact images and a confusion 
perception unit to enhance the ability to extract culture relic visually discriminative 
features.

Cultural Relic Image Retrieval Based on Artiﬁcial Intelligence 103
3 Sketch-Based Cultural Relic Image Retrieval 
3.1 A Cross-Domain Retrieval T ask 
Current cultural relic image retrieval techniques mainly belong to two categories: 
text-based image retrieval (TBIR) methods and content-based image retrieval 
(CBIR) methods (Wei et al., 2005a, b; Wen et al., 2011; Ren & Wu, 2006). TBIR 
is a kind of early image retrieval technique that mainly uses textual descriptions to 
describe the characteristics of an image, such as the author of a painting, the age, the 
genre, and the size. When retrieving, the images are generally queried by keywords, 
i.e., the name of the image, the textual information, and the indexing relationship. 
TBIR is simple and easy to use, but manual labeling of the index requires a lot 
of manpower and time, so it is difﬁcult to build a large retrieval database. At the 
same time, there are cognitive errors in manual labeling, and different people’s 
understanding of images and labels may be inconsistent, leading to inaccurate 
retrieval results. 
With the development of technology, CBIR has gradually appeared and been 
widely used. It no longer relies on manually labeled text information and is able to 
automatically extract and analyze visual information such as color, shape, texture, 
etc. of an image, calculate the similarity of the content features of the input and 
the image in the database, and match them to achieve retrieval. Compared with the 
text-based approach, content-based retrieval for cultural relic images can effectively 
avoid the tediousness and uncertainty of manual labeling and keyword search. 
However, there is a high scarcity of cultural relic images, and it is difﬁcult for 
general users to obtain high-quality colored cultural relic images, or even impossible 
to obtain the desired colored cultural relic images. In this case, CBIR also fails to 
satisfy the users’ needs, which is not conducive to the popularization of the cultural 
relic image database for the general public. 
To address the above problems (Yelamarthi et al., 2018; Dey et al., 2019; Dutta & 
Akata, 2019; Deng et al., 2020; Hu et al., 2021), we propose a sketch-based cultural 
relic image retrieval technique. Sketch (Y u et al., 2015; Xu et al., 2022)i saf o r m o f 
art and communication that can transcend national boundaries and time, regardless 
of age and language. We can still be touched by the Lascaux cave painting drawn 
by primitive man 15,000 years ago, and Picasso’s “Bull” reveals the inﬁnite charm 
and possibility of sketch. Today, with the popularity of smart touch screen devices, 
people can draw anywhere, anytime. The art form of sketch, as old as human history, 
has been revitalized in the new digital era, bringing new opportunities for cultural 
relic image retrieval. 
As shown in Fig. 5, sketch-based cultural relic image retrieval is the user input 
of a hand-drawn sketch, by matching the features with the color cultural relic 
images in the database, according to the degree of similarity to return to the user 
the sorting results of color images. It is easy to ﬁnd that sketch-based cultural 
relic image retrieval is a typical cross-domain retrieval task (Yelamarthi et al., 
2018; Dey et al., 2019; Dutta & Akata, 2019; Deng et al., 2020; Hu et al., 2021),

104 Y . Zhou et al.
Fig. 5 Illustration of sketch-based cultural relic image retrieval 
i.e., although the input item and the result item have consistency at the high-level 
semantic level, the low-level visual features of the two may be completely different. 
Cross-domain retrieval can overcome the limitations of traditional retrieval methods 
that only retrieve information based on a speciﬁc domain and comprehensively 
utilize information from multiple domains for ﬂexible and convenient retrieval, thus 
satisfying the retrieval needs of different users in a more intuitive way. We believe 
that the sketch-based cross-domain cultural relic image retrieval technique will bring 
new opportunities to the ﬁeld of cultural relic image retrieval. 
3.2 Methodology 
For the sketch-based cultural relic image retrieval task described in Sect. 3.1,w e 
propose a prototype contrastive learning algorithm. As shown in Fig. 6, the overall 
training process consists of two stages, intra-domain feature extraction, and cross-
domain feature alignment, each of which uses the proposed prototype contrastive 
loss. After training, samples of the same category from different domains will 
be clustered near the category prototypes in the public semantic space, while 
samples of semantically different categories will be distanced, thus realizing cross-
domain retrieval. This section describes the proposed prototype contrastive learning 
algorithm in detail and its application in intra-domain feature extraction and cross-
domain feature alignment stages. 
3.2.1 Prototype Contrastive Learning 
Retrieval methods usually apply triplet loss training, which pulls the anchor closer 
to the positive sample and moves it farther away from negative ones. Hence, models

Cultural Relic Image Retrieval Based on Artiﬁcial Intelligence 105
Fig. 6 The framework of proposed prototype contrastive learning method for sketch-based 
cultural relic image retrieval 
trained in this fashion show good retrieval performance. Nonetheless, this does not 
well-match the real-world situation. Speciﬁcally, the triplet loss-based approach 
assumes an equal proportion of positive and negative samples. However, when we 
conduct real retrieval tasks, many more negative than positive samples exist. 
We apply the prototype contrastive learning method to cope with this imbalance 
using prototype learning to aggregate samples of the same category (Snell et al., 
2017; Ji et al., 2020) while using contrastive learning to move the sample away 
from negatives (Wu et al., 2018; He et al., 2020; van den Oord et al., 2018). Our 
prototype contrastive learning draws on the main ideas of both methods, as shown 
in Fig. 7. Moreover, it is not bound to any particular modality and has the potential 
to transfer knowledge from seen to unseen classes. Thus, we apply it to the unseen 
cross-domain retrieval scenario. 
The prototype contrastive learning process contains two steps. First, we randomly 
choose the negative classes based on the training sample and calculate prototypes 
(including positives) by concentrating the samples in memory. Second, we update 
the network parameters in memory according to the prototype contrastive loss,

3.2.2 Intra-Domain Feature Extraction 
Inﬂuenced by the Siamese network, some models that deal with the cross-domain 
retrieval task use structurally similar feature extractors on both source and target 
domains and design a complex cross-domain loss function to reduce the inter-
domain gap. However, there is a huge semantic gap between sketches and cultural 
relic images, so we apply different image encoders to work with them and uses the 
prototype contrastive learning method for training. A prototype contrastive learning 
pseudocode feature extraction method is given in Algorithm 1. 
Algorithm 1: Steps of intra-domain feature extraction 
Input:intra-domain dataset D, max number of training epochs 
MaxEpoch, number of memorized samples per class k, number of 
negative classes n; 
Output:feature extraction network FE; 
Step1:initialize the feature extraction network FE and its 
parameter θ ; 
Step2: initialize the category label set C from the training 
dataset D in the according domain, randomly select k samples from 
each class of D, input the feature extraction network to get the 
features of these samples, and initialize the memory bank M; 
Step3:disrupt the order of the data in D and draw samples 
sequentially for training, let the currently drawn training sample 
be s, and its category label be c; 
Step4:input s into the feature extraction network to get its 
feature v;

Cultural Relic Image Retrieval Based on Artiﬁcial Intelligence 107
Step5:randomly draw n negative category labels c- from C based on 
the positive category label c; 
Step6:compute the clustering prototype p for each c and c- using 
M to obtain the prototype set P;. 
Step7:calculate the prototype comparison loss using v and P to 
optimize the network parameters θ ; 
Step8:randomly select a feature with category label c from M and 
replace it with v; 
Step9:repeat Step3 to Step8 until the network converges or reaches 
the preset maximum number of epochs MaxEpoch; 
3.2.3 Cross-Domain Feature Alignment 
Thus far, two single-domain feature extractors have been trained by the prototype 
contrastive learning method. However, as required by our cross-domain retrieval 
task, the semantically equivalent sketch and cultural relic image features must be 
mapped to adjacent locations in the common semantic space (i.e., cross-domain 
alignment). 
Because the prototype concept does not require a speciﬁc modality, we adopt the 
prototype contrastive learning method to solve the cross-domain alignment problem. 
We build sketch-based cultural relic image sample pairs using their class labels and 
their domains to cluster prototypes into common semantic spaces while assigning 
several common classes to each pair to train three fully connected network layers. 
Therefore, each sample, regardless of modality, can be near the prototype of the 
same category and far from others in the common semantic space. The speciﬁc 
steps are given in Algorithm 2. 
Algorithm 2: Steps of cross-domain feature alignment 
Input: sketch dataset D1 and corresponding feature extraction 
network FE1, cultural relic image dataset D2 and corresponding 
feature extraction network FE2, max number of training expochsMax-
Epoch, number of memory samples per class k, number of negative 
classes n; 
Output: sketch-publicspace mapping network Mapx, cultural relic 
image-public space mapping network Mapy; 
Step1:according to the sketch dataset D1 and the corresponding 
trained feature extraction network FE1 and the cultural relic 
image dataset D2 and the corresponding trained feature extraction 
network FE2, obtain the sketch feature set Dx and the cultural 
relic image feature set Dy, respectively; 
Step2: initialize the category label set C according to Dx and Dy, 
and construct the “sketch-cultural relic image” feature pair set 
D according to the categories. 
Step3: initialize sketch and cultural relic image mapping networks 
Mapx and Mapy and their parameters θ x and θ y; 
Step4: randomly select k feature pairs fx-fy from each class of D, 
input them into the corresponding mapping networks, and initialize 
the memory banks Mx and My;

Step5:disrupt the order of the data in D, and sequentially draw 
feature pairs to be used for training, and set the currently drawn 
training feature pair as fx-fy, and the corresponding class label 
as c; 
Step6:input fx and fy into the corresponding mapping network to 
obtain the common features vx and vy; 
Step7:randomly draw n negative category labels c- from C based on 
the positive category labels c; 
Step8:compute the common clustering prototype p for each c and c-
using Mx and My to obtain the prototype set P; 
Step9:compute the prototype comparison loss using vx, vy and P to 
optimize the corresponding network parameters θ x and θ y; 
Step10:randomly select a feature with category label c from Mx and 
My, respectively, and replace it with vx and vy; 
Step11:repeat Step4 to Step10 until the network converges or 
reaches the preset maximum number of rounds MaxEpoch; 
3.3 Summary 
In this section, we propose a prototype contrastive learning algorithm for the cross-
domain semantic gap challenges involved in the sketch-based cultural relic image 
retrieval task. The entire training process of our algorithm consists of two stages, 
intra-domain feature extraction and cross-domain feature alignment, each of which 
uses the proposed prototype contrastive loss. After training, samples of the same 
category from different domains are clustered near the category prototypes in 
the public semantic space, while samples of semantically different categories are 
distanced, thus realizing cross-domain retrieval. 
4 Experimental Results 
4.1 Dataset Settings 
To verify the effectiveness of the proposed semantic a priori induced cultural relic 
image retrieval algorithm, we conduct experiments on the cultural relic dataset 
which contains a total of 25,599 cultural relic images belonging to 450 ﬁne-grained 
categories under ﬁve coarse-grained categories, such as ceramics, sculptures, jade, 
calligraphy, and paintings. 
We performed data division for this cultural relic image dataset to realize the 
retrieval of cultural relic images in seen and unseen categories under two settings. 
The ﬁrst setting is the independent retrieval of seen and unseen categories, i.e., the 
query images of seen and unseen categories are retrieved in the seen and unseen 
category databases, respectively. As shown in Fig. 8, the categories of the whole 
dataset are divided into the ﬁrst 400 categories as seen and the last 50 categories

Cultural Relic Image Retrieval Based on Artiﬁcial Intelligence 109
Fig. 8 Data division in the 
ﬁrst setting 
Fig. 9 Data division in the second setting 
as unseen. And 80% of the images in these categories are used to construct the 
database, and the remaining 20% are used as query images to test the retrieval 
performance. In these four data parts, the seen database is used as the training set. 
The second setting is a joint retrieval of the seen class and the unseen categories. 
In this setting, the query images of the seen category and the query images of the 
unseen category are retrieved uniformly in the set that fuses the databases of the seen 
category and the databases of the unseen category, as shown in Fig. 9. Compared 
with the ﬁrst setting, the second setting is more challenging because the model needs 
to compare the query image with the cultural relic database of both seen and unseen 
categories, and the domain migration problem may cause the model’s judgment 
result to be more biased toward the seen category, thus requiring the retrieval model 
to have stronger generalization. 
To verify the effectiveness of our prototype contrastive learning method, we 
conducted experiments on the commonly used SHREC’13, SHREC’14, and D2O

110 Y . Zhou et al.
public sketch-artifact image retrieval datasets (Li et al., 2013, 2014a, b). All these 
three datasets contain a subset of sketch data and a subset of artifact image data. 
Among them, the SHREC’13 dataset contains 7200 sketches and 1258 artifact 
images, totaling 90 different categories. Each category of sketches contains 50 
training samples and 30 test samples; each category of artifact images has different 
sample sizes, ranging from only one sample to hundreds, with 23 categories having 
no more than 5 samples. In this chapter, 67 categories with more than 5 samples 
of artifact images are selected as seen categories for training, and the remaining 23 
classes are tested with zero-shot unseen categories. 
The SHREC’14 dataset contains 13,680 sketches and 8987 artifact images, for a 
total of 171 different categories. Each sketch category contains 50 training samples 
and 30 test samples, and each category has different artifact image sample sizes, 
ranging from only 1 sample to hundreds. In this chapter, 133 categories with more 
than 5 artifact image samples are selected as seen categories for training, and the 
remaining 38 categories are selected as unseen categories for zero-shot testing. 
The D2O dataset contains 8992 artifact image data and over 7 million sketch data, 
for a total of 50 different categories. Each category of artifact images has different 
sample sizes, ranging from 30 samples to nearly 1000 samples. Due to the very large 
number of sketch data in this dataset, this chapter randomly selects 1000 sketches 
from each category for the experiment. The training category and the zero-shot test 
category are then randomly split by 80–20%. 
4.2 Evaluation Metrics 
For the proposed semantic a priori induced cultural relic image retrieval algorithm, 
the performance evaluation metrics are R@K and NMI, which are commonly used 
in image retrieval (Schroff et al., 2015;G e , 2018; Zhai & Wu, 2018;Q i a ne t 
al., 2019), and are chosen for experiments to measure the retrieval performance 
of the proposed algorithm. Speciﬁcally, R@K indicates the probability that the 
same category as the query image appears in the K results obtained from each 
retrieval. If a result with the same category as the query image appears among the 
K results obtained by retrieval, it returns 1, otherwise it returns 0. The mean value 
of the retrieval results after several iterations is counted as R@K. NMI is known 
as Normalized Mutual Information and indicates the degree of clustering between 
different features in the same category. Given the clustering result C ={ C1, ... ,C n} 
and the true label /Omega1={ y1, ... ,y n}, NMI is deﬁned as NMI = 2 I(/Omega1,C )/(2I(/Omega1,C )) , 
where I (−,− ) measures mutual information and H (−) denotes entropy. 
For our prototype contrastive learning method, the performance evaluation met-
rics nearest neighbor (NN), ﬁrst-tier (FT), second-tier (ST), normalized discounted 
cumulated gain (nDCG), E-measure (E), mean reciprocal rank (MRR), and mean 
average precision (mAP) evaluators were used. They are metrics commonly used in 
the sketch-based cross-domain image retrieval methods (Wang et al., 2015; Dai et 
al., 2018; He et al., 2018; Dai & Liang, 2020). Speciﬁcally, NN, also known as Top-

Cultural Relic Image Retrieval Based on Artiﬁcial Intelligence 111
1 accuracy, reﬂects whether the system returns the highest ranked predicted result 
that matches the true result. FT is similar to ST, which are ﬁrst tier and second tier 
metrics, respectively. They are all used to quantitatively assess the quality of the ﬁrst 
few items of the sorted results. MRR and nDCG are capable of evaluating whether 
the results with a high degree of relevance to the input are placed higher or lower 
in the retrieval sort list; E is the balance between precision and recall; mAP is able 
to reﬂect the average precision of the retrieval system. Apart from E, the larger the 
metric, the better.

4.3.2 Experiments for the Prototype Contrastive Learning-Based 
“Sketch-Cultural Relic Image Retrieval” Method 
We compared our prototype contrastive learning method to those of state-of-the-
art methods, including Siamese (Wang et al., 2015), DCHML (Dai et al., 2018), 
TCL (He et al., 2018), and CGN (Dai & Liang, 2020), on SHREC’13, SHREC’14, 
and D2O using the same settings described in Sect. 4.1 for fairness. Codes are 
implemented using PyTorch. A resnet-50 (He et al., 2016) pretrained on ImageNet 
was used as the artifact image feature extractor backbone, whereas the sketch feature 
extractor applied Sketch-a-net (Y u et al., 2015). The maximum epoch number was 
50, and Adam was adopted to optimize our model with a learning rate initially set to 
1e−4 set to exponentially decay at a rate of 0.95. For testing, each positive sample 
tier was paired with nine randomly selected negative tiers. 
In Table 5, the best retrieval performances of each method on dataset SHREC’13 
are shown in boldface, respectively. Accordingly, our prototype contrastive learning 
method outperformed most extant methods on all metrics with SEEN and UNSEEN 
tasks. In particular, our prototype contrastive learning algorithm achieves an FT 
metric of 0.389 for the UNSEEN task on dataset SHREC’13, which is more than 
32% better than other methods.

To further demonstrate the validity of the proposed algorithmic innovations, we 
also conducted four ablation studies to validate the UNSEEN retrieval performance 
of our prototype contrastive learning method: 
• Clu (W/A): Learn prototypes via dynamic clustering with cross-domain align-
ment. 
• Anch (W/A): Fix anchor points for prototypes with cross-domain alignment. 
• PCL (O/A): Prototype contrastive learning without cross-domain alignment. 
• PCL (W/A): Prototype contrastive learning with cross-domain alignment. 
The results are shown in Table 8, where the best metrics are shown in boldface. 
It is easy to see that apart from the ST on D2O, our prototype contrastive learning 
method performed far better than the cluster and ﬁxed-anchor-point methods on all 
metrics on all three benchmark datasets. Furthermore, the semantic alignment was 
crucial for cross-domain tasks.

ﬁve attributes and the region that the model’s attention focuses on. 
Figure 11 gives the visualization results of the experiments. The leftmost of each 
row is the input cultural relic image, and the right side is the ﬁve closest results 
returned by the retrieval algorithm. It is not difﬁcult to see that the returned results 
are visually very similar to the input image, which can conﬁrm the good ability 
of the proposed algorithm to distinguish the discriminative features of subtle and 
complicated cultural relic images. 

116 Y . Zhou et al.

4.5 Summary 
In this section, we have done extensive experiments for the proposed semantic a 
priori induced cultural relic image retrieval algorithm and the prototype contrastive 
learning-based “sketch-cultural relic image retrieval” method. The results demon-
strated the superior performance of our proposed algorithms. 
5 Conclusion 
This chapter focuses on image retrieval technology for cultural heritage preser-
vation. Cultural relic image retrieval is one of the key technologies in regulating 
the circulation of cultural relics. It aims to ensure the legitimacy of cultural relics 
being traded by analyzing the images and matching them with the database of 
cultural relics prohibited for sale or historical transactions, as well as comparing the 
consistency of information in the cultural relic inventory and auction catalogue to 

Cultural Relic Image Retrieval Based on Artiﬁcial Intelligence 117 
prevent sellers from theft and false propaganda, thereby providing technical support 
for the research, conservation, and trade of cultural relics. 
We ﬁrst proposed a semantic a priori induced cultural relic image retrieval 
algorithm 
to deal with the large amount of subtle and complex discriminative 
information in the cultural relic images that are difﬁcult to be effectively extracted 
and recognized by general deep image algorithms. It uses the manually annotated 
semantic information as a priori knowledge to guide the deep model to learn and 
extract the key information in cultural relic images, improve the retrieval perfor-
mance, and thus achieve the regulation of private cultural relics circulation in a more 
efﬁcient way. Speciﬁcally, the proposed algorithm consists of two main units: (1) an 
artifact attribute matching unit to enhance the image encoder’s ability to extract 
semantic information from cultural relic images and (2) a confusion perception unit 
to enhance the ability to extract discriminative features for distinguishing cultural 
relics species. A large number of experiments demonstrate the superior performance 
of the proposed algorithm. 
Then, we introduced the sketch-based cross-domain cultural relic image retrieval 
task 
and proposed a prototype contrastive learning algorithm for the cross-domain 
semantic gap challenges. The entire training process of our algorithm consists of two 
stages: (1) intra-domain feature extraction and (2) cross-domain feature alignment. 
Each of the stages uses the proposed prototype contrastive loss. At the end of 
training, samples of the same category from different domains are clustered near 
the category prototypes in the public semantic space, while samples of semantically 
different categories are distanced, thus realizing cross-domain retrieval. Extensive 
experimental results on three publicly available datasets show that our prototype 
contrastive learning algorithm has superior cross-domain retrieval performance. 
Cultural heritage carries history, and the process of cultural development is a link 
between 
the past, present, and future. It is important to preserve cultural heritage, 
and our aim is to provide support and a fresh impetus to this cause. Through our 
research and introduction of cultural relic image retrieval technology, we hope 
to engage a wider audience and encourage greater participation in this essential 
endeavor that concerns the human spirit.

Part II 
Foundational Challenges Beyond Prompts: 
How Artiﬁcial Intelligence and Machine 
Learning Can Deal with Ancient Texts

The Artiﬁcial Papyrologist at Work 
Nicola Reggiani 
1 Introduction 
It has been sufﬁciently shown that papyrology, among classical studies, is par-
ticularly at the forefront regarding the proﬁtable use of digital resources. This is 
not just a methodological shift, as the ongoing development of Digital Papyrology 
is changing—slowly but constantly—the very idea of papyrological artifacts and 
the ways of dealing with them. The achievements of Digital Papyrology from the 
origins to the present day are discussed in two monographs published in 2017 and— 
with updates—in 2019 (Reggiani, 2017, 2019). Since then—or rather, between the 
two International Congresses of Papyrology of Lecce (2019) and Paris (2022)— 
new issues have emerged and contributed to alter the landscape, in some way, 
signiﬁcantly. First of all, several ongoing projects have reshaped the concept of 
the digital edition of the papyri and the digital representation of their various 
components (text, language, layout, materiality, script, etc.). This theme was faced 
by the international conference “Digital Papyrology 3.0 – Digital Encoding and 
Critical Edition of Greek Papyri: perspectives and progress” (University of Parma, 
30–31 May 2021), and I refer to its forthcoming proceedings for any further 
discussions about it. In this contribution, I will focus on another theme at stake: 
the rise of Artiﬁcial Intelligence. 1 
1 This contribution is provided within the framework of the research project “Selection, paleo-
graphical and chronological analysis of Greek papyri for the development of digital tools aiming 
at the automatic identiﬁcation of scribes and dating of handwritings” (University of Udine, P .I. 
Professor Giuseppina Azzarello).I concentrate my survey and my reﬂections on the primary tasks
