124 N. Reggiani
It is interesting—or at least amusing—to start from a test query submitted to 
the well-known AI chatbot ChatGPT, 2 asked the question Tell me about artiﬁcial 
intelligence in papyrology , in order to check what an AI seems to know about AI in 
Papyrology: 
Artiﬁcial intelligence (AI) has been increasingly used in the ﬁeld of papyrology, which 
is the study of ancient texts written on papyrus and other materials. The application of 
AI to papyrology can be broadly divided into two main areas: digital papyrology and 
computational papyrology. Digital papyrology refers to the use of digital technology, such 
as imaging and digitization, to study ancient papyri. AI can be used in this context to 
enhance the process of imaging and digitization, for example, by automatically detecting 
and correcting distortions in images, or by using machine learning algorithms to classify 
different types of papyri. Computational papyrology refers to the use of computational 
methods, such as natural language processing (NLP) and text mining, to analyze and 
interpret the content of ancient papyri. AI can be used in this context to support the process 
of transcription, translation, and annotation of the texts. For example, AI algorithms can be 
used to identify and transcribe different scripts, or to automatically classify texts by genre 
or date. Another area that AI is used in papyrology is the classiﬁcation of handwriting, 
which can be a time-consuming task for papyrologists. AI algorithms can be trained to 
recognize and classify different handwriting styles, which can help to identify the scribe 
and the date of a text. AI can also be used to enhance the searchability and accessibility of 
papyrological data. For example, AI-based search engines can be used to search for speciﬁc 
words or phrases in large collections of papyri, and machine learning algorithms can be 
used to automatically classify and tag papyri based on their content. In conclusion, AI has 
the potential to greatly enhance the ﬁeld of papyrology by providing new and efﬁcient 
methods for the study and interpretation of ancient papyri. However, it is important to note 
that AI should be used in conjunction with traditional methods of papyrological analysis, 
and should not be seen as a replacement for human expertise and interpretation. 
The speed and the structured arrangement of the response is impressive (the 
AI even created a new disciplinary sub-ﬁeld, “computational papyrology”!), 
although—while one cannot but agree with its conclusions—it is clear that an 
AI is not sufﬁcient to arrange a decent presentation on AI in papyrology. 
2 The Digital Papyrologist at Work 
Artiﬁcial Intelligence is deﬁned by the Oxford English Dictionary as 
the theory and development of computer systems able to perform tasks that normally require 
human intelligence, such as visual perception, speech recognition, decision-making, and 
translation between languages. 
of papyrology, so that I will not cover such topics as AI applied to the extraction and analysis of 
papyrological metadata.
2 ChatGPT is an artiﬁcial intelligence language model designed to communicate with humans 
through natural language processing. It can understand and generate human-like responses to a 
wide range of topics and questions, making it a powerful tool for virtual assistants, customer service 
chatbots, and other conversational applications. 

The Artiﬁcial Papyrologist at Work 125
These are precisely the intellectual tasks involved in the papyrological workﬂow. 
They were outlined exactly 50 years ago in one of the ﬁrst methodological 
reﬂections on the discipline, The Papyrologist at Work , the famous monograph (in 
fact, a collection of three lectures) published by Sir Eric Turner in 1973. Here, the 
primary papyrological task outlined by the leading British scholar is 
to set out precisely what the papyrus says, and to distinguish between what is certain or 
given by the text and what is a matter of inference. This is the prime responsibility of the 
papyrologist. (Turner, 1973,p .7 ) 
He then concentrates on the second stage of the papyrological task—i.e., making 
the reading hypotheses explicit—but the main scope of the philological work on 
the papyri remains to understand the text and to publish it in the most careful way 
possible—what we usually refer to as the editorial work. 
Later in his ﬁrst lecture, Turner summarizes this editorial workﬂow as a 
process of discovery and exploitation of a new piece of information, won unexpectedly from 
written relics of the past. The pleasure, indeed thrill, of discovery is the reward for a great 
deal of drudgery: meticulous attention to exact setting out what the papyrus contains, step-
by-step testing of the hypotheses on which even simple restoration is undertaken. This I take 
to be the meaning of editing, and this is the proper task of the papyrologist. He will not do it 
well unless he attempts a further step – to reconcile what is new with what is already known. 
But since he cannot be a universal polymath, he will defer here to the opinions of others. 
Unless his text, however, is completely reliable, counsel will be darkened, not lightened, by 
his discoveries. (Turner, 1973, p. 14) 
This is of course the narrower view of papyrology as a purely philological 
task aimed at decoding and restoring the papyrus texts at best, which makes a 
papyrologist be a “skilled copyist,” or also a “learned copyist,” as deﬁned, 1 year 
later, by Herbert Y outie in another important methodological work, The Textual 
Criticism of Documentary Papyri (Y outie, 1974, p. 14 and 53). From this standpoint, 
the papyrologist’s purpose is to decode the ancient texts with the help of his/her 
knowledge and provide a careful critical transcription as a reliable source to the 
other scholars—to be an “artiﬁcer of fact,” according to another famous, earlier 
deﬁnition provided by Y outie ( 1963). It is however important to underline this 
feature, in order to understand what happens when we turn to the digital side of 
papyrology. 
Precisely due to the never-ending push towards a perfect balance between the 
extant text and its editorial interpretation, papyrology is a “discipline in ﬂux,” 
as deﬁned by Ann Hanson ( 2002). Restorations, reuniﬁcations of fragments, 
new discoveries, new readings, corrections, and progress in the scholarship—not 
secondarily helped by the digital tools—contribute to outline a potentially ever-
changing text, which needs to undergo what we may call a “liquid philology” 
that envisages editorial changes and scholarly progress through time. 3 Recovering
3 I borrow the concept of ‘liquidness’ from Zygmunt Bauman’s ground-breaking reﬂections about 
“liquid modernity” as an age of quick changes and precariousness, of course without its negative 
aspects: e.g., Bauman 2000. 

126 N. Reggiani
Y outie’s deﬁnition of the papyrologist as an artiﬁcer of fact, we can say that actually 
we deal with ever-changing facts, so that the aim of the digital textual criticism 
of the papyri is to keep track of all of them in an open and liquid edition, which 
becomes a living (and live) digital representation of the papyrus text. This is what 
the Papyri.info database does through its contributors and editors. And this is what 
we may call “Digital Papyrology 2.0,” marking the transition from static repositories 
of texts and metadata to dynamic and collaborative resources. 
On the other hand, a papyrus is a complex network of material and cognitive 
interactions—the text with its linguistic features, the writing surface with its 
material features, and the writing act of the scribe with its graphical and mental 
features. A digital environment allows for more a careful critical representation of 
all such interactions, certainly better than traditional paper editions. From the digital 
viewpoint, this concept was deﬁned “meta-text” by Traianos Gagos as early as 1998 
(at the 22nd International Congress at Florence, proceedings published in 2001): in 
his own words, “in this new era of papyrological research, we cannot speak of a 
collection of papyri alone, but also of a collection of electronic ﬁles, data, metadata 
and digital images” (Gagos, 2001, p. 516). He was speaking of the Michigan papyrus 
collection, of course, but that concept can be easily exported to an idea of “meta-
papyrus” made up of a network of electronic resources describing and preserving 
all its multifaceted features. More recently, Marion Lamé described such an idea 
through Michel Foucault’s philosophical concept of “dispositive” (“dispositif”), 
according to which the message of the object bearing the text can be completely 
understood in relation to a complex net of many other heterogeneous pieces of 
information (Lamé, 2014). 
I think it will be inspiring to recover Gagos’ own words: 
The availability of huge amounts of information in fully searchable textual form with 
accompanying images through these new media is altering drastically the deﬁnition of 
what constitutes a ‘text,’ the way we experience reading it and, ultimately, the plurality 
of messages a text can offer to one or more readers. The new methods of presenting text 
with marked up images and the simultaneous availability of a variety of other research tools 
within the same electronic environment give us new ways of visualizing and approaching a 
given text. An edited text is no more a static, isolated object, but a growing and changeable 
amalgam: the image allows the user to look critically at the ‘established’ text and to 
challenge continuously the authoritative readings and interpretation of its ﬁrst or subsequent 
editors. Furthermore, the simultaneous access to and study of thousands of texts and their 
images that could be as far apart as a millennium, in a single search and through the same 
medium, has the potential to challenge our established notions of the ‘messages’ a text 
carries within itself, its textuality and intertextuality and, ultimately, the periodization of 
texts in strict chronology of political events. A text that was written, for instance, in the 
era of Caracalla contains information and ‘signiﬁers’ that operate beyond and above that 
particular period and era. The use of names, formulae, language at large, references to past 
events, and even the appearance of this text (e.g., the type of handwriting, often used by 
papyrologists to date other texts, or the layout) is in a constant dialogical relationship with 
other texts and their historical contexts, because it draws upon and is part of the multiplicity 
of meanings that circulate within culture and history. As Roland Barth[es] explains: ‘Any 
text is an intertext; other texts are present in it, at varying levels, in more or less recognizable 
forms: the texts of the previous and surrounding cultures. Any text is a new tissue of past 
citations. Bits of codes, formulae, rhythmic models, fragments of social languages, etc. pass

The Artiﬁcial Papyrologist at Work 127
into the text and are redistributed within it, for there is always language before and around 
the text.’ In one or another way, papyrologists have always recognized the ‘intertextuality’ 
of the Greek papyri from Egypt, because of the multicultural and multi-ethnic environment 
in which these texts were born. The development of the new electronic media in our ﬁeld and 
the capability to establish these cross-links—or these intertextual signiﬁers, so to speak— 
on the linguistic, cultural and historical level through the interaction of multiple texts, 
images and a variety of related tools places the notions of textuality, intertextuality and 
metatextuality on a new (electronic) platform which, in turn, becomes part of these notions 
as the ‘carrier,’ ‘interpreter’ and ‘distributor’ of these texts. (Gagos, 2001, pp. 514–516) 
This is what several existing and ongoing projects are doing right now in the 
ﬁelds of linguistics, sociolinguistics, paleography, layout, and formulaic studies, and 
we may call it “Digital Papyrology 3.0,” giving a nod to the current concepts of 
semantic digital networks and metatextual developments (Reggiani, forthcoming). 
The next step will be, hopefully, to digitize also the network connecting all such 
information systems itself, beside the individual resources that are being produced. 
If I have dwelt so much in an introductory recap of what is today Digital 
Papyrology, it is just to conclude by stressing that central in these digital critical 
workﬂows is still the character of the (human) papyrologist: reading and publishing 
a papyrus is still a matter of human criticism in terms of mental/intellectual 
process—for a comparatively long time, we have been recognizing and deciphering 
digital enhanced representations of papyrus fragments with our own eyes, typing 
and annotating papyrus texts (mostly) with our own ﬁngers, decoding handwritings, 
supplementing lacunas, and interpreting metadata with our own brains. 
In this regard, it is interesting to read what the pioneers of Digital Papyrology 
wrote, between the late 60s and the early 80s, about the relationship between 
humans and machines in papyrology. Arthur Bodson was one of the developers 
of a very early attempt to create a textual database of documentary papyri, at 
the Laboratoire d’ Analyse Statistique des Langues Anciennes (LASLA) at the 
University of Liège, in the late 60s, and he concluded his presentation of such a 
resource at the 12th International Congress (Ann Arbor 1968, proceedings published 
in 1970) with these words: 
Le rôle du papyrologue se réduit, à ce stade, à poser des questions. Le laboratoire 
est là pour trouver les moyens d’y répondre. Vient alors le travail de réﬂexion sur les 
documents fournis; mais ceci n’est plus de notre compétence: les machines peuvent aider les 
spécialistes dans leurs recherches en leur fournissant rapidement des données sûres; elles 
sont incapables de résoudre les vrais problèmes. Ilfaut encore d’excellentspapyrologues. 
(Bodson, 1970, p. 44) 
The same viewpoint was shared by Knut Kleve and Ivar Fonnes, who at the 
University of Oslo in the early 80s developed a computer program that was able 
to perform a task of automatic “gap ﬁlling” by searching suitable combination of 
characters in a provided textual databank. It was called Lacunology , and it was 
a sort of forerunner of some advanced search options that we still proﬁtably use 
when looking for possible parallels in the Duke Databank of Documentary Papyri 
via Papyri.info or in the Thesaurus Linguae Graecae . I quote a passage from their 
presentation of the tool:

128 N. Reggiani
We want to stress that we do not in the least expect that some time the scholar shall be 
replaced by the computer. On the contrary, as far as we can see, what now happens is that 
the scholar gets access to new aids and has been freed from many unnecessary burdens. He 
has, one could say, got a sort of magic lexicon in addition to the traditional reference books. 
In this magic lexicon there are endless possibilities of sorting and arranging text material 
in a minimum of time. But no other than the scholar is able to use that lexicon. Wilhelm 
Crönert once emphasized that there are three cardinal virtues for the papyrologist: Sehkraft 
[eyesight], Sprachgefühl [sense of language], Sachkunde [competence, expertise]. These 
virtues are today as relevant as ever they were, and can never be replaced by any computer. 
(Kleve & Fonnes, 1981, p. 165) 
However, since π ´αντα ῥε˜ι and we do live in a “liquid modernity,” things are slightly 
changed from those roaring 80s. Today (our today, not Kleve’s today), Artiﬁcial 
Intelligence has knocked on the doors of Digital Papyrology, and I would like to 
retain Crönert’s triad of Sehkraft—Sprachgefühl—Sachkunde , recalling the mention 
of the areas of visual perception, speech recognition, and decision-making in the 
deﬁnition of AI quoted at the beginning, in order to explore what this means for 
papyrology now. 
3 Sehkraft in Digital Papyrology 
Let us start from the ﬁrst “cardinal virtue,” Sehkraft , or the “eyesight.” This is 
primarily used to decipher the extant text on the papyrus and involves paleographical 
skills such as recognizing the ancient handwritings with a plenty of useful research 
outcomes. The help of the computer to perform this task was already envisaged 
in the early 70s by Knut Kleve, who developed a computational method, later 
called Literalogy , which was designed to exploit an electronic paleographical 
index of letter shapes, including any scribal habit or writing characteristic, to be 
compared quickly, but just manually on screen, with the incompletely surviving 
traces in the text under study, which consequently could be restored (Kleve et 
al., 1987). This was one step ahead with respect to the “simple” consultation of 
paleographical repertories, of which we now have electronic versions in PapPal and 
the Collaborative Database of Dateable Greek Hands . 
The idea to create a digital set of pictures of the handwritten characters was 
subsequently relaunched by Giovanna Menci at the 26th International Congress 
(Geneva 2010), where she presented the project called ALPHA— Alphabet Letters 
in Papyri Handwritings , a database of literary alphabets structured in online 
synoptic tables (Menci, 2012). This project unfortunately never saw the light and, 
just as Literalogy , did not involve any kind of machine-led automation. However, 
the storage of large datasets of letter shapes is the ﬁrst step towards the endeavor 
of teaching an AI to recognize characters automatically and eventually to read a 
papyrus on its own. 
In the early 2000s, an attempt was carried on at the Centre for the Study of 
Ancient Documents at Oxford, in relation with the Vindolanda ink and stylus tablets. 
After having analyzed the workﬂow of the papyrologists, the engineers managed to

The Artiﬁcial Papyrologist at Work 129
build an intelligent system able to compare similarities and differences between 
unknown shapes and a set of known characters already used to train it. Both known 
and unknown shapes were entered manually by annotating individual portions of the 
digital images and mapping the related text (Tarte, 2010). “Can computers ever read 
ancient texts?” asked Melissa Terras, one of the engineers involved in this project, 
during a Digital Classicist seminar at the London Institute of Classical Studies 
in 2007 (Bodard, 2007). For that moment, the answer was negative, because the 
described system still offered a range of possibilities to the researcher’s discretion, 
and was therefore no more than a very helpful assistant. 
More recently, other projects offered ground to the storage of massive alpha-
betical datasets: Ancient Lives at Oxford, which encouraged a crowdfunded papy-
rological editing by providing sample alphabets to be compared with the actual 
papyrus texts (Reggiani, 2017, pp. 152–153), and Anagnosis at Würzburg, which 
developed an automated alignment between text and image (Ast & Essler, 2018, 
pp. 71–73). At the 29th International Congress (Lecce 2019), an international team 
from Paris ( Scripta research program), Heidelberg (Rodney Ast) and Würzburg 
(Holger Essler, Anagnosis ), presented a poster dealing with “an automatic alignment 
of all available papyri transcriptions with the glyphs on the images.” The system is 
based on automatic line detection, with further steps involving image segmentation 
and the alignment with existing transcriptions of the papyri. It seems that this 
pipeline has already been successfully applied to Medieval manuscripts in Hebrew 
and Latin (Kiessling et al., 2019). 
A new challenge to digital paleography has been issued by the D-Scribes project 
led by Isabelle Marthot at the University of Basel (Marthot-Santaniello, 2021). 
It will be enough to report from the project’s website that its ﬁnal purpose is to 
create “an online interface through which papyrologists would be able to look for 
similar – or identical – handwritings to a given papyrus and for typical samples 
of writing for a given period” ( https://d-scribes.philhist.unibas.ch). I limit myself 
to highlight that one of the main theoretical goals of this project is admittedly to 
overcome the methodological limits of a traditional paleography based on subjective 
impressions and individual opinions, by providing objective classiﬁcations and 
criteria to understand similarity and difference in ancient handwritings. This looks 
very much like a ﬁrst true step towards the deﬁnition of an “artiﬁcial papyrologist” 
that can replace and even ameliorate some intellectual processes usually deployed 
by humans (we can recall what Turner said about distinguishing certainty and uncer-
tainty in the papyrological workﬂow). Automated recognition of dated documentary 
handwritings is also the focus of a new project that is being started at the University 
of Udine under the guidance of Giuseppina Azzarello: it will be both interesting and 
educational to see how it develops. 4 
It is very remarkable to mention also an experiment performed a couple of years 
ago by a team of Greek researchers, who compared the results of paleographical
4 At present, we are in the process of selecting relevant material from established papyrological 
archives and developing a software platform to host the desired process. 

130 N. Reggiani
dating of literary and documentary papyri by means of deep learning dating models, 
pre-trained on the images of objectively dated Greek papyri provided by PapPal 
and the Collaborative Database of Dateable Greek Bookhands , with the same task 
performed by human experts. The results of automated dating were 68% accurate 
in the case of the literary papyri and 55% in the case of the documentary papyri. As 
regards the human comparison, 
in the case of literary papyri, the models achieved a lower error than the average expert. In 
the case of documentary papyri, the performance was worse but did not signiﬁcantly differ 
from that of few experts. (Paparigopoulou et al., 2021) 
At the latest International Congress, last year in Paris, Rodney Ast addressed again 
these issues in a wishful paper, titled When will we start studying actual papyri , 
which I hope will be published in the congress proceedings because it was a most 
lucid reﬂection on the advantages of aligning digital annotated images with the 
digital critical edition of papyrus texts. He envisioned, for example, a possible 
future Papyri.info platform able to host image queries, and he also spoke of the 
potentialities of text-image alignment in view of automatic transcriptions. A proper 
automatic reading of the papyrus texts (a sort of papyrological OCR) will require 
further work, of course, but now we are certainly potentially closer to it than 40 years 
ago. 
One of the main problems contrasting this dream is the huge set of data required 
to teach a machine some good general paleography. For instance, it is not by chance 
that the past and the present digital paleographical projects mostly deal with literary 
texts or with homogeneous and quite formalized documentary texts, where the 
differences in the handwritings do exist, but can be conveniently managed. How 
many different shapes and sizes could a single character exhibit in the several 
thousands of documentary cursive texts preserved by the papyri? And what about 
fragmentary characters, lacking parts of their shape? This latter issue has been 
addressed by another very recent paper, presented at the 31st International Joint 
Conference on AI in July 2022 and involving technicians and papyrologists (among 
which James Brusuelas, Federica Nicolardi, Marzia D’Angelo, Claudio V ergara). 
They reﬂected on the opportunity to increase an existing dataset of ancient Greek 
character images (taken from the Ancient Lives project mentioned above) to be used 
for machine learning purposes, using synthetically generated character instances by 
means of other neural network algorithms (Swindall et al., 2022). This could be 
an effective way to overcome some quantitative problems: instead of teaching the 
machine, we could train other machines to teach the machine. How much virtual, 
however, the result will be? 
There is another area of papyrology where the human skill of “eyesight” plays 
a fundamental role: restoration and reuniﬁcation of fragments. “Reuniﬁcation” is a 
keyword in the D-Scribes project just mentioned, but there it means the automated 
process of recognition of two fragments of the same papyrus on paleographical 
ground. Physical reuniﬁcation is on the contrary the main purpose of another very 
recent project, currently ongoing at the University of Florence (Istituto Papirologico 
Vitelli) with the cooperation of the Consiglio Nazionale delle Ricerche. Presented

The Artiﬁcial Papyrologist at Work 131
in a poster at the latest International Congress in Paris, this so-called Papyrus 
Intelligent User Interface aims at exploiting automatic recognition methods based 
on Deep Learning in order to support papyrologists in more or less difﬁcult assembly 
works. Usually, when working on the reconstruction of a fragmentary papyrus, 
material features such as ﬁber patterns, fragment shapes, and writing layout are 
taken into consideration. Currently, this project is exploring the ﬁrst one (ﬁber 
patterns), assessing the feasibility of automatic matching based on the continuity of 
the ﬁbers on both recto and verso and the general pattern of the papyrus surface, as 
well as the fragment shape. The algorithm is trained with already known matching 
fragments. According to some preliminary tests, it seems that the thing might work, 
and it is certainly a great research perspective. 5 A similar task has already been 
attempted by an Israeli team few years ago. This particular algorithm was trained on 
a batch of items from the Dead Sea Scrolls and was limited to the match of pairs of 
fragments on the basis of the ﬁber patterns; also in this case, the application to new 
fragments seems to have produced positive results (Abitbol et al., 2021). 
Artiﬁcial Intelligence is deployed also in the complex algorithms developed for 
the virtual unwrapping of carbonized papyrus rolls, namely the Herculaneum papyri. 
As is known, the peculiar materiality of the Herculaneum rolls has always required 
the development of special treatments in order to unwrap the charred rolls and then 
read the darkened surface of the unrolled fragments. Digital Papyrology has done 
much in this respect, and a very recent monograph devoted to these matters by 
Kilian Fleischer reasonably speaks of two “revolutions” in the Herculaneum ﬁeld: 
digital imaging through multispectral photographs and related technologies aimed 
at enhancing the visible surface of the fragments, and virtual unrolling, i.e., the 
application of tomographic techniques in order to “scan” the wrapped rolls and to 
highlight the chemical contrast between written text and carbonized surface even 
without a physical and potentially destructive opening of the scrolls (Fleischer, 
2021; see Reggiani, 2023). This second “revolution” is remarkably deﬁned by 
Fleischer as in spe , since its results, though encouraging, are still at the beginning, 
and they are much improved by the application of AI techniques. Machine learning 
was ﬁrst applied to the virtual unrolling of the Herculaneum papyri by Brent Seales, 
who believed that reading the hidden text was a matter of algorithms rather than 
of chemical difference between the ink and the support. In 2019, using a sample 
item, he showed that the ink can be ﬁltered out from the background using suitable 
algorithms even if nothing is initially visible on the images of the synchrotron 
scans—basically, AI detects micro-changes in structure between papyrus with and 
without ink. Further progress in training the machines was stopped by the Covid 
pandemics, but it is going to restart also in connection with another big current 
project dealing with Herculaneum papyrology, the ERC Greek Schools project led 
by Graziano Ranocchia at Pisa (Brusuelas, 2021; https://greekschools.eu). A very 
recent competition, the so-called “V esuvius Challenge,” was launched in 2023 
to engage the general public in deciphering the Herculaneum papyri using AI
5 I thank Francesca Maltomini for preliminary information about this project. 

132 N. Reggiani
algorithms. Datasets from segmented 3D X-ray scans of unwrapped scrolls and 
additional scans of fragments were published and made available for various stages 
of automated ink detection, along with helpful tutorials. The ultimate winner, a 
computer science student, successfully recovered meaningful characters and even 
words in a section of a papyrus. 6 Overall, the V esuvius Challenge appears to have 
effectively combined technology, collaboration, and public engagement to advance 
the understanding of papyrus artifacts through the application of AI algorithms. 
4 Sprachgefühl in Digital Papyrology 
It is time now to turn to the second of Crönert’s “cardinal virtues,” Sprachgefühl 
or the “sense of language.” The automatic or semiautomatic linguistic analysis of 
ancient texts is by now a consolidated task in ancient studies. Started with such 
a huge linguistic annotation project as The Ancient Greek and Latin Dependency 
Treebank, this task has recently spread to papyrology. Big projects involving the 
digital linguistic annotation of papyrus texts such as PapyGreek (formerly Sematia ) 
led by Marja Vierros at Helsinki (Vierros, 2018) and Trismegistos Words , which 
is part of the increasing galaxy of metadata catalogues composing the Trismegistos 
platform, are based on semiautomatic linguistic tagging. 7 Semiautomatic annotation 
means that the automated task performed by a trained machine must always be 
checked and ﬁne-tuned by a human expert, because of the linguistic complexities 
of ancient grammars, the irregularities of the language of the papyri, and the 
fragmentation of damaged words and textual sections. The accuracy of TM Words 
is estimated around the 95%, which—as we read in the About section of the 
catalogue—“may seem high, but still implies that there are several thousands of 
mistakes in the current version” ( https://www.trismegistos.org/words/about.php). 
Few years ago, Giuseppe Celano conducted a comparison between the manually 
annotated papyri of Sematia and an automatic annotation performed by himself 
on the documentary corpus of Papyri.info using the analysis tools of the Depen-
dency Treebank . The resulting annotated corpus—called MALP , Morphologically 
Annotated and Lemmatized Papyri , available on GitHub —has revealed an accuracy 
amounting to just the 62% (Celano, 2018). I am not aware of projects currently 
deploying artiﬁcial intelligence (dynamic training of neural networks) to ﬁne-tune 
automatic linguistic analysis. 
A certain linguistic skill is required also to propose supplements to ﬁll the 
physical gaps affecting the ancient papyri. Filling a lacuna requires awareness of 
the narrower context of the papyrus text (what is written before and after and what
6 See https://scrollprize.org and https://scrollprize.substack.com 
7 PapyGreek relies on the annotation environment of Arethusa , which allows for a manual tagging 
supported by automatic suggestions, while TM Words relies on a trained algorithm developed by 
Alek Keersmaekers. See, e.g., Keersmaekers ( 2020) and Keersmaekers and V an Hal ( 2023). 

The Artiﬁcial Papyrologist at Work 133
is expected in between) and of the larger context of the papyrological corpus (more 
or less formulaic parallels, similar wordings, and so on). Automatic gap ﬁlling is 
perhaps one of the biggest challenges of digital papyrology together with automatic 
papyrus reading. Several different tools aimed at performing queries in electronic 
corpora in order to discover textual matches with the extant characters (the so-called 
fragment siting) have been developed through time, from the already mentioned 
Lacunology and the built-in research tools of the Ibycus machines running the Duke 
Databank of Documentary Papyri in the 80s (Reggiani, 2017, pp. 212–218), to the 
more or less complex features of research programs like Pandora, up to the current 
search options offered by Papyri.info . They are all tools performing mechanic 
comparisons of strings of text, submitting them to the human judgment. 
More advanced functions of automated text mining would involve an intelligent 
intervention by the machine in order to select the most probable supplements 
by itself, reducing the intervention of the human mind. Some 10 years ago, a 
project conducted at the University of Leipzig by Reinhold Scholl tried to apply 
more a complex text manipulation to the fragmentary papyri. The idea, part of the 
wider project eAQUA ( Extraktion von strukturierten Wissen aus Antiken Quellen 
für die Altertumswissenschaft )( http://www.eaqua.net), was to perform quantitative 
searches on digital text corpora like categorization (i.e., classiﬁcation of the text 
according to standard topical categories on the basis of recurring keywords), co-
occurrence analysis (i.e., analysis of the relationships between a word and the 
surrounding ones), and text recognition, a sort of advanced Lacunology , in which 
a partially missing or misspelled word is compared with the textual corpus and a 
list of possible candidates is generated automatically, relying on a word prediction 
system based on several classes of spell checking and text mining algorithms, which 
are essentially related to the analysis of the semantic, syntactical, morphological 
context of the words, on the word length, on the comparison of similar letter 
sequences, on Named Entity lists (i.e., onomastic and topographical indexes to 
identify personal or geographical names) (Rücker, 2010; Scholl, 2012; Büchler et 
al., 2012). Unfortunately, as long as I know, this tool remained in a beta-version and 
cannot be used regularly. Something very similar has been recently launched in the 
ﬁeld of Digital Epigraphy— Ithaca, an interface able to restore and attribute ancient 
texts using deep neural networks (Assael et al., 2022; https://ithaca.deepmind. 
com)—and it would be very interesting if Digital Papyrology could recover such 
an old desideratum too. 
Another aspect that papyrological research has experimented is the application of 
machine learning automation to stylometric analyses. A recent attempt applied to an 
unsupervised stylistic clustering of the literary papyri encoded in the DCLP corpus 
returned promising results, although there will be the need for further ﬁne-tuning 
(Ochab & Essler, 2019a, b). An interesting observation was that the best results 
were obtained with more normalized texts (i.e., with their spelling regularized, 
diacritics omitted, abbreviations expanded), the explanation being that “this removes 
the noise of scribal habit and convention, and thus leaves the author’s signal easier 
to detect.” Further attempts have been announced on the documentary papyri, where 
the task will be to query the Duke Databank for such information as genre or type

134 N. Reggiani
of texts, provenance, and time of origin. The Trismegistos automated linguistic and 
semantic annotation of the entire documentary corpus, mentioned above, is of course 
a wonderful starting point for deeper investigations in the papyrus texts: Named 
Entity Recognition and sociolinguistic annotation are just two main possible paths 
for future automatic analysis. 
5 Sachkunde in Digital Papyrology (Not a Conclusion?) 
What about, then, Crönert’s third “cardinal virtue,” Sachkunde or “competence, 
expertise”? A trained intelligent machine is expected to gain sufﬁcient competence 
to be able to replace a human papyrologist in his/her primary task of being a 
“learned copyist” of papyrus texts. This of course requires lots of information to 
be taught to the machine, especially as we likely expect such a learned machine 
to have less doubts and more certainties than human papyrologists when analyzing 
a papyrus. Today, it is perhaps more convenient and less time-consuming to try to 
decipher a complex text in the human way than teaching a machine to do so. We 
can start doing so, of course, as we do, and we can learn a lot in the meanwhile. 
As Rodney Ast signiﬁcantly remarked at the conclusion of his talk mentioned 
before, although for now it remains unclear whether computers will successfully 
learn to read the papyri, our efforts to teach them to do so can enhance our skills as 
papyrologists. In particular, by establishing stronger links between text and image, 
we can better analyze and interpret phenomena in the papyri that are difﬁcult to 
capture in traditional editions. 
This is a ﬁrst positive outcome of Digital Papyrology in general: a closer attention 
to several peculiarities of our object of study, which often escape the eye’s attention 
in traditional editions. Just think of the critical details that emerge when encoding 
papyrus texts in Papyri.info . Thus, ﬁrst of all, to work at the idea of an artiﬁcial 
papyrological intelligence is a way to improve and enhance our own papyrological 
intelligence. Secondly, we must note that all the current projects involving some 
machine learning are still using it as an intelligent and dynamic tool to help 
papyrologists in their further studies: artiﬁcial intelligence can detect fragment 
matches, similarities in handwritings, ink traces on carbonized surfaces, possible 
textual supplements, but is not able—at least so far—to come back to Turner’s 
papyrologist at work—“to set out precisely what the papyrus says, and to distinguish 
between what is certain or given by the text and what is a matter of inference” 
(Turner, 1973,p .7 ) . 
Will it be? Perhaps yes, since now we are facing technological progress that was 
just unimaginable few years ago. For now, as James Brusuelas noted in a recent 
reﬂection on this topic, 
It is probably not the type of AI about which our science ﬁction induced imaginations think 
and dream. It is an intelligence that makes predictions. But we cannot talk to it. We cannot 
interact with it. (Brusuelas, 2021, p. 68)

The Artiﬁcial Papyrologist at Work 135
Therefore, it is perhaps too early to consider it—quoting him again—“a critical 
assistant, if not full partner, in our work” (Brusuelas, 2021, p. 68) and including 
some new references to it in our current editions, as he starts proposing. But he is 
correct in stressing the fact that we must start thinking of it. In all other respects, I 
believe that it will take time before we can enter the era of Digital Papyrology 4.0 
and see the ﬁrst true artiﬁcial papyrologist at work.

AI for the Restoration of Ancient 
Inscriptions: A Computational 
Linguistics Perspective 
Alessandro Locaputo , Beatrice Portelli , Stefano Magnani , 
Emanuela Colombi , and Giuseppe Serra 
1 Introduction 
An inscription is a text carved or etched onto durable materials like stone and 
metals or painted on various surfaces made from different materials. This practice 
involves embedding language, symbols, or expressions onto enduring materials, 
aiding the preservation and transmission of information, culture, and history over 
time (Buonopane, 2009). 
In ancient Roman society, inscriptions were ubiquitous, serving a wide range of 
purposes. These purposes included keeping records of military activities, document-
ing legal matters, and making public announcements. 
The extensive use of inscriptions in these various aspects makes them incredibly 
valuable pieces of evidence from the past (Cooley, 2012). For instance, the analysis 
of honorary inscriptions can offer insights into the cursus honorum , which was 
the sequence of public ofﬁces that Roman politicians in the republican period and 
then in the imperial age aimed to hold (Buonopane, 2009). In addition, the huge 
number of inscribed funerary monuments offers a glimpse into the historiography 
of individuals and their “daily life” (Susini, 1982).

138 A. Locaputo et al.
However, the material on which the inscriptions were engraved is subject to 
deterioration over time. This renders the inscriptions difﬁcult to read and, in more 
dire circumstances, causes them to become entirely unreadable due to extensive 
damage or total erasure. In fact, it is estimated that only between 2 and 3% of all 
Latin inscriptions have survived to this day (Buonopane, 2009). 
The damage or the erasure of some portions of the text introduces gaps in the 
inscriptions, which are conventionally referred to as lacunae. In order to extract the 
information conveyed by the inscription, it is required to restore them. However, the 
process of restoring them is a time-consuming activity that requires the involvement 
of an expert epigrapher. This is necessary because restoring an inscription requires 
in-depth knowledge about the language, the historical context, and the time period 
in which the artifact was produced. These experts are difﬁcult to ﬁnd, especially 
for less common languages, because they need to be able to understand archaic 
scripts and languages, as well as track their historical evolution, including dialectal 
shifts. By carefully comparing similar inscriptions, these experts can piece together 
fragmented parts and thus conjecture over the missing text portion. Of course, when 
multiple copies of an inscription are available (e.g., laws and decrees), the conjecture 
can be proposed with a certain degree of certainty. This is particularly the case 
with the high formulaic level of Latin funerary inscriptions, which present a wide 
range of abbreviated formulae, such as D.M., H.S.E., S.T.L., V .F., VIX. ANN., 1 
etc. However, this is not the case when dealing with documents such as deeds or 
contracts, where usually no more than a single example exists, and thus it is more 
difﬁcult to ﬁnd evidence supporting the proposed hypothesis. 
Over the years, this task has been partially facilitated by the availability of 
digital corpora, enabling epigraphers to access previously inaccessible resources. 
This has given rise to the interdisciplinary ﬁeld of digital humanities, which 
combines traditional humanities disciplines with computer science and data analysis 
to explore and interpret historical inscriptions and cultural artifacts in innovative 
ways (Burdick et al., 2016). Furthermore, the increasing availability of digitized 
material, combined with increasing computational power availability, has opened 
up the possibility of applying deep learning techniques for numerous tasks within 
the humanities ﬁeld, including the development of systems to assist epigraphers in 
the restoration process. These techniques are capable of discovering patterns present 
in huge amounts of data. 
Testifying the signiﬁcance of digital humanities and the ferment in this ﬁeld, in 
2023 the Vesuvius Challenge was launched (Friedman et al., 2023), a competition 
with a prize pool of one million dollars. The goal was to read four passages of text 
contained inside two carbonized and ashen Herculaneum Papyri, without unrolling 
them, employing x-ray tomography and computer vision techniques.

AI for the Restoration of Inscriptions 139
The objective of this chapter is to emphasize the important role that ancient 
inscriptions play in our understanding of history and to provide an overview of the 
premises that led to the application of Artiﬁcial Intelligence for their restoration. 
This will be done by ﬁrst presenting the collective effort to digitize artifacts and 
make them machine-readable. Then, the problem of restoration will be formalized 
from a Natural Language Processing perspective. Following that, there will be an 
in-depth analysis of the evolution of AI methods, highlighting major breakthroughs 
and addressing the problems associated with these methods. 
Finally, there will be a discussion about the limits of these methods and what the 
next steps in the ﬁeld could be. 
2 Digitization 
The beginning of the effort to digitize artifacts can be traced back to the 1970s 
when, in what can be deﬁned as the ﬁrst wave of digital humanities, humanists 
embraced the usage of computers to expand the possibilities at their disposal. One of 
the initial attempts was, in fact, the digitization and standardization of corpora with 
the purpose of making them machine-readable and readily accessible to a wider 
audience. Later, especially thanks to the advent of the Internet in the 1990s, the 
possibility of collaboration greatly accelerated this process (Burdick et al., 2016). 
Before this happened, the collection of inscriptions in corpora was relegated to 
physical books, with all the limitations that come with it, such as the difﬁculty of 
updating or amending entries, and the inherent accessibility problems. 
One of the earliest and most signiﬁcant collections of Latin inscriptions is 
the Corpus Inscriptionum Latinarum (CIL). This work was initiated by Theodor 
Mommsen, a German historian and Nobel laureate, in 1847 and is an ongoing 
project that continues to be updated. It aims to compile and document all known 
Latin inscriptions from the ancient Roman world. CIL is organized into volumes 
covering different regions and themes, including inscriptions from a wide range of 
sources such as tombstones, dedicatory plaques, public monuments, and more. The 
CIL has played a crucial role in preserving and making accessible a vast amount of 
Latin epigraphic material. 
Other prominent corpora include L’Année épigraphique, a French publication 
that has been collecting, year by year, all newly found or reexamined inscriptions 
primarily in Latin and Ancient Greek concerning Ancient Rome since 1888, 
and Supplementum Epigraphicum Graecum , an annual survey of newly found or 
rediscussed Greek inscriptions. 
Something that unites the abovementioned corpora, aside from their common 
theme of interest, is that each of them transcribes inscriptions according to the 
Leiden Conventions (The Oxford Handbook of Roman Epigraphy, 2015). The 
Leiden Conventions, also known as the Leiden Guidelines, are a set of standardized 
rules and guidelines used by scholars to transcribe inscriptions accurately and 
consistently.

140 A. Locaputo et al.
In this way, epigraphers can annotate inscriptions, for example, by marking 
letters that are considered erroneous by experts or by introducing erroneously 
omitted letters. For instance, the introduction of missing letters from the text is 
denoted by surrounding square brackets, hence the common expression “history in 
square brackets” (Badian, 1989). 
In recent years, there have been numerous initiatives for the digitization of 
physical corpora, facilitated by the adoption of Artiﬁcial Intelligence. In fact, it 
is common to employ Optical Character Recognition models for the automatic 
transcription of text starting from scanned pages. These models tend to show 
high accuracy, especially for typewritten documents. However, the automatic 
transcription of handwritten documents (Handwritten Text Recognition) is a more 
challenging task, due to the higher variability in writing style. An interesting work in 
this regard is HisDoc (Fischer et al., 2012), an AI model designed for the automatic 
transcription and analysis of medieval Latin manuscripts. 
The most notable examples of digitization of physical artifacts and documents 
include the Perseus Project (Perseus Digital Library, 2024), which digitizes a large 
corpus of literary documents in both Latin and Greek, the EAGLE (Europeana 
network of Ancient Greek and Latin Epigraphy) project, an initiative born with 
the objective of digitizing Greco-Roman inscriptions originating from European 
museums, libraries, archives, and multimedia collections scattered across 25 Euro-
pean countries, and the Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative (CDLI), 2 which aims 
to preserve text and images of cuneiform inscriptions. 
For Latin inscriptions, the most complete collection available is EDCS 
(Epigraphik-Datenbank Clauss/Slaby). 3 Through it, it is possible to access not 
only the previously mentioned prominent corpora such as the CIL and AE but 
also all the inscriptions that are part of the EAGLE project, 4 as well as numerous 
datasets scattered only on the Internet, totaling 45 databases. 
Since the ﬁrst attempts at preservation through early editions, it immediately 
became evident how important standardization was, exempliﬁed by conventions like 
the Leiden Conventions. Over the following years, this need led to the development 
of the Text Encoding Initiative (TEI) (TEI Consortium, 2024), a set of more general 
guidelines and standards for encoding and representing texts in digital form, which 
found wide adoption in the digital humanities. 
Another important aspect to consider is that while one of the goals of the 
digitization process is to facilitate access to resources for a wider audience, this is 
not always completely achieved. Some resources are not available in open access 
due, for example, to copyright laws (this is especially true for photographs of 
artifacts), thereby undermining the overall accessibility.

AI for the Restoration of Inscriptions 141
3 Problem Characterization 
Addressing epigraphical gaps within a text resembles the well-known cloze task. 
This task is used to assess text comprehension. It involves removing speciﬁc 
words from a passage, creating gaps, which individuals are then asked to ﬁll in, 
inferring missing words or phrases based on the context. Widely used in education 
and language assessment, the cloze task evaluates language proﬁciency, reading 
comprehension, and the ability to deduce contextual meaning. This concept is 
rooted in Gestalt psychology, reﬂecting humans’ natural inclination to perceive and 
complete patterns (Taylor, 1953). 
In the machine learning ﬁeld of Natural Language Processing (NLP), the cloze 
task is commonly known as “text inﬁlling” (Zhu e al., 2019). Within text generation 
techniques, text inﬁlling consists in completing passages of text from which 
speciﬁc sections have been intentionally removed or concealed. The challenge is 
to seamlessly integrate the generated content into the surrounding context aiming 
for both completeness and coherence. 
Text inﬁlling in the context of NLP also resembles the concept of inpainting 
(Jam et al., 2021) in computer vision. Just as text inﬁlling involves predicting 
and completing missing words or tokens within a sentence, inpainting pertains to 
the process of ﬁlling in missing or corrupted parts of an image. In text inﬁlling, 
neighboring words provide hints about the missing content’s semantic role, while 
for inpainting surrounding pixels guide the choice of colors and textures for the 
incomplete regions. With its ability to restore missing or damaged portions of 
images, it ﬁnds valuable applications within digital humanities. Inpainting tech-
niques, for instance, can be employed to reconstruct historical artifacts, documents, 
and artworks that have undergone wear, tear, or degradation over time. For instance, 
the work by Lengauer et al. (2022) demonstrates how these techniques can be used 
to restore damaged patterns on ancient pottery. 
Notably, the recent emergence of diffusion-based models has led to signiﬁcant 
improvements in the quality of inpainting results. Moral-Andrés et al. ( 2022)u s e d 
DALL-E2 to explore the potential adoption of such models for the reconstruction 
of damaged ancient mosaics. The investigation concluded that while the results are 
promising, the model falls short in reconstructing large portions, faces, and handling 
nudity due to its policy constraints. 
The abovementioned tasks bear resemblance to the Masked Language Model 
(MLM) train objective used in NLP, as proposed by the BERT paper (Devlin et al., 
2018). It serves as a training objective, allowing the language model to capture 
intricate relationships between words, contextual nuances, and the grammar of the 
language by deliberately masking portions of the input text and forcing the model 
to predict them. In essence, these three approaches share a common objective of 
contextually guided completion, whether in images or text, contributing to the 
advancement of language understanding and generative models.
