4 AI Methods for Inscription Restoration 
Recently, the applications of Artiﬁcial Intelligence (AI) methods for ancient lan-
guages have seen a rise. The following section offers an overview of the most 
important ones with a focus on those designed speciﬁcally for the restoration of 
ancient inscriptions. 
4.1 Background 
Traditionally, the process of restoring inscriptions relies almost entirely on the 
knowledge of the epigraphist, their ability to detect common patterns based on 
context, and their capacity to draw parallels with inscriptions of a similar nature. 
The increasing availability of digitalized corpora of ancient inscriptions, coupled 
with the growing accessibility of more powerful computers, has enabled the 
application of AI methods for the semiautomatic restoration of inscriptions. 
However, the restoration of ancient inscriptions with AI can encompass a wide 
range of aspects not covered by NLP techniques. Numerous methods related to the 
concept of inscription restoration involve the ﬁeld of Computer Vision, for instance, 
the automatic reassembly of fragments of artifacts, which can be achieved other than 
by leveraging on textual information (Tyndall, 2012), also relying on images (Zhang 
et al., 2022), or even 3D scans (Collins et al., 2014). Convolutional Neural Networks 
have even been employed for the scanning of satellite images for the detection of 
archeological sites (Caspari & Crespo, 2019). 
Even when considering just the NLP ﬁeld, there exists a vast literature of methods 
for solving classical NLP tasks for modern languages. Recently, some of these 
problems have begun to be tackled for ancient languages. 
Among the classic NLP tasks that have found application in ancient languages 
(Sommerschield et al., 2023), there are: 
• Part-of-Speech tagging, which is marking each word in a text with its corre-
sponding grammatical part of speech (e.g., noun, verb, adjective, etc.) (Singh 
et al., 2021; Riemenschneider & Frank, 2023; Bamman & Burns, 2020) 
• Sentiment analysis, which means identifying the attitude of the writer as 
expressed in a piece of text (e.g., happiness, sadness, rage, and neural) (Sprugnoli 
et al., 2021) 
• Machine Translation, meaning the automatic translation of text from a language 
to another (Yousef et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2019; Kang et al., 2021) 
This was also favored by the development of tools such as the Classical 
Language Toolkit (CLTK) (Johnson et al., 2021), a Python library that provides 
a series of useful tools for the natural language processing of pre-modern languages 
such as Akkadian, Aramaic, Latin, and Sanskrit. As an example, CLTK provides

AI for the Restoration of Inscriptions 143
prepackaged tools for tokenization, lemmatization, Part-of-Speech tagging, and 
morphosyntactic analysis, among others. 
However, despite the increase in available data, in many cases, this information 
is not sufﬁcient to train a state-of-the-art model. Therefore, it may be necessary to 
train a less-performing model or rely on transfer learning techniques. 
The following sections will cover the evolution of these AI methods for the 
restoration of ancient inscriptions from the perspective of NLP, framing the problem 
solely as a text inﬁlling (Zhu e al., 2019) task. 
4.2 Statistical Methods 
Statistical methods, often considered the most traditional approach, have been 
fundamental to text restoration in archeological and linguistic research for decades. 
While historically these techniques have signiﬁcantly contributed to deciphering 
ancient texts, it is crucial to acknowledge their inherent limitations, particularly 
when dealing with severely damaged inscriptions or complex scripts. 
The ﬁrst examples of such models in the context of text restoration employed 
Markov chains (Rao et al., 2009) and n-gram models (Yadav et al., 2010)f o rt h e 
restoration of Indus scripts. N-gram models are one of the simplest approaches to 
language modeling as it is based on simple statistics. An n-gram is any sequence of 
n letters, and the probability of each n-gram’s occurrence is learned by observing 
how often it co-occurs with other n-grams in the analyzed corpus. This method 
of reasoning, where the probability of an n-gram occurring is determined solely 
based on the preceding one, without considering the entire history, is commonly 
known as the Markov assumption. Despite their simple assumptions, these models 
exhibit excellent performance, especially for very small datasets. They do, however, 
have certain limitations. For instance, they are highly dependent on the training 
set. In every language, there are some n-grams that, although not very common, 
can acceptably co-occur after other ones. If such occurrences are never observed 
in the training data, the model may erroneously learn to never output these 
valid combinations. Conversely, very common patterns could occur too frequently, 
causing the model to overpredict them. Another problem is dealing with characters 
not present in the training set, which can easily occur when working with ancient 
inscriptions and especially with small corpora. 
Although the abovementioned limitations exist, these statistical approaches 
demonstrated the usefulness of AI in restoring ancient inscriptions, paving the way 
for more sophisticated methods to assist epigraphers in their restoration workﬂow.

144 A. Locaputo et al.
4.3 Deep Learning Methods 
Deep learning (LeCun et al., 2015) presents a new avenue for overcoming the 
multifaceted challenges associated with text restoration. Driven by neural networks 
and advanced algorithms, deep learning models demonstrate an exceptional ability 
to discern intricate patterns and dependencies within textual data. This characteristic 
makes it particularly well suited for the restoration of text in ancient inscriptions. 
The fundamental building block of a neural network is the individual neuron, a 
computational unit that draws inspiration from the intricate workings of the human 
nervous system. The single neuron (also known as perceptron McCulloch & Pitts, 
1943) is a remarkably simpliﬁed information processor that takes in input a set of 
numbers, applies weighted connections to them, and then combines them through 
an activation function. This combination of inputs and weights enables the neuron 
to make basic computations. 
While a single neuron’s capabilities may appear rudimentary, it is an essential 
foundational unit for more complex neural network architectures. Neurons col-
lectively form intricate networks, capable of tackling increasingly complex tasks, 
ranging from image recognition to natural language understanding. 
4.3.1 Recurrent Neural Networks 
The ﬁeld of NLP witnessed a transformative moment with the ﬁrst applications 
of Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) ﬁrst introduced by Hopﬁeld ( 1982). RNNs 
brought forth a paradigm shift by introducing a novel architectural feature, recurrent 
connections, which fundamentally altered the way neural networks process an input. 
The network is now composed of a single unit, which “reads” the input one “word” 
at a time. RNNs possess a form of memory, allowing them to maintain a hidden state 
that evolves over time as new data is processed. In this way, they become aware of 
the direction of the information ﬂow and are capable of processing inputs of varying 
lengths. This temporal memory capability has proven to be exceptionally well suited 
for tasks that involve sequential data, such as natural language understanding and 
generation. Their capacity to capture dependencies across time steps allows them to 
excel in language modeling, machine translation, speech recognition, and sentiment 
analysis, among others. 
Some types of RNNs, known as bidirectional RNNs (BiRNNs), consist of two 
neural networks that analyze the input data not only from left to right (forward) 
but also from right to left (backward). This bidirectional approach enhances 
comprehension and allows the model to make predictions based on both preceding 
and succeeding information. 
Such architecture, for example, has been used for the inﬁlling of Linear B script 
found on Mycenaean tablets by training a language model (Papavassileiou et al., 
2023). This work underlines a common challenge in NLP when dealing with ancient 
languages: the scarcity of data. In fact, state-of-the-art models contemporary to

AI for the Restoration of Inscriptions 145
this work used a different architecture to solve inﬁlling tasks in other languages. 
However, these architectures typically demand a large training dataset, which was 
not available for the Linear B script. Therefore, the authors had to rely on RNNs, 
which can be trained with fewer samples. Although RNN models require less data 
compared to other architectures, the authors still had to resort to data augmentation 
techniques to increase the volume of training data. Data augmentation techniques 
allow to artiﬁcially increase the amount of available training samples by generating 
new synthetic ones, such as creating new sentences by replacing verbs with their 
synonyms. A downside of this approach is that data augmentation techniques are 
not trivial and they require careful choices and a deep knowledge of the language to 
create new plausible synthetic samples. A badly performed data augmentation could 
potentially introduce noise in the model, thereby reducing its prediction accuracy. 
4.3.2 Long Short-T erm Memory Networks 
An enhanced variant of the RNNs, known as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) 
networks, emerged as a notable evolution in the realm of recurrent neural architec-
tures. LSTM networks proved to be signiﬁcantly more effective and addressed some 
of the limitations encountered with traditional RNNs. 
The key innovation within LSTM networks is the introduction of specialized 
memory cells and gating mechanisms, such as the forget gate and input gate. 
These components enable LSTMs to better capture long-range dependencies and 
mitigate the vanishing gradient problem often encountered in standard RNNs, which 
limits the ability of the network to capture long-range dependencies. This improved 
capability to retain and selectively utilize information over extended sequences of 
data has made LSTMs a pivotal choice for a wide array of sequential data tasks. 
LSTM networks have also been applied to the ﬁeld of digital humanities, for 
example, Assael et al. ( 2019) proposed PYTHIA, the ﬁrst deep learning-based 
model for the semiautomatic restoration of damaged Ancient Greek inscriptions. 
One of the intuitions behind this model is that when dealing with damaged 
inscriptions, it is frequently the case that the damaged portion not only consists 
of entire words but often comprises only a few letters as well. As a result, PYTHIA 
operates both at the word level, which helps to convey context, and at the character 
level, allowing it to complete partial words. To be more accurate, PYTHIA is a 
sequence-to-sequence model (Sutskever et al., 2014) that is, as the name suggests, 
an architecture that is designed to handle sequences of data as input and generate 
new sequences as output. At its core, the idea is to employ one neural network 
as the “encoder” and another as the “decoder.” In both cases, PYTHIA utilizes 
bidirectional LSTM networks. The role of the encoder is to process the input 
sequence of tokens and convert it into what is commonly referred to as a “context 
vector.” This vector extracts essential information from the input sequence that will 
be used by the decoder to make the predictions. 
PYTHIA was speciﬁcally designed to assist epigraphers by providing the 20 
most likely ﬁlling hypotheses according to the model. It achieved a Character Error

146 A. Locaputo et al.
Rate (CER) of 30.1% for its top prediction, in contrast to the 57.3% CER obtained 
by “ancient historians,” two doctoral students with expertise in epigraphy. This 
performance showcases the model’s effectiveness in this ﬁeld. 
Building upon the insights from PYTHIA’s results, the concept of utilizing 
LSTMs for the restoration of ancient inscriptions was applied in a subsequent work, 
speciﬁcally targeted at Babylonian texts (Fetaya et al., 2020). Notably, this approach 
employed a single LSTM, in contrast to an encoder/decoder architecture. The LSTM 
model, achieving an 85.4% correct token prediction rate, outperformed a 2-gram 
statistical model, which still performed surprisingly well with a 74.8% accuracy 
rate. This comparison underscores how, even with a relatively small dataset like 
Akkadian, which is even smaller and more fragmented than the Ancient Greek one, 
these LSTM-based models can surpass traditional statistical methods. 
As mentioned before, sequence-to-sequence models are particularly valuable 
for tasks involving input sequences that require transformation. One such task is 
machine translation. For example, the work Zhang et al. ( 2019) uses bidirectional 
RNNs to translate ancient Chinese documents to modern Chinese. Conversely, in 
the paper Kang et al. ( 2021), the authors propose a multitask learning approach. 
This approach combines the translation of historical Korean documents into modern 
languages with the restoration of the same documents. 
Another interesting use of sequence-to-sequence LSTMs is grapheme-to-
phoneme transcription, for example, for the automatic phonological transcription of 
Akkadian clay tablets (Sahala et al., 2020). 
4.3.3 Transformers 
While the attention mechanism was introduced in a paper that explored its potential 
for use with RNNs in machine translation (Bahdanau et al., 2014), it was not until 
the introduction of the transformer architecture (Vaswani et al., 2017) that it gained 
traction in the ﬁeld. Transformer is an architecture that revolutionized the NLP 
world, becoming the de facto standard of the ﬁeld. Reversing the trend of RNNs and 
LSTMs, transformers are very wide models that can read long sequences of words at 
once, without the need for recurrent units. Transformers process the input in a non-
sequential manner (i.e., all words at the same time) and use attention mechanisms 
to understand how much each word has an impact on the other ones depending on 
the context. 
They are trained to optimize their efﬁciency in Masked Language Modeling, 
which is a task that consists in deliberately masking words and asking the model 
to reconstruct them, and therefore they are inherently good models for text 
reconstruction. 
The transformer is an encoder/decoder architecture that is the foundation of 
multiple state-of-the-art models for NLP tasks. For instance, GPT (Generative 
Pre-trained Transformer) models like GPT-3 (Brown et al., 2020) are decoder-
only transformers, meaning that they only use the decoder part of the transformer

AI for the Restoration of Inscriptions 147
architecture. These are also the core of the ChatGPT, which is a GPT-based model 
adapted for conversational tasks. 
In paper (Chang et al., 2021), GPT-2 (Radford et al., 2019) was employed for 
translating ancient Chinese text into modern Chinese. The authors were able to 
achieve great performances in the task, even without having access to large amounts 
of translated samples. The author simply trained the model with additional ancient 
Chinese poems without providing a translation. This underlines a very important 
aspect of transformer-based models, which is their remarkable transfer learning 
capability. In fact, transformers can transfer the knowledge learned during a task 
to other similar tasks via ﬁne-tuning, a process in which they are further trained on 
new tasks after having learned a main task. One of the ﬁrst papers to demonstrate this 
capability was BERT (Devlin et al., 2018) an encoder-only transformer which was 
designed speciﬁcally for being efﬁciently ﬁne-tuned. The training of a BERT model 
is divided into two phases. The ﬁrst phase is the pre-training, where the model is 
trained with a massive corpus in an unsupervised manner, that is without the need of 
having labeled data. In particular, Masked Language Modeling is used, as previously 
mentioned, randomly masking some parts of the input text and forcing the model to 
ﬁll the blanks. Once the model is pre-trained, it can be used for a speciﬁc task by 
just adding a very small new neural layer and ﬁne-tuning it to a speciﬁc task (e.g., 
sentiment analysis, part-of-speech tagging, etc.). 
T5 (Raffel et al., 2020), another transformer-based model, pushed the pre-
training idea further emphasizing the importance of transfer learning by introducing 
a uniﬁed framework. The key idea is to treat every NLP problem as a text-to-text 
task, allowing the model to be pre-trained effectively for various NLP problems 
simultaneously. The T5 pre-training process combines BERT’s Marked Language 
training objective with two additional objectives: language modeling (predicting 
the next word) and deshufﬂing (rearranging input tokens and having the model 
reconstruct them). Since T5 is capable of handling multiple tasks on textual input, 
the chosen task can be speciﬁed using task-speciﬁc preﬁxes (e.g., “translate English 
to German:” and “summarize:”). 
As mentioned, training from scratch of a transformer-based model requires a 
huge amount of data, especially when compared to LSTMs and even more when 
compared to statistical methods. This poses a problem for scenarios where there is a 
lack of data such as ancient languages. But, thanks to the ﬁne-tuning technique just 
described, it is possible to partially overcome this limitation. BERT-based models 
in particular found wide application in the digital humanities ﬁeld, including NLP 
tasks on ancient languages such as lacunae ﬁlling. 
A signiﬁcant work in this regard is the one proposed in Lazar et al. ( 2021), 
where the authors tried to train a BERT model from scratch for the ﬁlling of gaps in 
ancient Akkadian inscriptions. Given the low amount of available Akkadian texts, 
the results were not satisfactory as the pre-trained BERT performed similarly to 
the LSTM baseline. Then, given the lack of extensive resources of Akkadian text 
even considering the literature, the authors decided to ﬁne-tune the already-available 
multilingual BERT (Devlin et al., 2018) on the limited Akkadian texts. Multilingual 
BERT is a model pretrained on the Wikipedia pages belonging to the 104 most

148 A. Locaputo et al.
common languages. The intuition is that Akkadian, being an ancient language 
that was spoken in Mesopotamia, presents linguistic similarities with Hebrew and 
Arabic-Semitic languages, which were used to train multilingual BERT. In this way, 
even with a limited amount of data, the authors were able to reach state-of-the-art 
performances. Surprisingly, even the multilingual BERT model used in a zero-shot 
manner, without being trained on Akkadian texts, outperformed the model trained 
from scratch on the Akkadian corpus. 
The success of ﬁne-tuning is, of course, highly dependent on the pre-trained 
model, and sometimes the ﬁne-tuned model can inherit undesired features. This 
is precisely what happened with Ancient Greek BERT (Singh et al., 2021), which 
is based on the Modern Greek BERT model and ﬁne-tuned on a corpus of Ancient 
and Byzantine Greek texts. The limitation here arises from the necessity of limiting 
the model to the modern Greek alphabet, which, in turn, requires the omission 
of diacritic symbols that were widely used in Ancient Greek, starting from the 
Hellenistic period. This limitation restricts the applicability of this model. 
For Latin, there is currently no speciﬁc tool for ﬁlling gaps in ancient inscriptions. 
Although Latin BERT (Bamman & Burns, 2020) exists, it is a BERT model pre-
trained on a vast corpus of literary documents spanning from the classical era to 
the present, including data from the Latin Wikipedia. Subsequently, the model was 
tested to ﬁll gaps in literary documents from The Latin Library. 5 The test involved 
comparing expert emendations with those proposed by the model, resulting in a 
concordance rate of 33.1%. When examining this result, it is important to note 
that this model was trained on a vast amount of data spanning many centuries, 
during which the language underwent signiﬁcant changes. Consequently, it was not 
speciﬁcally tailored for working with classical documents such as those found in 
The Latin Library. 
Despite the abovementioned limitations of Latin BERT and Ancient Greek 
BERT, both models were able to improve the part-of-speech tagging, achieving 
state-of-the-art performances. 
When it comes to the application of a transformer-based model for the restoration 
of ancient inscriptions, one of the most notable examples is Ithaca (Assael et al., 
2022). This model has been proposed by the same authors as PYTHIA and can 
be considered its natural evolution. Being trained on the same cleaned dataset of 
ancient Greek inscriptions, the transformer-based model, which is built upon the 
Bigbird (Zaheer et al., 2020) architecture, outperforms the LSTM-based model 
with a Character Error Rate (CER) of 26.3%, compared to the latter’s 47.0%. 
Moreover, the Top-1 accuracy of the model is 61.8%, greatly surpassing PYTHIA’s 
accuracy of 32.6%. Despite this remarkable achievement, one of the most important 
takeaways from the paper is that Ithaca is able to effectively enhance the workﬂow 
of epigraphists by increasing their accuracy from 25.3 to 71.7%. The suggestion 
of restorative hypotheses is not the only way the model can assist epigraphists. 
In fact, Ithaca is also designed for spatial attribution of the region of origin and
5 https://www.thelatinlibrary.com/ 

AI for the Restoration of Inscriptions 149
chronological attribution, achieving a Top-1 accuracy of 70.8% for the former and 
an average deviation of 29.3 years from the ground truth for the latter. 
One of the most important aspects of Ithaca is that it was trained from scratch 
even with a relatively small dataset, made of just 76,608 inscriptions. As mentioned 
above, this would usually cause suboptimal performances for the restoration task, 
as there would be a concrete risk of overﬁtting. The authors overcome this obstacle 
by adopting several data augmentation techniques that are applied every time an 
inscription is fed to the model. The methods are the following: 
• Text clipping: Instead of always considering the full inscription, just a random 
portion of it is taken as input. This allows the model to better generalize partial 
input, as the clipping could happen anywhere in the text, even by cutting words 
in half. 
• Word deletion: Randomly deleting words from the text allows the model to better 
generalize over all the possible ways an inscription can be damaged. 
• Sentence swap: In addition to the Masked Language Modeling objective, the 
model employs the Next Sentence Prediction objective, which requires it to 
determine the correct order of randomly shufﬂed sentences. Thus, it becomes 
necessary to randomly swap sentences. 
Overall, all the models mentioned so far for ﬁlling gaps in ancient texts share a 
common limitation: They require prior knowledge about the gaps. This limitation is 
particularly pronounced in PYHTIA and Ithaca, as both models make predictions at 
the character level. Consequently, the user must not only specify the gap’s location 
but also mark every character they want the models to predict. This means that 
epigraphers must have precise information about the gap’s size in terms of the 
number of characters they wish to ﬁll. Instead, BERT-based models work at the 
token level, and thus it is required just to signal the location of the gap. Of course, 
the former models have an advantage because by knowing the exact size of the gap, 
they can rule out every prediction that does not correspond to the actual size of 
the gap, whereas the latter models do not incorporate this information. At best it is 
possible to specify the number of missing tokens, but since tokens do not possess a 
ﬁxed length, achieving correct predictions is not trivial. 
To address this issue, the Blank Language Model (BLM) (Shen et al., 2020) has 
been proposed. It dynamically generates text sequences, ﬁlling gaps by generating 
words and potentially introducing new gaps on either side of the generated 
word. When trained on the same dataset used by PYTHIA, it presented similar 
performances, even resulting in a lower Character Error Rate when the percentage 
of masked characters is 40 and 50%, with a difference of 4.4 and 3.3 points, 
respectively.

150 A. Locaputo et al.
5 Discussion 
After examining the main AI methods for the restoration of ancient inscriptions, it 
is possible to identify several critical factors that affect all the models equally. 
Firstly, one of the primary factors inﬂuencing the quality of the model is the data, 
as it serves as the main source of learning for the models. Given the limited number 
of artifacts that have survived to the present day, especially for dead languages, 
there is no way to increase the dataset size except for the occasional new discoveries 
made each year, which are valuable from a historical point of view, but negligible 
for training purposes. The only way to overcome this limitation is through data 
augmentation, which can be a nontrivial task since it requires a deep understanding 
of the language. Alternatively, transformers have demonstrated the effectiveness of 
transfer learning by relying on models pre-trained on a larger corpus of a language 
similar to the one desired, thus leveraging previous linguistic knowledge. 
Another problem related to the data is the quality or lack thereof. In fact, the 
quality of the data plays a pivotal role in the model’s predictive accuracy. Often, the 
digitization of an inscription can introduce some noise, especially when it involves 
OCR systems. Moreover, epigraphic texts may use markup notations, such as the 
Leiden Conventions (The Oxford Handbook of Roman Epigraphy, 2015), and non-
standard archival formatting, making it difﬁcult for machines to read them. Hence, 
again, it is vital to make use of domain experts to clean this data. Another source of 
added noise in the data is a result of the poor condition of the inscriptions. When 
the dataset is very small, every element, including severely damaged inscriptions, 
is considered. Therefore, the emendations made by epigraphers who have studied 
these inscriptions over the years are often treated as the ground truth, considering 
the possible newly introduced errors to the strenuousness of the errors that naturally 
may occur in the inscriptions. 
The other important problem is an issue that naturally arises from deep learning: 
explainability. Deep neural networks consist of a large number of interconnections 
between neurons, making it very challenging to understand the reasoning behind 
their predictions. As a result, these large models are often treated as black boxes. In 
the context of inscription restoration, having an assistive tool that does not provide 
any justiﬁcation can be problematic, especially because the restoration process 
needs to be thoroughly documented. 
Furthermore, providing epigraphers with only a list of predictions and no 
additional information would necessitate them to invest time carefully considering 
each suggestion, potentially diverting their focus from their primary objective. 
The Ithaca model has taken steps toward explainability by offering not only 
temporal and spatial attribution to better contextualize inscriptions but also a 
saliency map for the top prediction. Since Ithaca utilizes an attention mechanism, 
it can readily generate a heat map indicating which characters contributed most to 
each character’s prediction according to the model. 
On the other hand, the recent surge of Large Language Models, and particularly 
Multimodal Large Language Models (Yin et al., 2023), offers a potential avenue for

AI for the Restoration of Inscriptions 151
evolution by bridging textual information with visual data. This has the potential 
to improve prediction accuracy and provide new methods for better explaining the 
model’s reasoning. However, it would necessitate an additional effort to scan the 
inscriptions properly, at a resolution that permits such applications. 
6 Conclusions 
In this chapter, we have emphasized the pivotal role that inscriptions play in our 
comprehension of ancient societies. We discussed the ongoing efforts to preserve 
these invaluable artifacts and the initiatives aimed at enhancing their accessibility. 
Furthermore, we have formally deﬁned the epigraphic problem of restoration 
as a classical Natural Language Processing task. We then proceeded to provide 
an overview of the most signiﬁcant applications of Artiﬁcial Intelligence for this 
task. Beginning with simpler and less resource-intensive methods, such as statis-
tical approaches, we explored the evolution of the ﬁeld toward more demanding 
solutions, such as transformer models. These advanced models have demonstrated 
their ability to achieve state-of-the-art results across various NLP tasks, including 
inscription restoration. 
From this analysis, the importance of both the quantity and quality of data 
becomes evident. While there may be limited room for improvement in terms of data 
quantity, the quality of data crucially depends on the intervention of epigraphists. 
Additionally, it underscores one of the primary issues still affecting the ﬁeld of deep 
neural networks: the problem of explainability. 
In summary, this chapter highlights the importance of a collaboration between 
AI researchers and epigraphy scholars. As we explore inscription restoration and its 
intersection with advanced technologies, it becomes evident that these two domains 
have a mutually beneﬁcial relationship. 
This collaboration extends beyond academia to impact museums, archives, 
and cultural heritage institutions worldwide. Together, they advance research and 
enhance our understanding of history, culture, and civilization.

Part III 
How Data, Digitization and Reproduction 
Can Open Up New Realities in Visual 
Historical Heritage

Bridging the Gap: Decoding Abstract 
Concepts in Cultural Heritage Images 
Delﬁna Sol Martinez Pandiani 
1 Introduction 
The proliferation of images in modern mass media has reached unprecedented 
levels, with social media platforms alone hosting billions of images every day and 
cultural heritage (CH) institutions undergoing an unprecedented digitalization of 
their image collections (Bevan, 2015). This has resulted in a visually abundant 
contemporary culture where individuals are bombarded with heterogeneous visual 
data, and users are overwhelmed by an abundance of information that is not curated 
(Jansson & Hracs, 2018), making it increasingly important to become “lookers” in 
addition to being readers (Smits, 2022). The sheer volume of images in contempo-
rary culture makes manual indexing impractical. As such, automatic solutions for 
bridging the gap between raw visual data and meaningful interpretation, ensuring 
that users can navigate and comprehend the vast sea of images, are becoming 
increasingly important. 
CH institutions in particular are harnessing digital technologies to grant 
widespread access to and documentation of their visual collections, including 
via the association of linguistic tags to the visual content—such as depicted objects. 
However, visual forms like paintings and photographs not only provide links to 
depicted objects, through raw features like lines, colors, shapes, and sizes, but also 
convey additional layers of meaning, what Barthes called connotation , which is 
constructed from culturally coded elements (Barthes, 1980). In this sense, abstract 
concepts (ACs), such as comfort , power ,o r freedom, are powerful tools for the 
classiﬁcation and management of visual data, as they underpin humans’ expression 
of emotions, opinions, and ideas through language (Kousta et al., 2011a). For 
instance, examining Gentileschi’s Judith Beheading Holofernes (ca. 1611) might

lead a human observer to associate tags referring to depicted concrete objects, such 
as sword, yet grasping the painting’s essence usually involves perceiving an AC, 
such as violence (Fig. 1b). The indexing power of ACs is particularly recognized 
in the CH ﬁeld, where controlled thesauri and classiﬁcation systems include ACs 
to categorize visual materials (Rafferty & Hidderley, 2017). Shared vocabularies 
and ontologies, such as Iconclass, 1 Library of Congress, 2 and the Getty’s Art and 
Architecture Thesaurus, 3 offer pre-established ACs for association with visual 
content. 
While there exists a signiﬁcant interest in automating high-level visual under-
standing to enable automatic classiﬁcation of visual data based on ACs, this 
endeavor is fraught with technical and socio-cultural challenges. ACs, by their very 
nature, lack distinct, concrete referents and are instead especially subjective and 
evoked by a multitude of diverse scenarios (Davis & Yee, 2021). Such intricacies 
stand in contrast to the primary emphasis of the computer vision ﬁeld, which has 
traditionally concentrated on more objective and concrete categories. 
The intricacies in classifying visual data based on ACs set the stage for 
this chapter’s main goal: exploring the technical and socio-cultural landscape of 
automated decoding of CH visual data using the lens of ACs. This work offers a 
comprehensive overview of CV-based methods and specialized techniques for the 
automatic classiﬁcation of cultural images based on ACs. With a strong emphasis 
on interpretability alongside performance, this chapter strives to deliver a cohesive 
presentation and interpretation of these techniques. The investigation follows four 
key areas: 
1. Deep Learning for Abstract Concept Image Classiﬁcation : The effectiveness 
of conventional deep learning models in handling abstract concepts in image data 
is reviewed. 
2. Cognitive Intermediaries for Visual Data : The potential for visual data 
concrete descriptors to bridge the gap between raw pixels and abstract concepts 
is discussed. 
3. Cultural Bias in Visual Data Descriptors : An analysis of the role of visual 
data descriptors in subjective and cultural bias, along with proposed methods for 
addressing bias, is presented. 
4. Enhancing AC Image Classiﬁcation with Cognitive-Inspired Features :T h e 
fusion of sensory-perceptual semantics and cognitive-based information to 
improve abstract concept image classiﬁcation and interpretability is examined. 
The chapter’s structure aligns with this investigation. Section 2 situates the 
research within related work, while Sect. 3 addresses various facets of the chal-
lenges in abstract concept-based image classiﬁcation, covering subjectivity, scarcity, 
entropy, and ethics. Sections 4, 5, 6, and 7 delve into experimental results and case

2 Related Work 
2.1 Deﬁning Abstract Concepts 
By deﬁnition, ACs lack distinct, concrete referents and are triggered by diverse 
scenarios (Borghi & Binkofski, 2014), establishing a parasitic relationship between 
sensory-perceptual experiences and distributional linguistic data (Davis & Yee, 
2021). In the cognitive science ﬁeld, the term “abstract concepts” (Borghi et al., 
2018; Harpaintner et al., 2018; Villani et al., 2019; Yee, 2019) is used for concepts 
that do not possess a single and perceptually bounded object as referent and which 
have more variable content both within and across individuals than concrete con-
cepts (Barsalou, 2003; Borghi & Binkofski, 2014). The mechanisms that underlie 
the formation and use of ACs in human cognition are the object of study of the 
“Words As social Tools” (W AT) cognitive theory (Borghi & Binkofski, 2014), which 
sees words as tools to perform action modifying the state of our social environment. 
In this sense, ACs are seen as tools that change the state of humans’ inner processes, 
helping us formulate predictions and facilitating perception, categorization, and 
thought (Borghi & Binkofski, 2014). Advances in neuro-psychology posit that, 
as opposed to concrete concepts, ACs rely on semantic rather than categorical 
similarity relations (Crutch et al., 2006, 2009), on associative relations (Duñabeitia 
et al., 2009), on the social, event, and introspective aspects of situations (Barsalou & 
Wiemer-Hastings, 2005), and on evoked emotions (Kousta et al., 2011b; Vigliocco 
et al., 2013). 
As intended in this work, ACs are ontologically social objects (Gangemi & 
Mika, 2003) that refer to “cognitive objects with a social capital” (Giorgis & 
Gangemi, 2022), i.e., cognitive clusters of prototypical situations which often 
involve social interactions and societal dynamics. I adhere to Masolo et al.’s 
(2004) characterization of social concepts as immaterial constructs formed within 
a community, whose conventional constitution relies on intricate networks of 
interactions among social agents. These are concepts that depend on agents who, 
through established conventions, not only create, employ, and discuss them but also 
accept their signiﬁcance. In the context of this article, ACs include emotions (e.g., 
sadness), as well as abstract social, cultural, economic, and political values (e.g., 
freedom and leadership) and ideologies (e.g., racism and consumerism).

Bridging the Gap 161
2.2 Automating High-Level Visual Understanding 
The inception of Computer Vision (CV) aimed to achieve complete image under-
standing, encompassing the semantic interpretation of input images. While signif-
icant strides have been made in this ﬁeld, with remarkable achievements in image 
classiﬁcation, object detection, and image generation (Bagi et al., 2020), the explicit 
detection of ACs within visual data remains relatively underexplored. This gap 
may stem from the historical emphasis in computer vision on image segmentation, 
primarily targeting the detection of tangible (concrete) objects relying on discernible 
low-level features. In contrast, ACs inherently lack distinct physical attributes such 
as well-deﬁned form, color, and texture (Borghi & Binkofski, 2014). 
Expanding beyond abstract concept image classiﬁcation to broader realms of 
automatic high-level visual understanding, a comprehensive analysis of CV tasks 
related to high-level semantic units has unveiled four distinct clusters of related 
work within the CV research landscape:
 Situational Analysis : This cluster encompasses tasks related to common sense 
semantics, such as abstract reasoning, which handles logical global seman-
tic tasks, situation recognition, focusing on image summarization, and event 
recognition, including social and cultural events (e.g., Stabinger and Rodriguez-
Sanchez, 2017; Yatskar et al., 2016).
 Visual Sentiment Analysis : Aligned with emotional semantics, this cluster 
explores how images evoke emotions, covering emotion detection in natural 
images, group emotion analysis, and extending to other visual media like art 
images and memes (e.g., Ortis et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2021; Veltmeijer et al., 
2021; Cetinic et al., 2019; Achlioptas et al., 2021; Sharma et al., 2020).
 Aesthetic Analysis : This cluster focuses on detecting or predicting aesthetic 
value in various image types, including natural scenes, human faces, and entire 
images (e.g., Workman et al., 2017; Gray et al., 2010; Datta et al., 2006).
 Social Signal Processing : This cluster of CV tasks aims to sense and understand 
human social signals, including emotion, attitude, personality, and more. It 
involves tasks like detecting persuasive intent, deception, social relationships, 
and aspects of group images (e.g., Joo et al., 2014; Bruer et al., 2020; Zanette, 
2016; Li et al., 2020; Chu et al., 2015; Hung and Gatica-Perez, 2010; Kantharaju 
et al., 2020; Solera et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2018; Varghese and Thampi, 2018; 
Vanneste et al., 2021; Safra et al., 2020).
 Visual Rhetorical Analysis : This cluster relates to inductive interpretative 
semantics and explores visual persuasion and rhetorical techniques to understand 
the intrinsic meaning or purpose of images. It includes sub-clusters like visual 
persuasion, which assesses how images portray politicians (e.g., Hussain et al., 
2017a; Joo et al., 2014).

162 D. S. Martinez Pandiani
3 Challenges in AC-Based Image Classiﬁcation 
ACs wield the power to navigate visual data by connecting visual forms to cultural 
meanings, activating diverse scenes and situations (Borghi & Binkofski, 2014). 
However, this power introduces a challenge in reconciling disparities within their 
visual representation. ACs typically function schematically, specifying multiple 
semantic relations among entities (Fiske & Taylor, 1991), accommodating various 
entities and contributing to higher level scene and situation semantics. The intrinsic 
diversity and variability in visual cues evoking ACs pose signiﬁcant hurdles for 
conventional CV approaches. The intricate challenge AC image classiﬁcation is 
compounded by various factors. 
3.1 Subjectivity: Bridging Semantic and Cultural Gaps 
Computer Vision has to deal with the general challenge of the semantic gap (Smeul-
ders et al., 2000), as articulated by Smeulders: “the lack of coincidence between the 
information one can extract from the visual data and the interpretations that the 
same data has for a user in a given situation” (Smeulders et al., 2000, p. 1352). This 
challenge becomes particularly pronounced in the context of ACs, where the lack 
of distinct physical features and the reliance on generalized attributes exacerbate it. 
The absence of tangible characteristics closely associated with ACs ampliﬁes the 
gap between visual data and the connotations they hold, making it challenging to 
bridge the semantic divide effectively. Additionally, the challenge of establishing 
accurate ground truths is heightened for ACs by variable perceptions and cultural 
contexts among viewers, leading to unpredictable ground truth data affected by 
subjective interpretations and cultural diversity. Viewer-speciﬁc backgrounds and 
experiences result in distinct understandings of images, impeding the development 
of universally applicable ground truths for machine learning training. For example, 
emotions showcase pronounced inconsistency in ground truth generation, as a 
solitary image can evoke disparate reactions contingent on cultural inﬂuences, 
personal traits, and social circumstances (Zhao et al., 2018). The notion of the 
cultural gap in image understanding is introduced by van Noord et al. ( 2022), 
underscoring the variable nature of the semantic gap across images and extending 
it to encompass temporal and social dimensions. This perspective highlights the 
shifting meanings of images over time and across diverse social and cultural groups. 
The cultural gap signiﬁes the misalignment between extracted visual data and the 
interpretations made by cultural groups, with its prominence particularly evident 
in polysemic or partially described semantic images. For instance, the iconic 1989 
photograph Tank Man offers diverse cultural high-level interpretations: On the one 
hand, the most common reading as an evocation of the AC of protest, and on the 
other hand, Chinese ofﬁcials’ reading as an evocation of a different AC, military 
restraint, underscoring the range of understandings that can arise (van Noord et al., 
2022,p .3 ) .

Bridging the Gap 163
3.2 Scarcity: Ground Truths, Baselines, and Shared Methods 
The Computer Vision community has only recently “made ﬁrst attempts in tackling 
content which requires subjective judgment or abstract analysis” (Hussain et al., 
2017b). As such, the CV community has taken its ﬁrst steps in tackling AC image 
classiﬁcation. However, despite these recent efforts, progress remains notably con-
strained due to the scarcity of AC ground truths in publicly available image datasets. 
This scarcity is compounded by class imbalances in widely used image datasets 
like ImageNet and Google Open Images, which predominantly emphasize tangible 
object classes, leaving abstract social concepts underrepresented. Consequently, the 
skewed class distribution poses a formidable obstacle in effectively training models 
to accurately recognize and categorize abstract concepts, further exacerbated by the 
absence of well-deﬁned abstract ground truth annotations (Abgaz et al., 2021; Ahres 
& V olk, 2016). Additionally, the scarcity not only limits the amount of existing 
research and shared methodologies but also results in the absence of an explicit 
task deﬁnition and baseline benchmarks. In light of these challenges, addressing the 
scarcity of ground truths, class imbalances, and the associated limitations in shared 
methods and communication becomes essential to advance the task of AC image 
classiﬁcation with clear and shared terminology. 
3.3 Entropy: Going Beyond the Surface 
Abstract words are associated with higher dispersion ratings, resulting in a broader 
range of images returned from a query (Kiela & Bottou, 2014; Lazaridou et al., 
2015). This diversity in visual signals challenges the development of algorithms 
that can consistently recognize ACs from solely visual data. The wide variability in 
visual representation adds complexity to the training process and requires strategies 
to capture the essence of these concepts effectively. While strides have been taken 
toward achieving comprehensive image comprehension in computer vision, with 
impressive performance in tasks such as image classiﬁcation, object detection, and 
image generation (Bagi et al., 2020), this progression aligns with the focus on low-
level features for tasks focused on perceptually bounded ground truths. Speciﬁcally, 
CV has had a strong focus on Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) (LeCun et al., 
2015) and other methods that target images’ low-level features, which have largely 
banked on the decontextualized nature of visual signals. However, the ﬁeld’s focus 
on CNNs and their reliance on decontextualized visual signals becomes problematic 
for high-level visual understanding tasks, because CNNs are tailored for high intra-
class similarity situations (Benz et al., 2020; Shirali & Hardt, 2023). CNNs’ inherent 
optimization for tasks featuring high intra-class similarity poses a conﬂict, as CNNs’ 
capabilities do not align with the inherent diversity and nuanced cultural nature of 
abstract concepts, which by deﬁnition lack distinctive bounded perceptual features

164 D. S. Martinez Pandiani
(see Fig. 1a and b). As such, the inherent limitation of CNNs is a condition that 
contradicts the nature of cultural dependent tasks, including abstract concept-based 
image classiﬁcation. 
3.4 Ethics: Stabilizing Unstable Meanings 
The utilization of deep learning models prompts questions about the knowledge 
absorbed and echoed by them. The inherent cultural variance in abstract concept 
evocation not only adds complexity but also introduces ethical considerations 
regarding whose perspectives and values are being ampliﬁed by its automation. 
Cultural bias introduced and echoed through labels in CV pipelines in general 
raises a signiﬁcant ethical concern. To tackle this issue, novel frameworks have 
emerged aiming to explicitly represent the underlying knowledge assumptions 
within datasets and deployed AI systems (Gebru et al., 2021; Mitchell et al., 
2019). This concern becomes even more pronounced when dealing with culturally 
biased labels applied to images of human beings (Buolamwini & Gebru, 2018; 
Buolamwini, 2022). The ethical issue intensiﬁes with the increased abstractness 
and subjectivity of assigned labels, because ACs are socially constructed, giving 
rise to varied meanings based on cultural and historical contexts. For instance, 
assigning labels like “homelessness,” “beauty,” or “danger” to images portraying 
individuals is inherently inﬂuenced by the context of annotation, encompassing the 
cultural perspectives of the annotator. The critical idea here is not new: Automated 
systems are not inherently neutral and instead reﬂect the priorities, preferences, and 
prejudices of those who have the power to shape artiﬁcial intelligence (Mohamed 
et al., 2020; Birhane, 2020; Aroyo & Welty, 2015). The impact of these labels can 
have far-reaching and consequential effects on individuals and communities, and we 
cannot reduce them to simple technical problems to solve. That is, the consequences 
of these labels extend far beyond technical matters, affecting individuals and com-
munities profoundly (Ciston, 2023). Decontextualized labels used as training data 
easily get echoed through the development of automatic detection and classiﬁcation 
systems. The consequences of reusing AC image detection or classiﬁcation models 
without comprehending how they reached their conclusions can lead to harmful 
effects, including prejudice and racism. 
4 Deep Learning for Abstract Concept Image Classiﬁcation 
Based on the discussed challenges and related work, a nuanced and comprehensive 
investigation into the suitability of conventional deep learning models for the 
complex task of AC image classiﬁcation becomes imperative. This section primarily 
probes the capabilities of traditional deep learning models, designed for processing 
raw pixel values, in addressing the intricacies of image classiﬁcation rooted in

Bridging the Gap 165
abstract concepts. The structure of this section revolves around three key aspects 
for evaluating the model’s efﬁcacy in handling such classiﬁcation: representation, 
accuracy, and explainability. 
4.1 Deep Representations 
Idea The capability of off-the-shelf deep learning (DL) models to encode and 
represent intricate features related to abstract concepts within images was assessed. 
“Intra-class similarity” served as a measure to evaluate the extent to which image 
representations within the same target class exhibited shared features. Speciﬁcally, 
the fundamental question addressed was: To what extent can conventional DL 
representations effectively capture intra-class similarity among images labeled with 
ACs, in contrast to those associated with concrete concepts? The working hypothesis 
proposed that the deep representations of images linked to ACs would display 
lower levels of intra-class similarity compared to their counterparts associated 
with concrete concepts. This hypothesis was grounded in the inherent ﬂexibility 
of ACs and the resulting diversity of images evoking them, making intra-class 
similarity inherently more challenging to capture within the traditional deep learning 
framework.4 
Approach A VGG-16 convolutional neural network (CNN), pre-trained on Ima-
geNet, was used to compute feature vectors for each image within each of the 
seven target classes of the ARTstract dataset (Martinez Pandiani et al., 2023). 
Cosine similarity was used to quantify the similarity between each image and every 
other image in the same target class. To assess the signiﬁcance of the ﬁndings, the 
same steps were completed on the computer vision benchmark dataset, CIFAR10, 
consisting of ten concrete target classes. The CIFAR-10 dataset consists of 60000 
32x32 color images in ten classes, with 6000 images per class (Krizhevsky et 
al., 2009). Despite the dissimilarity in target classes, the perceptual content of 
ARTstract images resembles that of CIFAR10. Finally, a two-sample t-test was 
used to determine whether the differences in intra-class similarity for classes 
depending on the dataset hold statistical signiﬁcance. The resulting p-value allows 
the discernment of whether these distinctions are likely due to random chance or 
represent meaningful disparities. 
Results Results show that ARTstract exhibits signiﬁcantly lower intra-class simi-
larity than CIFAR10. On average, CIFAR10 classes attain 0.644 similarity, while 
ARTstract classes achieve close to half of that value, 0.344. Figure 2as h o w s 
intra-class similarity values for ARTstract and CIFAR10 classes. The two-sample 
t-test resulted in a basically negligible p-value (rounded to 0.00000) (see Fig. 2b), 
indicating statistical signiﬁcance.
4 This work has been recently published in detail in (Martinez Pandiani et al., 2023).

4.2 Deep Performance in Abstract Concept Classiﬁcation 
Idea Building upon the exploration of deep representations in the previous section, 
the performance of state-of-the-art deep learning models, including Convolutional 
Neural Networks (CNNs) and the Vision Transformer (ViT), for abstract concept-

Bridging the Gap 167
based image classiﬁcation was assessed. The goal was to determine how effectively 
these models could adapt to this specialized task in comparison to their perfor-
mance in conventional image classiﬁcation assignments. The hypothesis was that 
traditional deep learning models achieved lower accuracy in abstract concept-
based image classiﬁcation when contrasted with their performance in standard 
image classiﬁcation tasks. This expectation arose from the recognition that abstract 
concepts presented unique challenges, necessitating models to discern more subtle 
visual cues than those that might be shared by images tagged with the same concrete 
concept. 
Approach State-of-the-art deep learning models for image classiﬁcation were 
adopted, speciﬁcally, two Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), VGG-16 and 
ResNet-50, were leveraged. These networks had previously been pre-trained on the 
extensive ImageNet-21k dataset, which endowed them with a strong foundation in 
feature extraction. The approach was centered on transfer learning and ﬁne-tuning. 
Both models were ﬁne-tuned in two distinct manners: ﬁrstly, in the “head-only” 
fashion, where the classiﬁcation layer was adjusted while keeping the remaining 
layers immutable and subjecting them to a deﬁned number of epochs, and secondly, 
the “whole model” was ﬁne-tuned, involving the ﬁne-tuning of all layers. A suite of 
evaluation metrics, including accuracy, precision, recall, and the F1-score, derived 
from the ILSVRC multi-class formulation, was employed to comprehensively assess 
model performance. Additionally, for context, the same procedures were applied to 
the CIFAR-10 dataset, a standard image classiﬁcation benchmark. This allowed for 
a comparison of the models’ performance in abstract concept image classiﬁcation 
against a more conventional image classiﬁcation task. 
Results In the context of AC image classiﬁcation using the ARTstract dataset, 
challenges were evident for the CNN models in achieving high accuracy, with the 
top-performing model, head-only ﬁne-tuned ResNet-50, achieving approximately 
45% accuracy (refer to Table 1). This highlights the signiﬁcance of minimizing 
extensive ﬁne-tuning of the entire model, as it signiﬁcantly compromised pro-
ﬁciency in AC image classiﬁcation, emphasizing the importance of preserving 
features acquired during pre-training. As anticipated, substantial performance dis-
parities were observed when comparing the CIFAR-10 and ARTstract datasets. 
Notably, the models exhibited remarkable accuracy on CIFAR-10 (see Table 2). 
Both models encountered notably greater challenges in image classiﬁcation on 
ARTstract in comparison to CIFAR-10. This disparity underscores the unique com-
plexities associated with abstract concept-based image classiﬁcation, particularly 
for traditional deep learning models. 
4.3 Deep Explainability for AC Image Classiﬁcation 
Idea DL model explainability within the context of abstract concept-based image 
classiﬁcation was examined. The objective was to scrutinize the extent to which

DL models operate as black boxes when engaged in AC image classiﬁcation tasks. 
Additionally, valuable insights that could be gleaned through the application of 
explainability techniques were unveiled. The hypothesis underlying this investiga-
tion was rooted in the belief that traditional explainability techniques might struggle 
to provide interpretable explanations for CNN model predictions in AC image 
classiﬁcation. This challenge primarily arose because these techniques typically 
assumed the presence of concrete, bounding box evidence for target classes. 
Approach The classiﬁcation process was subjected to an in-depth analysis, with 
a particular focus on a VGG-16 model ﬁne-tuned for 1000 epochs. Confusion 
matrices were examined to identify challenging classes. The utilization of Grad-
CAM++ allowed for the generation of Class Activation Map (CAM) saliency maps, 
facilitating the pinpointing of inﬂuential regions within images. The exploration 
extended to the perceptual topology of the model, where Activation Maximization 
(AM) images were generated and optimized for each neuron responsible for a spe-
ciﬁc AC class. Additionally, a novel denoising method, SD-AM (Stable Diffusion 
Denoising of Activation Maximization), was introduced to render AM images more 
human-readable, thereby creating “hypericons” representing prototypical features 
related to abstract concepts. Qualitative analyses of the results were performed to 
draw meaningful insights. 
Results Grad-CAM did provide some insights into the relationship between spe-
ciﬁc perceptual semantics (e.g., depicted objects like swords or ﬂags) and abstract 
concepts (e.g., freedom) (see Fig. 3a). However, traditional feature visualization 
methods failed to yield human-readable results. The novel denoising approach, SD-
AM, incorporating stable diffusion, produced feature visualizations (“hypericons”) 
that closely resembled real instances from the dataset (see Fig. 4). This not only 
enhanced interpretability but also showcased the convergence of modern hyperpop 
aesthetics with SD-AM hypericons. This visual convergence prompted contempla-
tion on the parallels between the rapid pace of modern media consumption and the 
vast data ﬂow into deep learning models (see Fig. 5).

4.4 Discussion: DL for Abstract Concept Image Classiﬁcation 
Deep Representation and Intra-class Similarity The results indicate that there 
are differences in intra-class similarity between ARTstract and CIFAR-10 classes, 
which are highly unlikely to occur by random chance alone. The results shed light on 
the dependence of intra-class similarity in image representations on the concreteness 
or abstractness of the target class. The CNN-based model effectively captures shared 
features among images within concrete label target classes, resulting in higher intra-
class similarity. Conversely, images associated with the same abstract concepts 
exhibit lower similarity, signifying fewer shared features. The remarkably low p-
value underscores the signiﬁcance of these ﬁndings. This suggests that the model’s 
spatial resolution struggles to capture semantic nuances, leading the ConvNet 
to perceive all ARTstract images as similar, regardless of their speciﬁc abstract 
concept. These results underscore the inherent challenges of representing abstract 
concepts within traditional deep learning models. The lower average intra-class 
similarity in ARTstract highlights the difﬁculties posed by class variance and spatial

resolution limitations when compared to concrete classes. Further exploration and 
analysis of these distinctions may yield valuable insights into deep learning models’ 
ability to capture both abstract and concrete semantic information. 
The Performance of Deep AC Image Classiﬁcation The formidable challenge 
posed by abstract concept-based image classiﬁcation for traditional CNN models 
is exposed by the results. CNN’s proﬁciency in standard image classiﬁcation tasks 
does not seamlessly extend to the AC classiﬁcation context. Limitations in accuracy, 
precision, recall, and F1-score are observed, highlighting the intricate and high 
intra-class variability inherent in abstract concepts. Conventional models, designed 
for well-deﬁned objects and patterns, encounter difﬁculties with the nuanced and 
often elusive visual representations of abstract ideas. The performance contrast 
between CIFAR-10 and ARTstract, as demonstrated by the comparative analysis, 
further emphasizes these challenges. While concrete concepts in CIFAR-10 are 
well handled by traditional models, their performance signiﬁcantly deteriorates 
when confronted with the intricacies of ARTstract, resulting in a substantial drop 
in accuracy. This sharp disparity underscores the inadequacy of conventional deep 
learning models for the intricate task of AC image classiﬁcation. To address the 
challenges presented by abstract visual content effectively, future research should 
prioritize the development of dedicated AC image classiﬁcation models capable of 
capturing the subtleties and variations inherent in abstract concepts. 
The Explainability of Deep AC Image Classiﬁcation The exploration into deep 
learning model explainability within the realm of abstract concept-based image 
classiﬁcation has shed light on the interpretability challenges faced by conventional 
models. Our ﬁndings suggest that traditional explainability techniques, such as 
Grad-CAM, offer limited insights into the complex relationship between perceptual

5 Cognitive Intermediaries for Visual Data 
Results from Sect. 4 have yielded valuable insights into the relationship between 
speciﬁc perceptual semantics, such as depicted objects like swords or ﬂags, and 
abstract concepts like freedom. These ﬁndings strongly suggest the existence of 
visual data descriptors, potentially at the level of concrete depicted objects, that 
hold the promise of bridging the gap between raw pixel information and abstract 
concepts. Within this section, two ideas are explored. The ﬁrst revolves around the 
translatability of the cognitive concept of acquired embodiment into a computational 
method, with the aim of identifying concrete semantics that hold signiﬁcance for 
abstract concept representation. The second delves into the possibility of automating 
the reasoning process over the concrete semantics of visual data to evoke high-level 
concepts in an interpretable manner. 
5.1 Automating Acquired Embodiment 
Idea This research endeavors to investigate the feasibility of translating the 
cognitive concept of acquired embodiment into a computational method capable of 
identifying concrete semantics that hold signiﬁcance in the representation of abstract 
concepts. The core hypothesis posits that it is indeed possible to pinpoint concrete, 
sensory-perceptual features that provide visual grounding for abstract concepts by 
discerning patterns of co-occurrence involving dominant colors, depicted concrete 
objects, and depicted actions in images tagged with speciﬁc abstract concepts. 
Approach The research methodology was structured through several key stages. 
First, the data source selection involved identifying the Tate Gallery Collection 
metadata, a core dataset comprising a substantial archive of 70,000 artworks. Next, 
a list of 166 speciﬁc abstract concepts was meticulously crafted, drawing from 
the Tate’s comprehensive taxonomy. Subsequently, curated image datasets were 
assembled, each bearing tags associated with a chosen abstract concept. In terms 
of sensory-perceptual data extraction, sensory-perceptual features, encompassing

Bridging the Gap 173
concrete objects, actions, and colors, were systematically extracted from images 
that bore tags linked to abstract concepts. This encompassed the identiﬁcation of 
co-occurring physical object tags and a subsequent analysis of their co-occurrence 
patterns with abstract concepts. Similarly, action tags were identiﬁed, and their 
co-occurrence with abstract concepts was meticulously analyzed. Furthermore, a 
thorough examination of the dominant color characteristics was conducted for 
a select subset of images, with particular emphasis on two case study abstract 
concepts, namely “consumerism” and “horror.” 
Results Across the spectrum of 166 abstract concepts cataloged in the Tate 
taxonomy, a substantial variation emerged in the number of artworks associated 
with each concept. This variation ranged from 368 artworks tagged with the concept 
“death” to a mere 1 artwork tagged with “paranoia.” On average, there were 48 
matches for each abstract concept, with a median count of 27 matches. Likewise, 
the presence of physical object tags co-occurring with abstract concepts exhibited 
substantial diversity. The counts ranged from 288 object tags linked to “death” to 
just six object tags associated with “inﬁnity.” On average, each concept had 69 co-
occurring objects, with a median of 55 objects per concept. In stark contrast, the 
frequencies of co-occurring actions displayed a notable reduction, spanning from 
38 instances for “death” to zero occurrences for “void.” On average, each concept 
had 11 co-occurring actions, with a median count of eight actions per concept. 
Furthermore, the color analyses conducted on a subset of images, with a focus on 
two case study abstract concepts, “consumerism” and “horror,” unveiled distinctive 
visual characteristics. For instance, “consumerism” was characterized by brighter 
and more varied colors, while “horror” was marked by darker and less varied tones, 
as demonstrated through proportional color palettes. 
5.2 Interpretable Connections with High-Level Frames 
Idea Building upon the proof of concept that concrete features play a signiﬁcant 
role in the evocation of ACs within visual data, an intriguing avenue of exploration 
emerges. This exploration involves the automation of the reasoning process over the 
concrete semantics of visual data to unveil associations with high-level concepts. 
The hypothesis posits that by utilizing textual labels to represent image perceptual 
semantics, interpretable links between visual content and higher level conceptual 
frames can be established. This is achieved through the application of ontology-
based automatic reasoning techniques and the utilization of background common 
sense knowledge. In this context, the central question shifts to the feasibility of 
automatically extracting meaningful connections between visual data and high-level 
conceptual frameworks in a comprehensible manner. 
Approach The research involved the identiﬁcation and analysis of the data model 
of a CV ground truth dataset aligned with insights from cognitive theory, speciﬁcally 
the Visual Genome (Li et al., 2016) dataset. Next, an ontology was designed and

174 D. S. Martinez Pandiani
developed following the eXtreme Design (Blomqvist et al., 2010) methodology, 
which included competency questions formulation. The process extended to the 
extraction of frame knowledge from textual data using the Framester common sense 
knowledge graph (KG). Knowledge graph population was achieved by aligning 
the ground truth image data with the extracted frame knowledge via the ontology. 
To ensure accuracy and reliability, the approach incorporated SPARQL queries, 
unit testing, and veriﬁcation tests, with thorough documentation of test cases and 
results for validation. Finally, a case study analysis was conducted, involving a close 
viewing evaluation of case study images and frames. 
Results Visual Genome, a renowned computer vision dataset distinguished by its 
graph structure and relational focus, was chosen for frame knowledge enrichment. 
Among the dataset’s top 76 images in terms of activity richness, 17,566 frame 
evocations were derived. These frames include 163 emotions, 1,410 folk values, 
438 559 cultural values, 751 moral values, and 14,804 FrameNet frames. Leveraging 
this data, the Visual Sense Knowledge Graph (VSKG) was automatically populated, 
incorporating information from Visual Genome, frame evocations, and the Visual 
Sense Ontology. In VSKG, images are represented as information objects, and 
their information realizations are denoted as ImageBoxes, utilizing Framester-based 
URIs to signify conceptual frames. VSKG comprises comprehensive knowledge 
about images, depicted objects, relationships, attributes, pixel-based locations, 
evoked WordNet synsets, and Conceptual Frames. 
5.3 Discussion on Cognitive Intermediaries for Visual Data 
Automating Acquired Embodiment Empirical evidence is provided by our 
study,5 supporting the feasibility of employing computational techniques for 
capturing symbol grounding and acquired embodiment. Speciﬁcally, the capacity 
to identify common sense perceptual features that co-occur with abstract concepts, 
as exempliﬁed within the domain of art images, is demonstrated. Discernible 
regularities are revealed by our ﬁndings, such as the frequent co-occurrence of 
“consumerism” with concepts like “clothing,” “food and drink,” and “product 
packaging,” and the association of “horror” with terms like “monster,” “recoiling,” 
and “screaming.” It is crucial to note, however, that the frequencies of such co-
occurrences remain relatively low. This highlights the need for more extensive 
research to delve deeper into the substantial impact of speciﬁc objects and 
actions on the evocation of abstract concepts, allowing for a richer understanding 
of the underlying cognitive processes. Furthermore, valuable insights into the 
chromatic attributes of art images within the Tate collection, each linked to distinct 
abstract concepts, are offered by our color analysis, vividly illustrated through the

6 Cultural Bias in Visual Data Descriptors 
While the research conducted thus far has highlighted the remarkable power of 
visual descriptors, a degree of caution is warranted in their application. This section 
delves into an analysis of the role played by visual data descriptors in perpetuating 
subjective and cultural bias. Additionally, it introduces proposed methods for 
mitigating and addressing these biases effectively. 
Idea Exploring the potential for the introduction of subjective and cultural bias 
through the assignment of visual data descriptors and investigating strategies for 
their effective representation and rectiﬁcation is the central theme of this section. 
The hypothesis postulated that the general practice of data labeling serves as 
an entry point for subjectivity and cultural bias within AI system training. To 
address this challenge, an ontological approach is pursued, wherein ground truths 
are contextualized within their annotation contexts. This approach is anticipated 
to yield structured, machine-readable knowledge capable of mitigating subjectivity 
and cultural bias in AI systems by considering contextual annotation factors. 
Approach The approach involved a comprehensive investigation into potential 
subjective and cultural biases within visual data descriptors. This was accomplished 
through a multifaceted analysis that included an in-depth examination of the 
Visual Genome (Li et al., 2016) dataset, renowned as a gold standard in com-
puter vision datasets, characterized by extensive annotations encompassing object 
labels, attributes, object relationships, and scene descriptions. These annotations 
were performed by human annotators through crowdsourcing and their thorough 
examination allowed for the exploration of biases in image understanding and scene 
interpretation. Additionally, key situational factors that could introduce biases, such 
as the timing, location, and purpose of annotation, as well as the demographic 
characteristics of annotators, were investigated. To formalize this analysis, the Situ-
Annotate ontology was designed, utilizing the eXtreme Design methodology and 
incorporating competency questions (CQs) tailored to capture nuanced annotation 
contexts. Within this ontology, the Image Annotation Situations (IAS) module 
was introduced, specializing in tracing image-label meanings within culturally 
coded contexts. To evaluate the performance of the SituAnnotate ontology while 
capturing diverse contextual information, a comprehensive test dataset was created 
using the IAS module. Moreover, specialized CQs were formulated, translated 
into SPARQL queries, and executed to assess the capabilities of SituAnnotate. 
Finally, an automatic method was developed for translating SPARQL query outputs 
into understandable narratives, enhancing transparency by elucidating annotation 
contexts.
