6.1 Discussion Cultural Bias in Visual Data Descriptors 
The biases uncovered in the Visual Genome dataset underscore the need to consider 
cultural and subjective factors, even within benchmark datasets, to prevent potential 
misinterpretations when reusing data. These biases highlight the challenges of 
achieving complete objectivity in data annotations and emphasize the inﬂuence 
of cultural perspectives on image labeling (see Fig. 9). SituAnnotate emerges as 
a robust and superior alternative to traditional annotation methods, signiﬁcantly 
enhancing the precision and depth of annotations. Its ﬂexible architecture accommo-
dates diverse annotator types, from humans to automated systems, ensuring privacy 
protection and aligning with modern annotation practices. Automated reasoning 
through SPARQL queries streamlines annotation understanding, providing nuanced 
insights into annotation situations. SituAnnotate’s user-friendly interface and scripts 
bridge the gap between technology and human cognition, promoting transparency 
and comprehension, crucial in contemporary AI development. By contextualizing 
annotations within their broader context, it effectively mitigates bias and fosters eth-
ical AI development, meeting the growing demand for transparent, responsible, and 
bias-aware AI systems. The practical demonstration highlights SituAnnotate’s value

180 D. S. Martinez Pandiani
in providing insightful and human-understandable explanations of annotations, 
enhancing contextual understanding and elevating the quality of AI development 
practices. 
7 Enhancing AC Image Classiﬁcation with 
Cognitive-Inspired Features 
The results from Sect. 4 highlight the proﬁciency of deep learning models in cap-
turing concrete similarities within images, as evidenced by the notable performance 
disparities in image classiﬁcation between datasets such as CIFAR and ARTstract. 
Additionally, these models exhibit challenges in achieving explainability. Sections 5 
and 6, in contrast, shed light on the critical roles played by visual data descriptors 
and their assignment contexts. These ﬁndings not only underscore the potential for 
a more comprehensive understanding of the intricate relationship between pixel-
level data and the representation of abstract concepts but also suggest that visual 
data descriptors can be efﬁciently collected and situated within a broader context. 
Furthermore, they can serve as valuable components for reasoning over concrete 
semantics that may evoke speciﬁc abstract concepts. 
Consequently, a fundamental question arises: To what extent can a hybrid 
neuro-symbolic approach, blending subsymbolic deep learning (DL) with symbolic 
methods, enhance the performance and interpretability of abstract concept classiﬁ-
cation in images when compared to relying solely on raw pixel data? This inquiry 
delves into the feasibility of harnessing diverse perceptual data, including cognitive-
inspired features, to construct comprehensive common sense descriptions of abstract 
concepts based on their visual evocation. It further explores whether these features 
can effectively improve the classiﬁcation of abstract concepts in images, ultimately 
leading to enhanced performance and interpretability compared to the use of raw 
pixel data in isolation. 
7.1 Cognitive-Inspired Features for Image and AC 
Representation 
Idea The ﬁrst idea revolves around the effective integration of subsymbolic 
(deep learning) and symbolic methods to comprehensively capture the concrete 
semantics associated with abstract concepts in visual data. The hypothesis posits 
that the subsymbolic paradigm, including deep learning techniques, can be adeptly 
employed to extract various perceptual semantics such as objects, actions, art 
styles, emotions, and other visual data descriptors from images. Concurrently, 
symbolic technologies like knowledge graphs can be utilized to formally establish 
and represent meaningful connections between these extracted semantics and the

Bridging the Gap 181
images themselves. It is hypothesized that by curating an image knowledge graph 
that not only encompasses abstract concept labels but also incorporates cognitive-
based features at different levels of concreteness (e.g., objects, actions, style, and 
emotion), it becomes possible to generate data-driven, common sense descriptions 
of abstract concepts based on their visual representation. 
Approach In the proposed method and approach, the ARTstract Knowledge 
Graph (KG) was constructed using the ARTstract image dataset, and SituAnnotate 
was employed to establish connections between images and abstract concepts, 
meticulously recording the sources of image and abstract concept labels. Pre-trained 
deep learning models renowned for their proﬁciency in capturing diverse visual data 
descriptors, spanning objects, actions, art styles, emotions, and colors were identi-
ﬁed and chosen. These selected models were used to automatically extract pertinent 
visual data descriptors from each image within the ARTstract dataset. To ensure a 
formal and contextual representation, the extracted ground truths were meticulously 
embedded within the SituAnnotate ontology. The methodology also incorporated 
co-occurrence statistics, enabling the identiﬁcation of frequent and contextually 
relevant visual data descriptors closely linked to each abstract concept. Finally, 
leveraging the insights gained from co-occurrence analysis, abstract concepts were 
modeled as comprehensive frames, encompassing both perceptual semantics and 
cognitive-based features for a holistic understanding. 
Results The ARTstract KG provides comprehensive and context-aware metadata 
annotations for more than 14,000 cultural images, covering various perceptual 
semantic aspects of the images. These annotations include information about the 
original dataset source, the evocation context, automatically detected art styles, 
depicted objects, depicted actions, dominant colors, the presence of human subjects, 
age tiers, emotions, and image captions. This information was used to formalize 
human- and machine-readable representations of abstract concepts and to represent 
real data related to abstract concepts used in this study (see Fig. 11). 
7.2 Explainable Image Representations for AC Image 
Classiﬁcation 
Idea The core idea revolves around the exploration of the potential of cognitive-
inspired features in the development of enriched image representations, involving 
the extraction and seamless integration of image features that are indicative of 
abstract concept visual evocation. This exploration aims to enhance performance 
and explainability in the domain of AC image classiﬁcation. The hypothesis posits 
that cognitive-inspired perceptual semantic features can play a pivotal role naïven 
crafting image representations that are not only more meaningful but also highly 
interpretable. These enhanced image representations are envisioned to be compati-
ble with fully interpretable symbolic methods, with Bayesian networks serving as an

182 D. S. Martinez Pandiani
Fig. 11 Formalization of abstract concept clusters and their relationships with acquired embod-
iment characteristics. Top: T-box formalization. Bottom: A-box example featuring the concept 
comfort and its embodiment from objects like teddy bears and actions like hugging and sitting 
exemplary model in this context. The ultimate goal is to leverage this integration to 
signiﬁcantly improve the efﬁcacy of AC image classiﬁcation by marrying the power 
of cognitive-inspired features with the interpretability offered by symbolic methods, 
particularly Bayesian networks. Additionally, this approach emphasizes the strategic 
containment of deep learnin”s inherent black box, limiting its role to associating 
perceptual semantics with images and making these associations readily queryable. 
This strategic containment opens up possibilities for the systematic identiﬁcation of 
problematic data sources and offers avenues for addressing issues pertaining to bias 
and subjectivity in image annotation processes. 
Approach The proposed method encompasses several key steps: First, perceptual 
features are systematically extracted from images, with a speciﬁc focus on capturing 
components that reﬂect the visual representation of abstract concepts. Next, the 
relevance of each extracted perceptual feature in predicting abstract concepts is 
quantiﬁed using information theory, involving the calculation of feature entropy 
conditioned on the evoked abstract concept. These ﬁndings are then visually 
represented, both in a general context and concept-wise, through relevant graphs. To 
model the contextual dependencies among these features, a Bayesian Network (BN) 
is employed, featuring a manually designed network structure. A signiﬁcant portion

method in the realm of abstract concept image classiﬁcation, challenging the 
conventional notion that complex deep learning models are the sole solution.

7.3 Discussion on Enhancing AC Image Classiﬁcation with 
Cognitive-Inspired Features 
Cognitive-Inspired Features for Image and AC Representation The hybrid 
framework’s primary objective was the creation of a knowledge graph amenable 
to reasoning, thereby enhancing the comprehension of abstract concept visual 
evocation in images. This approach facilitated the systematic collection and uti-
lization of diverse perceptual data annotations from various sources, culminating 
in comprehensive, context-aware descriptions of abstract concept visual evocation. 
Importantly, it addressed the potential for subjective and cultural bias, treating 
annotations as contextual points rather than deﬁnitive ground truths. The pivotal

184 D. S. Martinez Pandiani
role played by the SituAnnotate ontology in situating these perceptual semantic 
annotations within the knowledge graph further enriched the framework’s capabil-
ities. This approach provided a multifaceted representation of images within the 
ARTstract KG, accommodating visual data descriptor labels with speciﬁc roles. 
This representation yielded a nuanced understanding of images, considering the 
origins and generation of these descriptors. Furthermore, it facilitated the extrac-
tion of common sense descriptions of abstract concepts from data-driven visual 
perspectives, formalizing these descriptions as multimodal frames for enhanced 
human and machine interpretability. By bridging subjectivity and visual represen-
tation, this methodology offered profound insights into the intricate relationship 
between cultural imagery and abstract concepts, contributing to the advancement 
of computational visual studies and addressing the complexities of abstract concept 
representation in cultural imagery. 
Explainable Image Representations for AC Image Classiﬁcation Our ﬁndings 
underscore the remarkable adaptability of machine learning models to meet task-
speciﬁc demands, with Naive Bayes emerging as a standout performer in abstract 
concept image classiﬁcation, particularly in achieving high F1 scores, while pre-
serving a crucial aspect—interpretability. These results challenge the conventional 
reliance on deep learning methodologies for tasks characterized by high abstraction 
and subjectivity, revealing a nuanced landscape in which deep learning shines in 
lower level image classiﬁcation tasks, whereas feature engineering and traditional 
machine learning methods excel in providing explainable decisions for higher level 
tasks. These alternative approaches yield fully interpretable systems with only 
marginal accuracy losses and potentially no F1 performance deﬁcits. 
8 Discussion and Conclusions 
In the pursuit of unraveling the intricate relationship between cultural heritage and 
digital tools, our ﬁnal discussion delves into the implications of decoding cultural 
heritage images through the lens of abstract concepts via computational methods. 
The exploration of abstract concept image classiﬁcation and the integration of 
cognitive-inspired features offer a multidisciplinary lens to foster a deeper com-
prehension of cultural imagery and creativity. In this comprehensive exploration of 
abstract concept-based image classiﬁcation, we delved into the intricate challenges 
and opportunities that deﬁne the intersection of deep learning, feature engineering, 
and interpretability. The following discussion synthesizes key insights from the 
study, shedding light on the multifaceted nature of AC image classiﬁcation and the 
imperative need for a multidisciplinary approach. 
Challenges in Abstract Concept-Based Image Classiﬁcation In our quest to 
decode cultural heritage images through digital tools, we confront the formidable 
challenges that abstract concept-based image classiﬁcation presents. While deep 
learning models excel in conventional image classiﬁcation tasks, decoding the

Bridging the Gap 185
nuanced visual representations of abstract ideas poses signiﬁcant hurdles. These 
challenges underscore the intricate nature of abstract concepts in the realm of 
cultural heritage, emphasizing the need for innovative solutions. 
The Role of Feature Engineering In the pursuit of decoding cultural heritage, 
the importance of feature engineering and traditional machine learning approaches 
emerges as important. While deep learning methods exhibit formidable capabilities 
for traditional image classiﬁcation, they often encounter performance limitations 
akin to those faced by conventional machine learning models for the task of AC 
image classiﬁcation. Critically, feature engineering techniques offer a unique advan-
tage by crafting fully interpretable systems—a pivotal element in comprehending 
and safeguarding cultural heritage through digital means. These approaches bridge 
the gap between the technical and the interpretive, enriching our ability to explore 
and preserve our cultural legacy in the digital era. 
Deep Interpretability Challenges and Innovative Approaches Interpretability 
proves to be a crucial facet of our journey to decode cultural heritage images. 
Conventional explainability techniques often fall short of revealing the intricate 
relationship between perceptual semantics and abstract concepts. However, the 
study introduces innovative approaches like the SD-AM denoising method, which 
produces human-readable “hypericons” capturing prototypical features associated 
with abstract concepts. These approaches underscore the pressing need for improved 
interpretability tools to navigate the complexities of decoding cultural heritage 
through digital analysis. 
Addressing Bias and Subjectivity The exploration into decoding cultural heritage 
images brings to the forefront the paramount importance of addressing bias and 
subjectivity. Cultural biases within benchmark datasets serve as poignant reminders 
of the impact of perspectives on image labeling. Here, tools like SituAnnotate 
emerge as ethical solutions, mitigating bias, and fostering transparency in the 
development of AI systems. This aligns seamlessly with the ethical considerations 
necessary for preserving cultural heritage through digital means. 
In summary, the insights gleaned from this study collectively emphasize the 
multifaceted nature of abstract concept-based image classiﬁcation. They underscore 
the need for a multidisciplinary approach that combines traditional machine learn-
ing, feature engineering, and innovative interpretability techniques to address the 
complexities of this task. Additionally, the study underscores the importance of 
ethical considerations, bias mitigation, and transparency in AI development, espe-
cially when dealing with cultural imagery. These insights advance our understanding 
of the intricate relationship between visual representation, abstract concepts, and 
cultural context.

Decoding Pictorial Collections Using 
Faces 
Doug Peterson and Hannah Storch 
1 Introduction 
Pictorial collections, rich in information and popular among the public, are essential 
in preserving our shared heritage. These collections serve as concrete and abstract 
content that represent not only the values of societies but also their growth, history, 
and heritage (Abgaz et al., 2021). As the scale of collections has increased, it has 
been increasingly important to have descriptive metadata with which to navigate 
these collections, and by which to understand how a cultural heritage object 
supports a given purpose (Bruce & Hillmann, 2004). Because of its core role in 
data management, metadata quality can sometimes even be associated with an 
institution’s effectiveness and value (Tani et al., 2013). Since this type of descriptive 
metadata frequently relies on the speciﬁc knowledge of individuals or subject 
matter experts, the contextual value of many of these collections and their inherent 
institutional value is often constrained by a lack of descriptive metadata, which can 
be time consuming and expensive to add manually. Many Artiﬁcial Intelligence (AI) 
technologies are emerging that can facilitate scalable metadata enrichment for such 
collections. In this chapter, we will discuss facial recognition, which promises to 
unlock the value of a collection using the key of the human face. 
Although many institutions have been delving into the possibilities of imple-
menting Machine Learning (ML), there are still several barriers to the wide-spread 
use of these technologies. Many of these AI use cases have been applied in “black 
box” conﬁgurations with relatively small data sets that are not generally publicly 
available (Fiorucci et al., 2020). Most AI models are trained using contemporary 
data sources, and they require considerable amounts of suitable data in order to

https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-57675-1_9

192 D. Peterson and H. Storch
train a given model and be adapted to historical collections (Neudecker, 2022). That 
being said, a number of organizations have begun focusing on ways to support the 
advancement and deployment of measured AI technologies in a measurable and 
meaningful way. The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) has 
created an AI Measurement and Evaluation (AIME) team to conduct research and 
development of metrics and measurement methods, contribute to the development 
of standards, and instill best practices. With their focused efforts, they were able to 
begin establishing common terminologies, deﬁnitions, and taxonomies of concepts 
pertaining to properties of AI systems in order to help assess the degree in 
which they succeed. NIST categorizes these AI metrics to include Trustworthiness, 
Explainability/Interpretability/Transparency, (Mitigated) Bias, Security, Privacy, 
and Safety (AIME Planning Team, 2021). 
Many of the current public concerns about AI center around the issues of 
personal data privacy violations, distribution of harmful content, and sensitive 
information disclosure, and while these are undoubtedly important concerns, they 
are more often relevant to tech, banking, and social media sectors than culture 
heritage, especially for historic collections. There are also general concerns about 
the transparency surrounding these types of advanced technologies as well as the 
potential ampliﬁcation of existing biases. To begin to address these apprehensions, 
the cultural heritage community needs to be cognizant of these potential pitfalls and 
continue to be transparent about the AI workﬂows utilized and their inner workings. 
It is with these standards and metrics in mind that we undertake and evaluate our AI 
applications in the cultural heritage ﬁeld in order to improve AI-generated results 
and establish best standards in our own applications and practices. 
In order to address the potential applications and implications of AI within the 
cultural heritage ﬁeld, the US National Endowment for the Humanities (NEH), 
and the Arts and Humanities Research Council (AHRC) founded the AEOLIAN 
(Artiﬁcial Intelligence for Cultural Organizations) Network. During their ﬁrst 
workshop, Thomas Padilla, the Director of Information Systems and Technology 
Strategy for the Center for Research Libraries, gave several strategies to allow 
GLAM (Galleries, Libraries, Archives, and Museums) organizations to distinguish 
themselves within the AI space while still engaging with the practice in a deﬁned, 
ethical, and innovative way. In his ﬁrst theme, Padilla discusses the non-scalability 
imperative and the problematic dependency where scalability is made possible by 
non-scalable processes, resources, and people. He elaborates to say that this type 
of heterogeneity and diversity can be overcome by AI and Machine Learning 
applications. Padilla also addresses the concept of “maintenance as innovation” 
through which he states that maintenance is sustained innovation and we must value 
the importance of maintenance to innovation and it is for that reason that we must 
continue to evolve, adapt, and innovate with expanding technologies like AI and 
Machine Learning (Padilla, 2023). 
By using AI, identiﬁcations made through facial detection can facilitate recog-
nition and research within a pictorial collection by providing contextualization and 
prompting further insights. Face recognition and related technologies are built on the 
unique attributes of the human face as a readily available identity marker. Images

Decoding Pictorial Collections Using Faces 193
of the face provide “facial landmarks” that can be measured to form a signature of 
that individual. Creating a facial signature (sometimes called a “faceprint”) from 
an image of a face is among the most mature areas of AI research and works 
successfully in a broader range of circumstances and challenges than most readers 
will assume. 
The signature is surprisingly robust and durable against aging, makeup, and 
apparel such as glasses or hats, and there are enough markers that differences 
in camera angle, lighting, and low resolution can usually be overcome. Along 
with supporting the cataloging of images and creating more complex metadata, 
using computer-aided AI often allows for more easily reproducible results and 
identiﬁcations (Fornaro & Chiquet, 2020). 
There are at least three ways heritage institutions can use facial recognition to 
enrich their pictorial collections:
 Custom-Trained Face Recognition : Uses known individual images to ﬁnd their 
additional instances in a collection, effectively identifying all appearances of a 
known person.
 Notable Individual Detection : Searches a collection for known individuals, 
identifying historically signiﬁcant people without prior knowledge of their 
presence.
 Frequently Occurring Individuals (clustering) : Converts all faces in a collection 
into signatures, clusters them by similarity, and identiﬁes the most frequently 
appearing individuals. 
Image description can be further enhanced by layering biographical databases 
and biometrics on top of face recognition. For instance, identifying John F. Kennedy 
in a photo dates it between 1917 and 1963. Biometric analysis of his face can further 
narrow the date range based on his estimated age at the time the photo was taken. 
If another individual appeared alongside Kennedy, then biometrics could be used 
to approximate the date of any other photo they appear in. Or if any photo has an 
already known date, then individuals in that photo can spread date approximations 
anywhere else they appear. Such network-based date approximation can cover an 
extensive portion of a pictorial collection, starting from a small number of known 
individuals. 
Facial recognition presents a transformative approach to managing and under-
standing pictorial collections. The human face can be a key that unlocks tremendous 
value in pictorial collections, making them more accessible, easier to search, and 
more fully described, signiﬁcantly contributing to our shared cultural heritage. 
2 Foundational Science 
Most AI face recognition tools work by quantifying various attributes of a face; 
these attributes, in sufﬁcient quantity and quality, form a ﬁngerprint unique to an 
individual and durable across time. The exact details of implementation vary and are

194 D. Peterson and H. Storch
Fig. 1 A highly simpliﬁed example of two faces represented in three-dimensional space where 
each dimension is an attribute of the face. In reality, even simple face recognition tools use far 
more than three attributes and weigh the importance of those attributes in complex ways 
always evolving. It is not essential to fully understand the underlying mechanism in 
order to use the technology successfully in a heritage context. However, a simpliﬁed 
example of this process can be informative as to the instances where we do or do 
not expect the process to work. 
The AI conducts ﬁngerprinting using face characteristics such as chin strength, 
nose size, and nose height. Similarity (or difference) between two faces can then 
be quantiﬁed as the distance in multi-dimensional space where each attribute is a 
dimension, or through a more simpliﬁed measure like weighted average (Fig. 1). 
In some cases, the weighting of these attributes is then automatically determined 
through Machine Learning on very large sets of faces. 
3 Main Methods 
3.1 Custom-Trained Face Recognition 
The most basic and intuitive face recognition workﬂow is to look for a speciﬁc 
person. The process is direct and straightforward—provide one or more examples of 
an individual’s face along with a label (typically their name) and then look for them 
in other images. Typically only a single-labeled image is required, but additional 
images can increase accuracy and robustness, especially if they add variety to the 
training set in terms of face angle, age, or lighting. This approach is common when 
you have prior knowledge or at least suspicion that a speciﬁc person will appear in 
images. 
For example, in 2021, Digital Transitions (DT) partnered with the Foellinger 
Foundation (The Foellinger, 1958) to digitize approximately 20,000 slides from 
their collection in anticipation of their 65th anniversary and to celebrate the 
family’s involvement in their local community (Digital Transitions, 2023). For 
this project, DT was tasked not only with digitizing the family’s slide collection,

Decoding Pictorial Collections Using Faces 195
but also with creating descriptive metadata information through the use of custom 
facial recognition. The goal of this AI collaboration was to identify sisters and 
organization co-founders Helene Foellinger and Loretta Foellinger Teeple, along 
with their mother, Esther Foellinger. Although these individuals were well-known 
and very inﬂuential within their community, they would not have been easily 
recognized using a broad database of notable persons for reference. 
By training on a few images of the women’s faces, AI was able to ﬁnd the 
family members in both the foreground and background of images, in a variety 
of places and contexts, as well as alone and with other people. As is typical for 
custom-trained face recognition, the identiﬁcations were made with extremely high 
speciﬁcity and sensitivity, as evaluated independently by the subject matter experts 
at the foundation for whom these faces were well known. 
Due to the fact that this model involves the preliminary work of creating a 
referential sample set, its accuracy is very high, but this method does rely on those 
individuals being identiﬁed at least once, accurately, at the beginning of the project. 
Other forms of AI analysis, such as notable individual detection, that use broader 
databases can require even less work upfront. 
3.2 Notable Individual Detection 
Notable individual detection is fundamentally the same as custom-trained face 
recognition in that speciﬁc faces are trained and looked for, but in notable individual 
detection, the set of trained faces is massive and less speciﬁc. That is, a large 
collection of notable individuals are trained into a pre-packaged model that can be 
used to search collections without applied custom training. 
The beneﬁt of this approach is that you do not need to know or suspect a speciﬁc 
person is in the collection in order for them to be found in your search. This can lead 
to unexpected discoveries like a famous actor performing in a play years before their 
big break, or a famous politician while they were still the mayor of a small town. 
As discussed later, the large number of people in the Target Face Set of a notable 
individual database greatly increases the likelihood of false positives, but there are 
techniques that can mitigate that tendency. 
For example, in 2021 Digital Transitions (DT) worked with the Smithsonian 
Center for Folklife and Cultural Heritage to describe a dark collection (lacking 
sufﬁcient descriptive metadata to facilitate searches) of digitized objects related 
to folk music (Halle, Cecelia, 2020). This collection included many photographs, 
most of which were not yet captioned or described in any item-level manner. 
Using a database of notable faces, DT was able to identify a variety of the 
individuals depicted (Fig. 2). While most of the faces could have been recognized 
by subject matter experts, the large size of the collection would have made manual 
identiﬁcation quite time-consuming.

196 D. Peterson and H. Storch
Fig. 2 Singer Big Joe Williams, journalist Charles Kuralt, and actress Jane Darwell identiﬁed 
correctly by AI in the Smithsonian Center for Folklife and Cultural Heritage collection 
3.3 Frequently Occurring Individuals (Clustering) 
Face clustering is the process of sorting a pool of faces into their constituent 
individuals, without any prior knowledge or guidance on who may appear. Unlike 
notable individual detection, the AI does not need to be trained on any face 
speciﬁcally and, unlike notable individual detection, the person need not be famous. 
Clustering has a self-reinforcing effect; each instance of a face creates a more 
complete understanding of that face, such that additional instances are more likely 
to be found. Therefore, clustering works most robustly on those individuals who 
appear most frequently in a collection. 
There are several beneﬁts to clustering. First, it is often the case that the 
individuals appearing most frequently in a collection have a prominent or interesting 
role in the events depicted, regardless of whether or not they were famous. For 
example, the research assistant who appears frequently alongside the famous Nobel 
winner, or the campaign manager that helped elect the president, might appear 
frequently grouped within a collection. Second, clustering can also ﬁnd a layperson 
who was not of historic signiﬁcance, but who can provide insight as to the 
experience of those living at that time and place. Third, clustering can connect 
narratives that span collections, time periods, or locations by ﬁnding people in 
different parts of their life and within different contexts. For example, clustering 
could identify an actress appearing on stage, attending a social party, and at a 
political rally. 
In 2020, 22 major museums, libraries, and archives of Estonia cooperated 
together on a joint project to digitize their respective photographic ﬁlm collections—

Decoding Pictorial Collections Using Faces 197

approximately 170,000 images, mostly from glass plates and 35 mm negatives 
(Digital Transitions, 2021). These collections represent the shared cultural heritage 
of the nation throughout the entirety of its history—the country having gained 
independence in 1918, well within the era of photography. The company Pixel 
Acuity was employed for both the digitization of the images and a pilot program 
to identify the most commonly occurring faces using the clustering technique (Figs. 
3 and 4).

198 D. Peterson and H. Storch
Fig. 5 A man identiﬁed in photos of the Estonian National Museum and Estonian Library Museum 
(bottom left) in a formal group portrait where he is readily identiﬁed as Ilmar Talve, writer, and 
ethnologist 
By ﬁnding and clustering all faces in the collection, Pixel Acuity was able to 
identify 279 individuals that appeared in two or more images. Of these, 211 of 
them appeared in 10 or more photos, implying they were of likely research value 
to the collection. Clustering of faces shows that a particular person appears more 
than once, but it does not identify them speciﬁcally (e.g., only a unique number is 
assigned to each person by the AI, not a name). But each face could be presented to a 
subject matter expert as a grouping of the photos he or she appeared in, making it far 
easier to make a speciﬁc identiﬁcation. For example, as seen in Fig. 5, one individual 
was identiﬁed as appearing 24 times in images of the Estonian National Museum, 
where he appeared primarily as a soldier in the context of photo documentary 
images taken during World War 2. In these photos from the National Museum, he 
would be challenging to identify. However, he was also identiﬁed as appearing in a 
formal group photo at the Estonian Library Museum where his identity, Ilmar Talve, 
Estonian writer, and ethnologist, is much more easily derived from context. 
Identiﬁcations that spanned across different institutions’ collections were com-
mon. A single face was identiﬁed as appearing 16 times in the Estonian Art 
Museum, 10 times in the Estonian Literary Museum, and once in the Estonian 
National Museum collection. As indicated in Fig. 6, in one of these 27 appearances, 
the glass plate itself is clearly labeled “Ants Laipman”—in face clustering, the iden-
tiﬁcation of a face in any of its appearances is an identiﬁcation of all appearances. 
Moreover, the identiﬁcation of a face in any image provides valuable context for 
identifying any other face in that image. One example of that effect is described in 
further detail in “Biometric Date Estimation Networks” later in this chapter. 
4 Robustness 
The current state of face recognition is more robust than most people are aware of; 
common obstacles like varied eyewear, side views, occluded views, low resolution,

Decoding Pictorial Collections Using Faces 199
Fig. 6 A man identiﬁed by AI as appearing in images from three separate institutions. Note that 
the left image is a glass plate clearly labeled with the name Ants Laipman 
blurry detail, and age are frequently non-problematic for a high accuracy, high 
conﬁdence match to an existing ﬁngerprint, as seen in Fig. 7. Much of this 
robustness is owed to the signiﬁcant investment in face recognition from the security 
and social media sectors. It does little good to have face recognition in those contexts 
if they are defeated by the head being turned at an angle or the eyes being blocked by 
sunglasses. Individuals can also be identiﬁed in a variety of garments, makeup, and 
environments, as seen in Fig. 8 with actor Aleksander Viilma. Even more extreme 
examples of cross-identiﬁcation can be found across different media formats. As 
seen earlier in the case of Ants Laipman, even paintings of a person, if done in 
a skilled manner and in a realistic painting style, may cluster together with their 
subject if photos of the subject also occur. 
This robustness of face recognition raises signiﬁcant ethical and societal concerns 
in broader use and among living populations in a contemporaneous manner. These 
concerns should not be ignored or assumed absent from use in historical heritage 
contexts. However, the further back one goes from current times, the more muted 
these concerns become. 
4.1 Accuracy Evaluation Terminology 
Face recognition is not perfect; it will misidentify an individual in some cases (false 
positives) and miss a face it should know in others (false negatives). 
The rate and importance of such errors will depend strongly on how many faces 
are in the training set and how often they actually appear in the corpus of images.

200 D. Peterson and H. Storch
Fig. 7 Detected instances of Ilmar Talve, used as a prior example. Note the robust detection on 
blurry and grainy images, with head turned and with hat, glasses, and cigarette 
Fig. 8 Actor Aleksander Viilma detected via clustering, despite large variation of costume, 
makeup, lighting, and scratches on the scanned photographic ﬁlm 
Before discussing this in detail, it is useful to introduce some relevant terminology 
that will help us describe the level of success of face recognition analysis:
 Prevalence: How often is the face actually present in the test set?
 Sensitivity: The success rate of detecting a face from the target face set, when 
present.
 Speciﬁcity: The success rate of correctly reporting that a face is not in the target 
face set.

Decoding Pictorial Collections Using Faces 201
 Conﬁdence: A metric returned by the face recognition tool indicating the 
conﬁdence of the match.
 Conﬁdence Threshold: A parameter in most face recognition systems that allows 
the user to balance sensitivity and speciﬁcity. 
4.2 Prevalence 
The most important driver of the accuracy rate is how frequently the face truly 
occurs in the corpus being searched. Although this metric can rarely be known with 
exactness (if it was, a test wouldn’t be needed), a rough estimate can frequently be 
made. As a thought experiment, imagine the extreme ends of the spectrum:
 High Prevalence: Training face recognition on Martin Luther King Jr. (MLK) in 
order to search for him in the personal archive of Coretta Scott King, his wife.
 Low Prevalence: Using a generalist “notable persons database” containing a host 
of individuals from a broad span of time and location, in order to see where they 
appear in a folk music collection at the Smithsonian. 
Let us examine the high-prevalence context. Assume there are 100,000 faces in 
the images of this collection and further assume that 1% of them (1000) belong 
to MLK. Modern face recognition has a very high sensitivity and a very high 
speciﬁcity—the exact rates vary signiﬁcantly by the engine and the quality of the 
images, as well as the conﬁdence threshold used (which will be discussed later). 
But, for the sake of instruction, let us assume 99.99% sensitivity and 99.999% 
speciﬁcity. And, for the sake of simplicity, let us assume we get the most average 
result. With these assumptions, we would correctly identify MLK all but one of 
the times he appears in the collection (99.99% sensitivity among 10,000 instances 
where he did in fact appear). Further, we would misidentify someone else as 
MLK one time (99.999% speciﬁcity on 99,000 faces that were not, in fact, MLK). 
Because MLK appeared frequently within the collection, the correct identiﬁcations 
overwhelmed the misidentiﬁcations so that nearly all of our total identiﬁcations were 
correct. We almost always identiﬁed him when he was present, and nearly all of our 
identiﬁcations of him were correct. 
Now let us consider the low-prevalence context. Assume there are 100,000 faces 
in the collection. Furthermore, assume that there are 100,000 faces in the notable 
persons database and that these notable individuals actually collectively appear 100 
times. Let us use the same sensitivity (99.99%) and speciﬁcity (99.999%) as before, 
but remember that these are per face in the target face set. When we go to examine 
the ﬁrst face in the collection, we will be comparing it to 100,000 notable persons for 
a match, and in each comparison our speciﬁcity is 99.999%. That means, on average, 
each such comparison would result in one false positive. For a face that actually is in 
the target face set, we would still expect one false positive, but we would also expect 
a match to the correct identity. Moreover, knowing that a given face can only be one 
person, if we choose the identiﬁcation with the higher conﬁdence that will be the

202 D. Peterson and H. Storch
correct identiﬁcation nearly all of the time (stated differently, even if another face in 
the database looks reasonably similar, the correct face will look most similar most of 
the time). The result is that we do, in fact, correctly ﬁnd the 100 notable individuals 
where they truly do occur, but we also falsely identify a notable person 99,900 times. 
Because we searched for a group of individuals that very rarely (on average; per 
individual) occurred in the collection, we ultimately received inadequate results. 
There are many potential solutions to this problem that would increase the 
accuracy of the analysis, including the creation of a more relevant test face set and/or 
a more precise match conﬁdence.
 Relevant Test Face Set: The more focused the test face set is to the times, places, 
and activities of a collection, the lower the chance of false positives.
 Higher conﬁdence threshold: The more strict you are on the match conﬁdence, 
the fewer false positives will occur. Of course, this does mean that there is a 
greater chance that you could miss an individual when they truly do occur. 
4.3 Improving Test Face Set Relevance 
We can call one approach to improving the relevance of the test face set, the ladder 
labeling approach. In this approach, you start with no test faces and use subject 
matter experts to identify important faces, which are then added to the test face set. 
The obvious disadvantage of this approach is that it requires upfront labor. However, 
the advantage is that your test face set will consist only of individuals who appear at 
least once in a collection. Depending on the nature of the collection, it is also likely 
that someone who appears once will also appear multiple times. This means that 
once you have sampled a small portion of the collection with subject matter experts, 
you can then run the nascent test face set on the remainder of the collection and ﬁnd 
all other instances of those individuals. Then additional labeling can be prioritized 
by searching for images with the most unlabeled faces. 
Since surfacing frequently occurring faces usually correlates with surfacing 
the most important faces in the collection, the ladder approach works best when 
combined with clustering and deﬁnitionally means the greatest return on investment 
in terms of faces labeled per person identiﬁed. This combination of approaches is 
also common outside of the cultural heritage ﬁeld and in the context of personal 
collections—for example, the Photos app on MacOS or iPhone attempts to cluster 
faces and surface the most common people in your life and, once you have labeled 
one, it tries to ﬁnd past and future instances of that person. 
Starting with a broad database of notable persons and then ﬁltering by biographic 
information is another approach to reﬁne the test face set. For example, you can 
ﬁlter out individuals who are born after the end of the date range of the collection, 
or those who died years before the start of the date range of the collection. The latter 
approach can result in a few anomalies, in that it is possible for individuals to appear 
in an image well after their death; for example, the photographs in the Estonian

Decoding Pictorial Collections Using Faces 203
National Archives frequently depict photographs, paintings, and busts of Vladimir 
Lenin many years after his death—although, usually they are not the main subject of 
the photo but appear as decorations around or behind the main subject. Additionally, 
some of the notable persons databases include famous individuals from antiquity 
as depicted in bust portraiture or art, allowing Roman busts or Greek statues to be 
identiﬁed as individuals. So depending on the collection and the goal of the labeling, 
it may be best to only ﬁlter those who were not yet born, rather than those who were 
already dead. 
Other biographic information such as occupation and location of birth and death 
can also be used to help ﬁlter out false positives. For example, let us say you are 
searching a collection of Japanese government photos of WW2 and looking for faces 
using a generalized notable persons database. Using the MediaWiki API, you can 
pull the occupation of the potential match, and if it is an actor, actress, or athlete (see 
Bias section for why these are over-represented in many notable person databases) 
and both, the birthplace and death place are both the United States. Then you can 
use a higher threshold for conﬁdence before recording the presence of an actor, 
actress, or athlete. It is plausible that such an individual is indeed in the collection; 
for example, if they were a POW or seen in TV footage within the ﬁlm image, but 
that is contextually fairly unlikely and a very high level of algorithmic conﬁdence 
would be required to surface such a result. 
If you do not have control over the database itself, as is the case with some 
commercial databases such as Amazon Rekognition’s Celebrity Detection, then you 
can apply ﬁltration on the results side; that is, you simply drop/ignore any result that 
does not comport with the allowed biographical date ranges, and apply a higher level 
of conﬁdence ﬁltration when biographical context is poor. This type of ﬁltration 
would help eliminate the identiﬁcations that fall outside of the user-set parameters, 
reducing the number of false positives. 
4.4 Increasing Conﬁdence Threshold 
The other main way to reduce false positives is to set a higher threshold for 
conﬁdence. Although a higher conﬁdence threshold means that fewer individuals 
will be correctly identiﬁed, it also means that more of those identiﬁcations will 
be correct. The trade-off is typically asymmetrical since the lower-conﬁdence 
identiﬁcations that are dropped are also the ones that were most likely to have been 
false positives. 
In the low-conﬁdence example that we used earlier, our sensitivity (99.99%) and 
speciﬁcity (99.999%) led to 99,900 false positives and 100 true positives, a truly 
awful result. By raising the conﬁdence threshold, we might reduce the false positives 
down to 100, while only reducing the true positives to 90. If that seems shocking, 
consider that most of the false positives were not of particularly high conﬁdence 
matches; they were random individuals whose facial characteristics tracked closely 
enough with one of the 100,000 in the database to be ﬂagged as a possible match.

204 D. Peterson and H. Storch
Although that random match may seem uncanny, it is usually the face recognition 
equivalent of a passing resemblance. In contrast, the true positives will usually be 
very high-conﬁdence matches and only occasionally be borderline. These types 
of borderline matches can often be caused by mitigating factors like image blur, 
low resolution, signiﬁcant age difference compared to the database, or a partially 
obscured face. By simply raising the conﬁdence threshold, we might change the 
ratio of errors to good results dramatically. 
4.5 Balancing Sensitivity and Speciﬁcity 
As a rule of thumb, it is impractical to have a large majority of your matches 
be incorrect, but the exact, ideal balance of “uncover every instance of someone” 
(sensitivity) vs. “ﬁlter out the mistakes” (speciﬁcity) depends on the context of 
the project. In academic research settings, it might be acceptable to have many 
false positives in hopes of making an extraordinary or unexpected identiﬁcation; 
researchers frequently have to comb through signiﬁcant amounts of data looking 
for something of interest. In general, consumer-facing settings, it might be more 
desirable to have extremely few false identiﬁcations, even if it means fewer correct 
identiﬁcations as well. It is simply a matter of weighing the costs of false positives 
against the value of additional true positives. 
Some of the costs of false positives are obvious, while other more pernicious 
costs are less so. Whenever a bad identiﬁcation is made, it costs time in Quality 
Control (QC), and if it slips past QC (as some small percent of errors always 
will) this risks reputational damage to the institution (see the Metadata section for 
suggestions on how to label matches in ways that mitigate this). Although this is 
fairly obviously bad, what is less obvious are the ramiﬁcations of bad identiﬁcations 
that carry negative emotional or societal implications. 
For example, to some, incorrectly identifying persons of color is reminiscent 
of the suppression of individuality found in historic slavery or in the common 
experience of some persons of color that those outside their race struggle to properly 
identify them. And in fact, where there are real discrepancies in facial recognition 
by race it is often caused by systemic biases and/or underrepresentation in the data 
sets used to train and test this technology (see Bias section). Another example is the 
errant identiﬁcation of someone with a bad reputation. For example, it would be very 
unfortunate to errantly label a person as Heinrich Himmler (a German Nazi) if they 
were, in fact, not Heinrich Himmler. Finally, because face recognition is typically 
so good, an errant identiﬁcation that is contextually plausible and visually hard to 
refute could lead a researcher down a rabbit hole. 
The best guard against these downsides is the appropriate contextualization 
of these answers as being AI-generated and non-deﬁnitive in nature, at least 
until/unless someone with subject matter expertise reviews and/or veriﬁes them.

Decoding Pictorial Collections Using Faces 205
5 Metadata Disclaimers 
Both humans and AI tools are imperfect and make mistakes when describing items 
in a historical collection. However, the types of mistakes AI makes can sometimes 
be unintuitive to human observers. Moreover, while the kinds of mistakes made by 
humans are broadly understood, the nascent and rapidly evolving nature of AI means 
the kinds of mistakes it makes are also constantly evolving. It is, therefore, vital that 
metadata generated by AI be labeled as such at least until they have been carefully 
vetted by human subject matter experts. Even after a human edits or approves the 
label, there is value in transparently documenting the role of AI in the creation of 
that label. 
5.1 Language for AI Disclaimers 
The appropriate language for this disclosure will vary depending on the existing 
practices of the institution, the context in which the information appears, and 
the amount of space available for the disclosure. Given this, we would suggest a 
framework of priorities that can help establish that wording for a given institution.
 Transparency: Be direct and clear about the use of AI. For example, “Generated 
by AI” or “AI identiﬁcation.”
 Speciﬁcity: Where practical, be speciﬁc—the engine, version, or date. For exam-
ple, rather than “Labeled using AI” say “Labeled using Amazon Rekognition 
May, 2023.”
 Conﬁdence: When available, provide the conﬁdence level. However, rather than 
a percent conﬁdence (which is usually the framework provided by commercial 
APIs), use categorical terms such as high/medium/low or possible/likely/very 
likely. The use of percentages implies a level of certainty about the conﬁdence 
that is likely unearned. The use of a question mark can serve as shorthand for this 
in the case that extreme brevity is required (“John Wilkes Booth?”)
 Further Exploration: Provide some link or resource identiﬁer where the viewer 
can go for more detailed information about the AI tools and QC processes in 
place at the institution.
 Feedback: Provide some capacity for the viewer to ﬂag the identiﬁcation if they 
believe it is wrong or offensive. The mechanism for feedback should be as low 
friction as possible. 
This framework is speciﬁcally meant to help the viewer understand that the 
information provided is infallible. By communicating clearly how the metadata was 
generated, the user is empowered to act in an informed manner.

206 D. Peterson and H. Storch
6 Bias 
Much has been written about the bias of facial recognition technology in a general 
consumer context. In general, the quality of AI depends on the quality of its 
training; so the quality of AI face recognition is highest for images of faces from 
demographics that are most represented in its training corpus. To handle minority 
demographics equally well would require disproportionately high coverage in 
training corpuses, while in fact the opposite is often true. Moreover, an ideal training 
corpus has a diversity of diversity—not just dark and light skin, but representation 
across the vast cornucopia of human variation, including many combinations of 
age, gender, physical condition, race, as well as variation in the conditions of the 
image, such as kind of camera, lighting, and resolution. Eliminating bias (or at 
least reducing it to the point where all individuals of any identity can expect the 
technology to work very well for them) is an important but daunting challenge. 
However, in the context of historical pictorial collections at heritage institutions, 
there are several other biases in these systems to consider. 
6.1 Born Digital vs Film Images 
Training corpuses tend to be biased toward born digital images. While nearly all 
images used to train AI face recognition systems are from modern digital cameras, 
many or most images from historic collections will have been captured with 
photographic ﬁlm or glass plates. Both digital cameras and ﬁlm cameras produce 
noise, but the noise in a ﬁlm image is typically stochastic grain, while digital images 
produce noise in a regular rectangular grid. Digital images frequently have contrast, 
saturation, and noise reduction applied in post processing that are higher than was 
typically common in the ﬁlm era. A face, as captured in a ﬁlm image and then 
scanned or digitized, is not fundamentally different from one captured by a digital 
camera, but they will vary in ways that could theoretically affect the speciﬁcity and 
sensitivity of detection. That being said, the authors are not aware of any controlled 
studies comparing face recognition in born digital as compared to ﬁlm images, but it 
is their subjective experience that face recognition works exceptionally well in ﬁlm 
archives, so any difference may not be of signiﬁcant practical importance. 
6.2 Recent, Rich, Western, and Entertainment 
Databases of notable individuals tend to be biased toward individuals for whom 
digital images are more easily accessible. This means that such databases tend to be 
far more recent, Western, wealthy, and far more concentrated in the entertainment 
business than the average experience across the world since photography was

Decoding Pictorial Collections Using Faces 207
Fig. 9 American actress Thora Birch, born in 1982, is a high-conﬁdence match to this girl found 
in a mid-twentieth century Estonian archive collection 
invented. While it takes primary research to locate images for speciﬁc actors and 
actresses in nineteenth century plays (if such images exist at all), one can easily 
locate name-labeled photos of nearly all 948 individuals who were credited for 
appearing on the television series Buffy the V ampire Slayer . Modern individuals 
have far more photos of them made readily accessible and those photos are far more 
often already labeled with a name in the metadata or found in a context in which 
the name can be reliably extracted, and for this reason, there can sometimes be false 
positives within historic collections when a modern individual is errantly identiﬁed 
rather than the correct historic one. For example, in Fig. 9, modern American actress 
Thora Birch, born in 1982, was misidentiﬁed as another young girl found in a mid-
twentieth century Estonian archive collection. 
Because such databases have far more modern faces than historic, and far 
more actors and athletes, the techniques described earlier to ﬁlter by the dates of 
birth/death and raising the threshold based on occupation can help overcome this 
particular bias and improve the overall accuracy of the analysis (see “Improve Test 
Face Set Relevance”). 
7 Biometric Date Estimation Networks 
The face detection process of the AI application provides estimation about the 
individuals in the photograph, including sex and the age range when the photograph 
was likely taken. Once a face has been identiﬁed as a speciﬁc person, any 
biographical information about that person can be combined with biometrics of 
their face in the image to date that image with reasonable conﬁdence. Through

208 D. Peterson and H. Storch
extrapolation, faces that appear more than once in a collection can become nodes 
in a Date Estimation Network such that identifying the date of any of those photos 
informs the date of all other photos in the network. Such network-based date 
approximation can cover an extensive portion of a pictorial collection, starting from 
a small number of known individuals or dates, providing valuable information not 
only about the people featured within the collection but also the relevant dates and 
time periods surrounding them. 
7.1 Dates via Biometrics 
Many face recognition engines also include basic biometric analysis that includes 
an estimation of an individual’s likely age, with conﬁdence intervals of roughly 
+/−5 years depending on the engine. Although this is an approximation, it still 
narrows down the likely date of a photo considerably. For instance, consider a photo 
that contains several faces, one of which is very conﬁdently identiﬁed as John F. 
Kennedy (JFK). That dates the photo between 1917 and 1963, his years of birth and 
death (with the exception of photos where his likeness is depicted, e.g., a portrait 
of JFK hanging on an unrelated person’s wall). But if biometric analysis of his face 
indicates he was 25–35 in the photo, then this narrows the date of the photo to 
1942–1952. If his brother RFK was also identiﬁed in the photo as 21–31 (implying 
a date of 1944–1954), then the middle of that range becomes more likely, and the 
conﬁdence of the estimate increases. Note that the proper statistics of combining 
probability distributions are signiﬁcantly more involved than this, but this simpliﬁed 
average of the middle of each range will often sufﬁce in most contexts for providing 
a reasonable estimate for the photo. 
7.2 Chain Inference 
The real power of biometric date estimation is in the network effect that it can create 
across the rest of the collection. Take, for example, our previous hypothetical of 
JFK and imagine that alongside JFK and RFK there was a third individual who 
could not be programmatically identiﬁed as a speciﬁc notable individual. Let us call 
that person John Doe. Doe’s birth date can still be estimated by back-porting their 
biometric analysis and the average estimate for the date of the photo. For example, 
if John Doe is estimated to be 40–50 years old in that photo, then a good estimate 
of his birth year would be 1903. Because we have an estimate for his birth year, we 
can thereby estimate the date of any other photo in which he appears—the dating 
authority of JFK and RFK can be extended, via John Doe, to other images. So if John 
Doe is found in a photo with Jane Doe and biometrics indicate he is approximately 
73 and she is approximately 25, we can say that photo was taken around 1976 
and she was born around 1951. If she then appears at approximately 40 years old

Decoding Pictorial Collections Using Faces 209
in a photo, that implies a photo date of around 1991. Through this type of chain 
inference, date information can be extrapolated to provide additional chronological 
context throughout entire collections. 
7.3 Conﬁdence and Distance from Ground Truth Nodes 
Within a collection, each photo represents a node in this network model, and dates 
are spread between the nodes (photos) by shared detected faces. The nodes where 
a date or an individual is known with conﬁdence can be considered ground truth. 
The further an inferred date is from such a ground truth node, the greater the error 
bars on those inferences. In the example above, the ﬁnal photo was dated by the 
following chain of inference: JFK/RFK (averaged) > John Doe > Jane Doe. Each 
of those inferences carries a margin of error, and those margins accumulate so that 
we are less sure of the date of the ﬁnal photo than we were of the photo containing 
JFK and RFK. Still, if there was no extant dating on the ﬁnal photo and it lacked 
context clues, such an inferred date, even with its higher uncertainty, could still offer 
signiﬁcant value. Therefore, when setting up code to generate a Date Estimation 
Network, one should adhere to some general principles:
 Use a higher conﬁdence threshold than for general detection. It is acceptable in 
some contexts to present a face that is low in conﬁdence (see the High Prevalence 
example earlier).
 Never replace ground truth with inference. It is plausible that the existing 
metadata record is in error, but one must start an inference process with 
assumptions, and existing vetted metadata is a far better starting point than 
inferred age or face recognition.
 Start with ground truth nodes, and work outward. Start with nodes where a date-
certain is known. From there expand ﬁrst to nodes where more than one face 
overlaps ground truth nodes; multiple faces allow averaging which improves 
the accuracy of the inference. Thereafter expand nodes, never replacing a less 
uncertain (closer to ground truth node) with a higher uncertainty node. In this 
way you avoid recursion and build all data from the least uncertainty. 
Although there are more advanced statistical approaches than those that have 
been outlined here, they would be predicated on an assumption that the algorithmic 
conﬁdence of face recognition tools is objectively accurate overall and, more 
importantly, that this accuracy would hold across their use in historic collections. 
8 Quality Control (QC) and Feedback 
Institutions wishing to use face recognition to enhance their pictorial collections 
will not be using these tools in isolation, but will instead be using them as part

210 D. Peterson and H. Storch
of a greater workﬂow that includes generating the raw results, ﬁltering or reﬁning 
them according to context clues about the collection, optionally using in-house 
human review as a quality control, deploying the results to some public-facing 
or at least stakeholder-facing system (e.g., a digital asset management system 
and/or website), and receiving feedback from stakeholders on the results. Since 
there are considerable efﬁciencies to be gained by combining digitization with 
the enhancement of the resulting digitized assets, these processes may also be 
prepended by digitization. In this next section, we will explore quality control and 
feedback in greater detail. 
8.1 Human Review 
Institutions are typically very conservative about placing unveriﬁed data into 
stakeholder-facing systems and rightly so. Providing access to trustworthy and 
authoritative information is both a core principle and the core value proposition 
of most museums, libraries, and archives. Any false or misleading information in 
their systems risks damage to their reputation. Therefore, institutions deploying 
AI to identify faces in their pictorial collections are well served to place human 
QC between the AI output and the ingestion of the results into stakeholder-facing 
systems. 
Although it would be ideal that all AI-generated identiﬁcations would be vetted 
by human subject matter experts, there may be situations where unﬁltered results 
could be used. Speciﬁcally, the main trade-off for human QC is the time and cost 
of that process, and in some cases, a shortage of either can mean that a collection 
would remain undescribed (“dark”) for an indeﬁnite period if human QC is made 
an absolute requirement. In such situations, the merits of providing unﬁltered AI 
data as a stop-gap until such human QC can be performed should be considered. 
Certainly, in the case that AI data is ever used without human QC, the wording and 
prominence of disclaimers about its nature should be signiﬁcantly increased (see 
Metadata Disclaimers). 
8.2 Feedback 
As with the descriptive metadata generated by human subject matter experts, the 
metadata placed into use from AI should never be considered ﬁnal, regardless of 
whether there was a human QC layer in the workﬂow or not. Even very high 
conﬁdence detections are sometimes in error; if you are searching large collections 
for large numbers of speciﬁc individuals, then one-in-a-million mistakes happen 
with surprising frequency (e.g., the Low Prevalence example earlier in this chapter). 
Even with QC, an errant identiﬁcation will slip through now and then. Institutions 
should embrace this, and actively enable their stakeholders to ﬂag labels for review.

Decoding Pictorial Collections Using Faces 211
This feedback mechanism can be as simple as a “suggest correction” button, but 
such language requires that the user feel conﬁdent that there is an issue, rather 
than merely having a suspicion that there might be an error. Therefore, language 
such as “ﬂag for review” is preferable. Even more open ended would be “accuracy 
feedback” with thumbs up ( ) and thumbs down ( ) emojis, with an automatic 
follow-up question asking for alternative suggestions or more details if stakeholders 
click the . 
Crowdsourcing issues with feedback of this manner leverage the wisdom of 
crowds and the power of the niche expertise that can be found among large numbers 
of individuals. Even if an institution has a world-leading expert in an area relevant 
to a pictorial collection, it is highly likely that for any given person or event there is 
or will be someone somewhere with more specialized expertise. 
Finally, the feedback mechanism serves as an additional reinforcement method, 
signaling to the user that the AI analysis is not infallible—infallible data would not 
warrant a feedback mechanism. 
9 Community Opportunity 
We have explained three main approaches to using face recognition in a her-
itage context: custom-trained face recognition, notable individual detection, and 
frequently occurring individuals (clustering). These need not be thought of as 
wholly separate techniques, but as three avenues for use of the same underlying 
technology. In fact, there exists a serious opportunity in the heritage community to 
combine these three approaches together to create a heritage-speciﬁc open-source 
face recognition database. 
Although there are more generic options available, a notable persons database 
is essentially the result of retained custom-trained face recognition. For a given 
institution, if each custom-trained face is retained, that institution will accumulate 
an institution-speciﬁc notable persons database—one where the training corpus is 
far more relevant to the times, places, and events of its collection. And rather 
than manually select faces for that database, that institution can use frequently 
occurring individuals (clustering) on its entire collection to ﬁnd likely candidates 
for identiﬁcation, then custom-train on those individuals. 
Moving wider than a single institution, groups of similar institutions could 
band together to follow this approach, uncovering connectivity between their 
collection that was previously unknown and defraying the development cost across 
their institutions. This is effectively what was done in Estonia, when two dozen 
institutions pooled their resources to do one large centralized digitization project; 
the face recognition performed by Pixel Acuity was not just performed for each 
institution, but each institution beneﬁted from the inclusion of the other institutions’ 
collections in the face recognition. The quality and quantity of face recognition was

212 D. Peterson and H. Storch
higher than what could have been achieved by any one of those institutions on their 
own. 
But why not dream bigger? Face recognition can be integrated into the 
broader open data ecosystem in the heritage community. Open data in a 
museum/library/archive context refers to the practice of making digital collections 
and associated metadata freely accessible to the public, researchers, and other 
institutions, promoting transparency, collaboration, and the reuse of cultural and 
historical information across institutions. Institutions across the world could work 
together on a universal heritage face database. Unlike commercially available 
notable persons databases, the corpus, the links to source material, and the resulting 
database could all be open source. There are, of course, practical obstacles to 
such a transnational, multi-institutional effort—the authors do not want to suggest 
such an effort would be fast or easy. But obstacles in similar large-scale academic 
references have been overcome by open collaboration—for example, the creation 
of botanical databases and linguistic corpuses. These types of databases such as 
The Plant Ontology Database generated by The Plant Ontology Consortium (POC) 
(Avraham et al., 2008) and various linguistic collaborations from organizations like 
the Linguistic Data Consortium (The Linguistic Data Consortium (LDC), n.d.), the 
American National Corpus, and others have taken on the responsibility of not only 
serving as community resources but also as the creators of controlled vocabulary 
and annotations for further study, research, and reference. Such open data initiatives 
have proven the potential of collaborative efforts in accumulating, preserving, and 
making accessible vast amounts of information, which would otherwise remain 
isolated within individual institutions. 
Furthermore, a technical framework for inter-institutional image sharing and 
description, International Image Interoperability Framework (IIIF) (The Interna-
tional Image Interoperability Framework (IIIF), n.d.), would allow a distributed 
implementation. Each institution could include face ﬁngerprints in their IIIF 
published images wherever they choose to clear that use, allowing any institution 
to independently search for a face across all IIIF accessible collections. 
The creation of a universal heritage-speciﬁc open-source face recognition 
database would not only democratize access to invaluable historical data but also 
provide a platform for cross-disciplinary research. This could enable historians, 
anthropologists, and other researchers to uncover new connections and insights 
about our shared past. Imagine looking through photos of a war, seeing a face that 
seems to tell a story of that time and place, and simply clicking to ﬁnd all other 
instances of that face in any participating heritage institution in the world. 
Moreover, this collaborative effort would also address the issue of representation, 
ensuring a more diverse and inclusive database that accurately reﬂects the breadth 
and depth of global heritage. This is a signiﬁcant improvement over commercially 
available databases, which tend to be skewed towards modern, entertainment, and 
Western-centric ﬁgures. 
While the task is undoubtedly challenging, the potential beneﬁts of a universal 
heritage face database far outweigh the obstacles. With the right level of commit-
ment, cooperation, and the leveraging of existing face recognition technology, it is

Decoding Pictorial Collections Using Faces 213
entirely feasible. The heritage community has an exciting opportunity to lead the 
way in this innovative use of technology, paving the way for a more inclusive and 
interconnected understanding of our global heritage. 
10 Conclusion 
The mature state of AI face recognition can signiﬁcantly enrich pictorial collections 
at heritage institutions, unlocking the contextual value trapped by the lack of 
descriptive metadata. The uses in heritage institutions are vast, ranging from 
identifying well-known individuals across a collection to surfacing lay persons who 
appear frequently in a collection. The integration of biographical databases and 
biometrics can further enhance image descriptions, providing more precise dating 
of images, spreading those dates in a network across the images. 
While the promise of these technologies is immense, it is crucial to approach their 
implementation with due diligence and transparency. If implemented effectively and 
collaboratively, this technology has the potential to establish a universal, heritage-
speciﬁc, open-source face recognition database. This could usher in a transformative 
era of research, enabling us to decode pictorial collections in ways that were 
previously beyond our imagination.

Digitization and Reproduction 
of Surface: Shedding New Light 
on Goya’s Black Paintings 
Carlos Bayod Lucini 
1 Introduction 
What can we learn from the surface of a painting, in light of the new digital tools 
for recording and reproducing its three-dimensional features? Can we acquire a 
deeper understanding of an original artwork through the process of replicating its 
superﬁcial appearance? This chapter discusses how digitization can be a tool for art 
historical research, using Factum Arte’s 3D scanning and reproduction of Goya’s 
Black Paintings as a case study, and suggesting an alternative layout for a physical 
reconstruction. 
The ability to accurately measure and visualize the skin of cultural artifacts is 
a relatively recent development. The earliest applications of high-resolution 3D 
scanning techniques in the study of paintings are only about 20 years old. Even now, 
with a few exceptions, the majority of museums do not carry out comprehensive 
three-dimensional documentation of their collections. And yet the surface relief 
is one of the fundamental sources of data for understanding the complexity of a 
work of art. A photograph of a painting captured exclusively with visible light can 
communicate, with more or less accuracy, the image represented in it, depicting 
its color characteristics. However, it will inevitably overlook the other half of the 
information—its surface texture—since paintings are not two-dimensional objects. 
The overall shape of an easel painting—or a wall painting for that matter—may 
tend to be ﬂat, but its texture is not. The painted surface registers the marks of every 
event that has shaped its current appearance: the weaving of a canvas fabric can 
produce a vibrant texture different from the smoother character of a rigid support; 
the brushstrokes applied by the artist sculpt a bas-relief that reveals a personal

216 C. B. Lucini
technique; the passing of time can generate inﬁnite varieties of craquelure lines, 
not too different from the effects of aging in human skin; and, last but not least, a 
painting’s restoration history is the cause of superﬁcial alterations with disparate and 
often unpredictable results. A painting’s history is embedded in its relief, amounting 
to an archive of information that must be decoded and interpreted with specialized 
tools. Therefore, in addition to an accurate photographic recording of color, it is 
necessary to conduct 3D scanning to complete the documentation of a painting. 
However, not every painting transmits the same amount of information through 
its surface relief: some are more articulate than others. In an article from the 
Boletín del Museo del Prado in 1984, Mari Carmen Garrido published photographic 
reproductions of two details of the painting Duel with Cudgels by Goya. 1 The 
painting was lit with raking light to emphasize its surface texture. The author chose 
these speciﬁc images to detail the condition of one of the most iconic works in the 
museum’s collection. The images highlight how “the pictorial layer comes off in the 
form of ﬂakes [though] in other cases it can be seen that the lifted layer is actually 
that of the repaints.” 2 This was the ﬁrst time in this publication’s history—and one 
of very few examples to date—in which the surface texture of a painting has been 
illustrated by photographs taken with raking light, which allowed to appreciate the 
unique material nature of Goya’s Black paintings. In this case, it made the relief of 
Duel with Cudgels visible and so enabled research into the painting’s history and 
the techniques used in its creation (Fig. 1).

Digitization and Reproduction of Surface: Shedding New Light on Goya’s ... 217
Francisco de Goya y Lucientes (1746–1828) painted one of the most intriguing 
series in the history of art directly onto the walls of his house. Universally known 
as the Black Paintings (due to their rather dark and disturbing subjects), these 
mysterious scenes created between 1819 and 1823 decorated the two main rooms of 
the Quinta del Sordo, the artist’s residency on the outskirts of Madrid. This property 
has since been demolished, but the paintings were removed from the walls and 
transferred onto canvas in 1874 and can now be seen in a dedicated space in the 
Museo del Prado. 3 Garrido describes the general condition of the series in these 
terms: 
The extraction of the paintings and their transposition to canvases was conducted in a 
somewhat irregular manner. This means that the thickness of the layers of its material 
structure is very different from one area to another within the same painting. ( ...  )T h e 
superﬁcial relief of the Black Paintings is not uniform, rather it could be said that in some 
respects it turns out to be an authentic “orography.” 4 
Orography is a geographical term that refers to the topographic relief of moun-
tains or elevated terrains. The author borrows this term to describe the conservation 
state of the painted surface of the Black Paintings speciﬁcally, highlighting the 
prominent three-dimensional features of the series. Such a metaphorical leap of ﬁeld 
and scale (from geography to pictorial art) was preceded by the literal removal of 
the images from their original architectural context 110 years earlier—where they 
formed the inner skin of a building—and their ﬁxing onto a new textile support, thus 
becoming moveable works of art. 
By changing the nature of the paintings, new layers of meaning were added 
onto them. With time, the Black Paintings have become the sum of the material 
remains of Goya’s creations intertwined with the alterations produced by the 
“somewhat irregular” transfer of their support. 5 During the journey from being 
part of a private house to becoming one of the main attractions of a museum’s 
collection, a series of dramatic events have eroded or deposited new strata on 
the paintings’ surface. 6 Texts like Garrido’s contributed to discerning these layers 
through technical studies precisely aimed at seeing beneath the surface. The x-ray 
radiographies and cross-section sample analyses carried out at the Museo del Prado 
opened up new information for understanding “the different stages suffered by the
