4 Garrido, op. cit., 36. “La extracción de las pinturas murales y su transposición a lienzos fue 
realizada de una manera un tanto irregular. Esto hace que el grosor de las capas de su estructura 
material sea muy diferente de unas zonas a otras dentro de un mismo cuadro. ( ... ) El relieve 
superﬁcial de las pinturas no es uniforme, más bien podría decirse que en algunos temas resulta ser 
una auténtica “orografía”.” 
5 For a reference summary of the alterations produced by the restorer Martínez Cubells, see the 
article: Nigel Glendinning, “The Strange Translation of Goya’s Black Paintings”, The Burlington 
Magazine, vol. 117, No. 868 ( 1975): 465–479. 
6 After being on show in Paris, the Black Paintings were donated to the Museo del Prado in 1881. 

218 C. B. Lucini
paintings until they reached their current state,” 7 which the author summarized in 
this order: 
1. Landscape scenes, ﬁrst made by Goya; 2. Change of the initial theme with the 
superimposition of the large ﬁgures; 3. Change of composition in the elaboration of the 
second scenes; 4. Loss and deterioration of the paintings while they remained on the wall; 
5. Losses and deterioration of the paintings during transportation from wall to canvases; 6. 
Restorations suffered from the moment they were transferred to the present moment [up 
to1984]; 7. V ery delicate current state, with lack of adhesion to the support, in many cases 
lack of adherence of some layers of paint with others ( ...  ) and much deteriorated surfaces 
through endless vicissitudes suffered by the paintings. 8 
Presented as a direct correspondence between physical and sequential layering, 
the technical documentation undertaken in 1984 offered new evidence for evaluating 
the changes suffered by the paintings throughout their history. As stated by Alfonso 
Pérez Sánchez, then Director of the Museo del Prado: 
The mysterious, dark spell of these captivating paintings multiplies when you 
enter them, even through the physical means that science puts within our reach. 
After studying the material provided here, it may be necessary to renounce some of 
the interpretations suggested up to now, but new ones are opening up. 9 
As will be argued next, recent advances in digital technology could further 
contribute to challenging certain assumptions made about the Black Paintings and 
open the door to new interpretations. However, these technological and physical 
means are no longer (or not only) based on seeing through hidden layers under 
the surface. Instead, the detailed study of their topographical relief with digital 3D 
scanning will shine a new light on Goya’s masterpieces.
7 Garrido, op. cit., 37. “En resumen, se pueden marcar las diferentes etapas sufridas por las pinturas 
hasta llegar a su estado actual. El conocimiento de las mismas será de suma importancia para su 
conservación futura.” 
8 Garrido, op. cit., 37. “1. Escenas de paisajes, primeramente realizadas por Goya; 2. Cambio de 
la temática inicial con la superposición de las grandes ﬁguras; 3. Cambio de composición en la 
elaboración de las segundas escenas; 4. Pérdidas y deterioros de las pinturas en su permanencia 
en el muro; 5. Pérdidas y deterioros de las pinturas durante el traslado del muro a los lienzos; 
6. Restauraciones sufridas desde que fueron arrancadas hasta el momento; 7. Estado actual muy 
delicado, con falta de adhesión al soporte, en muchos casos, falta de adhesión de unas capas de 
pintura con otras, a causa tal vez de la resina utilizada como adhesivo entre ellas durante el traslado, 
y superﬁcies muy deterioradas por el sinfín de vicisitudes padecidas por estas obras.” 
9 Garrido, op. cit., 4. “El hechizo, misterioso y sombrío, de estas subyugantes pinturas se multiplica 
al penetrar en ellas, incluso a través de los medios físicos que la ciencia pone a nuestro alcance. Tras 
el estudio del material que aquí se aporta, quizás haya que renunciar a alguna de las interpretaciones 
hasta ahora sugeridas, pero se abre camino a otras.” 

Digitization and Reproduction of Surface: Shedding New Light on Goya’s ... 219
2 A Landscape on the Wall 
In 2001, an innovative documentation project was carried out by Factum Arte, a 
Spanish studio founded by artists Adam Lowe and Manuel Franquelo, to explore a 
different form of wall painting. This project consisted of applying high-resolution 
3D scanning to record the painted reliefs in the tomb of Seti I. Considered to be 
the apex of New Kingdom funerary art, Seti I (c. 1300 BC) is the most profusely 
decorated tomb in the V alley of the Kings in Luxor, Egypt. Since its discovery 
in 1817 by Giovanni Battista Belzoni, the site has been subject to a series of 
interventions which have left their mark on the walls, often yielding unfavorable 
outcomes. Factum Arte carried out this project to demonstrate that it was possible 
to 3D-scan large surface areas to help preserve a site at risk of deterioration. The 
detailed documentation of the wall reliefs from Seti I was essential to ensure that an 
accurate record was made of their conservation state. Moreover, the high resolution 
of the recorded data enabled an exact facsimile to be made, to achieve “the balancing 
act between protecting the monument and allowing access to those who wish to 
study, admire and learn from it.” 10 
Factum Arte employed a technique known as triangulation laser 3D scanning 
to record these walls. Among the “numerous potential methods for surveying the 
surface it was found out that only laser scanning [was] capable of capturing the ﬁne 
detail.”11 This method was conducted with a custom-made Seti scanner prototype, 
created speciﬁcally for this job. The scanner mounted a Reversa scanning head— 
developed by the company 3D Scanners UK—onto a bespoke structural frame with 
motorized linear guides. 12 Using this system, it was possible to digitize an area of 
16 sqm in 6 weeks, with a spatial resolution of 100 microns (or 10,000 points per 
sq cm). “At such high resolution even the most minute details are reproduced, such 
as overlapping, brush marks and the grain of the painted surface.” 13 The color was 
captured “using a Hasselblad camera with a 120 mm digital lens ( ... ) mounted 
on a tripod at a ﬁxed distance from the wall.” 14 Both 3D and color data were 
captured in 52 cm wide tiles, which were then stitched together at a later stage with 
digital processing tools. With this information, Factum Arte was able to produce 
a facsimile of the tomb’s scanned area, through an experimental combination of 
digital fabrication technologies and craft techniques. 15

11 Lowe and Ahmon, op. cit., 13.

about 10 cm, recording an area of 52 cm wide by 300 cm high. 
13 Lowe and Ahmon, op. cit., 19.

220 C. B. Lucini
Fig. 2 Robert Barker, View of Edinburgh from St Giles Cathedral , 1796. The Royal Observatory, 
Edinburgh 
The use of digital technology for the high-resolution recording and reproduction 
of cultural heritage was novel in 2001. But the idea of making a replica of the tomb 
was not. In 1821, Belzoni exhibited in London a reconstruction of the tomb of Seti I, 
which he had recently discovered. From the ﬁrst moment he entered the royal tomb 
“to ﬁnd a sequence of thirteen rooms, almost all covered in superb wall paintings in 
relief in a state of pristine freshness,” Belzoni initiated an extensive documentation 
effort, producing “drawings of all the ﬁgures, hieroglyphics, emblems, ornaments, 
etc. [and taking] impressions of everything in wax.” 16 It was based on this 
documentation that Belzoni created his exhibition at the Egyptian Hall in Piccadilly 
(London). Visitors were invited to enter a full-sized reproduction of two of the 
rooms of Seti I (known as the Entrance Hall and the Hall of Beauties), completed 
with a scale model of the entire tomb and other material—including some original 
Egyptian antiquities. 
Belzoni’s “immersive” exhibition, which ran from May 1821 to April 1822, 
achieved success, coinciding with a period when the public was being challenged 
to view the world, both past and present, through innovative technologies. Precisely 
in 1822, Louis Daguerre introduced the ﬁrst diorama theater in Paris. This was 
followed by the diorama opening in London in Regent’s Park in 1823. Decades 
earlier, in 1778, the Scottish painter Robert Barker had patented the panorama , 
which as a revolutionary method for displaying a painted landscape image in a 360-
degree view. One year later, he showed a continuous view of the city of Edinburgh 
for the ﬁrst time in history (Fig. 2). 
In 1791, Barker’s second panorama—a view of London and Westminster— 
was exhibited near Leicester Square. This larger-scale panorama created an even 
greater and more convincing effect. The varying light tones across the image were 
also important, as often “the bright blue sky transforms into a yellow-pink sunset 
and enhances the illusionism.” 17 The success of these installations escalated in 
the early nineteenth century. Until the rise of photography (and, subsequently, the

replica of the visual characteristics of the original wall. For more information, see: Lowe and 
Ahmon, op. cit., 31–33. 
17 Susan M. Pearce, “Giovanni Batista Belzoni’s exhibition of the reconstructed tomb of Pharaoh

paintings depicted the progress of the Boat of the Sun below the Western horizon through the 
Hours of the Night in the Regions of the Dead, peopled by gigantic serpents and the souls of the

arrival of the motion picture), panoramas, dioramas, and other forms of immersive 
experiences enjoyed major success in London, Paris, and other cities across Europe 
and the United States (Fig. 3). 
The growing fascination with new modes of public entertainment helped to 
explain Belzoni’s desire “to exhibit a reconstruction of the tomb from an early 
stage.” He was able to achieve this thanks to his “continual insistence on the 
accuracy of the reconstruction” enabled by his detailed documentation of the 
walls.18 The methods employed 200 years ago to “record” the color (through 
drawings) and relief (through direct wax molding) of the wall paintings would not 
meet twenty-ﬁrst-century standards. 19 Nevertheless, part of the basic approach is 
dead, to the rebirth of the Sun in the Eastern dawn; this is, of course, analogous to the progress of 
the Pharaoh’s soul to eternal life”.

were erected exactly on the same plan, and of the same size, the ﬁgures might be placed in their 
situations precisely as in the original and thus produce in Europe a tomb, in every point equal to 
that of Thebes, which I hope to execute if possible”.

The exhibition “Scanning Seti: the Regeneration of a Pharaonic Tomb” (Antikenmuseum, Basel, 
October 29th, 2017—May 6th, 2018) reﬂected on 200 years of conservation of the site, reviewing 
the evolution towards a non-contact approach to the documentation of monuments, thanks to digital

222 C. B. Lucini
still valid today, namely the attempt to obtain the best possible record of the original 
surface in order to create a physical reproduction.
The prospect of constructing a life-sized replica of Seti’s tomb motivated Belzoni 
and his team to undertake this challenging endeavor. One hundred and eighty years 
later, the team from Factum Arte accomplished a similar feat, with all the necessary 
conceptual and technological updates: in 2001, the goal of making a material replica 
of Seti I (for preservation purposes rather than spectacle) led to the development and 
application of new, non-contact, high-resolution digital systems especially created 
for recording the color and topographical surface of painted reliefs. 20 
The Seti scanner originally developed for the tomb was then adapted for 
other projects, including the complete recording of the funerary chamber of 
Tutankhamun.21 In 2005, the Calcografía Nacional approached Factum Arte about 
the possibility of producing exact facsimiles of Goya’s plates for Los Caprichos to 
enable the originals to be preserved in a controlled environment. 22 This request 
presented an opportunity to test the capacity of digital technologies to record 
different mediums, such as Los Caprichos plates. But when recording these etching 
plates with the Seti scanner, the reﬂective surface caused an excess of noise resulting 
in invalid data. Again in 2008, while recording The Marriage of the Virgin by 
Raphael (which was undergoing restoration at the Pinacoteca di Brera in Milan), 
the color was correctly captured with composite photography, but the 3D scan of the 
surface showed errors in speciﬁc areas of the painting. 23 The scanner struggled to 
capture quality data on the darker and shinier regions. As became clear, the reﬂective 
and dark surfaces of paintings required a 3D scanner capable of adapting capture 
settings to multiple surface characteristics, in order to obtain valid information 
regardless of the object’s tone or glossiness. 
Following a period of extensive exploration testing a number of 3D scanners 
available in the market—none of which produced satisfactory results—Lowe and

Digitization and Reproduction of Surface: Shedding New Light on Goya’s ... 223
Franquelo decided in 2010 to develop a bespoke system, especially conceived for 
recording in high resolution the complex surface of paintings. The result of this 
research was the Lucida 3D Scanner , a system based on laser triangulation that 
captured relief data with a spatial resolution of 100 microns (the same resolution 
as the Seti scanner). Lucida ’s key difference was in the software conceived and 
developed by Franquelo and the algorithm which transformed the video footage into 
depth information. The scanning application included an automatic double-exposure 
feature which captures underexposed and overexposed data, thereby enabling the 
Lucida to record matte and gloss, dark, and light areas simultaneously. This avoided 
the need to digitize the same section twice or more and allowed the full dynamic 
range of a painting from the darkest black to the lightest white to be captured. 
In sum, the Lucida system was conceived to ignore a painting’s color or shine 
variations and focus on describing the topography of its surface. 24 
The Lucida 3D Scanner was the result of the collaboration between Manuel 
Franquelo and Factum Arte’s engineering team, with the support of the Factum 
Foundation.25 Since its creation, it has digitized paintings held by the world’s great 
museums and archaeological sites, recording more than 250 artworks and other 
cultural objects. The obtained information allows researchers to see and measure 
surface relief in high resolution, providing invaluable data for conservation and 
study; it also permits the production of exact facsimiles for dissemination and 
exhibition purposes. 
Lucida was ﬁrst used in the Museo del Prado in 2011 to digitize a panel by 
Peter Paul Rubens, in a research initiative aimed at evaluating the potential of 3D 
recording as part of a painting’s restoration process. The Triumph of the Eucharist 
over Idolatry (c. 1625) was painted by Rubens as one of the sketches for the great 
series of tapestries commissioned for the Monastery of the Descalzas Reales in 
Madrid.26 In 2011, the painting was to undergo a process of restoration which 
would modify the panel’s shape and texture. This meant it was essential to obtain 
an accurate scan of its surface condition before it changed. 
This painting was one of a series of six panels that underwent treatment by the 
Museo del Prado’s Conservation Department. The existing cradle was removed and 
substituted for a new, more ﬂexible support to prevent the appearance of further 
cracks, which were already visible on the painting’s surface. This new structural 
support gave the panel a more natural curvature, while providing room for certain 
movement of the material. As part of the intervention, the Prado removed sections 
on the panel’s perimeter that were not part of the original (as they have been added

1478/lucida-3d-scanner 
25 The Factum Foundation for Digital Technology in Preservation was established in 2009 with the

Cultural Heritage. For more information, visit: https://www.factumfoundation.org 
26 Museo del Prado ,“ The Triumph of the Eucharist over Idolatry ”, Museo del Prado, https://

224 C. B. Lucini
at a later stage). As a consequence, the size, shape, and texture of the panel radically 
changed, thus leaving the data obtained with the Lucida 3D Scanner as the only 
accurate record of the painting’s surface condition before treatment. 
This was the ﬁrst time a painting was scanned in three dimensions at the Museo 
del Prado. The captured data made it possible to appreciate the painting’s surface in 
detailed topographical form, like an aerial view of a terrain. Unlike other methods 
of analysis that look “beneath” the painted layer (such as infrared reﬂectography or 
x-ray radiography), 3D scanning focuses on the shape and texture of the surface, 
making it possible to perceive a painting as the volumetric object that it truly is. 
The depth map obtained through 3D scanning, which removed the “distraction” 
of the color, allowed key aspects of the artist’s technique to become clearer, such 
as the shape of Rubens’ brushstrokes. It also captured the effects of time on the 
painted surface, like cracks or blisters, which speak about the artwork’s conservation 
trajectory. 
Three years later, at a temporary exhibition at the Museo del Prado, entitled 
Rubens. El triunfo de la Eucaristía , the results of the conservation works carried 
out on the six paintings were presented. 27 In this bold installation, the panels were 
shown next to their corresponding tapestries, enabling visitors to see the direct 
connection between Rubens’ sketches and their derivatives as grand textile works. 
Additional materials on display included infrared images and information about the 
study and restoration process, in order to communicate to the public the complex 
tasks involved in art conservation. 
As part of this approach, the exhibition housed a white reproduction of the panel 
that was recorded in 3D, sharing the surface shape and condition before treatment. 
The reproduction, made by Factum Arte, was the physical materialization of the 
data recorded with Lucida . The surface was prototyped on a resin panel using high-
resolution CNC milling, and then a silicone mold was taken to produce a plaster 
cast. This resulted in an accurate recreation of the colorless sculptural bas-relief 
of the original painting. Displaying the bare surface before restoration next to the 
freshly restored original artwork confronted the public with the dynamic nature of 
artworks, highlighting that every painting is essentially an ever-changing landscape. 
3 New Light on the Black Paintings 
The potential of this new technology to deepen the knowledge of artworks led the 
Museo del Prado in 2014 to embark on a much larger and far-reaching research 
project: the digital documentation of Goya’s Black Paintings. Thirty years had 
passed since the analyses described in the aforementioned article by Garrido,
27 Museo del Prado , “Rubens. El Triunfo de la Eucaristía”, Museo del Prado, https://www. 
museodelprado.es/actualidad/exposicion/rubens-el-triunfo-de-la-eucaristia/329af1be-ee77-4b6e-
bbf1-61b217bc5b33 

Digitization and Reproduction of Surface: Shedding New Light on Goya’s ... 225
and digital technology had been integrated into the standard imaging methods 
employed for examining artworks. Moreover, advancements in 3D scanning, with 
developments like the Lucida system, provided unprecedented ways to look at the 
topography of paintings. 
Over a period of 2 months, a team from Factum Arte worked at the Museo del 
Prado to digitize the 14 canvases of the Black Paintings, capturing the color with 
panoramic composite photography and using the Lucida 3D Scanner to record the 
surface relief. This was the ﬁrst systematic three-dimensional recording of a series 
of pictorial works promoted by a major museum. 28 Alongside this, the Museo 
del Prado’s Technical Documentation Department carried out analyses of x-ray 
radiography, infrared reﬂectography, and ultraviolet photography. The goal of this 
comprehensive study was to acquire detailed information of the paintings’ condition 
and facilitate their in-depth study with new digital tools. 29 
One at a time, the paintings were temporarily removed from the gallery by the 
museum’s staff and taken to the laboratories downstairs for the various recordings, 
after which they were put back on display. 3D scanning was the most time-
consuming process. Lucida’s head operates from a set distance of about 10 cm to the 
painting, automatically sliding sideways at a constant speed. Surface is recorded in 
modular sections or tiles of 48 × 48 cm, each taking 1 hour to complete. The scanner 
functions according to a ﬁxed relation between its mechanical speed, the video 
frame rate, the USB’s connection speed, and the ﬁle’s spatial resolution, meaning 
there is no way to accelerate this process. 30 The smallest painting in the series, 
Two Old Men eating , whose dimensions are 49.3 × 83.4 cm, was scanned in just 
about 2 hours; however, a vast work like Witches’ Sabbath, or the Great He-Goat , 
measuring 140.5 × 435.7 cm, required a minimum of 32 hours to be digitized. 31 The 
combined area of the series covered approximately 33 square meters, equivalent to 
an estimated duration of 330 hours for the project’s completion. 
Observing a precise, slowly moving red line of light on a painting’s surface is 
mesmerizing. With a ﬂuid, uninterrupted motion, the line contorts and conforms to 
the painting’s topography. It meticulously portrays the artwork’s relief, presenting

francisco-de-goyas-black-paintings-c-1819-1823 
29 The project was instigated by Miguel Zugaza, Museo del Prado’s Director, 2002–2017, and 
Manuela Mena, Head of the Department of Conservation of 18th-century Painting and Goya, 
1978–2019. The work was supervised by Enrique Quintana, Head of the Paintings Restoration 
Department. From Factum Arte, the work was coordinated by Adam Lowe, Director and Carlos 
Bayod, Project Director. 
30 Factum Arte , “Lucida Manual”, Factum Arte, https://www.factum-arte.com/resources/ﬁles/ff/ 
manuals/01_web_assembly_lucida_booklet_2018_factum_foundation_pdf 
31 Museo del Prado , “Two Old Meneating”, Museo del Prado, https://www.museodelprado.es/en/ 
the-collection/art-work/two-old-men-eating/67eecb35-18d3-4377-9482-739713680b42 
Museo del Prado , “Witches’ Sabbath, or the Great He-Goat”, Museo del Prado, https://www. 
museodelprado.es/en/the-collection/art-work/witches-sabbath-or-the-great-he-goat/09559184-
cfeb-48fe-8acc-89b070b64d92 

226 C. B. Lucini
a sequence of evolving proﬁles on the computer screen. The recording process 
offered the rare opportunity to spend long hours in front of each painting, isolated 
from any distraction. This made the experience of observing the Black Paintings 
at the scanner’s pace radically different from the usual perception at the museum’s 
galleries. After some time of close, almost intimate inspection, certain details and 
general patterns on the surface began to become clearer (Fig. 4). 
In real time, the scanner showed on-screen different previews of the 3D data 
being captured. These images enabled a direct comparison between the naked-eye 
observation of a painting and the digital reconstruction of its relief. Unlike the 
photographs taken with raking light three decades ago, these shaded renders showed 
the painting’s orography without the color. And, perhaps more importantly, the 
scans allowed the relief to be measured. Through the mediation of the 3D scanner, 
the Black Paintings were translated into a new kind of visual language: a digital 
depth map waiting to be interpreted (Figs. 5 and 6). 
Upon completion of the recording phase, the processing of the data took place 
in Factum Arte’s studios. The individual shots of every image type, as well as the 
3D scanning tiles, were aligned using PTGui software, to compose the so-called 
panoramas of the entire painting area. The panoramas of each painting were then 
superimposed in accurate registration, to form a multilayered ﬁle in which all images 
were made to coincide. Taking the 3D render as a base of reference, the panorama 
of the visible color was registered on top with Photoshop. The process involved 
performing slight distortions to the color data, in a semi-automatic process to match 
every detail in the image with its corresponding detail in the surface relief. 
The same method was applied to each of the additional layers of information 
provided by the Museo del Prado, such as infrared reﬂectography, x-ray radiography, 
and ultraviolet photography. These multilayered ﬁles made it possible to inspect on 
screen, both in isolation and superimposed, ﬁve different recordings of each painting 
in high resolution. The result of this pioneer initiative was a new set of digital images 
that offered the most accurate, detailed, and complete documentation of the Black 
Paintings to date. 32 
In addition to the new recordings, the multilayered ﬁles also incorporated the 
well-known series of photographs of the paintings taken by Jean Laurent in 1874, 
not long before they were removed from the walls of the Quinta del Sordo and 
transferred to canvas. 33 These photographs show black and white depictions of each 
painting, photographed with artiﬁcial light. The images also prominently display

Aligning and merging extensive images to generate multilayered ﬁles proved a 
time-consuming task. The hours dedicated to ensuring each color detail synchro-
nized precisely with its corresponding element in the 3D render offered Factum 
Arte an additional chance for meticulous examination of Goya’s works, this time 
in front of the computer screen. Being able to examine the intricate surface of the 
Black Paintings as a layered stack of digital information, with the ability to activate 
or deactivate datasets, broadened the perception of the artworks and facilitated a 
deeper understanding that extends beyond the museum’s gallery. 
Through digital technology, the paintings underwent another transformation, 
this time in a non-contact, non-invasive manner: from canvas to the computer 
screen. While the murals were removed from the walls in 1874 using the strappato 
technique to become moveable artifacts, the 2014 recordings made the artworks 
accessible as digital images. However, unlike traditional ﬂat imaging techniques 
that offer a limited representation, the 3D scanning technology allowed the entire 
complexity of the surface to be transferred to a new virtual medium. This was 
particularly important for the Black Paintings because their surface relief holds a 
rich store of information about their historical journey.

Digitization and Reproduction of Surface: Shedding New Light on Goya’s ... 229
4 Learning Through Imitation 
And yet another transition is possible: the conversion of the digital data into 
physical replicas. After documenting the Black Paintings, Factum Arte successfully 
experimented with techniques to reproduce the color and relief of various artworks’ 
surfaces. The Lucida 3D Scanner has made it possible to capture the shape and 
texture of paintings, and composite panoramic photography captures the color. But 
the challenge has always been how to transfer this digital information back to a 
material medium, while maintaining the details and character of the original. 
The digital data’s resolution captured through these techniques is higher than 
what is realistically possible to obtain with subtractive fabrication. Therefore, 
CNC milling, which was employed in previous replicas of wall paintings (like the 
facsimiles of the tombs of Seti I or Tutankhamun) cannot be used to rematerialize 
the intricate detail of an oil painting on canvas, since vital details would be lost such 
as the brushstroke and the weave of the fabric. Thus, the focus turned to additive 
fabrication—or 3D printing—to achieve the greatest possible correspondence with 
the original’s surface. 
With this in mind, Factum Arte contacted the Dutch company Océ-Technologies 
BV (part of the Canon group), interested in their recent invention known as Elevated 
Printing.34 Evolved as an experimental adaptation of Océ’s series of large format 
Arizona printers, the patented technique of Elevated Printing allowed to print color 
and texture simultaneously, building surface relief up to a maximum of about 
20 mm. Using a special combination of UV-curable inks and resin, the relief is 
printed as a stack of layers of 10 microns (0.01 mm) thick, which solidiﬁes instantly 
under UV light. This technique can produce physical relief in high resolution using 
a grayscale depth map: just the ﬁle type generated by the Lucida system. 
A collaboration emerged in 2015 between Factum Arte and Océ that pushed 
Elevated Printing ’s development to meet the challenging needs of cultural heritage 
preservation. The focus was on the reproduction of “2.5D” surfaces, that is, 
generally ﬂat shapes with detailed texture features. Since then, Factum Arte has 
employed and adapted Océ’s Elevated Printing technology to reproduce the surface 
of hundreds of paintings and other objects of shallow relief. Unlike subtractive 
fabrication, this technique allows texture to be printed with the same resolution as 
the scanned data. 
However, Elevated Printing is just the start of the process. Making a facsimile 
involves a number of steps, complex blends of materials and techniques, and critical 
attention to detail. Digital technology and craftsmanship must be combined with 
each other to produce an accurate visual restitution of the original surface. 35 The 
Elevated Printing technology prototypes the relief information of a painting. The 
surface texture printed with the Océ system is used to obtain a silicone mold out of
34 Project Eiger , “Eiger. Elevated printing”, Project Eiger, https://www.projecteiger.com/ 
35 For more information about the facsimiles realized by Factum Arte, see: Factum Arte , “Digiti-
zation & Facsimiles”, Factum Arte, https://www.factum-arte.com/ind/559/digitization-facsimiles 

230 C. B. Lucini
it—as when copying a bas-relief sculpture. This is to cast the texture in a skin made 
with acrylic resin coated with gesso, a few millimeters thick, ﬁxed to a canvas. The 
aim of this operation is to obtain an exact reproduction in white of the 3D relief, 
attached to a ﬂexible material. The color is then printed (in perfect registration) 
over this white textured material, using a ﬂatbed printer designed and developed 
by Factum Arte. 36 The ﬁnal steps differ depending on each particular project, but 
typically involve hand-varnishing and ﬁxing the canvas to a stretcher (Fig. 7). 
The result of this process is an object that, although being made with different 
materials and techniques than the original painting, faithfully recreates its visual 
qualities. Unlike any ﬂat, 2D print (which offers a static or “frozen” version of a 
painting), the facsimile’s interaction of the color with the relief allows light to work 
on the surface in a dynamic way, just like it does on the original. Therefore, when 
the facsimile is observed under similar lighting conditions, it is indistinguishable 
from the original. 
A conservation facsimile seeks to accurately recreate all the complexity and 
character of an artwork, avoiding any simpliﬁcation so one can learn and appreciate 
it almost as much as in the presence of the original. Mastering the technique 
of reproducing paintings has taken Factum Arte many years of research and 
experimentation. From the non-contact recording of the original to the hand-
ﬁnishing of the facsimile, the task is nothing but a sophisticated process of imitation, 
aimed at grasping and transmitting the authenticity of the work of art: copying as an 
inquiry into the truth. 
What could we discover about the Black Paintings by making facsimiles of them? 
Could new insights emerge from reproducing the paintings and presenting them 
in a different context? Leveraging the digital data of relief and color captured in 
2014, combined with the advanced capabilities of current fabrication techniques 
for replicating 3D surfaces, there is now a deﬁnite possibility for another shift— 
from digital ﬁles to tangible facsimiles. Factum Arte has offered its technology 
and expertise to collaborate with the Museo del Prado in exploring the concept of 
producing one replica of each of the Black Paintings. These replicas could form 
part of a physical reconstruction of the interior spaces of the Quinta del Sordo, 
potentially becoming a traveling exhibition that serves to promote the preservation, 
examination, and dissemination of Goya’s masterpieces. This initiative would 
complement the unparalleled experience of viewing the originals in the museum 
gallery. 
5 Data for a Material Reconstruction 
Our current understanding of the appearance of the Black Paintings is based on our 
access to the series housed in the Museo del Prado alongside the digital surface

scans conducted a decade ago. This is sufﬁcient information to produce facsimiles 
of the artworks in their current condition. We also have an idea of how the paintings 
originally looked on the walls of Goya’s house, through the photographs taken by 
Laurent in 1874, combined with earlier engravings and verbal descriptions (mostly 
from the 1860s). These records would be essential to recover the paintings’ original

232 C. B. Lucini
dimensions or to perform a hypothetical process of digital de-restoration of certain 
elements, enabling the facsimiles to incorporate the characteristics of the paintings 
prior to their transfer to canvas. 37 However, there is no reliable information about the 
Quinta del Sordo’s interior spaces, or about the exact arrangement of the paintings 
on the walls. The only surviving sources are testimonies by the few individuals 
who visited the house in the nineteenth century. These written accounts contain 
varying levels of precision. 38 Thus, the proposed reconstruction would present exact 
facsimiles of the Black Paintings in a setting that is, necessarily, an approximate 
recreation. 
Nigel Glendinning’s article published in 1986 contains some of the most 
comprehensive research on the attributes of the vanished “Goya’s Country House 
in Madrid.” 39 More recently, the thorough research conducted by Carlos Foradada 
has made it possible to determine the precise morphology and dimensions of the 
building, with special attention to the rooms where the paintings were located on the 
ground ﬂoor and ﬁrst ﬂoor. In 2021, Foradada completed a detailed reconstruction 
of the interior spaces, which must be considered one of the main references for 
any recreation to be realized. In his research, Foradada concludes that the internal 
dimensions of the main spaces would have been 1005.8 ×  487.6 cm (33 ′ × 16′)f o r 
the ground ﬂoor’s dining room and 853.4 × 487.6 cm (28 ′ × 16′) for the ﬁrst ﬂoor’s 
living room.40

canvas and subsequent restoration: mainly changes of size and proportions, as well as alterations of 
Goya’s compositions, ﬁgures or the tonal balance executed by Martínez Cubells. The main events 
that occurred in this period are summarized by Glendinning as follows: “The French banker of 
German origin, Baron Frédéric-Emil d’Erlanger ( ...  ) bought the house in March 1873.” In 1874 
he commissioned to Laurent the photographs of the paintings, shortly before commissioning their 
transfer to canvas. The wing of the house where the paintings were located was demolished in 1876. 
The paintings on canvas were shown on the Great Exhibition in Paris in 1878 and were given “to the 
Spanish government three years later. Salvador Martinez Cubells (1845–1914), an artist who had 
been appointed Chief Restorer at the Prado ( ... ), supervised the transfer and restored the paintings 
between 1874 and 1878.” For more information, see: Nigel Glendinning, “The Strange Translation

The main hypothesis concerning the original arrangement of the paintings 
accepted today is built on the foundations of three testimonies from visitors to the 
Quinta del Sordo: an “inventory” of the contents of the house dated in the 1820s, 
attributed to Goya’s friend Antonio Brugada—the earliest known depiction of the 
Black Paintings; Charles Yriarte’s description of the paintings and their locations 
that appeared in his biography of the artist from 1867; 41 and a description written by 
the French journalist Pierre Imbert included in his travel book about Spain published 
in 1875.42 “Brugada’s inventory” lists a total of 15 paintings that decorated the walls 
of two rooms. Identifying them can be difﬁcult, as the provided titles are imprecise, 
and it is possible that he references the same painting multiple times. 43 Yriarte, a 
French writer of Spanish origin, seems to offer more clarity when allocating the 
paintings in each room. Although it contains some level of ambiguity, his text is 
regarded as the primary attempt to reconstruct the original arrangement of the Black 
Paintings. 
Yriarte begins by mentioning six paintings on the ground ﬂoor. The general 
assumption is that he locates the paintings in relation to his subjective viewpoint 
looking forward into the room as he enters through the door. For example, “the ﬁrst, 
the one on the left, represents a portrait of a woman whose mantilla is pulled down 
over her face” 44 —today known as A Manola: Leocadia Zorrilla . He then describes 
the painting that would have been on the same wall—entitled Two Old Men —in 
these terms: “The counterpart of this portrait is a character with a long white beard, 
strangely dressed.”45 The speciﬁc French term used is “le pendant,” which could be 
translated here as symmetric or equivalent , inferring that the two paintings on the 
same wall should be interpreted as forming a pair. 
He goes on by describing the two paintings on the opposite wall—entitled Saturn 
and Judith and Holofernes —and then the large paintings on the longer walls: “The 
one on the left can be called the Sabbath ”—this is Witches’ Sabbath, or the Great 
He-Goat; “The right panel, of the same size, represents The Pilgrimage to San 
Isidro.”46 This account has established the widely accepted arrangement of the

The placement of two paintings (or compositions) “to the right of the door” is 
thought to be an error made by Yriarte—possibly a memory lapse when transcribing 
his notes. The accepted assumption is that there would have been one painting on 
either side of the middle door: The Drowning Dog , which he regards as incomplete, 
and another painting that no longer exists, as per his own description, since it had 
already been detached from the walls and relocated to the palace of Vista Alegre (in 
Carabanchel). 
His narrative continues describing one of the four large paintings in the room: 
“The ﬁrst panel of the large wall on the left could be called In the Clouds. ”49 
Judging by his description, he is referring to Atropos or The Fates . But the question 
remains as to whether Yriarte was “looking” into the room when he refers to “the 
large wall on the left” or, instead, he was looking back towards the door he just 
crossed. The former option is generally assumed, but the latter is also possible. 
Next, he proceeds to describe Duel with Cudgels , considering it as forming a 
pair with The Fates : “The composition which acts as a counterpart represents two 
poorly dressed men, two herdsmen who strike each other with fury, armed with 
terrible sticks.” 50 Once again, the French term “pendant” is employed by Yriarte 
for a counterpart, so it is conventionally accepted that both paintings were on the 
same wall. 
The two paintings on the end wall, opposite to the entrance, are Reading and Two 
Women and a Man , “ﬁgures without a deﬁned action.” 51 Yriarte does not specify 
their respective position, but it is assumed that Reading is on the left and Two Women 
and a Man on the right, due to the order in which he describes them, from left to 
right. 
Yriarte concludes his report by describing the other two large paintings in 
the room: “The right side is divided, like the one facing it, into two parts. One 
is a beautiful landscape, with a path that runs alongside a rock.” 52 This is The 
Inquisition. It is subsequently presumed that the following painting was the second 
one on the same “right side” wall, though he does not explicitly say it. His words 
are: “The last composition obviously contains an allusion [sic].” This illusion (or, 
in fact, allusion to a classical text) can be identiﬁed as Asmodea : “This painting has 
a beautiful effect; it is the most colorful.” 53

accepted layout). From the lower right image, clockwise: Atropos or The Fates—Duel with 
Cudgels—Reading—Two Women and a Man—The Inquisition—Asmodea—The Drowning Dog — 
and, according to Yriarte, one that “no longer exists.”. Images © Archivo Fotográﬁco del Museo 
Nacional del Prado 
In summary, with the exception of the initial two compositions (one of which 
the author deemed unﬁnished and the other no longer in existence), he seems to 
have provided a consecutive account of the paintings in the room, following a 
clockwise order. It is based on this presumption that the widely accepted layout of 
the Black Paintings on the ﬁrst ﬂoor has been established, believed to be a faithful 
interpretation of Yriarte’s verbal description, despite some inherent ambiguities 
(Fig. 9). 
6 A Panorama of the Black Paintings 
The creation of facsimiles of the Black Paintings for a physical recreation of 
the interior of Goya’s house offers a unique opportunity to reassess established 
presumptions at 1:1 scale. Working with facsimiles rather than the original artworks 
allows literal room for experimentation, and the positioning of the paintings is 
among the elements open to reconsideration. Another intriguing aspect to consider 
is the possible incorporation of a facsimile of the “missing” painting on the ﬁrst 
ﬂoor that Yriarte could not describe because, as he explains, it was already removed

Digitization and Reproduction of Surface: Shedding New Light on Goya’s ... 237
from the walls—probably in the 1830s. 54 This painting could be the one known 
today as Heads in a landscape , which belongs to a private collector in New Y ork. 55 
In his catalogue of Goya’s works, Yriarte clariﬁes that this painting “would not be 
by Goya, but by his son.” 56 If it was possible to realize a digital recording of its 
surface for comparison with the data from the other Black Paintings, it could lead to 
the discovery of additional layers of knowledge. 
Irrespective of its authorship, should this painting have once been a constituent of 
the series adorning the house’s walls, its integration into a facsimile exhibition could 
contribute to a more comprehensive interpretation of the entire series. Heads in a 
landscape would have been the counterpart of The Drowning Dog . Both paintings 
would have shared the short wall at the entrance of the room on the Quinta’s 
ﬁrst ﬂoor, and both would have had a similar size and proportion. Heads ’ current 
dimensions are different from the Dog ’s. However, it is essential to note that during 
the challenging transfer from the wall to canvas and the subsequent restoration 
process, the painting’s dimensions might have been modiﬁed. The Drowning Dog 
is now a few centimeters higher than it seems to be in Laurent’s photograph, while 
Heads in a landscape has probably lost part of the image, along the left and top 
edges. However, if we look at the two paintings side by side, as they would have been 
in Goya’s house, there seems to be a clear continuation of the lines of the landscape. 
The curve of the Dog ’s foreground keeps ascending in the Heads . And the rock 
or mountain at the background of The Drowning Dog , whose contour was once 
more precise than it is today, continues in the background of Heads in a Landscape 
(Figs. 10 and 11). 
Now, let us broaden the perspective. Could the same landscape extend beyond 
these two paintings? The line in the foreground of The Drowning Dog continues 
its descent to the left in Asmodea (on the adjacent wall), then promptly ascends 
to outline another steep mountain, whose silhouette bears a resemblance to the 
preceding one. The cohesive expanse of color in the background of both paintings

appears to depict the same sky. But, if we direct our gaze to the right of Heads in a 
Landscape, we only discover continuity with Duel with Cudgels . Here, the horizon 
line seamlessly connects; the background is no longer a golden mass of color but has 
turned into a colder-toned clouded sky shared by the two images. No other painting 
in the room suggests a more natural continuation—certainly not The Fates , generally 
considered to be placed at the left of that long wall, opposite Asmodea . So, leaving 
aside for a moment any interpretation of Yriarte’s text and looking carefully at the 
pictures (both in their current condition and in Laurent’s images), a new hypothesis 
emerges that invites us to reconsider the original arrangement of the paintings on 
the ﬁrst ﬂoor (Fig. 12). 
To the right of Duel with Cudgels , the line of the landscape and the clouded sky 
continues in The Inquisition (traditionally believed to have been on the opposite 
wall). And to the left of Asmodea , the dark foreground with tree-like shapes extends 
in The Fates , whose sky and general tone is also warm and golden-hued. Thus, 
the resulting sequence would be like this: The Fates—Asmodea—The Drowning 
Dog—Heads in a Landscape—Duel with Cudgels—The Inquisition. As the main 
lines of the landscape align across the paintings, the sky’s hue gradually transitions 
from warmer (golden) to cooler tones, hinting at a potential cycle from night to day 
(Figs. 13, 14, and 15).

The two smaller paintings on the end wall, Reading and Two Women and a Man , 
currently show static ﬁgures on a black, undeﬁned background, so their speciﬁc 
order in the sequence is not evident. A study of the x-ray data might help discerning 
lines of a landscape underneath. It is important to recall that the depiction of 
landscape scenes on the wall, conceivably painted by Goya himself, preceded the 
addition of ﬁgures at a later stage. This ultimately culminated in the creation of the 
Black Paintings that we currently recognize and appreciate. As inferred by Carmen 
Garrido from the x-ray analyses conducted in 1984, 
The walls of the two rooms painted in the Quinta del Sordo had in the ﬁrst place 
a different meaning. Goya made a very simple decoration through clear landscapes 
and bright lights with very wide clouds. The lines that outline the mountains and

242 C. B. Lucini
deﬁne the perspective are in the foreground. It is frequent the drawing of mountains 
cutting the landscape diagonally from side to side. 57 
The continuation in the lines of landscape among contiguous paintings is not 
an unusual concept. The tradition of decorating a room with a continuous mural 
scene has a long history in art and architecture, spanning centuries. It has often been 
employed to dissolve the boundaries of walls and create an immersive representation 
of the surrounding natural environment. 
In the early nineteenth century, a similar experience was created, culturally and 
technically adapted to the spirit of the times: the panorama. Unlike a private room, 
panoramas were designed as popular spectacles for urban audiences. Built as 360-
degree representations of natural or artiﬁcial landscapes, panoramas were also used 
to place the viewer in the center of action of historic battles or events. 
It is unlikely that Goya had the opportunity to personally witness a panorama 
during his lifetime, at least not before his departure for Paris in 1824 when he 
left Spain and the Quinta along with the Black Paintings. However, he might have 
been aware of their existence through accounts in the press or through testimonies 
of others who had experienced them ﬁrsthand. In any case, Goya had already 
represented continuous or cyclic scenes, in the tradition of neoclassical fresco 
painting—e.g., in Saragossa’s Monastery of Aula Dei or in the church of San 
Antonio de la Florida in Madrid (Fig. 16). 
The proposed alternative layout of the facsimiles on the top ﬂoor arranges the 
paintings in a cyclic sequence; this challenges previously accepted hypotheses, but 
it is also compatible with numerous common interpretations of the Black Paintings’ 
iconography which, for example, suggest symbolic links between pairs of images: 
The Fates and Asmodea ; Duel with Cudgels; and The Inquisition. 58 The distinction 
lies in the fact that, rather than positioning these related paintings on opposite walls, 
each pair would occupy the same wall. 
To substantiate this prospect, let us carefully review Laurent’s images once more. 
His photographs are believed to depict the Black Paintings while they were still

con un sentido diferente. Goya realizó una decoración muy simple por medio de paisajes claros 
y luminosos de celajes muy amplios. Las líneas que contornean las montañas y delimitan la 
perspectiva se sitúan en primer plano. Es frecuente el dibujo de las montañas, cortando el paisaje 
en diagonal de un lado a otro. La presencia de personajes no es importante en este momento de sus 
pinturas, tan sólo aparecen algunas pequeñas ﬁguritas situadas en las partes bajas de las escenas”.

103–1183; Tzvetan Todorov, Goya. A la sombra de las luces (Barcelona: Galaxia Gutenberg, 
2017), 193.

situated in the Quinta, prior to their transfer onto canvas. Notably, a portion of 
the rooms’ decorative wallpaper is discernible in the images, surrounding each 
painting beyond the decorative frame. Our suggested reconﬁguration would position 
The Fates and Asmodea on the long wall to the right upon entering the room, and 
the alignment of the wallpaper pattern with the upper horizontal frame appears to 
bolster this hypothesis. On the opposite wall, Duel with Cudgels and The Inquisition 
also exhibit a cohesive arrangement. The row of pattern motifs is interrupted by the 
frame at the same height for the two paintings sharing that wall. When examining 
these details, it becomes difﬁcult to defend a different layout (Figs. 17, 18, 19, 20, 
and 21).

7 Conclusions 
The effort to recreate the interior of the Quinta del Sordo with facsimiles of 
the Black Paintings presents an exceptional chance to reevaluate long-standing 
assumptions regarding this extraordinary series. The inclusion of a facsimile of 
Heads in a landscape (possibly the 15th painting in the sequence) would help 
experts to compare it with the others as a life-sized recreation, potentially triggering 
fresh perspectives on its attribution. Moreover, the use of facsimiles could also 
test the hypothesis of an alternative arrangement of the paintings on the ﬁrst ﬂoor, 
opening the door to new lines of research. 
The facsimiles would add new layers of information for the study and appre-
ciation of the artworks, if only by allowing viewers to enter a recreation of the 
rooms in Goya’s house and see the paintings talk to each other. When viewed 
from a suitable distance and under historically appropriate lighting conditions, 
this recreation should enhance our comprehension of the signiﬁcance and intent 
behind Goya’s artistic endeavor. As a supplement to the experience of beholding 
the originals at the Museo del Prado, a faithful physical reproduction achieved with 
digital technologies would inevitably shed new light on the Black Paintings.
