Manufacturing of Sculpture in the Digital 
Age 
Francisco Javier Santos Martín , Elena Merino-Gómez , 
and Manuel San-Juan 
1 Introduction: “Lesœuvres acquerront une sorte 
d’ubiquité” 
“Comme l’eau, comme le gaz, comme le courant électrique viennent de loin dans 
nos demeures [ ... ] ainsi serons-nous alimentés d’images visuelles ou auditives, 
naissant et s’évanouissant au moindre geste, presque à un signe”1 (Valéry, 1934,p . 
84). Almost 100 years ago, Paul Valéry reﬂected in his famous essay “La conquête 
de l’ubiquité” on the immense possibilities that transmissibility granted for “con-
quering the ubiquity” of artistic work. However, Valéry thought that in the 1920s, 
one was still quite far from mastering and transmitting “visible phenomena,” unlike 
the possibilities that already existed then for reproducing music. Nevertheless, he 
emphatically asserted, referring to the future of the still “rebellious” transmission of 
“la couleur et le relief,” that “Cela se fera” (Valéry, 1934, p. 86). 
Paul Valéry’s prediction instantly evokes the immediacy with which it is now 
possible to transmit all kinds of information, including the artistic one, as if it 
were a household supply. With a simple gesture, practically with a signal, it would 
be possible, in the future envisioned by the French poet, for images or sounds to 
emerge or fade away, so that artistic expression would be capable of reaching distant 
destinations instantly. Valéry’s thought revealed a visionary intuition of artistic 
virtuality. 
1 “Like water, like gas, like electricity come from afar into our homes [...] so will we be supplied 
with visual or auditory images, arising and vanishing at the slightest gesture, almost at a sign” 
(Valéry, 1934, p. 84). 
Unless otherwise indicated, all translations are our own. 
F. J. Santos Martín · E. Merino-Gómez (/envelopeback) · M. San-Juan 
Universidad de Valladolid, Valladolid, Spain 
e-mail: francisco.santos@uva.es; elena.merino.gomez@uva.es; mansan@uva.es 
© The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2024 
F. Moral-Andrés et al. (eds.), Decoding Cultural Heritage, 
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-57675-1_11
249

250 F. J. Santos Martín et al.
While it is true that since the 1960s there have been artistic expressions that 
operate partially or exclusively in the digital realm, either in their creative processes 
or in their performative aspects (Paul, 2016), during their more than half a century 
of existence, they have proven to be complementary rather than substitutive to 
traditional physical art. The uneven reception of digital artworks, from their early 
and varied manifestations (Paul, 2003) to the controversial non-fungible tokens 
(NFTs), has led to their expansion in the art market being similarly diverse. The 
acquisition of tangible artistic creations currently enjoys excellent health despite the 
immense possibilities offered by purely digital environments. 
The exhaustive digitization of three-dimensional objects belonging to cultural 
heritage through photogrammetry or laser scanning (Argyridou et al., 2023) enables 
the creation of what Bolton and Cora ( 2021) refer to as Virtual Equivalents of 
Real Objects (VEROs). Major museums worldwide have been digitizing the most 
valuable pieces from their collections at extremely high resolutions for decades 
(Weber, 2018; Ulaby, 2021; Rühse, 2017; Eveno, 2018) for various purposes. The 
era in which, with the “slightest gesture,” we can make a digital representation of 
an artistic piece emerge or fade away instantly is here to stay. 
2 From Digital Data to Material Artifacts: “l’étonnant 
accroissement de nos moyens”2 
The open availability of high-resolution digitizations greatly increases the possibil-
ities of manufacturing authentic material clones from digital data. This is among 
the main reasons why institutions housing works of art are hesitant to share them 
(Wenman, 2019). The Smithsonian Institution began the massive task of digitizing 
its collection of 137 million objects in 2009 (Osborn, 2014). However, only a small 
quantity of them, and not necessarily the most signiﬁcant ones, are freely accessible. 
The economic return that the sale of VEROs in the form of NFTs (Maida, 2022) 
as well as high-tech reproductions of masterpieces (Holland, 2023; Sansom, 2020) 
could bring to museum institutions versus the democratizing possibilities entangled 
by virtual or material enjoyment of artwork, or by the repatriation of heritage in 
digital or physical formats, is part of a heated debate in the last decade (Alberge, 
2013; Samaroudi & Rodríguez Echevarría, 2019). 
Despite the ease with which digital data is transmitted and globally multiplied 
in the present, its materialization into physical objects poses various problems. On 
one hand, there are ethical-philosophical considerations questioning aspects such as 
the loss of aura (Benjamin, 1969) or the relative value of an original when copied 
massively or without rigorous criteria (Krauss, 1981), the control of copyright, and 
the immense possibilities of distorting original forms through digital techniques.
2 “The surprising increase in our means” (Valéry, 1934, p. 83). 

Manufacturing of Sculpture in the Digital Age 251
The questions regarding the materialization of three-dimensional artistic work 
from its digital data fundamentally depend on its nature and objectives. The manu-
facturing of complete replicas that even use the same materials as the original, the 
creation of facsimiles seeking the appearance of similarity from diverse materials, 
the production of unpublished works from existing historical data (Merino Gómez et 
al., 2021), the manufacturing of contemporary art from creations with digital tools, 
or the low-cost mass production of iconic objects from art history represent areas of 
three-dimensional production with very diverse consequences. 
“The surprising increase in our means” (Valéry, 1934, p. 83) has currently 
reached micrometric precision in data acquisition capabilities, to the extent that even 
two-dimensional works, such as serigraphs, frescoes, or paintings, can be treated 
as three-dimensional, almost sculptural objects (Bayod Lucini, 2022). However, 
when it comes to creating an artistic clone based on what data acquisition tools and 
software can store and process, technical means still suffer from limitations. Even in 
our technological present, with a wide catalog of highly roboticized manufacturing 
tools, with micrometric scopes and enormous programming possibilities, the manual 
component remains necessary, for the time being, in the production of high-quality 
replicas and facsimiles. 
On the other hand, the possibilities that 3D digital printing currently offers 
for the serial manufacturing of artistic reproductions are unprecedented. When 
pop art emerged in the late 1950s, reclaiming connections between artistic work 
and serial production through pieces that criticized or exalted mass production 
and consumption (Madoff, 1997), no one suspected the revolution that 3D digital 
reproducibility would cause in the art world in just a few decades. 
The instantaneous availability, despite restrictions often imposed by owners 
or exhibiting institutions (Sansom, 2021), of digitized data and the widespread 
use of 3D printing technology offer new perspectives in the large-scale physical 
dissemination of models, bringing us to some extent closer to the kind of telepor-
tation envisioned by Valéry when he referred to the possibility of “transporting or 
reconstituting in any place the system of sensations [ ... ] provided anywhere by any 
object or any event”3 (Valéry, 1934, p. 84). 
3 The Mass Production of Three-Dimensional Artifacts 
in Artisanal and Artistic Contexts 
The materialization of three-dimensional virtual data through highly sophisticated 
tools renews, improves, and multiplies the options for mass production compared 
to the possibilities that existed just over a century ago. During the Second Indus-
trial Revolution (Hounshell, 1985), mass production systems became widespread,
3 “[... ] transporter ou reconstituer en tout lieu le système de sensations [... ] que dispense en un 
lieu quelconque un objet ou un événement quelconque” (Valéry, 1934, p. 84). 

252 F. J. Santos Martín et al.
particularly efﬁcient for manufacturing identical objects. Assembly lines and the 
successive automation of processes contributed to modifying the social and eco-
nomic landscape globally. The possibilities of producing thousands of copies of 
virtually any object faced ﬁerce opposition in its early stages from those involved 
in traditional arts. The anti-modern desire to return to pre-industrial modes of 
production (Stankiewicz, 1992), however, contradicted some of the mass production 
systems that have characterized a signiﬁcant part of artisanal and artistic production 
throughout history. 
Repetitive manufacturing processes, traditionally employed in the production of 
practical objects such as amphorae, lamps, tiles, or bricks, were also applied to the 
methods of producing less utilitarian and more artistic items. Thus, in antiquity, 
the serial production of votive ﬁgurines destined for offerings in sanctuaries to 
express gratitude and piety or seek favors from the gods was common. Despite 
the exceptional nature of devotional objects and their transcendent function, their 
manufacturing processes were analogous to those of more mundane items. There 
is evidence that, in some cases, when it came to terracotta images, they were 
manufactured in the same facilities where everyday utensils like household pottery 
were produced (Barletta, 2006). 
The serial production of small-scale bronzes around 900 B.C. in the vicinity of 
the sanctuary of Olympia (Mattusch, 2006), the mass production of Egyptian votive 
bronze statuettes dating from the seventh century B.C. onwards (Leahy, 1988), the 
small terracotta ﬁgures molded in Tanagra (Greece) from 500 B.C. to 200 B.C. 
(Higgins, 1986, p. 66), or the affordable terracottas of Attis, mass produced in 
connection with the cult of the goddess Cybele in the second century B.C. (Turcan, 
1997, pp. 40–41), are just a few examples that demonstrate how, since antiquity, 
there has been a close relationship between serialization and the production of 
similar products in realms that transcend the mere functionality of the pieces. 
The mass serialization of ﬁgurines in archaic cults throughout the Mediterranean 
would gradually be replaced in the Christian period by the increasingly unique 
production of devotional objects. In artifacts such as altarpieces, funerary sculpture, 
or processional items, uniqueness will become a parameter adding value to manu-
facturing, and production will be subordinated to speciﬁc demand. Such productions 
are within the reach of wealthy individuals or collectives that can afford unique 
commissions through collaborative cost-sharing. 
However, in more popular aspects of Christian culture, small-scale widely 
distributed religious products continue to be made available to the public, whose 
religious functions little differ from those intended in antiquity (Talloen, 2011, 
p. 593). The mass production of reliquaries in various materials such as plaster 
or terracotta ensured their availability in the market at affordable prices (Renkin, 
2021). The production in multiple copies of small ﬁgurines of saints for small altars, 
domestic or urban, the mass production of ﬁgurines linked to Marian worship sites, 
or the production of all kinds of votive offerings in wax, plaster, plastic, silver, etc., 
depicting diseased body parts, whose healing is prayed for or thanked for (Weinyrb, 
2018) are many other objects that have been manufactured, marketed, and acquired 
on various scales from the Middle Ages to the present moment (Holmes, 2009).

Manufacturing of Sculpture in the Digital Age 253
Beyond devotional uses, from the Renaissance onward, decorative objects began 
to be integrated into the domestic setting. The Dovizie from the workshop of the 
Florentine Giovanni dellaRobbia (Randolph, 2002), and from the eighteenth century 
onward, the renowned ﬁgures from the Ginori workshops, or the highly prized 
decorative vases from Josiah Wedgwood (Holt & Popp, 2016), in the latter half 
of the same century, straddle the line between mass production and the creation of 
similar pieces with some variations. 
No movement had more impact than the Arts and Crafts movement in challeng-
ing the boundaries between artisanal craftsmanship and industrial production in the 
late nineteenth century (Boris, 1986). During the same period, the dissemination 
of small-scale domestic sculpture, produced through mold repetition, gradually 
moved away from the perception of luxury from previous centuries and began 
entering homes. At the same time, it sparked controversies about the originality 
and authorship of such manufactures (Gosse, 1895). 
Additionally, other aspects related to specialization and the loss of identity 
inherent in mass production processes (Luckman, 2012), or the decline in value 
that multiplication bestows upon the artwork, would extend into theoretical debates 
throughout the twentieth century (McDonald, 2004; Benjamin, 1969; Siebenbrodt & 
Schöbe, 2009; Mag Uidhir, 2013). These debates would be renewed with the advent 
of digital technologies in the twenty-ﬁrst century. The traditional perception that 
industrial multiplication is contrary to the singularity of the artwork is criticized but 
also fades through the serialized productions of many artists in the second half of 
the twentieth century. Works by artists like Sol LeWitt, Juan Muñoz, or Jeff Koons 
leverage the resources that mass production offers to create “new originalities” in 
the realm of artistic sculpture. 
4 Hoc Opus Hic Labor: The Difﬁcult Task of Producing 
Artistic Three-Dimensional Manufactures 
The intrinsic difﬁculties of reproducing visual information have been evident since 
the early days of printing (Bland, 1974). Woodcuts, engravings, or lithographs 
are based on the principles of laborious incision on rigid surfaces to allow for 
subsequent serial printing. It would be necessary to wait until the late nineteenth 
century, with the advent of photomechanical reproduction processes (Grifﬁths, 
1996) and their subsequent reﬁnement throughout the twentieth century, to observe 
the deﬁnitive democratization in the reception of visual arts. Mechanization in 
image reproduction would contribute not only to the dissemination and fame of 
many paintings and photographs now globally recognized (Beegan, 2007) but also 
to the knowledge, albeit in two-dimensional form, of the masterpieces of sculpture. 
Nevertheless, the “conquest of ubiquity” in terms analogous to those achieved for 
the dissemination of two-dimensional images or music still had to wait for three-
dimensional objects. Although, as mentioned in the previous section, the almost

254 F. J. Santos Martín et al.
industrial production of volumetric pieces has never been foreign to artistic contexts, 
the intrinsic difﬁculties in their manufacture, especially in larger-scale objects, have 
always limited them to a small number of copies and an eminently afﬂuent audience. 
The levels of industrialization reached by sculpture production in Italy in the sec-
ond half of the eighteenth century are well-known. Renowned workshops received 
commissions from all over Europe (Honour, 1972b), and the speed of production 
had to adapt to the growing demand. Manufactories, many of them producing 
copies of classical sculptures from the workshops of Bartolomeo Cavaceppi and 
Carlo Albacini (Howard, 1991), had extended their reputation to England, Germany, 
France, and Spain (Rotili, 2023). The serial characteristics achieved in the three-
dimensional production of the Piranesi workshop under the direction of his son 
Francesco (Bosso, 2006) satisﬁed, for a time, the extensive demand for artistic 
pieces from Grand Tour travelers. 
Despite the international success of Antonio Canova, spreading to the far reaches 
of Europe and even reaching the United States (Johns, 1998), his methods of 
sculptural manufacturing, incorporating components of mass production, were 
widely criticized by prominent ﬁgures of his time (Honour, 1972a). Stendhal, 
despite holding an excellent opinion of the Veneto sculptor, stating that he was “too 
great not to have opposition”4 (Stendhal, 1818, p. 139), observed, however, that his 
works were the result of the exact copying work done by his assistants in marble 
based on plaster models: 
Ses gens jettent du plâtre sur cette terre [the clayon which Canova hadmodeledhis 
sculpture], font un moule, et reproduisent la statue, en plâtre. Canova la perfectionne, ses 
gens font une copie exacte de la statue de plâtre, en marbre. On transporte le marbre dans 
l’atelier particulier de Canova, qu’il achève. V oilà son seul travail sur le marbre. Il se réduit 
à quelques coups de lime.5 (Stendhal, 1818, p. 139) 
The assembly line manufacturing of Canova’s work allowed him to produce more 
than 350 sculptures between 1769 and 1822 (Pavanello, 1976). This substantial 
production undoubtedly contributed to a literal globalization of the Canovian 
sculptural phenomenon. However, it also garnered numerous criticisms, and the 
production from his workshop almost immediately ceased after his death, despite the 
substantial delegation of the process to a signiﬁcant number of assistants (Fernow, 
1806, pp. 102–103). Four centuries earlier, Michelangelo, using more direct and less 
sophisticated methods, produced around 60 sculptures, many of them unﬁnished 
(Russoli, 1963), despite his sculptor career extending over 75 years (Hartt, 1968) 
and his quick stone carving skills. Blaise de Vigenère recounts how he had the
4 “trop grand pour qu’il n’y ait pas un parti contraire” (Stendhal, 1818, p. 139). 
5 “His people cast plaster on this soil [the clay on which Canova had modeled his sculpture], create 
a mold, and reproduce the statue in plaster. Canova perfects it, and his people make an exact copy 
of the plaster statue in marble. The marble is transported to Canova’s private studio, where he 
completes it. That is his only work on the marble. It comes down to a few strokes of the ﬁle” 
(Stendhal, 1818, p. 139). 

Manufacturing of Sculpture in the Digital Age 255
opportunity to witness the extremely rapid and seemingly tireless way in which 
Michelangelo worked: 
[ ... ] je puis dire auoirveu Michel l’Ange bien que aagé de plus de 60 ans, & encore non 
des plus robustes abattre plus d’escailles d’un tres dur marbre en un quart d’heure, que trois 
jeunes tailleurs de pierre n’eussent peu faire en trois ou quatre, chose presqu’incroyable qui 
ne le verroit: & y alloit d’une telle impetuosité& furie, que je pensois que tout l’ouvrage 
deust aller en pièces, abattant par terre d’un seul coup de gros morceaux de trois ou quatre 
doigts d’espoisseur, si ric à ric de sa marque qué s’il eust passé outre tant soit peu plus qu’il 
ne falloit, il y avoit danger de perdre tout, parce que cela ne se peut plus réparer par après, 
nyreplastrer comme les images d’argille, ou de stucq.6 (Vigenère, 1615, p. 855) 
The quantitative difference in the production of the two most celebrated sculptors 
of their respective eras owes much to the efﬁciency of Canova’s serialized method, 
timely implemented to meet demand, compared to the direct force employed by 
“le divine mani di Michelagnolo” 7 (Vasari, 1568, p. 725), even considering the 
collaborative processes of traditional sculpture workshops. 
Despite the notable leap in manufacturing methods during the Neoclassical 
period compared to the Renaissance, both serialized production and the singular 
creation of stone sculptures still required signiﬁcant effort. Antonio Canova recounts 
in his Roman diary that on June 15, 1780 “nello studio del signor Carlo Albagini 
[... ] vidimo molti giovani che stavano ristaurando delle statue, uno delli detti 
facceva la copia della testa di Lucio Vero di casa Borghese e mi dice che gli aveva 
lavorato quatordeci mesi nella sopradetta testa e che ci mancavano ancora cinque 
mesi di lavoro per terminarla” 8 (Canova, 1780). Indeed, despite the organization 
of work and the considerable manufacturing capacity of Albacini’s workshop, the 
effort involved in three-dimensional production is evident, even when it came to 
reproductions. 
While it was possible to improve subtractive processes in stone manufacturing 
during the eighteenth century, the challenges posed by additive methods, such as 
bronze casting, show that the methodological distance from traditional processes 
is practically nonexistent. The duration of work to sculpt large bronze pieces is 
measured in years, if not decades. Pliny the Elder mentions the 12 years needed to 
cast the Colossus of Rhodes (Pliny, 1961) in the early third century B.C. Twenty 
years were required for the casting and completion of the equestrian sculpture of
6 “I can say that I have seen Michelangelo though over 60 years old and not among the most robust, 
chip off more scales from very hard marble in a quarter of an hour than three young stonecutters 
could do in three or four, an almost unbelievable feat if one did not witness it. He went about it 
with such impetuosity and fury that I thought the entire work would shatter. With a single stroke, 
he would bring down large pieces three or four ﬁngers thick to the ground. If he had continued 
even a little beyond what was necessary, there was a danger of losing everything, because it could 
not be repaired afterward or patched up like clay or stucco images” (Vigenère, 1615, p. 855). 
7 “Michelangelo’s divine hands” (Vasari, 1568, p. 725). 
8 “In Mr. Carlo Albagini’s studio, where we saw many young people who were restoring statues, 
one of them was making a copy of the head of Lucius Verus from the Borghese house. He told me 
that he had been working for fourteen months on the aforementioned head and that there were still 
ﬁve months of work remaining to complete it.” 

256 F. J. Santos Martín et al.
Louis XV le Bien-Aimé, conceived by Bouchardon (McClellan, 2000; Mariette, 
1768) in the second half of the eighteenth century, and almost 20 years were needed 
for Clemente Papi to cast a bronze copy of Michelangelo’s David (Videtta, 2017)a 
hundred years later. Canova himself, in a letter to Quatremère de Quincy on January 
17, 1808, asserted his right to live in peace, refusing to deal with the bronze casting 
of Napoleon’s equestrian sculpture on behalf of Joseph Bonaparte: “Io non voglio 
impicciarmi per nulla nell’affari della fusione in bronzo della statua equestre. V oglio 
soltanto far i modelli, dirigere la cera, vigilar al ritocco del bronzo; ma voglio viver 
tranquillo, non voglio impicci” (Quatremère de Quincy, 1834, p. 372). 
5 Il a ôté tout ce qui estphysiquementpénible: 9 The 
Three-Dimensional Artistic Manufacturing in the Digital 
Era 
In his eagerness to get rid himself of the physical work associated with sculpture, 
Canova maintained ﬁve or six rooms in his “ofﬁcina statuaria” on via delleColonette 
in Rome, where his assistants worked, and an “atelier particulier,” in which “Il a 
ôté tout ce qui est physiquement pénible” (Stendhal, 1955, p. 1146). The arduous 
(“pénibles”) parts of the manufacturing processes referred to by Stendhal would 
undergo few changes throughout the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. To witness 
the true revolution, both in data capture and translation methods and in sculptural 
operations, it would be necessary to wait for digital data acquisition techniques and 
advances in software-directed robotization, which would not develop until the late 
twentieth and early twenty-ﬁrst centuries. 
In terms of data capture, digital photogrammetry and laser scanning techniques 
deﬁnitively surpass the age-old contact-based methods. The printing of negative 
molds of three-dimensional objects on various plastic materials (Sargentis, et al., 
2022) or point-based techniques for reproductions at the same or different scales, 
using pantographs and similar devices (Payne, 2023), will give way, from the late 
twentieth century onwards, to non-invasive methods where physical contact with the 
models to be translated or copied is no longer necessary. 
Regarding the manufacturing process itself, in the context of the automation of 
industrial processes in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, there was 
also room for “sculpturing machines” (Dunstan, 2014). Although their mechanical 
principles were practically the same as those of the earlier pantographs, their power, 
capable of “pass over the marble away like cheese” (Scientiﬁc American, 1903,p . 
260), foreshadowed a future free from the physical hardships that had always been 
associated with three-dimensional manufacturing. 
Whether the history of sculpture, beyond the creative genius, demonstrates its 
collective nature and the importance of delegating the hardest work to apprentices
9 “He has removed everything that is physically painful” (Stendhal, 1955, p. 1146). 

Manufacturing of Sculpture in the Digital Age 257
and assistants, never has the process of delegation in manufacturing and the 
liberation from physical labor been more evident than in the present. In both the 
realm of additive methods, with the revolution of 3D printers, and subtractive 
methods, the landscape for the manufacturing of three-dimensional artistic works 
is changing rapidly. 
The design of robots speciﬁcally crafted for sculpture, programmable with 
various types of software (Xuejuan et al., 2007; Lu et al., 2020), and equipped with 
high-precision tools is already capable of emulating the most intricate traditional 
manufacturing on moderately hard stone materials like Carrara marble in the present 
day (Bubola, 2021). Progress in three-dimensional production of metallic artistic 
objects is also rapidly expanding. The ability to melt metal powders of different 
compositions using high-power lasers is paving the way for the creation of works 
materialized in metal, representing an unprecedented qualitative leap in 3D metal 
printing (Eom et al., 2021). 
Regardless of the manufacturing processes available at the present moment, 
manual ﬁnishing is still employed to eliminate machining traces, reﬁne details, or 
give ﬁnished pieces a patina. These artisanal operations represent the last stronghold 
of human intervention, which will soon be more symbolic than necessary. 
6 Conclusions 
The “ultima mano” 10 (Cicognara, 1823, pág. 253), with which Canova pledged 
to complete the sculptures from his workshop (Ferando, 2015), will consist of 
a symbolic way of imparting to the artwork “quell’alito di vita, quel moto, e 
quasi [ ... ] quella parola” 11 (Teotochi Albrizzi & Cicognara, 1824, p. 101) that 
seemed to animate the sculptures of the Venetian artist. The mythology surrounding 
three-dimensional works, especially anthropomorphic ones, appears to demand the 
presence of Hephaestus, Pygmalion, or Pyrrha, capable of infusing them with their 
own vital nature. The highest praise that could be bestowed upon a sculptural 
creation in the traditional artistic conception was to be possessed by life itself: “La 
Notte, che tu vedi in sì dolci atti dormir, fu da uno Angelo scolpita in questo sasso; 
e perché dorme, ha vita. Destala se no’l credi, e parleratti” 12 sang an anonymous 
praise in the time of Michelangelo (Vasari, 1568, p. 741). 
The theoretical debates that began in the late nineteenth century would ultimately 
relegate the realism of ﬁgurative representations, both in two and three dimensions,
10 “The ﬁnishing hand” (Cicognara, 1823, p. 253). 
11 “That breath of life, that movement, and almost [...] that word” (Teotochi Albrizzi & Cicognara, 
1824, p. 101). 
12 “The Night, whom you see sleeping in such sweet poses, was carved from this stone by an 
Angel; and because she sleeps, she has life. Awaken her, if you do not believe, and she will speak 
to you” (Vasari, 1568, p. 741). 

258 F. J. Santos Martín et al.
to just another feature of artistic manufacturing. The new parameters introduced 
by digital models and total mechanization with results indistinguishable from tradi-
tional methods broaden the vexata quaestio of the necessity of human intervention 
in artistic manufacturing processes. 
Although the trend towards the digitization and total robotization of three-
dimensional art could portend effects analogous to what photography had on the 
two-dimensional, the truth is that episodes in the transformation of sculptural 
currents already occurred in parallel within the realm of twentieth-century avant-
gardes. 
The attention that these seemingly surpassed issues attract in the art world 
becomes evident when authors like Anish Kapoor (Clouston & Sayer, 2016) 
or Maurizio Cattelan (Lydiate, 2022) openly declare who they entrust with the 
manufacturing of their works, while others demand that the companies keep their 
identities secret (Bubola, 2021). The idea of the sculptor as someone who “nel fare 
la sua opera fa per forza di braccia e di percussione a consumare il marmo, od altra 
pietra soverchia, ch’eccede la ﬁgura che dentro a quella si rinchiude, con esercizio 
meccanicissimo, accompagnato spesse volte da gran sudore”13 that Leonardo (1498, 
p. 32) almost caricatured in the Quattrocento and which Harriet Hosmer ( 1864,
p. 734) lamented in the nineteenth century somehow persists in the imaginary o f
sculptural workmanship. The reluctance of some artists to reveal the manufacturing
companies and the means by which they execute their pieces undoubtedly conceals
the romantic ideal of the creator’s physical touch in the artwork even in the d igital
age.

Part IV 
Digitalisation and Artiﬁcial Intelligence for 
Architectural Heritage Intervention 
and Conservation

Digital Palimpsest: Transformation 
of Alois Riegl’s Modern Cult 
of Monuments 
Nikola Beim 
1 Introduction 
The following chapter focuses on adapting Alois Riegl’s Modern Cult of Monu-
ments, written in 1903 in Vienna, to the twenty-ﬁrst century, shifting monuments 
from their physical presence into the digital realm accessible globally. The chapter 
raises the following questions: What is the monument’s value in the twenty-ﬁrst 
century, and how is the monument represented in the digital realm? To answer 
these questions, I analyze a selection of digital technologies aiding the transition 
from Riegl’sModern Cult at the turn of the twentieth century toward a Cult beyond 
the Digital appearing within contemporary architectural discourse. During this 
process, I propose a monument’s value, a timeless value, for the twenty-ﬁrst century, 
reﬂecting on Riegl’s theory, and suggest a new digital documentation method of 
digital palimpsest that shifts the monument’s values from a physical to a digital 
environment. This process allows for a new relationship between the beholder and 
the monument, the concept deﬁned by Riegl within his art history scholarship. 
Due to recent technological advancements, the digital palimpsest can store multiple 
versions of a monument’s aging, in Rieglian terms called the age value of the 
monument, manage, and reveal them at any time, non-chronologically within the 
digital realm. 
The second part of the chapter focuses on mapping the relationship between 
technology and preservation, which has been interconnected throughout the history 
of the discipline. In developing the notion of the digital palimpsest, I analyze 
the technological possibilities allowing such representation that directly relates to 
Riegl’s theory of monuments. I present the shift in heritage preservation aided by 
the advancement of technology—from two-dimensional (drawing and photography)

to three-dimensional (digital replica) and four-dimensional (a digital palimpsest) 
representational models. In addition, this subchapter discusses the relationship 
between digital preservation and AI with the aim of proposing a new methodology 
for future preservation purposes. 
2 Beyond Age Value 
In 1903, Austrian art historian Alois Riegl published a seminal work on preserving 
cultural heritage, The Modern Cult of Monuments. Riegl lived during the period of 
ﬁn de siècle Vienna, which was characterized by the emergence of new theories 
and practices. Speciﬁcally, it was shaped by a certain duality: the rise of modernism 
on the one hand and the decline of historicism on the other. The longing for the 
past, representing historical styles, themes, and tradition, and its modernist outlook 
resulted in the city’s double character, inﬂuencing scholars and the development of 
their emerging theories, such as Riegl’s. His essay served as a preface to a legislative 
proposal for reorganizing public monument preservation methods in Austria in the 
early twentieth century, leading to the rejection of the proposal. 
In the essay’s opening, Riegl claims that “a monument is a work of man erected 
for the speciﬁc purpose of keeping particular human deeds or destinies alive and 
present in the consciousness of future generations” (Riegl, 1982, p. 21). This 
statement reﬂects on the original meaning of the word monument, derived from the 
Latin mon¯ere, meaning “to remind.” Therefore, a monument has a commemorative 
value and belongs to the cultural heritage of a speciﬁc society. In his axiological 
study, Riegl deﬁned monuments as either of art or of writingand also into intentional 
(gewollte) and unintentional (ungewollte) types. As part of the Modern Cult,R i e g l 
invented the notion of unintentional monuments as a visionary concept as opposed 
to the notion of intentional monuments that were already part of the historical 
discourse. He divided unintentional monuments into two additional categories: the 
artistic and the historical monuments defying the Modern Cult (Fig. 1). 
The concept of intentional monuments was known from antiquity throughout the 
Middle Ages as the only monument type. On the other hand, historical and age 
value monuments belong to unintentional monuments; thus, they represent the cult 
of modern monuments, as Riegl categorized them (Fig. 2). 
Riegl argued that the nineteenth century was of historical value as the monu-
ment’s utmost important value, while the twentieth century is the century of the age 
value, which is the most universal and modern value. However, I would argue that 
an underlying inner conﬂict is represented in Alterswert as the most modern value. 
It appreciates the traces of the past on the object in question and manifests the most 
modern value for the upcoming century. This tension between historical and modern 
is embedded in this particular value itself and thus challenges our understanding 
of it. 
It is essential to explore whether the concept of the age value of monuments, as 
initially posited by Riegl, diminished as we entered the twenty-ﬁrst-century digital

Digital Palimpsest: Transformation of Alois Riegl’s Modern Cult of Monuments 267
Fig. 1 Monument categories. (Diagram by the author, 2024) 
Fig. 2 Modern monument categories. (Diagram by the author, 2024) 
and beyond digital realms. The ﬁndings propose a twofold response. Reviewing the 
built environment, age value is still showing its effects on some monuments in the 
same way as the historical value is kept alive on some other types of monuments 
up to today. Moreover, age value allowed a new value to emerge while transitioning

268 N. Beim
from the built to the digital realm. However, the technological shift from physical to 
digital allowed the age value to be perceived physically and digitally under varying 
conditions. While the age value visible in the physical structure is perceivable only 
as a continuous change, and what has passed is forever lost, in the digital realm, the 
age value is documented as a “frozen” layer of time in the form of a single moment 
stored as a superimposition of multiple states, and thus no important state is lost as 
opposed to its the physical structure. 
This chapter’s main concern is to analyze how monuments transform from brick-
and-mortar construction to the digital environment and how they are represented. 
From the built environment into the digital realm, the monuments shift. Besides 
their material properties, they also shift their values, meaning, and functions. 
It is important to note that these monuments do not undergo the process of 
aging, informing their functionality or appearance due to their virtual existence, as 
opposed to what Riegl suggested in his theory concerning the age value of physical 
monuments. However, using the right tools and methods allows for interpreting 
an age value within the digital model in the form of a digital representation of a 
physically aging monument. 
Mark Wigley claimed, during the period classiﬁed as the “digital age,” during 
the 1990s, that buildings’ “memorializing function has been displaced by images. 
Buildings are, at best, fragile images, props in heterogeneous publicity campaigns. 
Digital archives have taken over storing memory from solid structures” (Wigley, 
1999, p. 409). Even though we care for buildings, including monuments, their 
lifespan is limited. On the other side, digital records have the potential to exist 
beyond the buildings’ life and provide their new image through a digital medium. 
2.1 Timeless Value 
The value of digitized monuments transforms from a physical environment where 
monuments undergo the process of natural aging to a digital environment unaffected 
by the passage of time. Therefore, these monuments are assigned timeless value as 
they do not change once they are digitally documented as opposed to their physical 
reference. 
We can observe the development of Riegl’s value system from the historical 
and age value of physical monuments to timeless value occurring within the 
digital domain. All physical monuments are undoubtedly affected by entropy, which 
provides evidence of the passage of time. It signiﬁes the deterioration of a structure 
under the passage of time as a natural condition. Deterioration of the object can be 
related to Riegl’s concept of age value represented by the traces of time causing the 
decay of the monument (Fig. 3). The monument’s decline is similar to the principles 
of the second law of thermodynamics, claiming that entropy always increases and, 
therefore, always leads to a less ordered state. It is important to note that this process 
is given naturally without human interference. In this way, architectural entropy

Digital Palimpsest: Transformation of Alois Riegl’s Modern Cult of Monuments 269
Fig. 3 Joseph Michael Gandy. A bird’s-eye view of the Bank of England. 1830. © Sir John Soane’s 
Museum, London 
stands against the stability of physical structures and contributes to their alternation 
and temporality, characteristic of objects in the physical world. 
On the other side, digitized monuments exist out of time; they are not affected 
in the same way as their physical references. Digitized monuments are comprised 
of zeros and ones and exist, therefore, only in digital space. The documented 
digitized monument has a timeless value because any collected data regarding the 
monument’s existence serves as a snapshot. 
2.2 Digital Palimpsest 
After the waning of modernist fantasies about creation ex nihilo and of the desire for purity 
of new beginnings, we have come to read cities and buildings as palimpsests of space, 
monuments as transformable and transitory, and sculpture as subject to the vicissitudes of 
time. 
Andreas Huyssen 
As timeless value represents the value of digitized monuments in the twenty-
ﬁrst century, a digital palimpsest serves as a method of preserving monuments 
within the digital realm. Digital palimpsest serves as a digital spatial framework 
offering a multiversal image of historical monuments in the twenty-ﬁrst century 
while redeﬁning their values and roles, mirroring society at the time. The digital 
palimpsest builds upon and goes beyond the notion of a Rieglian modern monument 
characterized primarily by the age value that was not accepted by the experts and 
public at the time of its creation but only multiple decades later. But is the age value

270 N. Beim
Fig. 4 The Bern Digital Pantheon Project. Comparison between Desgodetz’s 1682 longitudinal 
cross-section with the Bern Digital Pantheon Model (red line) (Desgodetz 1779, p. 7, pl. VI). 
2016. Digital Pantheon, Edition Topoi. DOI: https://doi.org/10.17171/1-4-166-1. License: Creative 
Commons BY-NC-SA 3.0 DE 
surpassed, or is it still in play at the current time? By an overlay of various collected 
“age value layers,” the value of the twenty-ﬁrst century is deﬁned as a timeless 
value showing changes visible throughout a monument’s aging with regards to its 
appearance, form, and materiality and allowing to create new connections between 
datasets—between monument’s various states within the digital environment. The 
monument is documented throughout its life, presenting us its historical value 
favored in the nineteenth century, revealing age value as the value of the twentieth 
century, and exposing traces of time on its material form. These documented stages 
of the monument and its values together form a digital palimpsest of the twenty-
ﬁrst century. Thus, this digital model offers a new representation of the past by 
overlapping layers with various information and, by doing so, creating new relations 
between histories that have not been perceivable before (Fig. 4). 
The word palimpsest is derived from the Greek palimps¯estos, meaning scraped 
again. According to the Merriam-Webster dictionary, the word originally refers to 
a writing material (such as a parchment or tablet) used one or more times after 
earlier writing has been erased. The concept of the palimpsest was invented during 
the Middle Ages due to the scarcity of vellum, animal skin, to write on. Therefore, 
the reuse of skin and the practice of overwriting were encouraged. However, the 
previously overwritten text might have appeared over time, and thus, a multilayering 
of text was revealed (Fig. 5). 
Palimpsest appeared in literature concerning memory and the human brain in 
the nineteenth century in the work of an English writer, Thomas De Quincey, “The 
palimpsest of the human brain.” He writes:

Digital Palimpsest: Transformation of Alois Riegl’s Modern Cult of Monuments 271
Fig. 5 The Codex Ephraemi Rescriptus, a Greek manuscript of the Bible from the ﬁfth century© 
Public Domain 
Such a palimpsest is my brain; such a palimpsest, oh reader! is yours. Everlasting layers 
of ideas, images, feelings, have fallen upon your brain softly as light. Each succession has 
seemed to bury all that went before. And yet, in reality, not one has been extinguished. 
And if, in the vellum palimpsest, lying amongst the other diplomata of human archives or 
libraries, there is anything fantastic or which moves to laughter, as oftentimes there is in 
the grotesque collisions of those successive themes, having no natural connection, which 
by pure accident have consecutively occupied the roll, yet, in our own heaven-created 
palimpsest, the deep memorial palimpsest of the brain, there are not and cannot be such 
incoherencies (1845). 
In the 1860s, French poet Charles Baudelaire in his poems titled Les Paradis artiﬁ-
ciels cites De Quincey’s thought on a palimpsest and continues with the following 
words: “Nevertheless, between the palimpsest that carries, one superimposed over 
another, the Greek tragedy, the monkish legend, and the knightly romance, and the 
divine palimpsest created by God, which is our incommensurate memory, arises 
this difference, that there is something in the ﬁrst of a fantastic, grotesque chaos, a 
collision between heterogeneous elements, whereas in the second the inevitability 
of temperament imposes a harmony among the most disparate elements” ( 1860). 
In the 1980s, an American historian and geographer, David Lowenthal, referred 
to De Quincy’s concept of the brain as a palimpsest by stating that “many saw 
memory itself as the receptacle. Because the past shaped everyone’s present, no 
transient impression could be expunged from the mind; the storehouse of memory 
permanently preserved them all” ( 1985, p. 16). Even though any of the previously 
mentioned literature works refers to any spatiality of the palimpsest directly, their 
description of the brain and its layers already introduces the multidimensionality of 
this concept.

272 N. Beim
Another perspective on the concept of palimpsest was given from the psycho-
logical point of view. In the 1920s, an Austrian neurologist and the founder of 
psychoanalysis, Sigmund Freud, wrote an essay, A Note Upon The Mystic Writing-
Pad, describing it as “nothing more than a writing-tablet from which notes can be 
erased by an easy movement of the hand. But if it is examined closely, it will be 
found that its construction shows a remarkable agreement with my hypothetical 
structure of our perceptual apparatus and that it can in fact provide both an ever-
ready receptive surface and permanent traces of the notes that have been made 
upon it” (1961, p. 228). Metaphorically, Freud’s mystic writing-pad is nothing else 
than a memory device of its time, using available technology for writing, rewriting, 
and storing. Freud shows the resemblance of perception and consciousness to the 
mystic writing-pad: two layers of the system where one “receives the stimuli” 
while the other serves as “the foundations of memory.” The mystic writing-pad 
allegory can be related to the idea of palimpsest, even though they are not exactly 
the same. Freud uses his concept to explain the formation of memory traces. In 
his view, the conscious mind can erase memories to allow the formation of new 
ones; however, the former memories never truly vanish as they leave traces in 
human unconsciousness. This process is similar to writing on a palimpsest sheet and 
reusing it repeatedly while individual text layers are never truly gone. Freud’s essay 
inﬂuenced French philosopher Jacque Derrida’s work on writing, memory, and 
traces. He explores the implications of Freud’s analogy in Writing and Difference, 
published during the 1960s. For Derrida, the concept of trace becomes a central 
theme in his deconstructionist philosophy. Even though he did not engage directly 
with the concept of palimpsest, his writing resembles conceptual similarities, such 
as the relation between presence and absence or the reference of one text to another. 
Within the ﬁeld of architecture, the technique of drawing on tracing paper evokes 
the concept of a palimpsest due to its multilayering technique. The drawing created 
on the tracing paper references the original drawing and adds new information to 
it by an overlay due to the paper’s transparency. The drawings on tracing paper 
as layers are semi-transparent, thus allowing the effect of “seeing through.” This 
technique can be considered a paper palimpsest applied in architecture before the 
method of palimpsest was used three-dimensionally. That occurred for the ﬁrst time 
during postmodernism, starting from the 1970s, signifying the return to memory 
and history. The Cities of Artiﬁcial Excavation projects designed by Peter Eisenman 
serve as great examples of the palimpsest technique applied spatially. Here, the 
method of palimpsest is based on the main principle of layering, overlaying, and 
juxtaposing historical layers within the urban context, forming a new type of 
architecture. 
Now, more than 50 years after the ﬁrst implementation of a palimpsest within 
the built environment, the method shows its limitations. Even though a palimpsest 
works with the layers of history within the context of its site, these layers are 
permanent as opposed to the primary characteristics of palimpsest, serving as a 
temporary medium for writing (text to be regularly erased). Following Riegl’s 
notion of temporality and age value, the palimpsest type I deﬁned in this text 
goes beyond the limitations of a physical palimpsest while working with digitally

Digital Palimpsest: Transformation of Alois Riegl’s Modern Cult of Monuments 273
documented layers of monuments forming the digital palimpsest. Thus, a digital 
palimpsest offers a temporary representation of a physical monument by continuous 
documentation. Within a digital realm, we are able to reveal and observe each 
layer of a digital palimpsest, both individually and collectively, as we request. 
In a physical palimpsest, we observe only the result—the selected and curated 
layers of history that offer only one subjective view of history—the one created 
by an architectural team. In a digital palimpsest, we can observe multiple histories 
simultaneously by the juxtaposition of a number of layers as well as a single layer 
that contributes to the object’s formation. Thus, we can review both the fragment 
and the whole within a digital model of palimpsest. Ruins, appreciated by Riegl, 
can also be viewed as fragments of reality. These fragments can be extracted from 
the physical environment and brought to the digital palimpsest, where they can 
contribute to the whole within other documented histories. The digital palimpsest 
model represents a part of reality; thus, it is also a reality fragment and consists of 
multiple fragments within itself. 
In a digital palimpsest, the main goal is to collect data about the existence of 
a physical monument as individual layers. By doing so, a monument is digitally 
preserved and serves future generations as a digital cultural heritage without altering 
the monument’s physical structure. In this way, the work of architecture is preserved 
in Rieglian terms using a “touchless” preservation method. No preservation version 
is lost, as it is a case in the physical realm when the preservationists decide what state 
the building should be preserved in. It is important to note that digital documentation 
of existing monuments always freezes one speciﬁc moment in time of a physical 
monument with age value. Therefore, each monument with a digitized age value can 
be compared to another by juxtaposition or overlay to review the aging differences 
and results of natural and human forces applied to a physical monument. This 
approach to preservation brings a new methodology into the preservation ﬁeld as 
well as a new way of representing monuments in the age beyond the digital by 
overlaying, overwriting, remixing, and reusing collected data. 
The model of digital palimpsest has a referential capacity similar to architectural 
drawings. It refers to architecture that will not be built as classical drawing does 
but refers to what was already built or unbuilt. Thus, as a representation, digital 
palimpsest points towards an external object other than itself. Speciﬁcally, its 
reference is always a physical monument located in a built environment. As Roland 
Barthes already deﬁned in the concept of an object and its referent as photography, 
these two are always bonded together. “They merge in meaning value, in which 
the former acts entirely in service of the real. In this context, without the “real” 
object, the virtual would have no meaning, no soul, no referential” (Cameron, 2007, 
p. 59). Digital palimpsest and models located within it are also completely related 
and bonded to real, original objects. They would have no meaning and no virtual 
presence without the existence of real objects; therefore, their creation depends on 
them. Once they are created as references, they can exist independently from their 
referential objects, and thus, they are not affected by the physical world. 
In digital space, digitized monuments are in a real scale (1:1) as they represent 
their physical reference. This representation model of a monument within digital

274 N. Beim
palimpsest consists of documented data from the physical site but does not include 
information characteristic of architectural digital images, such as inhabitation or 
suggestions on programmatic use of the space ﬁlled with people, atmosphere, social 
events, or services. 
2.3 Continuity of Riegl’s Theory in Digital Palimpsest 
The transition from Riegl’s view embedded in ﬁn de siècle Vienna to the digital 
and beyond the digital age informed the changes in the value system of digitized 
monuments accordingly. 
2.3.1 Relation Between the Artwork and the Beholder 
Heritage and heritage studies focus not on the object but on the relationships 
between an object and a society, the sociopolitical-cultural situation concerning 
an object. Therefore, the relationship between a beholder and an artwork in a 
Rieglian sense, in our case, the monument, is an important aspect when digitizing 
monuments. Thus, it is important to examine the process of digitizing monuments 
not only from one speciﬁc (technological) perspective but also from a relational 
point of view: that of technology, monuments and their values, and society. 
In this regard, we face the very question of how digital documentation includes 
the context of built heritage with its relation to the society and culture it belongs to. 
How does this process translate heritage’s social, cultural, and political relationships 
with the society into the digital format? While digital documentation is strongly 
focused on representing an object, it is crucial to include information that created 
or contributed to its existence within the physical space through other means, such 
as text, images, or recordings embedded in the digital model. All available data is 
reviewed by a contemporary beholder from elsewhere as a digital palimpsest exists 
online. Thus, the idea of a locally speciﬁc monument accessible only on its original 
site has shifted towards a globally accessible one due to the rise of the digital and 
the availability of tools worldwide. 
2.3.2 Role of Time and Temporality 
The notion of time and temporariness is present throughout Riegl’s work and 
is also brought into the concept of digital palimpsest. In digital palimpsest, a 
beholder can review the monument’s timeless value through historical layers in non-
chronological order and, thus, observe its temporary qualities as it continually ages 
in the physical realm. 
The temporality of architecture is endurance, and time is architecture’s channel 
of transmission. Architecture endures not only in the material but also in the

Digital Palimpsest: Transformation of Alois Riegl’s Modern Cult of Monuments 275
temporal sense. A building is not an ephemeral presence; it endures in the purest 
sense of temporality (Ernst, 2017, p. 63). 
A physical object can be transformed into a dematerialized one while maintaining 
its temporal properties. Thus, digital palimpsest can be considered a temporary 
structure presenting real-time data as they are collected. In that way, digital 
palimpsest is in a state of permanent temporariness . Authors Sandi Hilal and 
Alessandro Petti worked with the term “permanent temporariness” concerning the 
architecture of refugee camps that shares many conceptual resemblances to the 
digital palimpsest. They question if it is “possible to use the notion of heritage not 
as a ﬁxed representation of nation-state identity but rather as a right to freedom of 
movements across nation-state– imposed borders” (2022). Beyond Rieglian notion 
that emphasized the importance of the monument’s context, in digital palimpsest, 
digitized monument operates similarly to the notion of heritage in a refugee camp— 
beyond its original context, across nation-state borders, it only approximates the 
real. 
In the case of digital palimpsest, when the origin (a physical monument) no 
longer exists, a digital palimpsest provides the closest possible representation of an 
absent structure. The notion of heritage in a refugee camp is dual. It operates in two 
environments simultaneously: the space of exile and the space of origin. Similarly, 
a digital palimpsest refers to two different but connected spaces: the space of origin 
(physical) and the space of reference (digital). 
2.3.3 Optic and Haptic 
The qualities of optic and haptic, important when analyzing an artwork, have 
implications both on a physical and a digital object. They are perceivable by human 
sight from an early stage of life. 
Within the digital domain, haptic and optic properties strongly relate to the 
resolution of a representational model, including its form and texture. Depending 
on the resolution of the digital model, meaning the number of points forming the 
cloud potentially translating into faces forming the mesh, we are able to perceive 
both the optic and haptic qualities of an object. The resolution of a digital model 
also allows for the possibility of zooming into the model to review various details. 
These details can sometimes not even be perceivable by human eyes in the real 
world, making a digital palimpsest a unique tool for reviewing the intricacies of a 
physical monument. 
2.3.4 Touchless Preservation 
The important aspect of Riegl’s theory referring to a monument’s aging suggests 
that a man does not interfere with a monument’s natural decay. In other words, 
we can preserve the monument without touching it, as John Ruskin also brieﬂy 
suggested in his writings. Following this doctrine working within the digital realm,

276 N. Beim
digital documentation offers the preservation of a monument without modifying the 
original and thus storing information regarding its form, material properties, and 
appearance for future generations, scholarly research, or future preservation efforts. 
Riegl also claimed that all monuments are equal in terms of aging; they exist 
between life and death and cannot escape the arrow of time. The age value of a 
monument does not require any knowledge of the beholder to be recognized and 
appreciated because they can view it without prior knowledge just by their vision, 
seeing its traces, and its aging. In digital palimpsest, the aspect of the “equality” 
or “democratic” approach is presented through the availability of digital data for a 
global audience online. 
3 Instruments and Representations 
If we look at buildings as architects, what matters is not so much what digital technologies 
can do, but what we could not do without them. 
Mario Carpo 
Historically, preservation focused on preserving monuments located within a 
built environment. Yet only recently have digital tools enabled the ﬁeld of preser-
vation to digitally document, store, and three-dimensionally trace their evolution in 
ways previously unimaginable. 
In the following pages, I aim to deﬁne how and why the transformation from 
Riegl’s age value of a physical monument to the timeless value of a digitized one 
is possible in our time. To do so, I study the relationship between preservation 
and technology by examining the instruments available for digitizing physical 
monuments and analyzing their possible representations within the digital realm. 
It is important to note that Riegl, while developing his preservation theory, was not 
occupied by the question of preservation technology and the tools used for such 
processes. In the Modern Cult , he only stated the following: “The development 
of modern reproduction techniques promises that in the near future (especially 
since the invention of photography and facsimile reproduction) new and perfect 
means compensating for the loss of originals will be found. In this way, scholarly 
research, which remains a source of conﬂict for age-value, can continue without 
interfering with the original” (Riegl, 1982, p. 37). To follow his touchless preser-
vation approach, we can document physical monuments using various tools from 
analog to digital format and thus translate monuments to digital space. Historically, 
documentation methods included drawing, photography, or photogrammetry, among 
others. In the twenty-ﬁrst century, all previously mentioned documentation methods 
are already applied not only within the preservation of physical objects but also in 
the digital workﬂows and, thus, give us various possibilities for how to apply them 
further within the digital realm. 
Currently, we can use digital technologies to create a digital palimpsest and 
preserve our built environment in a digital format as opposed to previously used 
preservation methods that apply only to the physical realm. As the quote by Mario

Digital Palimpsest: Transformation of Alois Riegl’s Modern Cult of Monuments 277
Carpo suggests, we are able to preserve buildings digitally due to access to the 
technologies that allow for their digital preservation at the current time. Without 
them, we would only preserve physical objects. Therefore, in the following text, 
I brieﬂy present the shift in heritage preservation aided by the advancement of 
technology—from two- (drawing and photography) to three- (digital replica) and 
four-dimensional (digital palimpsest) representational models. In addition, this part 
of the chapter also provides an outlook for further research that goes beyond this 
text. It manifests the possibilities of digital preservation as a projective methodology 
utilizing AI while working with collected datasets to create future scenarios for 
preservation purposes. 
3.1 Digital Documentation Instruments 
In the twenty-ﬁrst century, the ﬁeld of preservation has the possibility to deploy 
new technological instruments to redeﬁne the methods applied when protecting 
monuments. Increasingly precise documentation technology allows for the virtual 
recreation of our human-built environment. 
As Michael Young stated, “Reality as mediated through images is a much larger 
cultural question than architecture’s internal disciplinary battles” (2022,p .3 ) .T h e 
debate around preserving architecture also touches many other ﬁelds outside of its 
discipline, especially when working with digital tools that mediate the image of our 
cultural heritage. Therefore, preservation methods have a greater impact than just 
on the discipline itself and the society it belongs to. When we preserve architecture 
digitally, we produce the digital representation that forms our perception of it. 
This mediated representation contributes to our comprehension of the physical 
object depending on how it is mediated. The instruments used to represent objects 
contribute to cultural heritage, identity-forming, and a sense of collectivity as they 
produce two-, three-, and four-dimensional records. 
The digital palimpsest is a model whose primary goal is to approximate reality 
as much as possible while documenting and storing all possible histories of the 
monument. At the same time, the palimpsest resists information loss. Collected data 
concerning a monument are of various formats: texts, two-dimensional drawings, 
photographs, diagrams, recordings, and three-dimensional documentation. Thus, 
the digital palimpsest serves as a monument archive with all its data available to 
depict the monument’s changes, its life, and even the afterlife. Stored layers of 
information within the digital palimpsest can be seen as a new form of archive— 
evolving, growing, and generating new layers. By doing so, the digital palimpsest is 
an active type of archive—it does not only store but also produces new information. 
In a traditional sense, archives are storages of past or present information, but the 
digital palimpsest serves as an archive for the future based on the possibilities 
of AI generating its upcoming artiﬁcial layers of possible changes. Furthermore, 
the digital palimpsest constantly evolves as new monument data occurs over time, 
such as changes in a monument’s materiality and form, relocation of a monument,

278 N. Beim
destructions, and others. In the digital preservation of monuments, preservationists 
survey an object as a starting point for digitizing monuments. The process of 
surveying has advanced from proximity when measuring the physical environment 
to the exact digital representation of surveying objects due to the development 
of technology and tools. Therefore, the current preservation techniques used for 
digitizing monuments can precisely represent the physical object and create an exact 
digital replica presented within the digital realm. 
With increasingly precise survey instruments, these cartographic programs gen-
erated exact virtualizations of the land and used the device of perspective projection 
at an immense scale to quantize national and colonial territory (Witt, 2022, p. 115). 
Technologies that signiﬁcantly advanced surveying throughout history (and also 
the preservation ﬁeld) are photography, photogrammetry, and 3D scanning, among 
others. 
Due to this technological advancement and the use of digital tools, the age value 
of a monument can be documented, stored, and represented, shifting from a physical 
to a digital environment. Even though these processes were not possible during its 
existence in the twentieth century, nowadays, age value can be stored in a digital 
space, offering a single layer of history—a moment frozen in time. In this process, 
it is important to understand that we can document and store a great number of 
layers of history, including various stages of the monument’s life from its original 
state—historical value to nature-exposing age-values at different points in time. 
What are the advantages of dealing with a monument’s development as indi-
vidual spatial layers? By doing so, we digitally document the evolution of the 
monument’s aging while preserving it without its physical modiﬁcation. Following 
Riegl’s approach of touchless preservation, the digital palimpsest builds upon 
Riegl’s theory by not intervening with monuments’ aging and their natural decay 
but preserving them for future generations through their documentation. Digital 
technologies allow us to document the state of a monument’s being and reconstruct 
its historical value by bringing it into its original state from the available sources 
such as drawings—plans, sections, sketches, or photographs to ﬁll in the missing 
information within the digital palimpsest retrospectively. The reconstruction instru-
ments, such as three-dimensional modeling software, allow for the reconstruction of 
layers and, thus, enable contemporary audiences to experience the past through the 
monument’s collected historical layers in a novel way. These layers are in constant 
ﬂux as they are the documentation of the age value of the monument that changes 
in the physical world as time passes. 
“While nineteenth-century architects imagined that monuments were either 
restored or not, twentieth-century monuments were more likely to be hybrids, 
equally damaged by neglect and zealotry” (Allais, 2018, p. 48). In the twenty-ﬁrst 
century, we can build upon the previously used term hybrid and situate it within 
a digital environment. Digital tools allow digitally preserved monuments to exist 
between two states—the original and the preserved. When a physical monument is 
digitally documented and translated into a digital environment, it is to be restored 
or modiﬁed from its original state. However, with the aid of digital modeling tools, 
a digitized monument has the capacity to be brought into its original state, f.e., as it 
was originally intended in technical drawings documentation.

Digital Palimpsest: Transformation of Alois Riegl’s Modern Cult of Monuments 279
3.2 Digital Photogrammetry 
Digital photogrammetry serves as a documentation technique for digitizing mon-
uments in the twenty-ﬁrst century alongside 3D laser scanning and others. The 
processes, such as photogrammetry and digital scanning, are not the exclusive 
property of the discipline of architecture or preservation, but they are utilized in 
a variety of ﬁelds with numerous applications. 
Historically, photogrammetry was built upon the advent of photography in the 
1830s, so it is important to acknowledge that its discovery brought a new possibility 
of spatial surveying. That means that photography has been one of the main 
processes included in photogrammetry. Even though a technique of photogrammetry 
was known during Riegl’s time, he did not express any interest in this new mode 
of surveying and documenting the built environment or in technology at large 
that could potentially support the preservation of modern monuments and relate 
to his doctrine of touchless preservation. Nevertheless, it is essential to deploy 
this method for preservation when dealing with digitizing monuments in our age, 
reﬂecting upon Riegl’s value system. Photogrammetry surveying allows for a new 
value of monuments to emerge, especially since the advent of digital. Even though 
Andrew Witt described photogrammetry as a “powerful new technique to record 
and dimension the visible world” (2022, p. 119), this method also allows for seeing 
a temporary aspect of the world—the time that has passed (Fig. 6). 
Photogrammetry was a term coined by German architect Albrecht Meydenbauer, 
who also invented its ﬁrst application within the ﬁeld of architecture—for purposes 
of cultural preservation (Witt, 2022, p. 119). Over the course of the twentieth 
century, photogrammetry as a method transformed from “mechanized visualization 
in architecture” (Allais, 2020, p. 22) performed by human labor into a digital 
documentation of a built environment aided by software. Photogrammetry, by 
deploying contemporary digital tools, is a way of virtualizing the built environment 
since the rise of the digital and, thus, serves as a method for digital preservation as 
a continuation of Riegl’s touchless preservation concept. 
With the development of surveying tools, photogrammetry evolved from an 
analog to a digital technique. While documenting the built environment, the 
digital tools used for photogrammetry allow for documentation of not only the 
visible world, as Witt stated previously, but also of an invisible time. Time as an 
invisible measure is made visible on the monument’s form that changes, and digital 
photogrammetry documents this process of transformation in a number of steps. 
The environment as scanned through digital images is a mapped, exploitable 
collection of data: it is reality modeled after images (Young, 2022, p. 13). 
Digital photography creates an image of a physical monument that is translated 
into a three-dimensional representation in a digital space. A physical monument 
becomes a digital one—from a large number of collected photographs. Thus, the 
physical reality is mediated and transformed into a data-based reality that can be 
manipulated within the digital environment.

280 N. Beim
Fig. 6 Auguste Mestral, Gustave Le Gray. The Ramparts of Carcassonne . Photograph, 1851. 
(Credits: Gilman Collection, Purchase, Harriette and Noel Levine Gift, 2005 © Public Domain) 
When the documentation instrument digitally records the work of architecture, 
it maps its surface only. During this documentation process, the instrument does 
not collect data on its inner structure or elements it does not “see.” Therefore, 
the inner structure of documented architecture will result in empty spaces instead 
of their physical material structures. But what can the instrument see other than 
human eyes? What is supplied with various materials and structures in a built 
work of architecture is represented by a void in a digital model created by digital 
photogrammetry. The instrument sees only what lies in front of it and not behind 
the surface. The data we collect during the photogrammetry process is information 
regarding the geometry of the outer surface and its texture, but not data concerning 
the geometry’s inner structure. 
This observation leads me to the argument that there is no interiority in the 
architectural form—of a digitized monument created by photogrammetry. Similar 
to Riegl’s concept of the aging monument, we can only experience changes visible 
on the monument by sight, meaning changes on the surface and not of its inner 
structures. Even though there could have been changes in the inner structure, other 
documentation tools must be deployed to analyze them and translate them into the 
digital model. Within the photogrammetry model, there is no differentiation of the 
form set by the relation of outside-inside, but there exists only outside or inside of 
the form. Therefore, once we review the palimpsest model, we are equally outside 
of the space as inside of the space due to its virtuality. There is no tangible border

Digital Palimpsest: Transformation of Alois Riegl’s Modern Cult of Monuments 281
between what is inside and outside, as the digital model only represents the outer 
structure while missing internal spatial data. An inner structure of the model in 
the digital palimpsest is represented by a void that signiﬁes missing information 
between point clouds or meshes as opposed to poché, known from the history 
of architectural representation as a solid hatch, for example, in a plan or section. 
Palimpsest’s inner void has no material evidence or digital data; thus, it becomes an 
unoccupied blank information space, a reverse of traditional poché. It is important 
to note that there is no hierarchy in the digital palimpsest—all the elements and all 
the layers are equally forming and contributing to the representational model. 
3.3 Resolution 
Digital monument documentation results in spatial recordings of a built environment 
as digital data. The recordings have various resolutions depending on the tools used 
or the advancement of technology in the current age. What is commonly known is a 
low-resolution and high-resolution image. This logic also applies when a monument 
is documented as a spatial record; therefore, it can be directly translated into the 
digital realm. The high-resolution models allow for closer viewing of elements in the 
structure, even those that are not perceivable by human eyes on the physical structure 
of the monument. With the ability to zoom into the structure within the digital 
model, the intricate details appear while offering a new experience to a beholder 
compared to viewing an original object where some details are not perceivable in 
their real scale. 
It is important to note that digital information is always discrete and thus contains 
gaps between points (in the point cloud) unavoidably opposed to the continuity of a 
built environment. These gaps are created regardless of the technological tools used 
due to the mediation of information from the physical to the digital realm; however, 
they relate to the resolution properties of the documenting instrument. Using the 
right technique in digital documentation can reduce the number of gaps in the 
model. For example, the combination of LiDAR 3D scanning and photogrammetry 
offers a higher-resolution three-dimensional model with its texture due to the higher 
precision of measurements. However, these two techniques greatly vary in capturing 
and processing data. 
While the LiDAR scanner uses a laser to measure the spatial information, 
the photogrammetry works with many photographs—a higher resolution of pho-
tographs results in a higher resolution of a digital model that is reconstructed from 
these photographs. In photogrammetry, two-dimensional images become three-
dimensional representations of a built environment. Once the photogrammetry is 
exercised continuously to capture the monument’s aging, there is a potential to shift 
from the two-dimensionality of architectural photographs into a four-dimensionality 
represented in the model of digital palimpsest through the collection of “states” in 
time and, thus, geometry deformations.

282 N. Beim
3.4 Representational Shift 
From the historical point of view, there have been various types of monument repre-
sentations, both analog and digital. These include two-dimensional representations 
of monuments in the form of a drawing (Fig. 7) or a photograph, three-dimensional 
representations such as a replica mostly occurring within the digital realm, and four-
dimensional representational models representing the passage of time. 
This shift in representation is due to the technological advancement in the 
discipline of architecture and preservation in particular. By building upon two- and 
three-dimensional models, digital palimpsest is a four-dimensional representation of 
a physical monument. However, it keeps certain properties of its previous models— 
two-dimensionality by the collected photographs or drawings necessary for the 
reconstruction and three-dimensionality given by the assembled digital model as 
a result of an assembly of collected spatial data as a digital replica. Therefore, the 
value of these two- and three-dimensional records lies in their ability to contribute 
toward creating a digital palimpsest. 
It is essential to distinguish two types of digitized spatial models: digital replica 
and digital twin. Even though they share certain similarities, their functions vary. 
The three-dimensional representational model of a digital twin gained popularity in 
the early 2000s. Its primary goal has been to simulate the real environment under 
various conditions, monitor its reference in real-time, or analyze the collected data 
about the original object to make predictions about its future performance. Shifting 
from its original application in, for example, manufacturing, automotive industry, 
aerospace, healthcare, or building industry to digital preservation, it brings a new 
approach to the preservation of the built environment. On the other hand, a digital 
replica serves for archiving purposes and digital preservation while also allowing 
for the study of an artifact without damaging the original. By storing digital replicas 
online, they can become accessible to a wider audience—the general public and 
researchers. A great early example of a digital replica is the project of Digital 
Pantheon (Fig. 8) undertaken by Bern University between 2005 and 2008 by 3D 
scanning the architectural monument with a laser scanner on multiple occasions to 
reconstruct the structure in the digital space further. 
“Today, the increased accessibility of geospatial technology, open data laws, 
urban dashboards, the public engagement and multimedia options afforded by online 
platforms, and the burgeoning arena of civic tech engender a raft of quantitative 
and qualitative data, tools, and methods for understanding the relationships between 
people and their communities, and for informing policy decisions toward just 
and ecologically sustainable development” (Avrami, 2019). These technological 
advancements accelerated the preservation methods in our time and contributed 
to the development of four-dimensional digital representations of monuments 
accordingly.

Digital Palimpsest: Transformation of Alois Riegl’s Modern Cult of Monuments 283
