3.5 Four-Dimensional Monument 
Digital palimpsest represents a four-dimensional object existing in a digital envi-
ronment. It maps the aging of a physical monument while manifesting detectable 
changes in its form and material over time. Monument’s digital records show the 
duration of its life through a series of layers. Digital palimpsest is also considered

284 N. Beim
Fig. 8 The Bern Digital Pantheon Project, Laserscan 2005, 2016, Digital Pantheon, Edition 
Topoi© Public Domain 
a hyperdimensional object because it relates to a space with more than three 
dimensions. 
How can we review four-dimensional objects such as digital palimpsest? The 
three-dimensional building is represented by a series of two-dimensional drawings, 
such as plans and sections. Then, a four-dimensional object can be represented by 
a three-dimensional model if the same logic applies. Reviewing a four-dimensional 
model of digital palimpsest is enabled by technologies, for example, virtual and 
augmented reality, while it provides a new experience to the contemporary beholder. 
Concerning four-dimensional models, it is crucial to understand that human senses, 
as described by Ozenfant and Le Corbusier, are incapable of recognizing the fourth 
dimension in space and must be mediated. 
The four-dimensional digital representation of a physical monument is mediated 
through a digital palimpsest. Due to a documentation process, a digital palimpsest 
consists of a series of three-dimensional models (the same monument documented 
in different stages of its existence). The constructed digital model is based on the 
collection of records about the reference monument. These records represent the 
physical monument and its environment and serve as a reproduction of a reality. 
Consequently, a digital palimpsest also serves as a reproduction of a physical 
monument in a digital space. Each time a palimpsest is viewed as a reproduction 
of the real, the representation will vary based on the device it is displayed on. The 
digital model of the real is always of a lower resolution than the reality it represents.

Digital Palimpsest: Transformation of Alois Riegl’s Modern Cult of Monuments 285
When we digitally document monuments and their existence, we can categorize 
them into two categories concerning their relation to the original object. The ﬁrst 
type refers to digitized monuments existing in parallel with their physical reference, 
while the second deals with digitized monuments existing after the death of their 
physical reference. The latter type is concerned with monuments in a digital space 
existing without further documentation of their reference. In this case, digitized 
monuments gain complete independence from the physical environment and from 
documentation of any changes that should be implemented in the model. They have 
a life of their own. 
An example of a digitized monument that exists after the demolition of its 
physical reference is the Nakagin Capsule Tower in Tokyo. Its recent disassembly 
instigated the digital preservation of the metabolism monument that was not part of 
the World Heritage List, and thus, the physical protection of the building was not 
initiated. However, the Japanese activists decided to digitally preserve the building, 
claiming that: “the entire real space information is converted into 3D data. In 
addition to the three-dimensional recording of complex shapes and structures that 
cannot be recorded with only two-dimensional photographs and drawings, it also 
records the trajectory of changes over time of the building as the residents have 
ingeniously lived. By doing so, we can accurately grasp the architectural shape and 
leave it as a digital archive for future generations” (Gluon, 2022). 
In this project, the contemporary beholder can review the palimpsest character 
of the building as the changes occurring during its existence are embedded in the 
digital model. The group utilized laser scanning technique and a large volume of 
photographs to build a high-precision, complex model of the tower. Gluon initiated 
the crowd-funding campaign titled “3D Digital Archive Project” with the goal of 
releasing the tower’s 3D point cloud data as an open source. Therefore, we can 
observe a participatory approach of the public to protect a heritage site. The open-
source model has the potential to be represented by various technologies, such as 
virtual or augmented reality of 3D printing, for research purposes, similar to the 
digital palimpsest applications in or outside of its original location. 
3.6 Digital Preservation and AI 
The following text focuses on the relationship between the digital palimpsest and 
artiﬁcial intelligence tools in order to propose new methods of digital preservation. 
I delve into the idea that digitized monuments extend beyond the digital realm by 
arguing that our interaction with digitized monuments involves not just viewing, 
storing, and managing vast amounts of digital data but also includes the creation of 
new entities from that data, for example, for purposes of digital preservation while 
utilizing AI. 
Using AI and machine learning is nothing new when working with large datasets. 
The introduction of the Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) by computer 
scientist Ian Goodfellow in 2014 was followed 1 year later by the publication

286 N. Beim
of the paper titled “A Neural Algorithm of Artistic Style” by machine learning 
researcher Leon Gatys. Gradually, these AI techniques have spread from computer 
science to a wide range of ﬁelds, including art, architecture, and also possible to 
digital preservation. By now, AI can analyze large volumes of digital content and 
automatically generate metadata, making it easier to categorize, search, and retrieve 
information. This is particularly useful for large archives where manual cataloging 
is impractical. However, working with 3D datasets adds complexity and brings 
novel solutions to various disciplines, such as architecture and preservation, in 
generating spatial outputs. Architect Matias del Campo calls this type of architecture 
“neural.” He examines the contribution of neural architecture to the discipline of 
architecture by stating the following: “For one, it critically interrogates the role 
of the architect in the creative process of architecture design. Neural architecture 
embraces the possibility of design methods that are deeply informed by existing 
information in the form of databases and understands that the artiﬁcial modeling 
of neural processes can aid in harnessing the information in big data” ( 2022). Del 
Campo’s approach manifests the tendency to employ innovative methodology in 
architecture. Therefore, there is potential to translate the abovementioned method 
to the discipline of preservation when working with large amounts of digitized 
historical data on a monument. 
Returning to the notion of a digital palimpsest as a spatial model consisting of 
collected information about a monument, such as St. Stephen’s Cathedral in Vienna 
(Fig. 9), it has the ability to become a preservation tool utilizing AI to generate 
new data beneﬁcial for its future preservation. Thus, digital palimpsest is not seen 
as a mere architectural representation of a monument but rather as an instrument to 
preserve it in the future. 
Digital palimpsest, already serving as a spatial database, can be used beyond 
its archiving character by introducing the processes of AI and machine learning, 
such as neural networks (computing system consisting of layers), when working 
with palimpsest’s database. The application of AI would not be possible in relation 
to digital palimpsest without the initial step of digitizing a monument and storing 
its available data in large volumes. It is precisely due to AI’s characteristics of 
working with large datasets to generate new content that reﬂects learned patterns 
and styles through the use of, for example, a StyleGAN application. This algorithm 
is represented by processing thousands of existing images in order to produce a new 
one. Its application can be seen in the work of architects such as SPAN (Matias del 
Campo and Sandra Manninger), M. Casey Rehm, Stanislas Chaillou, and others, but 
it is still rather limited in the ﬁeld of preservation at the time of writing (2024). 
In a digital palimpsest, thousands of images or individual spatial layers (as 
obj. ﬁles) forming the database are processed by GAN, which identiﬁes common 
characteristics occurring in this database. GAN is then able to interpolate these 
common features and create new outputs or versions building upon available data 
of a digitized monument that were collected over a certain time. It is important to 
note that this process introduces a new set of relationships: between an architect (a 
creator of a historical monument), a digital surveillant (a trained expert who digitally

Digital Palimpsest: Transformation of Alois Riegl’s Modern Cult of Monuments 287
Fig. 9 Top: West Facade of St. Stephen’s Cathedral in Vienna. Construction progress from the 
12th to the 15th centuries, drawing (Dahm, 2008). Bottom: Axonometric diagram of building 
phases as individual layers forming schematic three-dimensional palimpsest. (Diagram by the 
author, 2024)

288 N. Beim
documents the physical monument and provides digital data), and a machine 
(algorithm which provides digital output). 
Architect Karel Klein incorporates AI in her work; in particular, she reﬂects upon 
the notion of AI in architecture in her article “Machines à Rechercher,” building 
upon the notion of anamnesis in memory recollection. She argues that “the claim 
for anamnesis to be both a search for the unknown in memory and the production 
of fantastic images that result from this problematic endeavor might indeed be the 
bridge across the abyss of not knowing ﬁrst confronted by Plato” ( 2022, p. 103). 
Whatever information is lost in the documented digital layers of the monument (e.g., 
in a case of a ruin) could be ﬁlled by machine learning through memory recollection 
and imagination as a transformation of collected data into something new. This type 
of ﬁlling data in memory is not exactly what is classically deﬁned as a process 
of remembering but rather as inventing memory, already deﬁned by Marcel Proust 
as mémoireinvolontaire. Therefore, digital palimpsest can be supplemented by an 
artiﬁcial layer, meaning the model includes a new outcome of a machine, serving 
preservation purposes while bringing novel preservation methods into the ﬁeld. This 
result resembles a hybrid of the work of a human and a machine, of a human’s 
documentation of physical changes done by a man and nature on the monument 
over the course of time and a machine’s imagination of ﬁlling in missing information 
while producing something new. Therefore, reﬂecting on Riegl’s Modern Cult,t h e 
digital palimpsest offers an updated type of Cult in the twenty-ﬁrst century: The 
Cult beyond the digital, in the age of AI. 
Because the images produced are not simple retrievals of stored memory but 
seemingly elaborate reimaginings of that memory, AI seems to possess a capacity 
for imagination. It is tempting to propose that AI is, in fact, not an acronym for 
artiﬁcial intelligence but artiﬁcial imagination (Klein, 2022, p. 101). 
Various architects studied the relationship between remembrance and archeology. 
For example, Eisenman’s conceptual basis of the Berlin Excavation project recalls 
Freud’s analogy between archeology and “preservation in the sphere of the mind ...  
Since we overcome the error of supposing that the forgetting we are familiar 
with signiﬁed destruction of the memory- trace- that is, its annihilation- we have 
been inclined to take the opposite view, that in mental life, nothing which has 
once been formed can perish- that everything is somehow preserved and that in 
suitable circumstances (when, for instance, regression goes back far enough) it can 
once more be brought to life” (Bédard, 1994, p. 23). In the essay “Remembering, 
repeating, and working-through,” Freud introduces the concept of working through 
the missing, blurred memory. This methodology is comparable to the Artiﬁcial 
Intelligence process of creating something new from available datasets that appear 
incomplete. Thus, by working through ( Durcharbeitung) the collected data stored 
in the digital palimpsest in Freudian terms, new, missing information can be ﬁlled 
in based on the rewriting principle. As Klein further writes, “AI- produced images 
are the anamnesis of its curiously trained artiﬁcial memory” (2022, p. 98). The term 
anamnesis, meaning an “unforgetting,” comes into play in this chapter in a different 
context. Digital palimpsest serves as a method to not forget while collecting, storing, 
and producing new data about physical monuments. The information, such as

Digital Palimpsest: Transformation of Alois Riegl’s Modern Cult of Monuments 289
destroyed parts of monuments, can be refound again by a machine. Consequently, 
the image of the past becomes artiﬁcially constructed as a hybrid of collected 
data and the imagination of the machine. Therefore, this new representation of a 
monument can also be seen as a hybrid of reality and ﬁction. Even though we 
digitally preserve the monument, we reconstruct its form into previously unexisting 
conditions by a machine imagination. 
Digitally documented histories of a physical monument in the spatial model 
offer a base for machine learning to perform its statistical optimization and ﬁnd 
differences between layers, producing a new one: the future-oriented layer of a 
palimpsest. The use of machine learning can help, in a wider sense, “to draw 
generalization, to infer patterns, and to predict future outcomes based on prior 
experience encoded as data. But data are never neutral– they are cultural artifacts 
situated in social and material settings. This means that data themselves are not 
inherently truthful but constructed, and thus their production and the processes for 
collecting, curating, and visualizing them are acts of design” (Llach, 2021, p. 19). 
When we produce data collected in a digital palimpsest, there are multiple 
variables, such as the expertise of human labor, the time of the documentation, and 
changing light and weather conditions, among others. All these factors impact the 
data construction, and thus, they inﬂuence the digital representation of a monument 
and future outcomes of monument preservation. 
In his book on Artiﬁcial Intelligence, architect and theorist Neil Leach argues that 
“AI, after all, is all about predictions. It recognizes patterns and predicts the future. 
And its success lies in the accuracy of its predictions” ( 2022, p. 159). Therefore, I 
would claim that the more data is collected in digital palimpsest, the wider range of 
results it can offer once predicting and creating new layers. Through interpolating 
collected datasets of historical layers stored in digital palimpsest, digital tools, such 
as machine learning, suggest a new scenario of monument preservation within a 
digital environment. The digital palimpsest is in a constant state of temporariness; 
every new layer serves only as a monument’s temporary condition at some speciﬁc 
point in time that allows for the production of new information by a machine. 
4 Conclusion 
The emergence of digital preservation methodologies within the discipline is 
relatively new. 
The advancement of preservation is possible through implementing new tech-
nologies into already established processes. Dealing with digitized monuments 
offers a ground for various disciplines to be involved. The new methods for digital 
preservation might ﬁnd applications and interest within art history, architecture, 
design, and history, among others. 
The Modern Cult of Monuments proposed by Riegl more than a 120 years ago 
was represented by the age value of monuments. The Cult transformed accordingly 
in the twenty-ﬁrst century, driven by digital tools. Hence, Cult Beyond the Digital is

290 N. Beim
represented by a timeless value that reﬂects upon age and historical values deﬁned 
by Riegl. Digitized monuments forming the new Cult can be reviewed through 
digital palimpsest forming a multiversal image of history. 
The digital palimpsest’s application is twofold: it digitally preserves cultural 
heritage for future generations as a four-dimensional digital replica, and at the 
same time, it serves as a digital preservation tool for experts utilizing AI pro-
cesses. Based on the collected data, palimpsest can generate future scenarios 
for monument preservation. It offers new ways of understanding preservation 
methodology, technological applications, geometry, architectural representation, 
and working with data. It helps predict how the physical monument might evolve 
under the consequences of its historical past. The predictions are calculated using 
the collected data and artiﬁcial intelligence, for example, machine learning. Even 
though preservation has been a strongly subjective decision process of multiple 
agencies, with the application of AI using collected data about a monument, the 
method of digital palimpsest stands for more optimized processes in the digital 
preservation ﬁeld.

3D Scanning of an Architectural 
Sculpture Using a Smartphone 
with LiDAR Sensor: The Case of the Late 
Gothic Helical Stair 
Patricia Benítez Hernández and Iker López Consuegra 
1 Introduction 
This chapter focuses on the application of LiDAR (Light Detection and Ranging) 
technology integrated into smartphones for the 3D modeling of helical staircases, 
also known in Spanish as caracol 1 con ojo or caracol de mallorca , a characteristic 
element of the Spanish late Gothic architecture. 
When addressing the study and rehabilitation of this type of staircase, it is 
not unusual to ﬁnd that the only available source of knowledge is the element 
itself: speciﬁc references to its existence do not usually provide any additional 
information; it is rare to ﬁnd any measured or drawn record of it and the only 
existing documentation typically consists of schematic representations on the gen-
eral building plans that merely indicate its circular typology without distinguishing 
between spiral with helical staircases. For this reason, to enhance our understanding 
of these staircases and propose well-founded interventions, it is essential to start 
with a meticulous examination of each part and detail that deﬁnes them, which 
means conducting a comprehensive survey. 
The use of scanners for 3D documentation of built heritage elements is not a 
novel issue. Although this type of staircase is not a usual subject of study, 3D surveys 
of helical staircases are not uncommon. There are speciﬁc researches in which 3D 
scanning was conducted, such as those accomplished by Argenziano, Fiorillo, and 
Marcantonio in 2014 (Zerlenga et al., 2022), Paris ( 2016), and Mancini and Farroni 
(2023) focusing on Italian Renaissance models. However, these previous studies 
1 The Spanish term caracol refers to a circular stair, spiral or helical. 
P . Benítez Hernández ( /envelopeback) · I. López Consuegra 
Department of Architecture and Construction, Universidad Nebrija, Madrid, Spain 
e-mail: pbenitezh@nebrija.es; ilopezc@nebrija.es 
© The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2024 
F. Moral-Andrés et al. (eds.), Decoding Cultural Heritage , 
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-57675-1_13
293

294 P . Benítez Hernández and I. López Consuegra
have predominantly employed terrestrial laser scanners or portable laser scanners, 
which come with signiﬁcant drawbacks. Firstly, the use of such devices implies an 
initial investment in their purchase or rental. Secondly, expertise knowledge of tool 
operation is essential for its optimal use. Thirdly, prior detailed planning is required 
for data capture to prevent areas from being unscanned. The scan planning process 
depends on the shape and size of the object to be scanned and should determine ﬁxed 
points for scanner placement during data capture. This aspect is particularly critical 
for circular staircases, which requires a minimum of three ﬁxed scan points per 
revolution due to its shape. Lastly, it is often necessary to export the acquired point 
cloud data to computer software for their processing and generation of the ﬁnal 3D 
model, which further extends the time investment. These issues collectively hinder 
the widespread adoption of this surveying technique. 
In contrast, this research focuses on 3D scanning using LiDAR technology 
integrated into smartphones. While the origin of LiDAR technology dates back to 
the 1960s, its integration into smartphones is relatively recent. Being integrated 
into a device commonly used by the general population, its application offers 
signiﬁcant advantages: quick accessibility, lower cost, as well as lightweight and 
easy portability due to its compact form factor. Another major advantage is the user-
friendliness of this technology through an intuitive and often updatable application, 
which works with unorganized images. In other words, data is collected while the 
technician moves along the object to be scanned, eliminating the need for meticulous 
data capture planning. This simplicity, in turn, results in signiﬁcant time savings 
during data collection. 
As research object, the helical staircase located in the Chapel of Inmaculada Con-
cepción in Segovia Cathedral was selected. Following an initial visual inspection of 
both the exterior and interior of the chosen model, instrumental inspection for data 
capture was carried out. This involved the use of a LiDAR sensor integrated into a 
state-of-the-art smartphone equipped with a 48 MP primary camera. The signiﬁcant 
advantage of this sensor is its capability to capture high-quality photos and videos 
with sharpness in low-light environments, a common circumstance in late Gothic 
small-sized circular staircases. This sensor was employed to create a point cloud in 
space with coordinates (x, y, z) and to capture high-deﬁnition videos. The combined 
processing of both the point cloud and video, using an application installed on the 
same device, facilitated a rapid 3D survey of the staircase without the need for 
subsequent processing on a computer. 
The application of this technique allows for a comprehensive 3D overview of the 
entire staircase. It deﬁnes not only the geometry of each step, whose revolution 
around the central axis forms the staircase, but also detects masonry variations 
to accommodate access openings or various architectural constraints. In addition 
to geometric deﬁnition, this technology facilitates the deﬁnition of other crucial 
construction-related aspects in assessing its current state. This includes masonry 
changes that may have occurred during its construction or due to the presence of 
pathological processes that could degrade its condition. This survey represents an 
essential initial step for the cataloging, as well as for subsequent individual and/or 
comparative analyses of this type of staircase.

3D Scanning of an Architectural Sculpture Using a Smartphone with LiDAR ... 295
The ultimate goal of this work is not so much the survey itself, but to assess 
whether the results obtained by applying this technology provide additional accurate 
information for its subsequent use in conservation projects. 
The work presented in this chapter is organized as follows. After this introduc-
tion, the second section gives a brief overview of the different technologies and tools 
which are employed to heritage data collection. The third section brieﬂy presents the 
helical stairs as well as the model selected as aim of this chapter. Then the speciﬁc 
methodology followed is outlined in the fourth section. The ﬁfth section gathers the 
results obtained and their discussion and ﬁnally the conclusions are drawn in the 
ﬁnal section. 
2 Heritage Data Collection Techniques 
The surveying of plans and data collection are intrinsically associated with archi-
tecture and territory. In both cases, representation is generally carried out after 
a rigorous preliminary data collection using the most suitable technique for the 
type of survey to be undertaken, and a subsequent graphic survey of plans. The 
documentation obtained is essential to work on heritage with precision and at 
the necessary scale whatever the purpose of the study is, whether constructive, 
restorative, research-oriented, or informative. 
As Antonio Almagro Gorbea points out in his book Architectural Survey (2004), 
architectural survey lacked a concrete deﬁnition until the approval at the congress 
“AIl rilievo dei beni architettonici per la conservazione” (Cundari & Carnevali, 
2000) of a document promoted by Professor Cesare Cundari of La Sapienza 
University. Almagro’s book establishes clear guidelines for the morphological 
understanding of the object to be surveyed, the technical knowledge of its materials, 
and its direct historical observation. It transcends the scope of drawings that 
simply delineate the surveyed elements, aiming to establish connections with the 
context and its design decisions. This approach allows for deeper understanding 
of the heritage considered, facilitating a more comprehensive survey execution. 
Almagro deﬁnes architectural surveying as a discipline, as a research activity. He 
emphasizes the relationship between representation and content without closing off 
new avenues of connection, assuming that any branch of knowledge can be valuable 
for the morphological and material deﬁnition of architecture. He highlights the 
research importance of analysis and is keenly aware of the relationships between 
the architectural entity and its environment. 
The scale is a fundamental concept in the survey and must align with the 
type of ﬁnal document required, as well as the level of rigor, precision, and 
tolerances needed. Its deﬁnition should vary depending on the representation needs. 
A small scale provides a broad understanding of the heritage element for a quick 
understanding of spatial relationships, while a large scale delves into detail and 
accuracy. Employing a speciﬁc scale in a survey entails a particular information 
level and requires speciﬁc data collection tools. For instance, an initial assessment

296 P . Benítez Hernández and I. López Consuegra
helps to identify the basic connections of the heritage piece under examination 
with its immediate environment, without the need for great precision but still 
generating sufﬁcient documentation for an overall understanding of the element 
to be surveyed. At this stage, tools that enable easy and quick measurements are 
employed. This phase is crucial as it serves as the ﬁrst approach to architecture. 
Subsequently, a more in-depth exploration into detail is necessary, making a leap 
in graphic representation with the assistance of digital tools and incorporating 
additional documentation like photographs and videos. This requires being more 
rigorous both in the level of deﬁnition and in the selection of measuring tools. This 
generated documentation enables more speciﬁc analyses. Finally, a level of detail 
deﬁnition is sought, employing much more speciﬁc tools with greater rigor and 
narrower tolerances to meticulously deﬁne the analyzed elements. 
The necessary measurements for an accurate survey can be classiﬁed into two 
main groups: direct measurements and indirect measurements. 
Direct measurements, as the name suggests, refer to those taken directly on 
the element, allowing for the acquisition of absolute measures. The most common 
tools for taking such measurements due to their simplicity and low cost are the 
ﬂexometer, the measuring tape, and the laser meter. The traditional ﬂexometer is 
the most conventional tool, employed by most professionals in architecture. It is 
suitable for small-format measurements, being easy and quick to use. To date it is 
the most used method in heritage studies because of its advantages, such as speed 
of measurement and minimal post-processing requirements. Due to its cost and 
satisfactory precision in many applications, it has always been considered “a good 
heritage documentation method ( ... ) [with] adequate precision in many projects” 
(Lodeiro Pérez, 2010, p. 13). On the other hand, the measuring tape is used for 
measurements of larger-scale elements and, until the advent of laser measurers, 
was a common tool in construction layouts. The use of the measuring tape is more 
intricate than the ﬂexometer since it often requires two people to keep the tape taut 
in order to prevent its deformation, thus avoiding errors in measurement. As an 
evolution of the ﬂexometer and measuring tape, the laser measurer emerged. This 
tool enables quick and precise measurements and can be easily operated by a single 
operator. Additionally, it has the advantage of reaching areas that are difﬁcult to 
access or even inaccessible. The choice between these tools will depend on factors, 
such as cost, time availability, size of the object to be measured, accessibility of the 
element, and required precision. Each tool has its advantages and limitations, and 
its use will depend on the speciﬁc needs of the architectural survey. 
Although the tools described above are the most employed ones for direct mea-
surements, the use of 3D Terrestrial Laser Scanner (TLS) is becoming increasingly 
common in architectural elements of considerable size. This scanner allows mass 
data capture with great precision at high speed. Depending on the generated point 
cloud matrix and its density, different levels of rigor and tolerances can be achieved. 
This tool allows for the analysis of complex elements by generating a 3D point 
cloud mesh model. Subsequently, a computer program is employed to recognize 
and triangulate the point surfaces to create a 3D model. Despite its signiﬁcant 
advantages, the application of this tool comes with important drawbacks that limit

3D Scanning of an Architectural Sculpture Using a Smartphone with LiDAR ... 297
its widespread use: it is an expensive measurement tool due to the high price of the 
required equipment; it requires expertise in handling the tool; it needs a minimum 
workspace that allows for stable and ﬁrm positioning of the tool, as well as a 
minimum distance to the element being measured; it needs a prior measurement 
plan; and ﬁnally, the amount of information obtained requires a demanding post-
production phase of both hardware and software, since it generates a complex point 
cloud that is difﬁcult to handle due to the weight and complexity of the scanned 
ﬁle. 
The aforementioned tools and techniques are used when direct access to the area 
for measurement is feasible. However, this is not always possible. In such situations, 
other techniques are needed to obtain indirect or relative measurements, that is, 
those obtained in relation to a reference element whose dimensions are known. 
There are multiple techniques for indirect measurement, such as theodolites, total 
stations, or those others based on photography. Among them, the photography-based 
techniques are the most used in heritage surveying due to their simplicity, low cost, 
minimal logistics to obtain results, and the capability to achieve high precision levels 
depending on the technique and equipment employed. Among these photography-
based techniques, photogrammetry stands out, and speciﬁcally, SfM (Structure from 
Motion) photogrammetry. 
SfM photogrammetry is a technique based on the overlap of 2D images taken 
from various perspectives. This approach is similar to traditional stereoscopic 
photogrammetry; however, in this case the identiﬁcation of homologous points is 
automated by algorithms, swiftly generating a cloud of points located in space with 
coordinates (x, y, z). By processing this point cloud with speciﬁc software, a 3D 
model of the analyzed element is obtained (Peña Senín, 2019, p. 36–38). 
Both techniques, 3D Terrestrial Laser Scanning and SfM photogrammetry, are 
the most modern methods that permit mass data capture, deﬁning not only the 
geometry of the analyzed element but also its texture. Although SfM photogram-
metry is a much cheaper measurement technique compared to terrestrial laser 
scanning, it also demands expertise in software for processing the acquired data—a 
proﬁciency not universally held by professionals in architecture and construction. 
Consequently, both techniques are predominantly utilized by experts in the ﬁeld, 
limiting their widespread use, and causing the ﬂexometer to remain the most widely 
used measurement tool among professionals as well as amateurs. 
In addition to the aforementioned techniques, new digital tools can be found 
in the general market, halfway between direct and indirect measurement. These 
tools leverage the hardware and software capabilities provided by mobile devices, 
simplifying the process, measurement, and surveying. These tools are readily 
accessible to everyone and are becoming increasingly popular for measurement 
purposes. Users simply need to open the application, scan the area they wish to 
survey using the phone camera and/or laser sensor, and obtain a mesh of points 
or a triangulated 3D surface. These applications utilize the camera and various 
sensors included in smartphones and tablets, operating through a combination of 
photogrammetry and laser measurement. The phone application interprets the image 
and identiﬁes surfaces, allowing users to ﬁx points on them. This even includes

298 P . Benítez Hernández and I. López Consuegra
mapping textures, facilitating the creation of a 3D model with rich information for 
subsequent work. 
At present, there are two types of depth sensors integrated into high-end 
mobile devices: the LiDAR sensor integrated into Apple mobile devices and 
tablets and other Time of Flight (ToF) sensors integrated into Android devices. 
Both sensors have speciﬁc limitations in terms of range or size of the surface to 
be scanned, as well as accuracy. The latter factor is directly inﬂuenced by the 
quality of the camera, the algorithms used, and the lighting conditions. While these 
techniques are still subject to improvement, they have recently undergone signiﬁcant 
enhancements, allowing for a rapid and low-cost survey. This makes them a 
powerful tool for heritage surveying, accessible to both non-expert professionals 
and amateurs. 
In this chapter, the application of the LiDAR sensor integrated into an iPhone 14 
Pro is analyzed. 
3 The Late Gothic Helical Staircase 
The helical staircase is one of the most characteristic elements of the Spanish 
Late Gothic style. Despite the fact that its origin dates back to Greek and Roman 
architecture, it did not ﬂourish until the ﬁfteenth century (Templer, 1994b, p. 54), 
mainly linked to late Gothic architecture in the Mediterranean area. 
From that moment on, this singular staircase became widespread in the Iberian 
Peninsula, and it was built in both religious and civil buildings even in the 
Renaissance-style ones. Examples of this kind of circular stair can be found in 
Spain in civil buildings like Lonja in Palma de Mallorca, Lonja de los Mercaderes 
in V alencia, Casa de las Conchas in Salamanca, Colegio Arzobispo Fonseca in 
Salamanca, or the castle of Cabrera Island, as well as many religious ones like 
the cathedrals of Segovia, Salamanca, Baeza, Cáceres, or the churches of Barco 
de Ávila or Santa María in Cazorla. 
This architectonic element stands out for its inner hollow which set it apart from 
the traditional spiral staircase (Fig. 1). Other representative characteristics are its 
small size and a strongly private use together with an often-concealed positioning 
inside the masonry walls (Vicens Pedret, 2005, p. 17). These last features frequently 
caused to consign this element to oblivion and be totally abandoned, leading to its 
general state of ruin. 
It is important to note that, like any staircase, this element is essential for the 
proper functioning of multi-level structures, making its preservation crucial for 
the overall building rehabilitation. In other words, for the accurate survey of this 
element, it must always be considered its location and its relationship with the 
building in which it is integrated. 
From a geometric point of view, the circular staircase, whether spiral or helical, 
is generated by a single step with a more or less triangular tread. This step is 
uniformly replicated in the horizontal plane, revolving around a central axis while

3D Scanning of an Architectural Sculpture Using a Smartphone with LiDAR ... 299
Fig. 1 La Concepción helical staircase ( a) View from above (left) ( b) Intrados view (right) 
simultaneously moving vertically (Templer, 1994a, p. 175). Achieving an optimal 
geometric design involves a complex process that must harmonize construction, 
structure, comfort, safety, economy, and ornament. The proposed geometric solution 
must fulﬁl all these functions to achieve the desired success and dissemination 
(Alsina & Catalá, 2005, p. 8). In many staircases, these functions are often fulﬁlled 
by different elements (Vicens Pedret, 2005, p. 23). However, in the staircase aim 
of this study, the step itself serves multiple purposes: (i) it serves as the structure 
as it is part of the wall of the case in which it is embedded as well as supports 
the next step; (ii) it acts as an ornamental element, as its inner ﬁnishing forms the 
molding around the staircase interior hollow; (iii) it serves as the ﬁnishing material, 
as it has no added components; (iv) the monolithic step design not only allows 
for construction simplicity and economic efﬁciency but also provides the necessary 
dimensional regularity for the safety of those ascending or descending through it. 
Furthermore, the proportions between the different parts of the step and between the 
step and the entire staircase ensure stability, as well as comfort for the users, since 
they are designed in accordance with human dimensions. Consequently, the analysis 
of the caracol involves examining both the staircase as a whole and the geometry 
of the step, which is the elemental module which repetition gives rise to the entire 
structure (Carreiro Otero, 2007, p. 15). 
From a constructive and structural point of view, it is important to consider that 
the masonry is a construction whose behavior is directly inﬂuenced by the properties 
of the material used. For this reason, a rigorous survey and assessment of the current

300 P . Benítez Hernández and I. López Consuegra
Fig. 2 La Concha Chapel 
condition of this type of staircase requires an analysis of the type of stone used, 
potential variations in the stone throughout the masonry, as well as any pathological 
processes that may have initiated its degradation. 
3.1 The Helical Staircase of the Chapel of La Concha 
This work focuses on one of the helical staircases constructed in the Cathedral 
of Nuestra Señora de la Asunción y San Frutos in Segovia. There have been 
numerous studies conducted on late Gothic architecture in Segovia in general, and 
the cathedral in particular. Notable among these are the research efforts undertaken 
by Moreno Alcalde ( 1990), De Cáceres ( 1991), Cortón De Las Heras ( 1997), Ruiz 
Hernando ( 2003a, b), and Alonso Ruiz ( 2009). 
Speciﬁcally, this study centers on the circular staircase that starts from the chapel 
of the Inmaculada Concepción, also known as La Concepción Chapel or just La 
Concha Chapel (Fig. 2). It is situated next to El Perdón facade and provides access 
to the exterior of the rooﬁng of the gospel nave, from which other staircases can 
be reached for accessing to higher levels. This helical staircase was constructed 
in 1526, and its authorship can be attributed to Rodrigo Gil de Hontañón. This 
master, transitioning from Gothic to Renaissance architecture, incorporated the

3D Scanning of an Architectural Sculpture Using a Smartphone with LiDAR ... 301
helical staircase into many of his works, contributing to its dissemination throughout 
Spain (Hoag, 1985). 
This late Gothic master was involved in signiﬁcant constructions across the 
Iberian Peninsula, including the Monterrey Palace and the New Cathedral, both 
in Salamanca, the San Ildefonso College in Alcalá de Henares, and the Plasencia 
Cathedral. Speciﬁcally in Segovia, he participated not only in the cathedral but also 
in other buildings such as the San Sebastián Parish Church in Villacastín, the Church 
of San Miguel (De Lozoya, 1962 and Casaseca Casaseca, 1988). 
The choice of this particular helical staircase as aim of this study is not 
random. As noted in the introduction, the purpose of this work is not the 3D 
modeling of a structure but rather to analyze and assess whether the use of LiDAR 
technology integrated into a smartphone provides a sufﬁciently precise survey. For 
this reason, one of the few helical staircases with detailed previous information, 
including metric, architectural, and construction details, has been selected. The 
helical stair in La Concha Chapel was thoroughly analyzed by Benítez ( 2016, 2021) 
using traditional methods. Geometric data was collected then using the traditional 
ﬂexometer. Although this method has a certain margin of error in measurements, 
given the small dimensions of the model under study, it can be assured that in 
this case, the precision was adequate, and measurement errors were minimal and 
acceptable. 
Alongside the ﬂexometer, the capture of high-resolution photographs was 
another crucial resource for data acquisition. The high-resolution photographs 
obtained allowed for the measurement of dimensions of elements located in 
inaccessible areas, as well as the identiﬁcation of architectural and construction 
details that are not visible to the human eye. Thus, the collection of photographs 
not only served as a visual record but also, through subsequent analysis, provided 
metric and construction data. 
In accordance with the preliminary study conducted, typologically, this is a 
helical staircase with a circular plan inscribed in a 280 cm diameter cylindrical 
case, which is only visible from the outside. This cylindrical volume is popularly 
identiﬁed as Cubo de la Almuzara and constitutes the right-hand lateral ﬁnish of 
the northern elevation of the cathedral. The case is capped internally by a simple 
spherical dome and externally by a conical spire and a small sphere (Fig. 3). 
This work focuses on the 3D scanning of the interior of the staircase, where the 
use of a mobile device is possible, either with or without the assistance of extender 
accessories to reach those points that are farther from the user. For scanning the 
exterior volume, other technologies would be necessary to visualize the high points 
reached by the enclosure and its upper ﬁnish, which are not the subject of this study. 
The staircase consists of a total of 75 steps, each one is formed by a monolithic 
stone piece that is embedded in the outer wall as well as supported by the previous 
step. Each step is deﬁned by (i) a riser of 20 cm in height, directed towards the 
geometric center of the staircase; (ii) a tread length of 105 cm measured from the 
outer edge next to the wall to the molding of the inner opening; (iii) a tread width 
with a maximum value of 36 cm measured at the outermost part next to the wall 
and a minimum value of 9 cm measured at the inner part next to the molding of the

302 P . Benítez Hernández and I. López Consuegra
Fig. 3 Cubo de la Almuzara 
central opening; (iv) a triangular cross-sectional shape, cut at the necessary angle to 
ensure continuity between one step and the next, except for the outermost part of 
the step which is designed to integrate with the wall structure forming the staircase 
enclosure. 
The upward counterclockwise rotation of this step around the central axis 
generates a left-handed stair with 24 steps per revolution. According to the solution 
used to create the central opening, the staircase corresponds to a helical staircase 
by radial solution (Benítez & V aliente, 2015) that generates an interior hollow, 
including the molding, within a diameter of 68 cm (Fig. 4). The continuous intrados 
creates a continuous helical lower surface. The average headroom clearance is 
480 cm. 
The staircase is equipped with a handrail that is embedded in the outer wall which 
forms the enclosure of the staircase. It starts with a vertical section before the ﬁrst 
step, reaching the appropriate height. From that point on, it continues, maintaining a 
consistent section and distance from the step—between 75 cm and 90 cm measured 
at the outer and inner ends of the tread, respectively—forming a simple helix that 
disappears with the opening of the ﬁrst door leading to the roofs. The handrail has a 
circular section with a diameter of 12 cm integrated into a Scotia molding embedded 
in the wall. This molding is joined to the wall below by a convex section. 
The helical staircase also has another handrail next to the central aperture of the 
staircase, formed by the molding that internally cap the step. These are two simple

3D Scanning of an Architectural Sculpture Using a Smartphone with LiDAR ... 303
Fig. 4 La Concha helical staircase layout 
circular convex moldings of different diameters, connected by a concave one. The 
larger one is placed next to the riser. A cut in the inner end of the tread accentuates 
its appearance, to the point that when viewed from above, it resembles a helical with 
a round newel, as the smaller diameter molding is only visible from the side and the 
bottom of the staircase. This molding is slightly altered in the ﬁrst three steps to 
form the start of this handrail. 
Throughout the volume of the staircase, there are four openings: two window 
openings and two door openings. The two window openings are on nearly opposite 
vertical axes of the cylinder. The ﬁrst one is located above step number 14 and 
opens next to El Perdón facade. The other one is above number 29 step and opens 
towards the room adjacent to the chapel. Both openings have a ﬂared rectangular 
section and similar dimensions ranging from just over 60 cm to less than 70 cm 
in width and between 130 and 140 cm in height. They are closed with wooden 
joinery and glass or wire mesh. In both cases, the joinery, set slightly back from the 
inner limit, is narrower than the opening and is closed with new strips or cement 
mortar. Regarding this issue, the helical staircase of La Concha Chapel is scarcely 
illuminated, as only two window openings illuminate three turns of the staircase. 
This signiﬁcantly affects the quality of the images to be obtained. The door openings 
are located at the end of the staircase. The ﬁrst one is above step number 74 and

304 P . Benítez Hernández and I. López Consuegra
opens towards the roofs of the lateral chapels. The second one is at the level of step 
number 75, behind a small wooden platform of recent construction. Both openings 
have a rectangular section topped with a lowered segmental arch. Both doors are 
made of metal. 
The staircase is constructed with limestone extracted from quarries in the Segovia 
area. To assess its state of degradation, a detailed visual study was conducted, which 
revealed common pathologies found in many staircases from that period, such as the 
black patina, a large number of grafﬁti painted or scratched on the stone wall, and 
frequent pitting, some of which have been ﬁlled with mortar in previous restoration 
work (Esbert et al., 1997). Despite these pathologies, it can be conﬁrmed that the 
staircase of La Concepción Chapel is in good condition. 
4 Methodology 
Once La Concepción Chapel helical staircase was selected as aim of this study, the 
ﬁrst phase involved the collection of both written and graphical information. In this 
regard, the previous work by Benítez ( 2016, 2021) served as a valuable starting 
point, providing context and a theoretical framework, among other things. 
The mobile device used for the work was an iPhone 14 Pro with 256 GB of 
storage capacity and a 3200 milliampere-hour battery. Both features are important 
because recording video and taking a large number of photographs require signiﬁ-
cant storage memory and consume a lot of battery power. For this reason, an external 
portable battery with 26,800 milliampere-hour capacity was used. The use of this 
element contributes to the goals established at the beginning of this study: economy, 
ease of use, lightweight, and portability. The employed iPhone has a lens with a 
resolution of 8064 × 6048, which translates to a 48-megapixel main camera sensor 
and 4 K video recording at up to 60 frames per second. The presence of an image 
stabilizer is also important as it allows for sharper images compared to other devices. 
Then the required applications for 3D scanning were installed on the smartphone: 
Scaniverse and Polycam. Both applications were selected for being highly rated on 
the market for 3D scanning using the LiDAR sensor and for being freely accessible. 
Both applications have similar features. Scaniverse is a completely free application 
exclusively available on iPhone and iPad. This application creates 3D models 
from meshes or by applying photogrammetry to frames automatically extracted 
from the video recorded using the LiDAR sensor. On the other hand, Polycam 
is an application that, unlike the previous one, offers two possible LiDAR data 
capture modes: (i) automatic mode through video recording and (ii) manual mode 
through taking photographs. This latter application, while free to use, requires prior 
registration and payment of a fee to access some options, such as exporting the 
scanned models. In both applications, the obtained data is subsequently processed 
using integrated software, resulting in a 3D image in just a few seconds. 
Once the applications were selected, we proceeded with the scanning of the 
staircase. For data collection from the furthest areas from the user, an Eligiant brand

3D Scanning of an Architectural Sculpture Using a Smartphone with LiDAR ... 305
extension pole was used. This extender allows for distancing the smartphone up to 
100 cm from the user and adjusting the device angle as needed. The use of this 
device aligns with the initial goal of this research, which aimed for economy, user-
friendliness, lightweight equipment, and ease of transport. 
As mentioned, the analysis of the helical staircase involves examining both the 
staircase as a whole and the geometry of individual steps. Therefore, the scanning 
process focused on three areas: scanning step number 26, scanning the entire 
staircase, and scanning a complete turn. 
An important point to consider when approaching 3D scanning is the frequent 
alignment problems that tend to arise during data processing. These issues are a 
result of the lack of reference points due to the excessive uniformity of the scanned 
element. In the case of the helical staircase aim of study, uniformity is the governing 
principle in the generation of the staircase. The regularity of the step piece is 
essential to ensure user safety and comfort. Additionally, the revolving around a 
central axis while moving vertically, with each step embedded in the outer wall, both 
made from the same material, embodies the economy and simplicity characteristic 
of Gothic architecture. All these elements create a structure that clearly seeks 
uniformity in both geometric and textural aspects. Initially, this uniformity does not 
provide enough reference points to reduce potential alignment issues. To address 
this, as usual, colored targets were located at the outer ends of each step tread near 
the wall and adjacent to the interior molding of the central opening. 
For the scanning using the Scaniverse application, the following general settings 
were initially adopted: meters as the unit of measurement, no point cloud sim-
pliﬁcation, and data saved in Raw format. The Raw format retains uncompressed 
data, which offers the advantage of being able to reprocess the model by changing 
the initially adopted settings, but requiring more storage capacity. Subsequently, 
for each scanning area, it was necessary to select the following factors: ﬁrst, the 
object size (Small object, Medium object, Large object/Area), which determines the 
LiDAR sensor range (0.8 m to 2.5–5.0 m); and second, the processing type (Speed-
Area-Detail), which determines either the creation of a point cloud and its voxel size 
(10 mm–5 mm) or the processing through photogrammetry. 
The scanning process began with step number 26. The Small Object option was 
selected as the object size, as recommended by the application for scanning items 
like food, toys, pets, or ﬂowers, which sets the LiDAR range to 0.8 m. Once the 
step tread and riser were scanned, the Detail processing mode was chosen, which 
is also recommended by the app for textured objects. In this processing mode, the 
application automatically extracts various frames with minimal overlap from the 
recorded video to apply photogrammetry in the 3D model it provides as a result. 
At the start of the scanning of the entire helical staircase, selecting the object 
size was once again necessary. It is essential to note that this type of architectural 
element does not easily ﬁt into the typologies initially offered by the application. 
The helical staircase should, due to its overall dimensions, be considered a large 
object. This automatically sets the LiDAR sensor capture range to 5.0 m. However, 
this distance greatly exceeds the distance from the device carrier to the elements 
being scanned. For this reason, the Medium Object option was ﬁnally selected,

306 P . Benítez Hernández and I. López Consuegra
Fig. 5 Scaniverse ( a) Scan size selection (left) ( b) Scanning (center) ( c) Processing (right) 
recommended for scanning people, vehicles, and furniture. By default, this option 
sets a maximum LiDAR range of 2.5 m. Nevertheless, this value was manually 
readjusted to 1.5 meters. This choice was made because it roughly corresponds to 
half the diameter of the staircase, as determined by direct measurement methods. 
Once the desired area was scanned, the Detail processing mode was chosen again to 
achieve the most precise results. 
For the entire staircase, the object size was set to Medium Object mode, and 
the LiDAR range was set to a maximum of 1.5 meters for the same reasons as 
before. After scanning the desired area, the Detail mode was chosen for processing. 
However, the application did not allow this due to the video being too extensive. 
Finally, following the application recommendation, the video was processed using 
the Area mode, which utilizes LiDAR to create a 3D mesh with a voxel size of 
5 mm. 
The application itself marked areas left unscanned with a striped pattern, so its 
instructions were followed to avoid them (Fig. 5). 
With Polycam application, the scanning process for individual steps and the 
entire staircase followed a similar approach. At the beginning of each new scan, 
the application offers the choice between the two possible 3D scanning modes it 
provides: Auto (video) and Manual (photography). Priority was given to the ﬁrst 
mode because it is recommended when fast and straightforward scanning of large 
spaces is desired. Simultaneously, the app offers options like LiDAR-Room-360

3D Scanning of an Architectural Sculpture Using a Smartphone with LiDAR ... 307
Fig. 6 Polycam scan ( a) Scamming (left) ( b) Processing (center) ( c) Result (right) 
Photo. LiDAR was chosen for this research project. It is important to note that the 
application guides you on how to proceed with scanning in each mode but does not 
offer explicit recommendations on when to use one or the other. For processing of 
the data obtained in each case, Polycam provides three types of processing options 
(Fast-Spatial-Object). For each of these, you can adjust parameters like depth range, 
mesh voxel size, simpliﬁcation, automatic cropping, and loop closure. While the 
application explains the meaning of the ﬁrst three parameters, it does not provide 
information about the last two. Polycam also offers a valuable feature that allows 
for the duplication of scans, enabling you to save various processed versions of the 
same scanned area. 
Again, the application itself marked areas left unscanned with a purple color, and 
its instructions were followed to avoid them (Fig. 6). 
Once this 3D scan using the LiDAR sensor was completed, an individual analysis 
of the data quality was performed, along with a comparative study between both 
applications and a comparison with data obtained through traditional techniques. 
It was also veriﬁed that the obtained scan could be easily exported to other 3D 
modeling software. Speciﬁcally, the obtained ﬁles were exported to the Blender 
program. Blender is one of many available tools that allow working on the 3D 
scan obtained with the application. It is open-source and completely free software, 
aligning with the research initial goal of economizing.

308 P . Benítez Hernández and I. López Consuegra
From the results of the analyses conducted, both individual and comparative, 
conclusions have been drawn that address the research problem stated at the 
beginning of the study. 
5 Results and Discussion 
Once the data collection was completed and 3D models of the scanned areas were 
obtained, the following results have been achieved. It should be noted again that the 
goal of this study is to verify if the 3D scanning performed using the application 
installed on the smartphone provides sufﬁcient data for use in the survey of the 
helical staircase. To achieve this, both geometry and texture obtained in the ﬁnal 
model will be analyzed. 
5.1 Results of the Scanning of Step Piece No. 26 
Scanning the step number 26 was simple. The 3D scanning of its tread and riser was 
performed in detail. The 3D model did not take more than a couple of minutes to 
complete. It is worth noting that although reference targets were initially added to 
the ends of the tread during data collection to prevent potential alignment issues, 
it was observed that their inclusion did not improve the ﬁnal result; in fact, it 
obstructed the accurate view of the scanned piece. Therefore, the decision was made 
to remove the targets. This could be possible due to the numerous pathologies on 
the stair, mainly the pitting, which acted as reference points. As a result, model A 
was obtained with Polycam, and model B with Scaniverse (Fig. 7). 
Regarding the geometry, both models appear to be quite faithful to the real 
dimensions of the step. As mentioned in Sect. 3.1, the dimensions of the step 
Fig. 7 Step 26 ( a) Model A – Polycam (left) and ( b) Model B – Scaniverse (right)

3D Scanning of an Architectural Sculpture Using a Smartphone with LiDAR ... 309
Fig. 8 Step 26 dimensions ( a) Model A – Polycam (left) ( b) Model B – Scaniverse (right) 
obtained through traditional direct methods are as follows: a tread length of 105 cm, 
a maximum width of 36 cm, a minimum width of 9 cm, and a riser height of 20 cm. 
In Fig. 8, it can be seen the dimensions of models A and B obtained directly 
in the application. Both models match the measured dimensions, while there is 
less of 1 cm difference between these dimensions and the ones obtained using a 
ﬂexometer. It is important to note the difﬁculty of using the measuring tool in both 
applications, which arises from the challenge of accurately placing points on the 
small screen of the device by tapping with a ﬁnger to measure the desired distances. 
Additionally, the measurement provided by the application is a total distance and 
does not distinguish between the x, y, and z coordinates, making it essential to 
determine the exact starting and ending points of the dimension. Therefore, it is 
not possible to accurately extract the dimensions of the step directly from the 
smartphone application. To achieve precision, it is recommended to export the 
model to a computer software where it can be manipulated with ease and accuracy.

310 P . Benítez Hernández and I. López Consuegra
Furthermore, it is also advisable to verify the dimensions through traditional direct 
measurements, for example, a ﬂexometer. 
In terms of texture and ﬁnish, while both models faithfully reproduce the step, 
there is a clear difference in quality between them. The quality of the result was 
assessed based on the following parameters: the accurate reproduction of color, 
brightness, contrast, sharpness, and overall appearance, as well as resolution and 
compression. 
Regarding color, both models are quite similar, displaying real-color digital 
images that are fairly true to reality. However, there is a noticeable difference in 
brightness and contrast. Under the same lighting conditions and camera sensor, 
model B appears much brighter and has higher contrast without generating overly 
dark areas that limit the correct perception of the texture. The contrast and brightness 
of the inner molding, the staircase wall, and the riser of step number 25 stand out. In 
terms of sharpness, it is clear that model B has a higher level of detail compared to 
model A. This is particularly noticeable in the edge where the tread and riser of the 
step are joined, where it is possible to recognize areas with material loss in model 
B, while the same area in model A appears blurred. This results in a better overall 
perception of model B, where it can clearly be seen textures, pathologies, and the 
boundaries of the piece with a great ﬁdelity to the original. 
In terms of resolution, model A (Polycam) consists of 115.9 K vertices, and the 
ﬁle size is 50.2 MB. On the other hand, model B (Scaniverse) has more than twice 
the number of vertices (382 K) and is twice the size of the previous one (104.3 MB). 
This information conﬁrms the higher quality of the scanning performed with the 
Scaniverse application. 
5.2 Results of Scanning the Entire Staircase 
As previously mentioned in Sect. 2, the analysis of a staircase entails examining 
not only the individual step but also the staircase as a whole. Therefore, after 
scanning the step element, the entire staircase was scanned. The 3D scanning 
process took approximately 40 minutes for each application. During data capture, 
the use of reference targets was once again discarded, and an extension pole was 
employed. This approach resulted in the creation of model C (Polycam) and model 
D (Scaniverse) (Fig. 9). 
Despite the challenging lighting conditions, with low and uneven illumination, 
the models obtained allow for a global perception of the entire staircase, something 
that would not have been possible otherwise, as the circular nature of the staircase 
restricts visibility beyond a single turn. These models can be compared to a kind of 
X-ray of the internal structure of the helical staircase. 
However, upon detailed analysis of both models, signiﬁcant alignment issues 
were detected, particularly in the window openings and the handrail embedded in 
the outer wall of the staircase. These problems were more pronounced in model C 
compared to model D, as can be observed in Fig. 10. Additionally, both models

3D Scanning of an Architectural Sculpture Using a Smartphone with LiDAR ... 311
Fig. 9 Entire staircase ( a) Model C – Polycam (left) ( b) Model D – Scaniverse (right) 
exhibited occasional blurred areas on the steps and problems with deﬁning the 
texture of the staircase. It is worth noting that the use of an extension pole to reach 
distant areas during data capture could have contributed to the image instability and 
consequently caused a reduction in quality. The use of a gimbal stabilizer was not 
considered as it is not a common tool among the general population, and its use 
would have involved an additional ﬁnancial investment. 
Regarding the handrail embedded in the outer wall of the staircase, it was not 
possible to capture the detailed geometry of its section due to the presence of 
electrical cables inside, which are part of the cathedral lighting installation. For a 
detailed deﬁnition of the geometry of this molding, it is recommended to conduct 
a 3D scan of a section in detail, similar to what was done with the step piece. 
Additionally, verifying its measurements through direct methods, such as using a 
ﬂexometer, is advisable. 
It is essential to highlight that model D (Scaniverse, 4653.6 MB raw data) 
provides a signiﬁcantly higher image quality than model C (Polycam, 198 MB).

312 P . Benítez Hernández and I. López Consuegra
Fig. 10 Alignment issues ( a) Model C – Polycam (left) ( b) Model D – Scaniverse (right) 
Model D clearly deﬁnes the volume and geometry of the entire structure, including 
the inner dimensions of case, its upper cap with the spherical dome, the number 
of steps per turn, the offset of the inner molding from the central axis, the overall 
layout of the handrail embedded in the wall, the arrangement of windows and access 
doors, and a better overall delineation of the elements. Model D was subsequently 
exported to the Blender software, where its proper and straightforward manipulation 
was conﬁrmed (Fig. 11). 
5.3 Results of the Full Turn Scan 
The primary goal of scanning just a single full turn was to obtain a shorter video 
sequence in order to perform a better processing and thus reduce the alignment 
issues observed in the full staircase model. While the result does not provide a 
comprehensive view of the entire staircase, it offers an intermediate perspective for 
analyzing both the proportions of the individual step and its relationship with the 
entire staircase. Models E (Polycam) and F (Scaniverse) were obtained using this 
method. 
Once again, Scaniverse outperformed Polycam in this issue. Model F signiﬁ-
cantly mitigated alignment issues and texture distortion, as shown in Fig. 12.T h i s

(right) 
model proved to be exceptional, capturing not only the geometry but also the texture 
and existing structural irregularities accurately. 
In order to determine the geometric quality of the obtained models, a series of 
points were identiﬁed (Fig. 13), and a comparison was made between the measures 
of these points and the measures obtained using traditional techniques. Slight 
deviations were observed in the interior dimensions of the exterior wall, as well as 
in the dimensions of the inner hollow and interior molding. These elements deﬁned 
not perfect circles but slightly deformed ones, causing the diameter of the staircase 
to ﬂuctuate between 280 and 278 cm. Similarly, the dimensions of the step showed 
small deviations, although on average, they maintained the dimensions measured 
using the ﬂexometer.

However, the most notable ﬁnding from this analysis is that the riser of the steps

6 Conclusions 
This chapter has focused on the assessment of the results obtained through LiDAR 
technology integrated into smartphones for the 3D documentation of late Gothic 
helical staircases. 
The application of new digital techniques for 3D documentation of built heritage 
is becoming increasingly common. Although faster and more precise 3D scanners 
are being developed, they are often more expensive, complex to operate, and 
occasionally bulkier, which limits their use to speciﬁc cases. Simultaneously, 3D 
scanning applications available for smartphones are also undergoing signiﬁcant 
technological advancements, offering increasingly better possibilities for document-
ing heritage elements. With this technology, it is possible to capture a large amount 
of data at high speed, as laser scanning does. However, in contrast, it requires 
less planning time and post-processing of the obtained data. Additionally, using 
these applications offers several signiﬁcant advantages, including portability, ease 
of transportation as they are integrated into a small, commonly used device among 
the general population, lower cost, and intuitive application use. In other words, it 
is a valuable and readily available resource accessible to the majority.

316 P . Benítez Hernández and I. López Consuegra
This study aimed to assess whether a 3D model of a late Gothic helical staircase 
obtained through a 3D scanner application integrated into a smartphone provides 
sufﬁcient information for its comprehensive documentation. This particular type 
of circular staircase is relatively small, and its unique morphology prevents a 
global interior view of the whole structure. For this reason, 3D documentation 
is necessary for its accurate deﬁnition. Traditional 3D documentation techniques 
face signiﬁcant challenges with these staircases due to their distinct geometry, 
necessitating detailed planning when using traditional 3D scanners. Additionally, 
the limited and uneven lighting negatively impacts data capture for traditional 
photogrammetry. The application of LiDAR technology aimed to overcome these 
challenges and provide data that contributes to the proper documentation of the 
staircase. 
This study focused on the helical staircase of La Concepción Chapel in the 
Segovia Cathedral. 3D scanning was performed in three different areas: a step, 
speciﬁcally step number 26; a complete turn; and the entire staircase. Two freely 
available applications, Polycam and Scaniverse, were used on an iPhone 14 Pro 
with a 48-megapixel main camera. Each of the 3D models provided a reasonably 
faithful view of the scanned area. However, it was evident that the models obtained 
with Scaniverse were of higher quality. 
The 3D model of the entire staircase provided an overview that would not have 
been obtainable otherwise and served as the physical framework for locating the 
other scanned areas and any associated information. It also allows the detection of 
potential problematic points that may require closer examination. The scanning of a 
single step and a complete turn provided fairly precise and detailed information 
about the scanned area, both regarding its texture and geometry. While making 
measurements directly in the application required a considerable effort, the models 
were easily exported to Blender, a freely available and free software program, 
from which necessary adjustments could be made for proper documentation and 
subsequent measurements. Although the data obtained are usually less precise than 
traditional 3D scanning methods, such as photogrammetry and laser scanning, 
the models offered an acceptable level of accuracy. It allowed the validation of 
the dimensions obtained through traditional measurements techniques. But most 
importantly, it enabled the detection of a potential design uniqueness, which should 
be examined in detail using more precise techniques. 
Furthermore, 3D documentation obtained through these applications has the 
signiﬁcant advantage of being easily shared through instant messaging, further 
accelerating the time needed for model analysis and subsequent decision-making. 
For the creation of 3D models intended for more than just dissemination, careful 
selection of the application is recommended. The quality of the results obtained 
depends not only on the mobile device used but also on the application installed. 
Additionally, it is advisable to follow a procedure similar to the one used in this 
study, which involves scanning in at least three areas: the step generating the 
staircase, a complete turn, and the entire staircase. Each area provides different and 
necessary levels of information. Furthermore, to achieve the best results during data 
capture, it is essential to have a previous scan plan to avoid leaving areas unscanned, 
reduce scanning speed, and ensure the device stability.

3D Scanning of an Architectural Sculpture Using a Smartphone with LiDAR ... 317
While these 3D scanning applications using LiDAR sensors cannot compete with 
laser scanners or photogrammetry in terms of accuracy and precision, it has been 
demonstrated that they are a fantastic support for professionals in the construction 
ﬁeld. However, it is essential to keep in mind that data capture using this technology 
is an indirect method that does not, in any case, replace the taking of photographs or 
direct measurements of elements that the responsible professional deems necessary. 
As future lines of research, it is proposed to study the use of these applications 
installed on Android smartphones with ToF (Time of Flight) sensors other than 
LiDAR. In addition, it is also proposed to carry out 3D documentation of the exterior 
to achieve a complete 3D deﬁnition of the helical staircase volume and establish its 
relationship with the entire building.

The Impossible Cathedral of Mejorada 
del Campo, Madrid: Utilizing 
Digitalization to Comprehend Its 
Geometry and Behavior 
Juan Carlos Arroyo Portero and Fernando Moral-Andrés 
1 Introduction 
On the ninth of April 2021, just over 2 years ago, the cathedral in Mejorada del 
Campo, Madrid, was donated to Mensajeros de la Paz, an NGO run by Father Ángel, 
an Asturian priest who has dedicated his life to helping the poor. This donation 
occurred around the time when Justo Gallego, an exceptional man, was nearing the 
end of his life. Justo Gallego, born in 1925, commenced the construction of the 
cathedral single-handedly in 1960. For over 60 years, with sporadic assistance and 
no technical support, he accomplished the remarkable feat of building this cathedral. 
This chapter focuses on the cathedral, delving into its sustainability, construction, 
resilience, and future. The NGO approached the structural engineering company 
CALTER to ensure the cathedral’s structural capacity. Their intention was to utilize 
it as a place of worship and a meeting point for diverse cultures and religions, 
Catholic and non-Catholic. 
Assessing the structural state of the building posed a challenge, as the work had 
no documentation aside from the possibility of taking samples, conducting tests, 
and consulting with the author, extensively documented in numerous videos and 
interviews (primarily on YouTube). Important testimonies were also provided by 
Ángel, the person who assisted Justo in the last years of his life. The cathedral’s 
structural restoration project received the Madrid College of Civil Engineers “best 
work of the year.” 
The objective of this chapter is to illuminate the reasons behind Justo’s construc-
tion of the cathedral, how he built it despite academic ignorance, and to elucidate, 
from the perspective of a team of structural experts, the reasons for its surprising 
stability and resistance. It particularly focuses on the construction process and
