Figure 1 showcases a magniﬁcent and extraordinary work of art—an improbable 
achievement. It is termed “impossible” because it appears incredible that someone, 
under such challenging circumstances, could accomplish this feat: an individual, in 
a relatively short span of time achieving a work of this magnitude, without technical 
knowledge. 
2 Justo Gallego, the Man Who Built a Cathedral 
Justo Gallego was born in 1925, the son of farmers, in the town of Mejorada del 
Campo. His family owned land, and the town of Mejorada was relatively large in 
the region. It can be said that his family had a certain economic capacity; they were 
not poor, but rather farmers who earned their living from their work. 
The third of four brothers, he entered the convent of Santa María de Huerta in 
Soria at the age of 27. Eight years later, he left the monastery due to an illness that 
was unpopular among the monks and returned to his village with the ﬁrm conviction 
that he had done something wonderful and had offered it to God and the Virgin. 
Upon returning to his village, he began the construction of the cathedral. In the 
initial stages, Justo traveled to Madrid several times, where he encountered an urban

The Impossible Cathedral of Mejorada del Campo, Madrid: Utilizing... 321
Fig. 2 Digniﬁed posture and 
stacked bricks. Justo’s 
personal collection 
world that did not align with his concept of sanctity. He disliked the noisy, seemingly 
impersonal, and selﬁsh life there. He purchased several books about cathedrals and 
then returned to his village. 
He is a straightforward man, obsessed with holiness, avoiding sin, especially 
the sin of vanity, a term he frequently employs. He expresses genuinely interesting 
thoughts with an attitude that is both close and ﬁrm, polemical, and digniﬁed (see 
Fig. 2). 
He ate very little and hardly any meat, although he was not a vegetarian. 
He was a religious man, as evident in some of his statements: “I saw that the 
cathedral was so beautiful that I didn’t want to look at it.” This sentence reﬂects 
both his pride in the beauty of his work and his awareness that such vanity is 
inappropriate. The author reiterates the idea of vanity several times throughout the 
text (see Fig. 3). When a journalist asked him if he was happy after completing the 
work, he responded, “I am not the one to say if I am happy. You have to say it, but 
if I say it, it’s vanity.” The man consistently wore the same outﬁt, which comprised 
blue overalls, a rope belt, and a small red beret on his head.

322 J. C. A. Portero and F. Moral-Andrés
Fig. 3 Bike wheels and paint cans 
This excerpt provides insight into the subject’s personality and beliefs, particu-
larly concerning views on vanity, food, and dress. It also illustrates his unwavering 
determination to express these beliefs and desires throughout his 60-year career. 
3 The Cathedral: History and Structural Considerations 
In 1961, Justo began the cathedral with some very clear ideas. What is unusual is 
that from the ﬁrst moment, he had the entire project mapped out in his mind—the 
geometry, the morphology, the materials, and the ultimate goal of his work. 
It is surprising, just like a twenty-ﬁrst-century engineer, Justo had such a clear 
vision right from the start, from the initial excavation to laying the ﬁrst brick. The 
early photos reveal that he knew precisely the dimensions of his ambitious work. 
Even after 60 years, the original dimensions remain visible. Photographs from 
the 1960s showcase the ﬁrst brick walls with meticulously placed masonry. The 
brick walls exhibit well-executed verticality and signiﬁcant thickness, indicating 
the intended height of the cathedral. Certain materials, especially the bricks, hold 
signiﬁcant importance for him, along with other elements such as the lap length of 
the reinforcements of the columns and stairs. These aspects are more a consequence 
of construction requirements than aesthetic choices; they symbolize an eternal 
construction, always ongoing and never entirely ﬁnished. 
The cathedral follows one guiding principle that motivated Justo throughout its 
construction: to build a church for the poor using old materials, serving as a clear 
representation of a church for those most in need. 
Key structural aspects of the cathedral that captivate a structural engineer include 
the early conception of the entire work by a single person with minimal assistance, 
the leadership of an individual without formal education or travel experience, and 
the achievement of verticality without a plumb line.

The Impossible Cathedral of Mejorada del Campo, Madrid: Utilizing... 323
During his visit to Mejorada after receiving the Prince of Asturias Award, 
Norman Foster commented, “I’m sure that you deserve the award more than me.” 
Upon reviewing his YouTube videos, the only available source of information, 
it is evident that he possesses a certain wisdom not derived from books but rather 
from intuition. “You must create structures that are both aesthetically pleasing and 
efﬁcient while also being constructed in a timely manner.” This statement embodies 
the principles of beauty, efﬁciency, and speed essential in the ﬁelds of engineering 
and architecture. The term “Vitruvian” has been removed to avoid confusion as it is 
not commonly understood. The author’s vision of construction is conveyed through 
the emphasis on these three principles. 
Justo’s statement, “I am not concerned if the methods I use are too precise...” has 
been retained to preserve the author’s intended meaning. This statement suggests 
the author’s awareness of the magnitude of their work and a sense of urgency to 
complete it, rather than indicating an inability to be more precise. 
3.1 Recycling 
Justo’s lifestyle revolves around recycling, reusing, and austerity. He utilizes his 
construction to convey a message to the world, emphasizing its purpose for the 
less fortunate. At various junctures, Justo could have opted for new materials. 
For instance, the local brick factories offered him pallets of new bricks, yet he 
favored the old ones—the discarded bricks, the less afﬂuent materials. He employed 
recycling as a metaphor, selecting waste (Fig. 3).1 
Justo used bricks that contained faults during the treatment in the kiln. As shown 
in Fig. 4, the majority of the bricks appear to be defective. 
On the left side of the Fig. 5, concrete braces made from tomato jars can be seen.
1 In a way, it is a contradiction; he undertakes the creation of an immense cathedral, a colossal 
endeavor for one man, yet he strives to avoid drawing attention to himself through this monumental 
work. His desire is for us to recognize the cathedral as a tribute to God, rather than a showcase of 
his construction prowess or formidable will. Justo does not seek admiration; he prefers to remain 
inconspicuous, eschewing celebrations in his honor. His goal is to complete the cathedral and 
present it humbly as a place of worship. Nevertheless, within this vast construction, he infuses 
subtle details to express his humility, and recycling stands out as one of them. In this attitude, his 
life philosophy becomes evident: vanity is a sin, presumption is futile, beauty is divine, and when 
presented with the opportunity to showcase beauty, he wishes it not to be associated with himself 
but with God.

3.2 Loads 
During the Filomena snow storm, the most aggressive in the last century that 
demolished numerous industrial buildings, the dome remained exposed with its zinc 
tiles. It is impossible to determine what would have transpired if the dome had been 
covered. 
Nevertheless, the fact that Filomena passed without causing damage to either 
the dome or the towers served as clear evidence of their resilience. The nave 
ﬂoor, housing a crypt below, has endured the weight of people and extreme loads 
throughout construction, including that of the truck (Fig. 5).

The Impossible Cathedral of Mejorada del Campo, Madrid: Utilizing... 325
3.3 Concrete 
Justo produced two types of concrete: one with a light aggregate and the other 
with conventional aggregate. Lightweight aggregate concrete is typically employed 
for ornamental purposes, while conventional concrete is utilized for structural 
applications. Donations from commercial companies often supply lightweight 
aggregate, among other materials. 
One of the tasks involved in characterization was to assess the strength of the 
concrete (refer to Chap. 5). Concrete crafted manually exhibits strength results 
equal to or surpassing the standard concrete of that era, constructed by experienced 
professionals. 
3.4 Construction Scenes 
While the construction scenes may not facilitate analysis or safety inspections, they 
do demonstrate the ingenious construction methods that Justo, a single man, had to 
undertake. 
It is worth noting that although the legend of the construction speaks of a single 
man, Justo did receive sporadic help from children in the town and also from 
families who had beneﬁted from the real estate operations he undertook on land 
inherited from his family. Justo ﬁnanced the cathedral and provided housing for 
needy families in exchange for their assistance with construction. 
Ángel, a worker from a neighboring town, joined the construction team in the 
last decade, initially working sporadically before becoming a full-time member. 
One of the ﬁlms about Justo draws a curious comparison between Ángel and 
Justo, and Don Quixote and Sancho Panza. One was associated with divinity, 
while the other served as their earthly ofﬁcer and assistant. Their relationship was 
respectful until Justo’s demise. 
The construction scenes are terrifying, as Justo is depicted walking on a tightrope 
(Fig. 6). 
These images not only induce vertigo due to Justo’s position but also highlight 
the extreme slenderness of the nascent trusses. 
Justo’s foresight is evident in his design process, as he had already planned for 
skylights—the circular elements seen (Fig. 7) at the top of the nave. These skylights 
are a modern architectural feature, currently used in several works by prestigious 
architects. Additionally, Justo incorporated domes above the skylights, which were 
part of his original plan. 
No construction documentation exists, as it was deemed unnecessary by the 
individual who did not possess the knowledge to create it. They expressed a disdain 
for the engineering concept of a project, believing that drawing and projecting were 
a waste of time. They conﬁdently asserted that they had all the necessary information 
in their head, stating that it was passed on to them by a higher power. “God is the

326 J. C. A. Portero and F. Moral-Andrés
Fig. 6 Non-comment construction scene 
architect,” he conﬁdently responded to the repeated questions, as the journalists and 
documentary ﬁlmmakers were obsessively documenting their visit to Mejorada. 
3.5 Craftsman, As W ell As Builder 
Justo was a designer, a builder, and a craftsman who approached his work with a 
Renaissance-like interest in all aspects, particularly in addressing the problem of 
detail. 
The domes, covered with zinc tiles, showcase his expertise and attention to detail. 
Each zinc sheet is folded individually, taking into account its ﬁnal position and 
making the necessary folds to ensure resistance against water, time, and wind. 
This meticulous and patient work results in domes like the one shown in the

As an artisan (Fig. 9), Justo created stained glass windows that possess three 
main features:

 Circular geometry
 Radial composition 
Justo meticulously crafted the perfect and equidistant circle, representing the 
sun’s rays, with patience and precision, ensuring each piece is placed in its ﬁnal 
position with expert skill.
2 The image disappeared due to wrong and disrespectful decisions towards the spirit of Justo. 

The Impossible Cathedral of Mejorada del Campo, Madrid: Utilizing... 327

Although some may view the cathedral as a shoddy and unreﬁned work, 
especially when accustomed to expensive modern methods carried out by teams 
of people, a discerning eye will perceive its true value. This is particularly evident 
when discovering the stained-glass window being carefully and dedicatedly crafted 
on the table, which ﬁts perfectly into the hole left in the wall of discarded bricks. 
The cathedral’s rough appearance does not diminish its impressive compositional 
capacity and precision in construction, which surpass any technical evaluation of 
tolerances.

3.6 Cathedrals in Spain: Comparison of Dimensions 
When it comes to the constructive complexity of a cathedral, we usually refer to its 
width and depth as the deﬁning dimensions. As for the length, it is often determined 
by the available budget. 
A comparison of several Spanish cathedrals with the Mejorada cathedral yields 
interesting data (Table 1).

The León Cathedral measures 30 m × 30 m, the same as Mejorada. The Burgos 
cathedral, although not a single nave and with many openings, measures 60 m wide 
and 88 m high, making it a very special cathedral. Seville and Santiago are both just 
over 30 m in height, similar to Mejorada. Barcelona, on the other hand, is 40 m wide 
and 53 m high, making it considerably taller than the former. 
The construction time and year of construction are perhaps the most signiﬁcant 
comparative data points. Cathedrals are typically constructed over the course of one 
or two centuries. However, this particular cathedral was built by a single individual 
in just half a century. While the materials used may not be comparable, the number 
of workers and investment also differed signiﬁcantly. 
An aerial view of the cathedral (Fig. 10) allows a better understanding of its 
layout and comparison with other cathedrals. 
The image displays the central nave, vault, dome, cloister, two side buildings 
(one with four domes and the other with towers), and a private patio. Compared to 
this scheme, there are others that are very similar. For example, the Santa Eulalia

scheme in Barcelona has a main nave, two side naves, and a cloister to the right. 
The cathedrals of Santiago and León are also comparable examples. 
4 Structural Elements 
The use of circular geometry in elements such as the stained glass window, the 
railing, and the arch represents the divine, as Justo explains. Circular geometry is 
often associated with religion. 
The arch is a prominent feature throughout the building process. 
The walls begin with a signiﬁcant thickness and gradually become lighter as they 
ascend, thanks to the implementation of circular arch structures. 
The thickness of the walls shows that Justo had a great understanding of the scale 
of his work 60 years before it was ﬁnished. He used low-quality materials but made 
up for it by ensuring a very sturdy thickness. 
Justo transitioned to using concrete arches with unique technology, after initially 
constructing the arches with bricks. 
One of the most remarkable features of Justo’s work is the formwork of the 
arches. The arch formwork used as self-supporting formwork represents Justo’s use 
of a technical advance, based solely on his intuition, without any study. 
Justo frequently utilizes the arch as a design element with great skill. The arches 
vary in size and complexity, ranging from small, simple arches to larger, more 
grandiose structures consisting of smaller arches stacked on top of one another. 
The two large arches, particularly those ﬂanking the side doors (Fig. 11), can be 
described as majestic for several reasons. Firstly, they are built at a great height and 
have a slender design (length-thickness ratio). Secondly, they were constructed by 
a single person with minimal assistance, using on-site concrete manufacturing and 
innovative techniques (designed by a farmer). 
Circular geometry is a popular choice in old stone constructions, despite not 
being the strongest option. However, its historical signiﬁcance and aesthetic appeal 
make it a valuable choice for many architects and builders. 
The construction process begins by arranging the reinforcement acting as 
formwork and then placing the concrete. The structure is built autonomously from 
the bottom to the top, with each new part being supported by the previous one. 
This technique is known as the “Movable Scaffolding System” and has been used 
in bridges such as the Martín Gil viaduct (1939) and in many modern bridges. It is 
an interesting technique that allows for efﬁcient construction. 
Top-level construction companies use these techniques to build structures that 
cover much larger spans (Fig. 12). Although the cathedral only has a span of 15 m, 
it is important to note that Justo invented this method and it was not found in 
engineering books. 
The columns are made using prefabricated cylinders (paint cans) as formworks, 
that are superimposed with horizontal joints every 50 cm. The joints that seem to be 
evenly spaced are actually a result of the construction process. The columns were

The Impossible Cathedral of Mejorada del Campo, Madrid: Utilizing... 331
Fig. 11 Arch at the side 
entrance 
formed using paint cans, which left a metal ﬁnish on the top and created the ﬁnal 
pattern in the concrete. This pattern appears at a distance equal to the height of the 
can. 
This creates an apparent disconnection in their height, but almost all the columns 
are actually made of continuous concrete. This provides them with the necessary 
rigidity for stability during construction and in the ﬁnal state. 
It’s clear that this pattern was intentional, most likely due to the economy of the 
construction. The builder took advantage of this circumstance to give an aesthetic 
order to the columns of the construction. 
The lap length for reinforcements, which wait for the next section of the pillar to 
be built, is included in the construction. This is because Justo likely intuited the need 
for continuity not only in the concrete but also in the reinforcement, and therefore 
overlapped it. It’s possible that he copied this detail from conventional, everyday 
works around him. 
When reinforcing, it seems that Justo may have overlooked some conceptual 
aspects. The reinforcement provided may not be sufﬁcient for a construction of this 
size and there appears to be some overlap. It is unclear whether the reinforcement 
was intended to guarantee durability or if it was due to a mistaken intuition about

332 J. C. A. Portero and F. Moral-Andrés
Fig. 12 Construction of the 
Martín Gil bridge, Soria, 
Spain 
the central work of the support. Furthermore, the length of the reinforcement seems 
to be too long for the diameters used (Fig. 13). 
One notable fact about the columns is that they are already in their ﬁnal position, 
where they will remain until the completion of the cathedral 50 years later. It’s 
great to know that the placement of the columns is deﬁnitive and harmonious. 
There are no misaligned or twisted pillars in the structure. All vertical elements, 
including pillars and walls, are perfectly vertical. Justo claims to have a method for 
determining verticality using his body. While this method may not seem scientiﬁc, 
it was effective and did not involve the use of a plumb line. The achieved level of 
verticality is really impressive. 
Justo demonstrated a clear understanding of the structural schemes of the primary 
and secondary arches, as evidenced by his awareness of the position of the columns, 
the height of the cathedral, the length of the openings, and the staining of the arches. 
To ensure correct structural behavior, it is crucial to consider scale and slender-
ness. A structure with appropriate scale (height/base) and slenderness (depth/span) 
is well equipped to withstand external forces. 
It can be argued that the most important factor in ensuring resistance is 
appropriate slenderness, while the most important factor in ensuring stability is 
appropriate scale. 
On the other hand, a structure lacking in scale may be able to resist, but only in 
a more strained manner, just as a structure without scale will face greater stability 
issues when subjected to horizontal forces.

The Impossible Cathedral of Mejorada del Campo, Madrid: Utilizing... 333
Fig. 13 Reinforcement 
overlapped 
It’s important to note that scale pertains to the external dimensions of the 
structure and is more closely related to aesthetics. When a structure has scale, it 
becomes easier to construct, even for builders without academic backgrounds in 
architecture or engineering. To determine an appropriate scale, we can examine 
similar structures, such as cathedrals in Spanish cities. It’s interesting to note that 
Justo researched extensively before beginning his work, even purchasing books 
from bookstores in Madrid. 
However, determining the slenderness of the structural elements is more chal-
lenging without appropriate studies. The cathedral’s structural elements are slender, 
which can only be explained by the intuition of the builder, Justo Gallego. 
Despite having many theoretical and technological deﬁciencies, the scale of the 
cathedral ensures that small defects do not destabilize the structure. 
Justo conveys the harmony of the construction through the geometric deﬁnition 
of his work. 
The cathedral’s scale and harmony are achieved by scaling the diameter and 
height of the towers, the number of towers, the thickness of the walls, the depth 
of the slabs, the distance between columns, the height and diameter of the columns, 
and even the ﬂoor plan. The use of scale ensures a logical and balanced structure.

334 J. C. A. Portero and F. Moral-Andrés
Fig. 14 Dome 
The building is not a cathedral because it does not serve as a place of worship. 
Nevertheless, the ﬂoor plan, cloister, and side naves adhere to the correct proportions 
of a cathedral. 
The dome is the most photogenic element of the construction (Fig. 14), possibly 
due to its unﬁnished state. It is not covered with zinc tiles but is structurally 
complete. The dome is formed by generating radii of a single curvature that Justo 
had meticulously measured and raised with strictly homemade auxiliary means. 
Justo’s concern for the dome’s structure is exactly the same as that of a structural 
engineer. He expressed that he is not concerned about the weight of the roof, but 
rather the wind, which is why bracing is necessary. He demonstrated the wind as a 
horizontal force with hand gestures and closed his hands in a circle to illustrate his 
idea of bracing the dome.3 
3 Something unique occurs in Justo Cathedral that can be experienced in other signiﬁcant 
architectural works: the photographs always turn out well because they are inherently photogenic 
structures. This same sensation can be felt, for example, in Siza’s work. The provided example 
consists of captivating photos showcasing a vault with half-rusted sheet metal and an unﬁnished 
dome.

The Impossible Cathedral of Mejorada del Campo, Madrid: Utilizing... 335
Fig. 15 Vault 
Justo demonstrated his intuition during the construction process of the cathedral 
by discussing the bracing of the dome. Overall, the construction of the cathedral was 
a success due to careful planning and execution of the building process. To achieve 
the effect of tying and conﬁning the entire structure, the entire nave must be well 
ﬁnished. The vaults were built before the dome, as stabilizing them only required 
the construction of the side walls. The cathedral’s stability is attributed to the use of 
lightweight elements in the construction of its vaults. 
The metal vault (Fig. 15), which has the scale of a cathedral but not the weight, 
rests on brick walls that are more than capable of supporting its vertical loads. 
The nave vault of the cathedral is constructed using a material that contributes 
to its structural success. If stone or concrete were used, the weight would require 
much greater structural strength. It is important to note that the process of structural 
thinning, from Romanesque to Gothic constructions, was motivated by the need to 
resist the tremendous weight of the stone roofs of the cathedrals. The cathedral has 
the architectural structure of a classical cathedral but is signiﬁcantly lighter. This is 
one of the reasons for its construction. 
The concrete gusset is a unique and innovative element. The cartouches of the 
cathedral bear a striking resemblance to those of a Galician Mozarabic church 
(Orense, 1000 years ago) that had the same ornamental ﬁgure (Fig. 16). However, 
the brace in Orense is made of stone, while the one in Justo’s cathedral is made of 
concrete with tomato jars. 
The crypt, located beneath the main nave, is a unique space due to its access, 
architecture, wall decorations, and lighting. Structurally, the crypt is the most 
compromised part of the building, with a span of 10 m, exceeding the typical span of 
7 m in conventional buildings, and exhibiting unidirectional behavior. The structure

336 J. C. A. Portero and F. Moral-Andrés
Fig. 16 Corbels formed with tomato cans. Church of San Miguel de Celanova 
of the crypt’s roof, while less visually striking than other parts of the cathedral, 
is more precarious due to its straight design lacking the added support of curved 
shapes. 
Justo’s typical structures rely on arches and vaults for support, while the crypt 
relies on bending, a less common and more complex shape that requires careful 
structural analysis. It is important to note that this shape is currently the most 
economical option, as it has been for over a century. However, the author relies on 
slender design to resist the forces. Justo built a straight slab with a variable edge that 
has competent proportions for this type of structure. The reinforcement can then be 
arranged intuitively, but ensuring adequate slenderness is the ﬁrst step to ensuring 
safety. 
The trusses in the naves are a clear example of Justo’s lack of technical 
knowledge. Many of the trusses exhibit poor structural capacity due to defective 
details. During a tour of the building, it becomes evident that Justo had only a 
general sense of the shape of the trusses but did not pay attention to the necessary 
details. 
Note the point where the lower metal proﬁle of the truss ends, which must 
strictly reach the support (Fig. 17). The adjacent nave pictured below provides a 
poor structural example of the cathedral. The truss was constructed with incorrect 
details and a bottom chord alone that cannot resist the total load. 
The slabs are constructed using conventional techniques and consist of unidirec-
tional slabs with joists. Justo’s innovative approach lies in the use of the material 
between the joists. 
It is worth noting that the joists used in the construction are obtained from charity. 
The length of the joists remains ﬁxed, as there is no need for adjustment, and leaving 
them longer than necessary does not interfere with their purpose. Additionally, 
adjusting their length would divert the worker’s attention from their main objective, 
which is to complete the cathedral quickly and safely.

The Impossible Cathedral of Mejorada del Campo, Madrid: Utilizing... 337
Fig. 17 Bad examples of 
structure 
Fig. 18 Slab made with ceramic pieces 
The material between the joists is primarily waste ceramic material, consisting of 
various shapes, origins, and colors. Justo’s intention when constructing the cathedral 
was to showcase the beauty in things that may not be immediately visible. The ﬁlling 
ceramics are arranged in a way that makes them visible, even using broken waste 
ceramics and carefully placing them pretty side down. 
It is clear that one of his goals is to create a beautiful cathedral, with a focus on 
showcasing the ceiling of slabs (Fig. 18). 
The construction of Justo features a recurring element in both structural and 
ornamental components. 
Justo employs a leitmotif4 in his cathedral through the use of spirals. The spiral 
serves as a metaphorical representation of circular perfection and eternity (Fig. 19). 
When choosing which arches to ﬁll with lightweight aggregate, it is important 
to select those that are structurally understressed. For the remaining arches, 
conventional concrete with a strength of 25 MPa should be used.
4 Similar to Wagner’s use of leitmotifs in his operas. 

338 J. C. A. Portero and F. Moral-Andrés
Fig. 19 Spirals in the roof/in the stairs/in the arches 
Ángel, who was Justo’s assistant during the last few years, explains how the 
project was constructed: “The small-diameter steel bars are bent using human force, 
leveraging against an already-built column. Once the straight spiral is generated, it 
is given the desired circular shape and ﬁlled with concrete of the desired quality.” 
Justo’s spiral utilizes the property of conﬁnement, a well-known concept in 
materials science. Materials with a high Poisson’s ratio, meaning their perpendicular 
deformations are signiﬁcant (around 15–25% of the deformation in the direction 
of the load), exhibit increased resistance and can withstand greater deformation 
when conﬁned. It is important to limit their transverse deformation to achieve this. 
The transverse reinforcement of concrete prevents its transverse deformation and 
breaking under tension perpendicular to the compression. This is induced by the 
Poisson effect (Fig. 20). 
This property, long recognized in the engineering world, was ofﬁcially intro-
duced in reinforced concrete standards in the late 1990s. However, Justo had been 
utilizing it since the 1960s.

The Impossible Cathedral of Mejorada del Campo, Madrid: Utilizing... 339
Fig. 20 Conﬁnement of concrete 
5 Structural Inspections 
CALTER Engineering conducted a structural inspection and performed several 
tests to determine the strength of the concrete. Breakage tests were carried out 
on specimens extracted from various columns, walls, and slabs, revealing concrete 
resistance values of approximately 25 MPa. 
To contextualize this resistance value, it is worth noting that during that time in 
Spain, concrete used in city works by professionals with concrete plants typically 
had a speciﬁcation of 17.5 MPa. The concrete used in the cathedral is of higher 
quality than usual, with a 40% improvement. It appears that Justo was meticulous in 
measuring the cement and may have had the foresight to avoid adding excess water, 
which can be detrimental. 
Geotechnical assessments were also conducted, revealing that the land on which 
the cathedral stands is stable.

340 J. C. A. Portero and F. Moral-Andrés
6 Digital Models 
Geometric modeling primarily serves two essential purposes for a comprehensive 
understanding of the cathedral: geometry and structural behavior. Accessing a 
comprehensive geometrical deﬁnition of an existing construction is challenging 
without modern digitization methods. 
Several techniques are commonly used for digitizing existing building geome-
tries. One popular option is 3D laser scanning, which captures the building’s 
shape and dimensions with great precision using a laser. Another technique is 
photogrammetry, which involves taking photographs from different angles and then 
using specialized software to reconstruct the geometry in 3D. Drone scanning can 
also be used to capture aerial images and generate digital models. The choice 
of technique depends on factors such as budget, required precision, and building 
complexity. 
3D laser scanning is a cutting-edge technology that has revolutionized the way 
we model and document existing buildings. This technique involves using a laser 
scanner to capture millions of data points on the surface of a building, creating a 
detailed and accurate 3D model of its geometry. The process is non-invasive and 
can be completed relatively quickly, making it an ideal method for capturing the 
intricate details of complex architectural structures. 
The ﬁrst step in 3D laser scanning is to set up the equipment in strategic locations 
around the building. The laser scanner emits a beam of light that sweeps across the 
building’s surfaces, measuring the distance to each point it hits. As the scanner 
rotates and moves, it captures data from all angles, creating a comprehensive point 
cloud that represents the building’s exterior and interior. 
Once the scanning is complete, the data is processed using specialized software 
to create a 3D model of the building. This model accurately represents the building’s 
geometry, including its shape, size, and intricate details such as ornate facades 
or decorative elements. The level of detail captured by 3D laser scanning is 
unparalleled, allowing for precise measurements and analysis of even the most 
complex architectural features. 
One of the key advantages of 3D laser scanning is its ability to capture details 
with incredible accuracy. This makes it an invaluable tool for documenting existing 
buildings, especially those with historical or cultural signiﬁcance. By creating a 
detailed 3D model of a building, architects and engineers can accurately assess its 
condition and plan renovations or restoration projects. 
Another application of 3D laser scanning is in the ﬁeld of Building Information 
Modeling (BIM). By integrating scanned data into BIM software, highly detailed 
digital representations of existing buildings can be created. 
Equipment: Laser scanner, which is a highly specialized piece of equipment. 
These scanners can range from handheld devices to larger tripod-mounted or 
vehicle-mounted systems. The cost of these scanners can vary signiﬁcantly based 
on their capabilities, accuracy, and range.

The Impossible Cathedral of Mejorada del Campo, Madrid: Utilizing... 341
The specialized software allows for the registration and alignment of point cloud 
data, as well as the creation of detailed 3D models. 
Photogrammetry is a powerful technique used to model the geometries of 
existing buildings. It involves capturing and analyzing photographic images to 
create accurate 3D models of structures. This method offers a non-invasive and cost-
effective approach to creating detailed digital representations. 
The process of photogrammetry begins with the capture of a series of high-
resolution photographs of the building from various angles. These images are taken 
using specialized cameras or drones equipped with high-quality lenses to ensure 
precise and detailed data capture. The photographs should cover all aspects of the 
building, including its exterior, interior, and surrounding environment. 
Once the images are captured, they are processed using photogrammetry soft-
ware. This software analyzes the photographs to identify common points or features 
in multiple images, allowing it to triangulate the position of these points in 3D space. 
By comparing the positions of these points across multiple images, the software can 
reconstruct the 3D geometry of the building with remarkable accuracy. 
One of the key advantages of photogrammetry is its ability to capture highly 
detailed and realistic textures. The high-resolution photographs used in this tech-
nique allow for the creation of 3D models that accurately represent the visual 
appearance of a building, including its surface materials, colors, and architectural 
details. This level of detail makes photogrammetry an ideal method for creating 
visually stunning and lifelike digital replicas of existing buildings. 
Similar to 3D scanning, photogrammetry is increasingly being integrated into 
Building Information Modeling (BIM) workﬂows. By combining 3D models 
created through photogrammetry with BIM software, architects and engineers 
can develop comprehensive digital representations that accurately reﬂect existing 
building conditions. This integration allows for more informed decision-making 
during design and construction processes. 
Photogrammetry relies on high-resolution cameras to capture a series of pho-
tographs from various angles. While professional-grade DSLR cameras are often 
used for this purpose, advancements in drone technology have made it possible to 
capture aerial imagery using drones equipped with high-quality cameras. Special-
ized photogrammetry software is used to process the captured images and generate 
3D models. This software analyzes the photographs to identify common points or 
features in multiple images and reconstructs the building’s geometry. 
Drone scanning, along with drone photogrammetry or aerial surveying, is a 
cutting-edge technique used to model the geometries of existing buildings and 
structures. This innovative method involves the use of unmanned aerial vehicles 
(UA Vs), commonly referred to as drones, equipped with high-resolution cameras 
and LiDAR sensors to capture detailed imagery and data from the air. The captured 
data is then processed using specialized software to create accurate 3D models of 
buildings and their surroundings. 
The process of drone scanning begins with careful planning and preparation. 
A ﬂight plan is established to ensure comprehensive coverage of the building and 
its surroundings. The drone is then deployed to ﬂy over the target area, capturing

342 J. C. A. Portero and F. Moral-Andrés
a series of high-resolution images from different angles and altitudes. In addition 
to traditional photography, LiDAR sensors may be used to collect precise distance 
measurements, enabling the creation of highly detailed point clouds that accurately 
represent the building’s geometry. 
Once the data collection is complete, the images and LiDAR data are processed 
using photogrammetry or 3D scanning software. 
One of the key advantages of drone scanning is its ability to capture detailed 
information about a building’s exterior, even in hard-to-reach or inaccessible areas. 
Drones can ﬂy at varying altitudes and angles, allowing for comprehensive coverage 
of complex architectural geometries. 
Drone scanning, like other related techniques, offers signiﬁcant advantages in 
terms of efﬁciency and cost-effectiveness compared to traditional methods. 
The cost of drones can vary based on their capabilities, payload capacity, ﬂight 
time, and camera quality. LiDAR sensors add an additional cost to the equipment 
setup, and specialized software is used, similar to photogrammetry and 3D scanning. 
6.1 Comparison of T echniques 
The three commonly used methods related differ in their approach, equipment, 
and capabilities. Three processes are non-invasive and can be completed relatively 
quickly, making it an ideal method for capturing intricate details of complex 
architectural structures. 
3D scanning captures millions of data points on the surface of a building. 
The level of detail captured by 3D scanning is unparalleled, allowing for precise 
measurements and analysis of even the most complex architectural features. 
Photogrammetry involves capturing a series of high-resolution photographs. 
Photogrammetry is very interesting to capture highly detailed and realistic textures. 
The high-resolution photographs used in this technique allows a very realistic 
representation of the visual appearance. The three commonly used methods differ 
in their approach, equipment, and capabilities. All three processes are non-invasive 
and can be completed relatively quickly, making them ideal for capturing intricate 
details of complex architectural structures. 
3D scanning captures millions of data points on the surface of a building. 
The level of detail captured by 3D scanning is unparalleled, allowing for precise 
measurements and analysis of even the most complex architectural features. 
Photogrammetry involves capturing a series of high-resolution photographs. 
Photogrammetry is very effective for capturing highly detailed and realistic textures. 
The high-resolution photographs used in this technique allow for a very realistic 
representation of the visual appearance of a building, including its surface materials, 
colors, and architectural details. 
Working with drones allows for the capture of detailed information about a 
building’s exterior, even in hard-to-reach or inaccessible areas. Drones can ﬂy at

The Impossible Cathedral of Mejorada del Campo, Madrid: Utilizing... 343
varying altitudes and angles, allowing for comprehensive coverage of complex 
architectural details such as facades, roofs, and ornamental elements. 
The cost of each method for modeling existing buildings—3D scanning, pho-
togrammetry, and drone scanning—can vary based on several factors, including 
the equipment and software required. Generally, 3D scanning tends to be the most 
expensive of the three methods due to the specialized hardware involved. 
In summary, while all three methods require specialized equipment and software, 
3D scanning tends to be the most expensive due to the high cost of laser scanners. 
Photogrammetry and drone scanning also require an investment in quality cameras 
or drones with advanced imaging capabilities but may be relatively more affordable 
compared to 3D scanning equipment. It’s important to note that beyond initial 
equipment costs, ongoing expenses such as maintenance, training, and software 
updates should also be considered when evaluating the overall expense. 
It is also important to note that the data storage capacity in photogrammetry must 
be much greater than in 3D scanning, which, for extensive work in large projects, is 
a value to take into account. 
6.2 Cathedral Modeling 
At the cathedral, the structural engineering team utilized 3D scanning images. The 
images taken from the ground and the drone were compiled into a complete point 
cloud, enabling the precise determination of the geometry of the cathedral and its 
adjacent buildings. Both exterior and interior measurements need to be completed. 
LiDAR scanning emits multiple laser pulses that bounce back to the sensor. The 
device measures both the satellite positioning and the bounce data of the geometry to 
obtain the exact position of the measurement. This is essential for aligning different 
ﬂights or sweeps. 
Speciﬁc software is used to assemble the various point clouds. 
LiDAR is becoming increasingly popular compared to photogrammetry, which is 
cheaper but requires well-deﬁned lines for accurate measurements, such as in civil 
works, roads, dams, and canals. 
LiDAR has the added advantage of providing direct measurements in point 
clouds, resulting in smaller ﬁle sizes compared to the high-resolution photos 
required for photogrammetry. The smaller ﬁle sizes and ease of post-production 
are advantageous. 
The images display the point clouds of the 3D model generated from multiple 
laser ﬂights (Fig. 21). 
However, the amount of information and precise geometry determined by the 
laser may not be easily understandable. Therefore, simpliﬁcations are necessary to 
aid comprehension, as in any intelligent process. To transfer the information from 
the generated point models to working models, perfect planes must be formed. 
This transition from the cloud to the model is accomplished with the help of 
modeling, drawing (Fig. 22), BIM professionals, and structural software. We have

used sketches made by the site personnel with measurements taken in situ, which 
provide clear references, and photos of the sites to understand the point geometry.

Fig. 23 BIM model, cut

From this data, the structural engineers generate comprehensible models, primar-

(Figs. 23 and 24).

346 J. C. A. Portero and F. Moral-Andrés
6.3 Structural Modeling 
From the BIM models, which are geometric, the next step is to deﬁne the structural 
models that have a high accuracy requirement. The error in the intersection of 
two elements, in order to be analyzed by any matrix or Finite Element Method 
(FEM), needs to be coincident, unlike geometric models that allow non-visible 
imperfections (Fig. 25). 
Fig. 25 Structural models, made with SOFISTIK

The Impossible Cathedral of Mejorada del Campo, Madrid: Utilizing... 347
Soﬁstik creates structural models that accurately reﬂect the ﬂexibility of the 
evaluated concrete. Bar models are used for this purpose. For walls, slab models 
with in-plane and perpendicular loads are employed, while for slabs with bidi-
rectional behavior, only slab models with perpendicular loads are used. In cases 
where the behavior is unidirectional, beams and their top layer are modeled. The 
structural engineering team created models of all parts of the cathedral, including 
the dome, vault, and different naves, while considering structural details, wind, 
and vertical loads to ensure the construction’s longevity. The results determined 
the overall structural suitability and detailing of the cathedral. The conclusions are 
clear. The cathedral will perform effectively as long as the recommended actions are 
implemented. We have taken speciﬁc measures to address certain details that were 
not provided by Justo due to his limited knowledge or construction ability. 
7 Conclusions 
The structural engineering in this project presents a greater challenge than in many 
other due diligence cases. This challenge is unique compared to the more conven-
tional challenges faced by forensic structural engineering of existing structures. The 
cathedral’s structure was built without graphic tools or plans, resulting in a lack of 
prior geometric or mechanical documentation of the structure, both in general and 
in its assembly and details. 
The depth of the issue is exacerbated by the fact that the structure was not 
constructed under the guidance of professionals. In such cases, the evaluation 
tasks are more akin to those of geotechnical engineers than structural engineers, 
as the material being studied is largely unfamiliar and must be approached from a 
statistical perspective. 
However, the cathedral’s geometry is not repetitive but rather reﬂects the 
unconventional and unexpected ideas of its designer. Comprehensive geometric 
data collection is crucial in this type of construction, and modern digitalization 
techniques make it possible. 
In addition to collecting data to determine the mechanical characteristics of 
materials and soils, both destructive and non-destructive tests are necessary. The 
chosen method for geometric digitization is 3D scanning using ﬁxed stations and 
drones, synchronized and geolocated by LIDAR. The deﬁnition of surface textures 
was not crucial in this case. 
After obtaining the point clouds, modeling work is required to estimate the 
position of the real planes. It is important to note that their deﬁnition requires 
precision to ensure that the structural models can accurately represent the geometry. 
The involvement of experts in this type of modeling is necessary to avoid signiﬁcant 
delays or errors in deﬁning calculation models.

Harnessing Audio-Based Augmented 
Reality for Digital History and Cultural 
Heritage Experiences 
Brian Knoth 
1 Introduction 
In recent years, augmented reality (AR) has emerged as a powerful tool for 
presenting historical narrative and cultural heritage experiences in an engaging and 
immersive manner. The integration of sound within AR applications offers a unique 
opportunity to enhance usability and storytelling potential while creating a more 
immersive and captivating experience bringing historical events to life. However, 
much of the literature focuses on the visual, and there is a need for a more in-
depth investigation of the research on the effective utilization of sound and audio 
in AR history and heritage applications. This chapter will answer that call with a 
focused exploration of sound and audio’s creative and innovative use within such 
AR experiences. 
The main objective of this chapter is to demonstrate how sound and audio 
can be leveraged to enhance the storytelling potential of AR applications focused 
on historical narratives and cultural heritage. This chapter will provide practical 
guidance for researchers, public historians, and cultural heritage professionals 
interested in creating immersive audio-driven AR experiences by examining various 
techniques and strategies. This chapter will also suggest a theoretical framework, 
informed by early experiments, two more recent project summaries, and one 
expanded case study (on the author’s own recent work), for leveraging sound and 
audio to enhance the immersive storytelling experience in digital history and cultural 
heritage applications. This framework will encompass key elements, such as Sound 
Design, Sound Spatialization, Interactive Audio Narrative, and the Preservation of 
Historical/Heritage Soundscapes.
