349

350 B. Knoth
By highlighting best practices through covering an array of projects, this chapter 
will contribute to advancing the ﬁeld of AR by inspiring researchers and practition-
ers to consider sound and audio as essential and/or even primary elements in the 
design and development of immersive digital history and cultural heritage experi-
ences. The research will also encourage interdisciplinary collaborations between 
experts in sound design, digital history/heritage, and AR technology, fostering 
innovation and further advancements in the ﬁeld. By effectively integrating sound 
and audio (including music), AR experiences can foster emotional connections and a 
deeper understanding and appreciation of history and cultural heritage. The ﬁndings 
and guidelines presented will be valuable for museums, cultural institutions, and 
heritage sites seeking to leverage AR technologies to engage visitors and convey 
historical narratives and heritage experiences innovatively and memorably. 
2 Digital History, Cultural Heritage, and Augmented Reality 
Digital history is deﬁned as “[ ... ]historians’ use of modern computer and com-
munication technologies [ ...  ] ranging from basic web publishing applications to 
the latest virtual reality (VR) and augmented reality (AR) tools, digital historians 
present materials in new ways to various audiences” (What Is Digital History? 
A Guide to Digital History Resources, Museums, and Job Description, 2020). 
Likewise, cultural heritage sites and experiences can utilize similar technologies 
to present “[ ... ] the full range of our inherited traditions, monuments, objects, and 
culture—in tangible and intangible forms” (What Is Heritage? |  Center for Heritage 
& Society, n.d.). 
Heritage is much more than preserving, excavating, displaying, or restoring a collection 
of old things [ ...  ] Heritage is both tangible and intangible, in the sense that ideas and 
memories—of songs, recipes, language, dances, and many other elements of who we are 
and how we identify ourselves—are as important as historical buildings and archaeological 
sites. (What Is Heritage?|  Center for Heritage & Society), n.d.) 
Augmented Reality (AR) is described as, “[ ... ]an experience where designers 
enhance parts of users’ physical world [ ... ] ranging from sound to video, to 
graphics to GPS overlays and more [ ... ]” (What Is Augmented Reality?, n.d.). 
The British Computer Society offers a simple yet elegant deﬁnition of AR, stressing 
the relationship between the real and virtual. 
Augmented reality (AR) is all about combining the digital world with the physical one and 
therefore augmenting the real-world experience. It brings the real and virtual worlds closer 
together by adding graphics and sound to what the user is experiencing. (Augmented Reality 
Learning, 2014) 
The same article highlights quick reference (QR) codes as being one of the earliest 
(and simplest) forms of AR in comparison to more recent developments that 
make use of computer vision technologies, GPS, or some combination of the two 
(Augmented Reality Learning, 2014). Even with the understanding that AR can be

Harnessing Audio-Based Augmented Reality for Digital History and Cultural... 351
as simple as a QR code, the costs of augmented reality have often been so prohibitive 
that designers and creators could only develop projects with specialized software 
and hardware. More recently, the technology has become so accessible that even 
the more advanced augmented reality experiences are available on common mobile 
devices (Augmented Reality – The Past, The Present and The Future, n.d.). 
Although clearly useful for presenting location-based content, much of AR to 
date has been based on visual augmentation of the physical environment. 
[ ... ]a rich body of research also shows that AR can be incredibly valuable for exploring 
various cultural, historical, and geographic aspects of an environment. This type of app 
typically operates on the basis of a user pointing his mobile device towards an object or a 
site, in order to see superimposed content on the screen. (Javornik, 2016) 
The subject of this chapter differs in the sense that it is focused more than most 
on the aural components of a multimedia experience, which some would argue can 
offer more emotionally rich content, which might be a beneﬁt to a user or audience. 
[ ... ]they want technologies that weave themselves seamlessly into their activities. Con-
sumers expect their digital experience to be more human and empathic, to be ﬁlled with 
emotional content[... ]. (Javornik, 2016) 
3 Augmented Reality Applications for Digital History 
and Cultural Heritage 
Augmented reality for history and cultural heritage experiences has a great beneﬁt as 
being physically present at a historical site provides a user with a sense of empathy 
for the past that cannot be achieved by just reading a book or watching a movie 
(Challenor & Ma, 2019). 
We feel that augmented reality is the ideal choice of technology because it can be 
used to recount experiences that require the user to be physically present at the site to 
truly comprehend [ ... ] Augmented reality technology could assist with displaying and 
preserving these parts of history which may be difﬁcult for a visitor to imagine or no longer 
exist as they once did[... ]. (Challenor & Ma, 2019) 
On that note, some would argue that historians have long been interested in 
“augmenting the present with the past” (Kee & Compeau, 2019). 
In many ways, historians and antiquarians had always been interested in AR, long before we 
had a name for it. Plaques on a building, bronze and concrete monuments on a battleﬁeld, 
signs and historical sites, and other markers alerting visitors and passersby that something 
signiﬁcant happened at that speciﬁc place are all, in a sense, original forms of AR. It is as 
if there is an innate human urge to annotate our environments and reveal the hidden stories 
and meanings. (Kee et al., 2019) 
Yet, “digital technologies increase the possibilities” of how the present can be 
augmented with a better sense of the past (Kee & Compeau, 2019). 
For example, AR at museums or historical sites can provide on the spot supplementary 
information, telling hidden stories or offering lesser-known facts to enhance the visitor’s

352 B. Knoth
knowledge of an item or space [ ... ] And GPS linked AR can prompt location speciﬁc 
historical data, guiding visitors at sites of interest, and increasing their sensory engagement 
with a place. AR applications can provide a seemingly magical way to tease out the history 
all around us[ ... ]. (Kee & Compeau, 2019) 
These days, teams of researchers work together to study and express history using 
a multitude of digital tools and media (Kee & Compeau, 2019). The real promise 
of augmented reality projects for history and heritage lies within the power to offer, 
“an immediate and [... ] affecting experience in which we [ ... ] encounter history 
with multiple senses” (Kee & Compeau, 2019). In addition, it should be noted that 
the digital history tools media practitioners are using and experimenting with “are 
becoming an additional form of scholarly publishing, adding to how historians and 
humanists tell stories and share knowledge with academic and public audiences” 
(Kee & Compeau, 2019). 
McGrath feels that digital experiences are something all historians and preserva-
tionists need to accept and embrace. He highlights the role of augmented reality as 
a method of communicating the work to the public. 
But preservationists who are skeptical or otherwise critical of the uses of digital tools, 
platforms, and other resources in the context of their work must also acknowledge that, 
for many of the publics they serve, their approaches to curation and education will always 
be mediated by the conditions of augmented reality, thanks in large part to the ubiquity 
of smart phone devices networked to various digital spaces and resources (and games). 
(McGrath, 2018) 
McGrath further argues that the beneﬁts of digital experiences and augmented 
reality outweigh the potential downsides in terms of the audience’s pushing back 
on a perceived overuse of technology. He argues that such tools have the capacity to 
“restore and re-materialize histories lost to gentriﬁcation, urban development, and 
other events impacting a region’s material, social, and cultural dimensions over the 
passage of time” (McGrath, 2018). 
4 Early Experiments in Audio-Based Augmented Reality for 
Digital History and Cultural Heritage 
4.1 Bronze Age Roundhouses 
Stuart Eve, for instance, employed a unique approach to investigating a Bronze Age 
settlement (Fig. 1) on Bodmin Moor, a granite moorland in northeastern Cornwall, 
England (UK). He made use of a form of aural AR that allowed people to navigate 
and immerse themselves in the landscape. Eve utilized the Unity3D gaming engine 
to create 3D audio sources that corresponded to the locations of the settlement’s 
houses. The ancient houses are now barely visible on the ground as circles of stones 
and rocks, making it difﬁcult to discern where each house is. However, with the

Harnessing Audio-Based Augmented Reality for Digital History and Cultural... 353
Fig. 1 A virtual computer-generated reconstruction of a Bronze Age Roundhouse. (From Soluis) 
geolocated app, users could walk around the settlement and hear the augmented 
sounds of the houses, such as indistinct voices, laughing, and babies crying, which 
became louder or quieter depending on their distance from each sound source. 
Furthermore, Eve introduced virtual models of the houses that simulated the effect 
of the house walls and roofs dampening the sounds coming from within, allowing 
only unobstructed sound to emit from the doorways. Sounds served as auditory 
markers indicating where the doorways of the houses were located. People could 
walk around the houses and hear when the sounds got louder, signaling the location 
of the doorway. In this way, users could immerse themselves in the landscape and 
experience the site in a truly unique way (Graham et al., 2019). 
By considering the sound sources and their relationship to the archaeological 
ﬁndings, interesting questions emerged for Eve about the Bronze Age settlement on 
Bodmin Moor. For example, if certain houses were used for rituals, what types of 
sounds would be associated with these rituals and how would they spread throughout 
the settlement? Additionally, if animals were kept in a speciﬁc area within the 
settlement, how would their sounds impact the inhabitants? Moreover, how far 
could people communicate across the settlement area by using calls or shouts? Such 
explorations can potentially help visitors to better understand the site while also 
allowing them to explore it in a more immersive and engaging manner (Graham et 
al., 2019).

354 B. Knoth
Fig. 2 Screen shot of historical friction generating location-based information. (From Shawn 
Graham and Stuart Eve) 
4.2 Historical Friction 
At the time of its creation, the Historical Friction app also offered a new and 
innovative way to experience historical sites. Still in existence on the web, it uses 
sound immersion to help users better understand the history of the location they 
are visiting (Fig. 2). The app was inspired by the work of Ed Summers. Summers 
created a web app called Ici, which uses a browser’s location capabilities to ﬁnd 
and display Wikipedia articles tagged to that location (Summers, 2013). The app 
encourages users to contribute to Wikipedia by expanding coverage of the area they 
are exploring. The density of digital annotations on a map can visually indicate the 
historical signiﬁcance of a location. 
Historical Friction uses an innovative approach to explore the historical signif-
icance of different locations taking this concept a step further by using sound to 
create a more immersive and interactive experience. It’s a unique way to explore 
history and learn about the stories behind different locations. It intentionally creates 
a disruption in the user’s experience by incorporating sound to draw attention to 
areas that are densely annotated with historical information. Initially, the app used a 
musical generator to create an acoustic soundscape that varied in tone and volume 
as users moved through space. Later, a text-to-speech algorithm was introduced to 
whisper abstracts of Wikipedia articles at slightly different speeds and in varied 
tones. The goal was to create a sense of discomfort that would encourage users to 
pause and observe their surroundings with a fresh perspective. By doing so, users

Harnessing Audio-Based Augmented Reality for Digital History and Cultural... 355
Fig. 3 Main view of the voices recognition app. (From Stuart Eve, et. al.) 
might discover new places and gain a deeper appreciation of the history behind them 
(Graham et al., 2019). 
4.3 V oices Recognition 
At the 2014 York University Heritage Jam, a yearly cultural heritage event, 
a team consisting of archaeologists, artists, and coders drew inspiration from 
Historical Friction and developed an Audio-Augmented Reality app named V oices 
Recognition (Fig. 3). The makers of the app stated that it was created to enhance 
one’s interaction with York Cemetery, its surroundings, and visible features, by 
giving voice to the unseen elements that were the primary reason for the cemetery’s 
establishment; the buried bodies underground (Graham et al., 2019). 
The V oices Recognition app accomplished its goal by utilizing geolocation 
technology to connect each grave in the York Cemetery to an online database of 
census data, burial records, and biographies of those interred there. When the user 
was within 10 meters of a grave, the app narrated the corresponding information 
from the database. At the time, the app used actors’ voices, but the full version was 
expected to use computer-generated voices due to the vast amount of data available. 
This innovative approach to sound and place created a tactile and visceral experience 
for users, allowing them to hear individual stories and clamoring voices throughout 
the grave sites. Overall, this app provided a unique twist on the conventional 
cemetery experience (Eve et al., 2014).

356 B. Knoth
During a guest lecture to a digital history class at Carleton University in the fall 
2014 semester, Colleen Morgan shared her impressions of the V oices Recognition 
app during its testing phase. She described the app’s implementation in a cemetery 
as an incredibly impactful and immersive augmented reality experience. Although 
the app never got past the prototyping stage, the concept emphasizes how audio can 
establish a closer and more personal connection to a cultural location compared to 
relying solely on visual overlays and presentations (Graham et al., 2019). 
5 More Recent Project Summaries of Audio-Based 
Augmented Reality for Digital History and Cultural 
Heritage 
5.1 Echoes Labs and the Zollverein UNESCO World Heritage 
Site 
In 2013, Echoes Labs began with the goal of creating a GPS-based audio tour. How-
ever, as they collaborated, they realized they could build a superior product: their 
own platform. Today, Echoes is a thriving worldwide community that collaborates 
with an array of individuals and organizations, including businesses, non-proﬁts, 
educational institutions, and sports teams. The team provides customized app 
development, consultation services, and content creation advice to many partners. 
Echoes is driven by a passion for sound and creativity, and they are dedicated 
to fostering creativity and providing unrestricted resources. Their apps are free 
of advertisements and data sales, funded by Echoes Labs initiatives and an Open 
Collective community (About us – Echoes Labs, 2020). 
The Zollverein UNESCO World Heritage Site, located in Essen, Germany, was 
once a signiﬁcant ex-colliery and coking plant that played a crucial role in the 
development of heavy industry in Europe. The site is known for its exceptional 
Bauhaus architecture. Nadelør, an artist duo, created an audio walk they dubbed 
Klangtour Kunst (loosely meaning “sound art tour” in English) that adds a new 
and fascinating dimension to the art at the UNESCO World Heritage Site. The app 
provides an up-to-date map of all locations on the site, and the 3D map encourages 
visitors to explore Zollverein on their own. GPS-guided tours are also available, 
including a children’s route, and the app provides information about the current 
and historical use of the buildings and facilities. Visitors can enjoy a unique and 
educational experience at Zollverein (Zollverein UNESCO World Heritage Site, 
2023). 
The site needed an audio guide system that could be incorporated into the current 
application. This was a difﬁcult task because the system had to be multilingual 
and integrate with outdated technology. Despite these challenges, Echoes Labs was 
able to successfully add a GPS-triggered audio guide technology to the existing 
application. Later, Zollverein requested Echoes to rebuild the whole application

Harnessing Audio-Based Augmented Reality for Digital History and Cultural... 357
Fig. 4 Zollverein UNESCO World Heritage Site app. (From Echoes Labs and Zollverein) 
using modern technologies to make it more resilient to upgrades and newer 
technologies (Fig. 4). As a result, the application’s reach increased from 45% 
to 88%, covering a broader range of operating systems and devices. The new 
application provides visitors with a smooth and uninterrupted experience while 
exploring the site (Zollverein UNESCO World Heritage Site, 2023). 
5.2 Invisible Ground 
Brian Koscho is a media artist, historian, and producer from Athens, Ohio, who 
founded the Invisible Ground project. When he enrolled in the Communication and 
Media Arts MFA program at Ohio University in 2019, Koscho knew that his future 
endeavors would blend his passions for history, community, audio storytelling, and 
visual design. Koscho had a strong dedication to history and community, which was 
reﬂected in his 12-year involvement in non-proﬁt work at Stuart’s Opera House in 
Nelsonville, Ohio. Upon pursuing a graduate degree in creative media production, 
he chose to focus on audio storytelling and visual design as a means of promoting 
the value of history and making it more accessible to his community (Koscho, 
2022a). 
Koscho’s passion for media production and storytelling extends beyond creating 
compelling narratives. He recognizes that studying history offers characters, lessons, 
connections, self-reﬂection, and a way to connect with the past. As he pursued 
his education, he discovered that these areas of interest were all intertwined, and

358 B. Knoth
he could utilize his skills in audio storytelling, augmented reality, visual design, 
public history, and community collaboration to share his love of history with others. 
Koscho strives to approach his subjects from a unique perspective, utilizing different 
artistic tools to make history more accessible and emphasize its signiﬁcance within 
a community (Koscho, 2022a). 
The Invisible Ground project started as a podcast that aimed to showcase the 
stories of southeast Ohio’s community, which are not always visible but play an 
essential role in everyday life. The podcast focused on cemeteries, starting with the 
historic West State Street Cemetery in Athens. The creator of the podcast, Koscho, 
worked there as a seasonal maintenance employee for the city of Athens when he 
was 23 years old. While walking around the cemetery, he became fascinated with the 
stories of the people buried there, which he later discovered were documented by a 
historian, lawyer, and author named W.E. Peters. As Koscho continued his graduate 
studies, more episodes of Invisible Ground were published, covering topics such as 
Mound Cemetery in Marietta, Tablertown, and the Little Cities of Black Diamonds. 
These podcasts used music, sound, and documentary interviews to engage the 
listeners in the stories (Koscho, 2022a). 
For his thesis project, Koscho aimed to take this further by creating a visual 
and physical connection to the stories creating an “Immersive Historic Marker.” 
These markers look like regular interpretive signs, but contain a QR code that, when 
scanned, allows users to download an app that uses augmented reality to bring 
history to life. By using their smartphone’s camera, visitors can use the Invisible 
Ground app to see a historical photo overlaid on their camera view. In addition, there 
is a brief audio introduction, an interpretive panel, and a longer podcast episode 
that presents local history in a captivating way. Visitors can experience the physical 
space while also using digital technology and audio to enhance their experience 
(Koscho, 2022b). 
The ﬁrst Invisible Ground Immersive Historic Marker was revealed in April 
2022, located across the street from the former site of the renowned Berry Hotel on 
Court Street in Athens. The Berry Hotel, a signiﬁcant early Black-owned business 
established by Edward and Martha Jane Berry, had a reputation that extended 
beyond Ohio, attracting prominent ﬁgures such as US presidents, Bob Hope, Carl 
Sandburg, and others. The Berry family’s story is also intertwined with the Albany 
Enterprise Academy, one of the earliest educational institutions in the United States 
to focus on providing education for Black individuals, taught by Black educators. 
The Berrys are also associated with the Mount Zion Baptist Church, which has 
been a pillar of the Black community in Athens and southeast Ohio for many years. 
The Berry Hotel proved to be an ideal ﬁrst test for the Immersive Historic Marker 
technology in the context of Invisible Ground, as it was demolished in 1974. Visitors 
can use augmented reality on their mobile devices to experience the hotel as it once 
was (Koscho, 2022b). 
The community has responded positively to the podcast and marker, prompting 
Koscho to expand the project (Fig. 5). He plans to create eight markers in Athens 
County by 2023, with support from various organizations and individuals such as 
the Southeast Ohio History Center, the Ohio History Connection, and others. These

Harnessing Audio-Based Augmented Reality for Digital History and Cultural... 359
Fig. 5 Invisible ground project website. (From Brian Koscho) 
markers will be part of a tour that showcases signiﬁcant places in the area, including 
Albany Enterprise Academy, The Ridges, and Mount Zion Baptist Church. The 
podcasts will also continue to be produced. Koscho believes that technology can 
connect people to place-based storytelling, amplifying important stories from the 
past. The blending of digital and physical spaces is a powerful tool for achieving this 
goal (Koscho, 2022b). For further details on the Invisible Ground project, including 
additional information on the podcasts, one can visit https://ﬁndinvisibleground. 
com/. 
6 Case Study (Highlighting the Author’s Work): The 
Germania Musical Society in Newport, Rhode Island; 
Multimedia Tour and Podcast Episode 
6.1 F ellowship Research 
The beginning of this project commenced with fellowship funding from the 
Preservation Society of Newport County (PSNC). I, Brian Knoth (the author), was 
awarded a full-year research fellowship, which included $24,000 in funding and 
accommodations. I started working on the background research phase of the project 
in July 2015. Ultimately, I found an original research focus which centered around 
the role of the Germania Musical Society in relation to Newport’s emergence as

360 B. Knoth
a world-class summer resort destination. The main point of this focused research 
emphasized that music and dancing were not just routine pastimes but integral 
features of Newport as it rose to signiﬁcance to become “The Queen of Resorts.” 
Moreover, the role of the Germania Musical Society became highlighted. As a result 
of this research, an original article was accepted for publication in Newport History. 
The article titled “Music and Dancing at the ‘Queen of Resorts’: The Impact of 
the Germania Musical Society on Newport’s Hotel Period” was praised by Dr. 
Nancy Newman, the foremost scholar on the Germania Musical Society who is also 
Chair of the Department of Music and Theatre at the University at Albany (State 
University of New York). 
6.2 The Rhode T our Project 
From that point on, I meticulously adapted my original research for a multimedia 
documentary-style delivery format. Although the realization of a digital media 
experience based on my research could have taken many forms, the platform I chose 
to focus on was the innovative public history platform Rhode Tour (Fig. 6). Rhode 
Tour, “a statewide, multimedia mobile application and website for the interpretation 
of and engagement with local, place-based thematic history” was developed in 2014, 
by the Rhode Island Council for the Humanities, the John Nicholas Brown Center 
for Public Humanities and Cultural Heritage at Brown University, and the Rhode 
Fig. 6 Rhode tour home page. (From Rhode Tour)

Harnessing Audio-Based Augmented Reality for Digital History and Cultural... 361
Island Historical Society. It is an editor-reviewed mobile app and website that uses 
text, sound, and images to bring Rhode Island history to life in place-based narrative 
form. It uses the Curatescape framework, “following the principles and practices 
established at Cleveland State University” (Curatescape, n.d.). The app is available 
for both iOS and Android devices and requires a reliable mobile internet connection. 
The app also has a related website, and the content on both the app and site are the 
same, but the visual appearance is somewhat different (Rhode Tour Style and Use 
Guide, 2015). 
The app is designed to tell stories about speciﬁc places. As the developers of 
Curatescape have articulated, “A story can be told in many ways [ ...  ]f r o mt h e 
historical to environmental or from the literary to the architectural, but effective 
Curatescape projects must take an interpretive stance that builds meaning through 
evoking context, place, or identity” (Curatescape, n.d.). The creators of Rhode Tour 
have developed thorough guidelines for content production, media formatting, and 
the editorial process, while providing a ﬂexible and coherent set of standards to 
consider for developing such a mobile digital media experience (Rhode Tour Style 
and Use Guide, 2015). 
Because Rhode Tour is a place-based application, individual stories must be 
linked to speciﬁc locations. Stories that are thematically or geographically linked 
then form a “tour.” Brief stories about particular people or events connect the 
places (or “pins”) on a map to broader meaning or relevance. Each place-based 
story is most effective when containing multiple media, such as images, archival 
documents, music or audio clips, and/or video links that deepen the written narrative 
and encourage the user to make connections back to the overarching theme of the 
tour (Rhode Tour Style and Use Guide, 2015). 
The Rhode Tour guide also speciﬁes a very speciﬁc “Tour Content Hierarchy” 
with stylistic requirements for both the “Tour Introduction” and each “story/place.” 
Each tour begins with an introduction of around 250 words, including an engaging 
opening and overview of the tour’s overarching narrative subject. A map with pins of 
the key locations (and addresses) helps the user navigate between places. In addition, 
the introduction page includes a list of places on the tour with numbers, story titles, 
and summaries for each place-based narrative. From there, the user clicks on the 
title which takes them to that particular place/story. Each place starts with a title and 
a story of around 400 words which connects back to the theme of the tour. Images 
and audio clips augment the experience for the location-based story, in addition 
to “Facts” which are engaging text snippets providing additional context about the 
locale, and “Tips” which provide information about how to further engage with the 
place, person, sources, or themes. A map is also included towards the bottom of 
each place/story page and includes a clickable pin with an address or other location 
identiﬁer (Rhode Tour Style and Use Guide, 2015). My project titled “Music and 
Dancing at the ‘Queen of Resorts’” is available for public distribution at this link: 
http://rhodetour.org/tours/show/37 (Knoth, 2018).

362 B. Knoth
The tour introduction starts as follows: 
On this tour, explore the role of music and social dancing during Newport’s rebirth and 
ascent to becoming a premier summer resort destination in the mid-nineteenth century. 
Known as Newport’s “hotel period,” the era between 1840 and 1865 captures Newport’s 
revitalizing economic boom, spurred on by the emergence of luxurious public hotels, before 
the age of private mansions. Music and dancing were not just routine pastimes, but main 
attractions of the Newport summer experience as it rose to the ﬁrst-rate status of the “Queen 
of Resorts.” 
During the “hotel period” boom years of the 1850s, an extraordinary group of musicians 
called the Germania Musical Society were instrumental to Newport’s rebirth as a ﬂourishing 
resort town. 
Locations for the tour include the Atlantic House, Ocean House, and Bellevue 
House hotels, in addition to Chateau-sur-Mer, and Fort Adams (Fig. 7). 
For additional context, here is an opening excerpt of one of the stories developed 
for the Ocean House Hotel tour location (Fig. 8). 
In his memoir, the Germania Musical Society’s Henry Albrecht painted an interesting 
picture of the ensemble’s relationship to Newport during the “hotel period,” stating: “the 
magical effect of the sounds of the orchestra aroused not very solemn thoughts in the breasts 
of art-loving ladies, affections more than on the level of Platonic friendship.” He added that 
their concerts “brought to the fore the reality of the words that ‘Music is the language of the 
heart.’ ” Such memories included pleasurable and cozy evenings at the Ocean House. 
When the original Ocean House opened on Bellevue and East Bowery in 1844, it instantly 
rivaled the most luxurious European hotels. The Ocean House offered summer visitors top-
notch accommodations, ﬁne-dining, and a variety of attractions. A Newport Mercury article 
in 1884 reminisced about “Old Time Newport” highlighting the new Ocean House and the 
hundreds of people assembling daily and nightly to the music of the “celebrated Germania 
Band.” 
After the story, additional media and text elements are provided to augment the 
historical narrative experience for that location. For the Ocean House Hotel page, 
images include carefully curated archival photographs of the Ocean House Hotel in 
both of its manifestations and an image scan of the title page for a relevant piece of 
sheet music. 
Two audio clips of relevant pieces composed by the Germania Musical Society’s 
conductor Carl Bergmann are also embedded and linked to complement the story. 
I recorded and produced these pieces, which were performed by the Newport 
String Project in the historic surroundings of the Old Colony House in Newport, 
RI. Additional text elements include a “Fact” which elaborates on the Germania’s 
penchant for composing many of the dance compositions they would perform, and 
a “Tip” which provides an educational video clip that helps to illuminate a new 
category of group dancing emerging at the time called a “cotillion.”

Harnessing Audio-Based Augmented Reality for Digital History and Cultural... 363
Fig. 7 Tour introduction page. (From Rhode Tour) 
6.3 Incorporating Multimedia Elements 
In the Rhode Tour “Guidelines for Photographs,” it is suggested that photographs 
“are a critical part [ ... ] They help bring stories to life.” In many ways, I agree, 
as indeed, “photos provide visual comparisons of the landscape between present 
and past.” In addition, given the time period I was working with, photos are the 
only actual archival option (besides what is written) representing the reality of that 
time. That said, some limitations do exist with the Rhode Tour platform regarding 
incorporating imagery. For instance, “3-5 relevant, high-quality photos that relate 
to the story” are considered optimal, as the “use of more photos will cause the app

364 B. Knoth
Fig. 8 The Ocean house hotel tour location/story page. (From Rhode Tour) 
to load too slowly.” Thus, my plan was to incorporate photographs that especially 
help the users/audience visualize the past locations and structures, in addition to the 
experience of a Newport summer at the time, and important archival imagery related 
to the Germania and their music (Fig. 9). 
Although the Rhode Tour “Guidelines for Videos” stress the importance of 
“Interesting and relevant videos” being potential assets to a story, one is equally 
warned that “videos that are of poor quality, overly long, or tangential to a story’s 
content can detract from the users’ experience.” The one video component I 
thoughtfully incorporated into the experience included a reenacted representation 
of a cotillion from Dancetime Publications (on YouTube) which does a good job of

Harnessing Audio-Based Augmented Reality for Digital History and Cultural... 365
Fig. 9 Clickable images and sheet music. (From Rhode Tour) 
Fig. 10 Clickable YouTube link. (From Rhode Tour) 
capturing that piece of social dancing history (Fig. 10). A cotillion was a popular 
period dance style and helps the users/audience imagine that aspect of the resort 
experience, and/or hotel life, in Newport at the time. That said, for this project, the 
video functions more as a complement to the rich audio content, which is really 
what brings the stories to life, as will be discussed in the next section. 
6.4 Audio Enhancements 
One unique focus of this project, inﬂuenced by my substantial experience as a sound 
artist, composer, and music producer was also to create rich and immersive audio 
elements to bring the narratives to life. Since the focus of this project was largely 
based on the role of music (as well as social dancing) during the “Hotel Period” 
resort experience in Newport, music clearly is a major component of the historical 
narrative. Although the Rhode Tour “Guidelines for Audio” are somewhat vague and 
mostly centered around incorporating oral interviews or historians’ interpretations, 
I saw the clear potential for using music to enhance the historical subject matter for 
my tour (Fig. 11). In many ways, I saw the musical elements as being key to the 
audience experience, enhancing engagement with the stories, and augmenting the 
immersive qualities of the multimedia experience for each location/story (Rhode 
Tour Style and Use Guide, 2015).

366 B. Knoth
Fig. 11 Playable music samples. (From Rhode Tour) 
However, since there was no access to recordings from that time period (as audio 
recording technologies did not yet exist), the music needed to be re-created. Sheet 
music versions of compositions by the Germania Musical Society exist (in relative 
abundance), and since they also played well-known pieces of the time, that sheet 
music also exists, as well as recordings of ensembles since then that might sound 
similar (in terms of instrumentation and orchestration). What is not known is how 
they really sounded. 
As mentioned, period recordings are not an option as a reference point. In 
addition, there aren’t any known arrangements that exist of the music they played 
(i.e., parts for each instrument’s contribution to the whole sound). Therefore, any 
recreations are largely educated speculation. But to be honest, that is an interesting 
problem to have for a composer and sound designer like myself, as some creative 
liberty should be assumed. My plan then was to incorporate some of their own 
compositional work (largely dance tunes like polkas, etc.) and some of the more 
well-known canonic pieces they excelled at and brought to American listeners’ ears 
for the ﬁrst time (in a way never experienced before). 
On that note, I collaborated on a lecture/performance event with the Newport 
String Project (NSP) in April 2017 and they played such pieces in a small ensemble 
format, and I captured the performances with a quality recording. The Germania 
members were known to perform together in smaller units, so it would not be a 
stretch to include some of this work as a representation of their sound. As the 
NSP’s calendar posting read, the event featured “[ ... ]discussion and performances 
of music closely associated with the Germania Musical Society, including Newport-
inspired dance music such as the ‘Fancy Ball Polka Redowa’ and ‘Ocean House 
Polka.’ In keeping with the Germania Musical Society’s promotion of works by 
Felix Mendelssohn, the event will close with a performance of Mendelssohn’s ﬁery 
String Quartet No. 6 op. 80 dating from 1847.” In addition to the aforementioned 
pieces, I also captured NSP performances of Germania conductor Bergmann’s

Harnessing Audio-Based Augmented Reality for Digital History and Cultural... 367
“Love Polka” and “Bellevue House Polka Redowa,” in addition to Mendelssohn’s 
“Nocturne for A Midsummer Night’s Dream.” 
It could be argued that the text and image components are potentially more 
introductory and contextual complements to the featured audio content. Notably, 
the Rhode Tour guidelines suggest that it is important that audio elements do not 
simply restate, or paraphrase information already included in the text-based “story.” 
Particularly, in the case of my tour and the stories told within, the audio content does 
signiﬁcantly expand upon and enhance the narrative experience (Rhode Tour Style 
and Use Guide, 2015). 
6.5 The Complete T our 
The complete tour included the introduction mentioned above, in addition to ﬁve 
media-rich stories for each linked location, including, the Atlantic House, Ocean 
House, and Bellevue House hotels, in addition to Chateau-sur-Mer and Fort Adams. 
As stated in a previous section of this chapter, the ﬁnished multimedia tour can be 
accessed and experienced at this link: http://rhodetour.org/tours/show/37. 
6.6 Rhode T our Analysis 
McGrath situates Rhode Tour as a simple, yet effective, augmented reality platform 
for digital history projects when one harnesses the full potential of the technology, 
“to augment textual narratives with multimedia resources that illustrate what has 
changed over time” (McGrath, 2018). The narrative power of the Curatescape 
framework is evident within Rhode Tour as it: 
[ ... ]emphasizes storytelling [ ...  ] using any approach that builds meaning through evoking 
context, place, or identity. Good storytelling, then, builds context through text, images, and 
multimedia, and is fundamental to humanities interpretation. The information architecture 
of Curatescape is built with this approach in mind. (About Curatescape |Curatescape, n.d.) 
With McGrath’s contextualization in mind, I’d like to pause to reﬂect on making 
and embracing this choice to utilize the Rhode Tour platform. 
Clearly, there were other options for communicating this history through a 
multimedia platform. For one, I could have designed a customized website or mobile 
application and leaned into the creation of more complex interactive experiences and 
other augmented reality experiments. In addition, a custom-made platform could 
have allowed for more media content and less restrictions in terms of content design. 
That said, my choice to utilize Rhode Tour was based on a few simple principles. 
For one, the platform is established and has a built-in user base and community 
supporting and promoting it. In addition, the content is curated and edited by 
experts in the public humanities. Lastly, the framework, partly due to its own system

368 B. Knoth
limitations, restricts the number of media elements that can be incorporated into the 
experience, which in turn demands extra curatorial thought. 
It’s very possible that a less constrained process driven by customized interactive 
media elements and augmented reality technologies could have led to an interesting 
experiment, but also less-than-optimal storytelling. As McGrath has articulated, the 
temptation to add elements without restraint is real when one considers a more 
freeform technological approach: 
Digital contexts often tempt novice practitioners with the potential to create and add more 
and more content: do your audiences share this desire for additional context at the scale 
you’re imagining, or in the formats you’ve adopted? (McGrath, 2018) 
One could argue that the more constrained aspects of Rhode Tour are a feature that 
potentially leads to a more elegant, albeit technologically simple, narrative-driven 
augmented reality experience. 
Others may argue that a platform like Rhode Tour offers an easy way out for 
digital history experience design and does little to advance the ﬁeld of augmented 
reality history technologies. As Kee, Poitras, and Compeau point out: 
We are only beginning to scrape the surface of this new medium, and future developers 
will perhaps look back on these early attempts as quaint. The potential for developing new 
methods of storytelling and sharing with AR is immense and we cannot foresee the most 
transformative advances. (Kee et al., 2019) 
I believe Rhode Tour offered a framework that demanded the kind of clarity that 
was necessary for this project. It also did allow for the key audio augmentations 
that enhanced my speciﬁc subject. Even in Rhode Tour’s simplicity it offers a way 
forward for thinking more deeply about aural augmented reality approaches. 
With our contemporary focus on the visual, we tend to prioritize sight over other senses 
[ ... ] we suggest that “hearing” the past is a more effective and affective way of providing 
immersive AR. (Graham et al., 2019) 
Yet, one must also be honest that such an expertly curated and edited model does 
potentially leave out the public’s input, which could be viewed as another limitation 
when considering the potential for advancing the ﬁeld. As Hsu has pointed out, 
“Content and design considerations should be informed by conversations with the 
public, whether over social media or in civic contexts like town hall meetings” (Hsu, 
2016). 
6.7 The Podcast Episode 
A podcast episode based on my original research was also produced for the 
regionally popular podcast program Mosaic (Knoth, 2019). Mosaic is a program 
featuring regional immigration stories produced by Rhode Island Public Radio 
(doing business as the Public’s Radio), which is a National Public Radio afﬁliate 
for the state of Rhode Island and southeastern Massachusetts. The episode produced

Harnessing Audio-Based Augmented Reality for Digital History and Cultural... 369
Fig. 12 Podcast episode web page. (From The Public’s Radio) 
was entirely based on my research and published article about the Germania Musical 
Society’s impact on Newport’s “hotel period” in the mid-1800s. The episode was 
broadcast regionally and is also available for streaming and download with an 
accompanying web page that also incorporates some of my own curated imagery 
and links to other published works associated with the project (Fig. 12). A link to 
the episode and all associated materials is located here: https://thepublicsradio.org/ 
episode/ep-24-think-bob-dylan-was-newport-s-ﬁrst-headliner-think-again 
As the lead producer for the podcast episode, one guiding principle that I took to 
heart was to think in terms of both macro and micro-story structures for the scope 
and content of the piece. The story structure of any audio documentary program 
should operate on multiple levels. The macro level addresses the overall structure 
of a documentary story, while at the micro level, one considers the structure of 
each small section. Having created the Rhode Tour experience before developing the 
podcast, I used the overarching themes of the tour to guide the macro structure while 
using the “stories” for each location as an approach to the micro-level structure 
(Lewis & Shaw, 2014). 
I should mention right away that it was important to collaborate with seasoned 
podcast professionals throughout the process. I worked extensively with co-host 
Alex Nunes planning the episode. The episode was edited by Sally Eisele along with 
production help from James Baumgartner, and co-host Ana Gonzalez provided a 
key voice to the production. One element of our plan was to incorporate on-location 
interview content into the story mix. Although a narrator-driven approach could 
have easily worked for communicating the stories, we believed that multiple voices 
would make the stories more engaging. 
I was a natural ﬁt as the interview subject since my research was the foundation 
for the episode, and I could offer an authoritative voice on the subject. Alex Nunes 
recorded the interview content for each location, which mirrored the locations 
of the Rhode Tour experience. After the interview content was recorded, the co-
hosts, Alex and Ana, worked on a rough edit, while assembling the narrative pieces

370 B. Knoth
and developing scripted content based on my research text and their own creative 
personal perspectives on the research. In addition to the voice elements, which 
included both scripted and interview segments, music and sound effects would 
round out the overall sound design. 
Sound effects are another way to help propel a story forward or underscore ideas, 
themes, and/or create a sense of place and set a scene. In this case, given the period 
I was working with, there isn’t even a notational, or paper, representation to turn to 
for how the resort experience in Newport might have sounded. I knew from the start 
that my use of sound effects would be sparse, and most likely only after the music 
and voices were in place. In the end, we chose to just use some of the ambience 
of the on-location interview segments to create a sense of place as we moved from 
location to location to tell the story. Interestingly, the juxtaposition of the present-
day soundscape with stories of the past creates an interesting dynamic. 
Music was key to the sound design, however, and the recordings of the Newport 
String Project (NSP) would serve the piece well. Carefully chosen snippets were 
used as transitional pieces between story segments, which provided rich sonic 
context for the historical narrative. Alex made the choice to contrast Bob Dylan’s 
notable place in Newport’s music history with the story of the Germania Musical 
Society, which created an interesting mash-up of the importance of music to 
Newport’s summer culture from the 1840s all the way to modern times. Hearing 
the NSP’s renderings of nineteenth-century dance music with Bob Dylan makes for 
an interesting and entertaining musical history lesson. 
As McGrath asserts, an effective audio narrative would be one that “balances the 
voices [ ... ] in a mixture of conversational and scripted content” (McGrath, 2019). 
Not all podcasts need to be monologues or one-on-one interviews! Public history’s 
investments in collaboration, dialogue, and diversity (among other areas) can and should 
inform the work of making podcasts. This can be difﬁcult and time-consuming work. It can 
take a while to become comfortable having conversations in public, to create a comfortable 
structure and rhythm, to stay on topic, and to edit with an ear attuned to amplifying key 
talking points. (McGrath, 2019) 
I can conﬁrm that the work of producing an effective podcast is indeed “difﬁcult and 
time-consuming work” as McGrath points out. All elements, including the voices 
(interview segments and the scripted co-hosts), sound effects, and music needed to 
be carefully assembled and mixed. 
Throughout the editing, mixing, and mastering process, the concept of balance, 
along with effective pacing, ﬂow, and layering were all guiding principles. Having 
veteran podcast producers review my work and provide feedback throughout the 
process was instrumental to the success of the episode. Ultimately, we achieved an 
engaging episode that was both educational and entertaining, while making original 
and inventive connections between the past and present-day summer music culture 
of Newport, Rhode Island.

Harnessing Audio-Based Augmented Reality for Digital History and Cultural... 371
6.8 Podcast Episode Analysis 
In addition to situating the Rhode Tour platform within the space of augmented 
reality-driven digital history experiences, McGrath also argues for the potential of 
audio storytelling and narrative-focused podcasts as an approach to a more sonically 
immersive form of augmented reality for digital history projects. McGrath states: 
I try to encourage students and community partners to think about podcasts as a form of 
augmented reality. Many of us listen to podcasts as we commute to work or run errands. 
What if more of us in public history saw these listening habits as an opportunity to tell 
stories about space as it changes over time, to call attention to landmarks or objects we 
might otherwise quickly pass by, and to invite listeners to think about how our uses of 
space and ideas of place have been and continue to be mediated by a range of historical and 
cultural forces? (McGrath, 2019) 
As with the decision to use the Rhode Tour platform for the augmented reality 
multimedia tour experience, I found the collaborative process of producing an 
episode for an established podcast program very beneﬁcial. Once again, I could 
have had more freedom with the structure and content of the piece if I had created 
an original podcast, but that would have had its own limitations. For one, it would 
have made it more difﬁcult to reach an audience. In addition, making the decision to 
work with seasoned producers led to an editorial process that was illuminating and 
focused. 
Communicating my subject through an established entity had the built-in capac-
ity to broaden my subject’s reach. Not only did the episode itself make that possible, 
but a web page was created for the episode, which included links to the research 
article and Rhode Tour experience. That level of promotion would have been next to 
impossible, especially in that short amount of time, if I had created my own program. 
As McGrath asserts, “Podcasts present new opportunities for public historians to 
tell stories [...  ] and in some contexts these audio narratives can be invitations for 
listeners to visit [ ... ] archives or exhibitions” (McGrath, 2019). 
In addition, working with professional content editors was an amazing learning 
experience and essential to adapting the content in a way that made sense for the 
form. McGrath highlights the importance of editing and an iterative process by 
stating, “Don’t be afraid to revise and refocus; you might ﬁnd, for instance, that 
some elements sound better scripted [ ... ] Cultivating an attentiveness to what is and 
is not working is a key part of the podcasting process” (McGrath, 2019). Working 
with seasoned podcast producers made the process of reﬁning the most essential 
elements of the story that much more efﬁcient and effective.

372 B. Knoth
7 Reﬂections and Future Directions: Location-Based 
Storytelling, Sonic Immersion, and Aural-Augmented 
Reality 
The early experiments, project summaries, and one expanded case study covered 
in this chapter provide examples of location-based storytelling and augmented 
reality that can advance the practice of creating digital history and cultural heritage 
experiences. The music and audio components add depth and a greater sense 
of immersion to the experience of the place-based historical narratives. Much is 
assumed about the importance of the visual to augmented reality-driven digital 
history projects, but these projects demonstrate how sonic and musical components 
enhance the immersive multimedia qualities of such experiences, including web or 
mobile-based tours, and podcast-style narratives. 
All of these examples combined provide a foundation for future explorations 
of augmented reality as a digital history and cultural heritage tool. As McGrath 
emphasizes, a judicious approach to content selection might be one of the most 
important principles to consider throughout the process of designing experiential 
enhancements. 
Successful augmented reality projects work to enhance, illuminate, and re-frame your 
objects, tours, and resources; less successful projects may distract from or obscure the 
material, histories, stories, and pedagogical aims that drew you to the digital in the ﬁrst 
place. (McGrath, 2018) 
These projects also provide a foundation for future explorations of podcast-style 
documentary audio storytelling as a digital history tool and augmented reality 
platform (in itself). McGrath’s advice within this realm should also be highlighted. 
Consider [ ...  ] a subject that you’ve already done work on elsewhere that might lend itself 
to new possibilities via audio storytelling. Set up some metrics for success and further 
evaluation, and give yourself time at various points before, during, and after the process 
to discuss these goals and concerns with your collaborators. (McGrath, 2019) 
Kevin Kee, Eric Poitras, and Timothy Compeau point out that there is much 
still to experiment with and learn from. Place-based AR for historical and cultural 
heritage contexts as a practice is still in its infancy and future technologies will 
provide tremendous potential for AR as a tool for communicating the stories of the 
past. 
Just as an explosion of user-generated content helped us reimagine the internet, the same 
will happen with AR. Additionally, wearable computers such as AR glasses, watches, and 
other technology will no doubt revolutionize AR and its ability to transform spaces into 
interactive playgrounds without the need for handheld screens. (Kee et al., 2019) 
Furthermore, as this chapter emphasizes, AR is not limited to vision. One could 
argue that humans suffer from a preoccupation with the idea of visualizing content 
or culture, and in the case of history projects, an obsession with seeing the past. 
Aural AR can greatly expand sensory immersion for historical and heritage sites

Harnessing Audio-Based Augmented Reality for Digital History and Cultural... 373
while allowing users and audiences to be more present for the experience (Kee & 
Compeau, 2019). 
[ ... ]the majority of AR apps currently available privilege the visual, overlaying recon-
structions or text on an image of the present [ ...  ] the clunky visual overlays, create [ ... ] 
a “break in presence” [ ...  ] preventing us from seeing the past and understanding it in any 
meaningful way. (Graham et al., 2019) 
Graham et al. make a compelling case for a more sonically immersive form of 
location-based storytelling or aural augmented reality whereby experimenting with 
soundscapes might help to evoke emotions that sight cannot (Kee & Compeau, 
2019). 
We argue from cognitive and perceptual grounds that audio, spoken word, soundscapes, 
acoustic horizons and spaces, and spatialized audio, should be a serious area of inquiry 
for historians exploring the possibilities of new media to create effective immersive AR. 
(Graham et al., 2019) 
The project examples covered in this chapter provide lessons to help consider the 
potential of more sonically immersive digital history experiences. One could even 
imagine the beginnings of a framework for a more articulate approach to Aural 
Augmented Reality (AAR)-driven digital history experiences. 
7.1 T owards a Framework for Integrating Sound and Audio 
in AR Applications for Digital History and Cultural 
Heritage 
Drawing from the experiments, project summaries, expanded case study, and 
associated ideas articulated throughout this chapter, one can start to imagine a 
framework encompassing the following key elements:
 Sound Design: Understanding the importance of sound design in AR experiences 
and exploring techniques to create a coherent and immersive audio environment 
that complements the physical location or visual elements of the augmented 
scene/site.
 Sound Spatialization: Investigating the integration of modern spatial audio tech-
niques to enhance the user’s perception of virtual sound sources in conjunction 
with the physical environment.
 Interactive Audio Narrative: Exploring the potential of interactive audio nar-
ratives to provide users with a personalized and engaging historical/heritage 
storytelling experience. This involves designing branching narratives, dynamic 
soundscapes, and interactive techniques that respond to user actions or move-
ments, allowing for a deeper level of immersion and exploration.
 Preservation of Historical/Heritage Site Soundscapes: Exploring the potential of 
audio-based AR to preserve and recreate historical/heritage site soundscapes, as 
well as the challenges and opportunities of integrating archival audio materials.

374 B. Knoth
This will involve examining how sound and audio can be used to create a sense 
of presence and transport users to different historical periods or locations. 
7.2 Public Design Considerations 
Practitioners in the realm of the digital humanities who want to communicate 
content to a general audience should also be reminded that involving the public 
in the design workﬂow is important, and a focus on process and experimentation 
over ﬁnal products can be liberating and help promote innovative advancements in 
the ﬁeld. This principle is well articulated by Wendy Hsu in a book chapter titled 
Lessons on Public Humanities from the Civic Sphere , where Hsu asserts: 
[ ... ]we should think of public work in the humanities as a process, not a product, and that 
we should do more to include the public at earlier phases of our work. Using the digital to 
learn from the public is a listening practice, one that yields more efﬁcacious and engaged 
public humanities work. (Hsu, 2016) 
In past multimedia projects, I have conducted qualitative survey research with 
public participants on project design ideas, usability, and the audience experience 
of both work-in-progress systems and ﬁnal products (Knoth, 2012). The approach 
was akin to how software developers utilize alpha and beta testing with public 
participants to test products in various stages of development to acquire feedback on 
what works, what doesn’t, and what design ideas should be pursued further. In my 
practice, the insights gained from testing systems with potential users and audiences 
have provided a deeper understanding of the work, providing helpful guidance in 
reﬁning the multimedia experiences. In that light, as I imagine the potential of 
developing new place-based and/or augmented reality-driven multimedia platforms 
or experiences for digital history/heritage in the future, I can certainly envision 
engaging public participants in similar qualitative survey research as part of the 
design and testing process. 
8 Conclusion 
At this point in time, the practice of digital history and cultural heritage should be 
less about knowing and more about listening. Hopefully, the ideas presented here 
provide another jumping-off point for continued conversations, experimentation, 
and process-driven explorations that further propel the scholarly and creative 
practice of designing digital history and cultural heritage experiences. 
This chapter makes an original research contribution by critically analyzing and 
synthesizing the academic literature, while also using speciﬁc projects to highlight 
key research ﬁndings, methodologies, and design considerations for incorporating 
sound and audio within AR experiences for digital history and cultural heritage.

Harnessing Audio-Based Augmented Reality for Digital History and Cultural... 375
Through this synthesis, the chapter also presents a comprehensive framework for 
integrating and/or focusing on sound and audio in AR applications for digital history 
and cultural heritage. 
Overall, this chapter contributes to the growing creative ﬁeld of digital history 
and cultural heritage by focusing speciﬁcally on the role of sound and audio in 
enhancing historical narratives and heritage experiences within AR applications. 
Through the development of a comprehensive framework directed by practical 
examples, this chapter provides valuable insights, guidelines, and inspiration for 
researchers, practitioners, and professionals interested in leveraging the creative 
potential of sound and audio within the intersecting realms of history, cultural 
heritage, and AR technology, ultimately informing the innovative design and 
development of immersive and captivating applications.

3D Heritage: Preserving Historical 
and Cultural Heritage Through Reality 
Capture and Large-Scale 3D Printing 
Jose Daniel Garcia-Espinel , José María López-Galiacho González, 
and Manuel Fernández Torres 
1 Introduction 
Over the last few years, the evolution of techniques for creating digital models of 
real elements through laser scanning techniques has evolved in a very important 
way, to the point that replicas of elements of our historical and cultural heritage can 
be achieved with a high degree of realism and precision. 
Likewise, 3D printing technology has allowed these elements to be “printed” on a 
real scale, maintaining the same dimensions and appearance as the original objects. 
Even with the evolution of the size of the printable volume of these pieces, what 
is called large-scale 3D printing, has allowed these pieces to acquire sizes greater 
than 1×  1×  1 m, allowing us to recreate artistic and architectural elements in large 
formats. This technique is also called additive manufacturing. 
In the same way that these two technologies have evolved enormously in recent 
years, another technique, that of milling stones using a robotic arm, has come to 
make it possible to sculpt solid blocks of stone or concrete with high precision, 
being able to faithfully recreate all the details of the digital model of the piece to be 
recreated. This technique is known as subtractive manufacturing. 
All these developments allowed initiatives to emerge around the world in the last 
decade of the twenty-ﬁrst century that sought to preserve, thanks to technology, the 
artistic and architectural elements of our cultural heritage that could be at risk of 
disappearing due to armed conﬂicts, natural disasters, or even vandalism.

378 J. D. Garcia-Espinel et al.
In 2003, the Cyark1 initiative was founded, pioneering the use of 3D technologies 
to preserve the world’s cultural heritage and make it accessible to future generations. 
Its main objective was digital documentation and the creation of web, mobile and 
immersive digital experiences that inspire reﬂection, conversation, and imagination 
based on the digital models created in historic sites with a strong cultural and 
identity component for the community. 
Cyark’s most representative project was the digitization of the Mount Rushmore 
National Memorial2 whose original monument depicts the efﬁgy of several Ameri-
can presidents, such as George Washington, Abraham Lincoln, or Teddy Roosevelt 
and is located in the Black Hills in South Dakota (USA). 
Then, in 2012, one of the most prestigious institutions emerged, the Institute of 
Digital Archeology (IDA) 3 founded by Roger Michael, which was born with the 
spirit of promoting the fusion of new digitization and manufacturing techniques 
with traditional archaeology. 
One of the ﬁrst actions carried out by the Institute of Digital Archeology (IDA) 
was the preservation of the “Triumphal Arch of Palmyra”. In May 2015, a group 
of students and enthusiasts decided to create a digital model of one of the most 
iconic triumphal arches in the ancient Roman city of Palmyra, Syria, using Reality 
Capture technology. This happened prior to the ISIS occupation of Syria in 2015, 
which resulted in a large part of the historical heritage of the Roman city of Palmyra 
being devastated and disappearing due to the cultural censorship campaign. 
Faced with the worldwide reaction to these acts of vandalism on such precious 
elements of our culture, a global heritage preservation movement emerged that 
promoted the project to create a replica of the “Triumphal Arch of Palmyra” led 
by the Institute of Digital Archeology (IDA). 
In April 2016, a replica made of marble by the subtractive manufacturing 
technique was erected in Trafalgar Square in London, 4 weighing more than 11.5 
tons and 5.5 m high, which was exhibited to the public in a ceremony led by 
the mayor of London at the time, Boris Johnson. Later in September 2016, this 
replica was exhibited in New York, Dubai and ﬁnally in Florence and Arona in 
Italy. The response of society to this project was overwhelming, being visited by 
tens of thousands of people. 
From this project, multiple projects were carried out around the world aimed at 
the preservation of historical and cultural heritage, such as the following:
 “A World of Small Things”—Exhibition of V&A at the Architecture Biennale 
in Venice (2016). Reach.5 This exhibition of the V&A museum demonstrated 
how scanning and additive manufacturing (3D printing) were applied to preserve
1 CyArk (n.d.-a). 
2 CyArk (n.d.-b). 
3 People – The Institute for Digital Archaeology (2023). 
4 Morby and Morby (2016). 
5 Mairs rom digitaand Mairs (2022). 

3D Heritage: Preserving Historical and Cultural Heritage Through Reality... 379
cultural heritage at risk, due to natural disasters, intentional destruction, and 
negligence, creating different statues of Nefertiti, made from different materials 
and different 3D printing processes. A replica was also created of a refugee 
shelter used by refugees in Calais’ Jungle using subtracting manufacturing over 
synthetic stone.
 Replica of the winged bull of the Lamassu Statue of Nimrud. 6 On November 
6, 2017, the general director of UNESCO with Italy and Iraq inaugurated the 
replica based on the original sculpture that was destroyed in spring of 2015 by 
ISIL/Da’esh. The Statue of Lamassu, which once protected Ashurnasipals II’s 
North-West Palace in the ancient capital of the Assyrian Empire, was rebuilt 
using substractive manufacturing techniques led by the Associazone Incontro di 
Civiltà and supported by the Fondazione Terzo pilastro. The replica reﬂected the 
joint efforts of the international community in responding to these threats, which 
resulted in the adoption of the historic UN Security Council Resolution 2347, 
the ﬁrst resolution to address exclusively the protection of cultural heritage in the 
event of armed conﬂict.
 Lier mammoth at the Stadsmuseum in Lier, Belgium (2018). 7 Materialise, 
a Belgian software and 3D printer maker, has 3D printed a replica of Lier 
mammoth and it can now be visited at the Stadsmuseum Lier. For this purpose, 
320 bones of the skeleton have been scanned. The 3D-printed replica is more 
accurate than the original, considering that the original fossil has damaged bones 
and is missing a tusk. The printing was carried out using stereolithography 
printers for 52 days. The fully assembled skeleton is 5 m long and 3.5 m high. For 
the support inside the bone structure, a carbon ﬁber support frame was designed. 
It uses laser polyamide ﬁtting to hold the skeleton together.
 Dragon’s sculptures of Kew’s Great Pagoda at Richmond, England (2018).8 The 
company 3D systems carried out a 3D printing project of 72 dragons by the 
selective laser sintering process (SLS) for the Royal Botanic Gardens in London. 
This project is the restoration of a 256-year-old building to its original state. Due 
to the age of the structure, the dragons had to be very light. Each dragon was 
printed in ﬁve parts, all of them hollow inside. A dragon weighs approximately 
10 kg. The printing process for the 72 dragons lasted approximately one year, 
using two printers in the UK and two in the Netherlands.
 Replica of Yungang Grottoes’ Buddha Statue (Datong, Shanxi Province, China).9 
In 2019, technicians and researchers from the Yungang Grottoes Research Insti-
tute and Zhejiang University’s Cultural Heritage Research Institute successfully 
duplicated a smaller cave: Yungang Grottoes’ Cave No. 12. It was the ﬁrst 
cave duplicated. Thereafter, cave No. 3 was done, which is currently displayed 
at the Yungang Grottoes Art Museum in Qingdao, east China’s Shandong

Province. The third cave is known for its vast, impressive carvings. The identical 
reproduction strictly matches the appearance and scale of the original. The copy

stands at 9.93 meters tall reproduced in ﬁne detail. During the replication process,
