In Spain, the ﬁrst element that was digitized using Reality Capture technology 
and then 3D printed using large-scale additive manufacturing was the Arch of the 
Monastery of Dueñas, which is currently on display at the entrance of the National 
Archaeological Museum and which we will talk about later in this chapter. 
2 Reality Capture: From Physical to Digital 
“Reality Capture” is a term that refers to the process of capturing the shape and 
appearance of physical objects using digital devices, such as cameras, lasers, drones, 
or sensors. The captured data can then be processed and transformed into 3D 
models that represent the objects with high accuracy and detail. Reality Capture 
can be applied to various ﬁelds, such as architecture, engineering, construction, 
archaeology, art, and entertainment. 
Reality Capture can be performed using different methods and technologies, 
depending on the type, size, location, and complexity of the heritage elements. Some 
of the most common methods are:
 Photogrammetry: This method uses a series of photographs taken from different 
angles and positions to reconstruct the 3D shape and texture of an object. The 
photographs can be taken with any camera, such as a smartphone, a DSLR, or a 
drone. The photographs are then processed with specialized software that aligns 
them and extracts the 3D information from them.
 Laser scanning: This method uses a device that emits a laser beam and measures 
the distance and angle of the reﬂected light to capture the 3D shape of an object. 
The device can be handheld, mounted on a tripod, or attached to a vehicle. The 
device scans the object by moving the laser beam across its surface and recording 
the data points. The data points are then processed with specialized software that 
connects them and creates a 3D mesh.
 Structured light scanning: This method uses a device that projects a pattern of 
light, such as stripes or grids, onto the surface of an object and captures the 
image with a camera. The device can be handheld or ﬁxed. The device analyzes 
the distortion of the light pattern caused by the shape of the object and extracts 
the 3D information from it.

3D Heritage: Preserving Historical and Cultural Heritage Through Reality... 381
Reality Capture can offer many beneﬁts for the preservation of heritage elements, 
such as historical buildings, monuments, sculptures, paintings, and artifacts. Some 
of these beneﬁts are:
 Reality Capture can create digital replicas of heritage elements that can be 
stored, shared, and accessed online, without the need for physical access or 
transportation. This can reduce the risks of damage, theft, or deterioration that 
may affect the original objects.
 Reality Capture can provide accurate and detailed documentation of the current 
state and condition of heritage elements, which can help monitor their changes 
over time and identify potential threats or issues. This can facilitate the planning 
and execution of restoration and conservation projects.
 Reality Capture can enhance the understanding and appreciation of heritage 
elements by allowing users to explore them in immersive and interactive ways, 
such as virtual reality, augmented reality, or 3D printing. This can increase the 
awareness and engagement of the public and the stakeholders with the cultural 
and historical value of the objects. 
Reality Capture technology is the ﬁrst step that is always taken to generate 
a digital 3D model of the piece to be preserved. It is the step prior to additive 
manufacturing or subtractive manufacturing and allows the heritage element to be 
preserved in a digital format, guaranteeing that it will not be altered over time. 
3 Additive Manufacturing: From Digital to Physical 
by Adding Material 
3D printing, also known as additive manufacturing, is a process that creates physical 
objects from digital models by depositing layers of material on top of each other. 
3D printing has been used for various purposes, such as prototyping, art, education, 
medicine, and aerospace. However, one of the most promising and challenging 
applications of 3D printing is the construction of large-scale structures using 
concrete as the main material. 
Concrete is one of the most widely used and versatile materials in the construc-
tion industry, due to its strength, durability, and low cost. However, conventional 
methods of concrete construction, such as casting, molding, and formwork, have 
some limitations, such as high labor and material costs, long construction time, and 
environmental impact. 3D printing in concrete aims to overcome these limitations 
by using robotic arms, gantries, or cranes to extrude concrete layers in a controlled 
and precise manner, following a predeﬁned digital model. This way, 3D printing 
in concrete can create complex shapes, reduce waste, save time and money, and 
enhance sustainability and creativity in the construction sector.

382 J. D. Garcia-Espinel et al.
The basic principle of 3D printing in concrete is similar to other 3D printing 
technologies, such as fused deposition modeling (FDM) or direct ink writing (DIW). 
The two most commonly used techniques for 3D printing concrete are as follows:
 Contour Crafting:10 this is a technology for concrete 3D printing that Behrokh 
Khoshnevis from the Information Sciences Institute of the University of Southern 
California’s Viterbi School of Engineering in 2010. The process of 3D printing 
in concrete consists of four main steps: design, printing, curing, and ﬁnishing. 
In the design step, the structure to be printed is modeled using a computer-aided 
design (CAD) software, and then sliced into layers using a slicing software. The 
slicing software generates the toolpaths and the printing parameters, such as the 
speed, the ﬂow rate, and the layer height, for each layer. In the printing step, the 
printer follows the toolpaths and extrudes the concrete mixture layer by layer, 
forming the structure. This technique is characterized by its performance and 
productivity; however, the parts manufactured with this technique lack sufﬁcient 
resolution and have a wavy ﬁnish motivated by the superposition of their layers. 
Additionally, this technique requires that there be a support material to be able to 
add one layer on top of the other, which prevents the deposition of cantilevered 
material or without support material, which limits the geometries that can be 
manufactured.
 Powder Bed (D-Shape): 11 this technology uses a 3D printer that can produce 
stone-like objects from sand. It uses binder-jetting, a technique of printing layer 
by layer, to bind sand with a cementitious-based binder. The inventor of D-Shape 
is Enrico Dini, who founded Monolite UK Ltd. in 2006 and patented the ﬁrst 
model. The system works starting with a 3D model of the element to be printed. 
The 3D model ﬁle is then sent to the printer head. The printer head spreads a 
layer of sand mixed with cement that is 5–10 mm thick, over the area inside a 
frame, to start the printing process. The printer head divides the 3D model into 2D 
layers. Then, it begins with the lowest layer, and moves over the base, spraying 
the binding liquid at a resolution of 25 DPI (1.0 mm). The sand and the binder 
react chemically to form a material like sandstone. The material takes about 24 h 
to harden completely. The material is like concrete by composition. 
The most widely used technique of additive manufacturing on a large scale has 
been that of Powder Bed, since the need to obtain the highest possible resolution 
and have freedom of manufacturing forms advises to use this technique instead 
of Contour Crafting. This manufacturing technique can be combined with the 
subtractive manufacturing technique that we will see below to achieve maximum 
resolution.
10 Contour Crafting (2023). 
11 D-Shape (2023). 

3D Heritage: Preserving Historical and Cultural Heritage Through Reality... 383
4 Subtracting Manufacturing: From Digital to Physical 
by Material Milling 
Subtractive manufacturing, also known as milling, is a process that involves 
removing material from a solid block to obtain a desired shape. This technique can 
be applied by means of a robotic arm, which is equipped with a milling or drilling 
tool, and which is controlled by software that tells it how to move according to the 
three-dimensional model of the object to be manufactured. The robotic arm can have 
different degrees of freedom, allowing it to access different areas of the block and 
make complex and precise cuts. 
To perform a replication using subtractive manufacturing, you need to follow the 
following steps:
 Three-dimensional scanning: A 3D scanner is used to capture the shape, color, 
and texture of the original element. The scanner can be portable or stationary, 
depending on the size and location of the object. The result is a digital ﬁle 
containing the geometric and chromatic information of the element.
 Modeling and simulation: Computer-aided design (CAD) software is used to 
create the 3D model of the replica, based on the scan ﬁle. The model can be 
modiﬁed or adjusted according to the user’s needs or preferences. Simulation 
software is also used to predict the behavior of the robotic arm and cutting tool, 
as well as the time and material required for manufacturing.
 Manufacturing: A robotic arm is used to perform the subtractive manufacturing 
process, following the instructions of the control software. The robotic arm is 
positioned in front of the material block, which can be made of stone, metal, 
wood, plastic, or another suitable material. The robotic arm begins to remove 
the excess material, following the outline of the 3D model. The process can take 
anywhere from a few hours to several days, depending on the complexity and 
size of the replica.
 Finishing and assembly: A ﬁnishing process is performed to polish, paint, or 
varnish the replica, as appropriate. An assembly process can also be carried out, 
if the replica is composed of several pieces that must be joined together. Finally, 
the quality and ﬁdelity of the replica is veriﬁed, comparing it with the original. 
Subtractive manufacturing using a robotic arm is an innovative and versatile 
technique that offers many advantages for the replication of historical and cultural 
heritage elements, such as:
 Speed and efﬁciency: the manufacturing process is faster and more efﬁcient than 
other traditional techniques, such as hand carving or molding.
 Precision and detail: the manufacturing process allows the details and dimensions 
of the original to be accurately reproduced, without deformations or errors.
 Customization and creativity: the manufacturing process allows the replica to be 
customized according to the user’s needs or preferences, as well as creating new 
shapes or designs from the original.

384 J. D. Garcia-Espinel et al.
 Sustainability and respect: the manufacturing process reduces material and 
energy consumption, as well as environmental impact. In addition, the manu-
facturing process respects the original element, without damaging or altering it. 
The technology of robotic arm subtractive manufacturing is quite suitable for 
the creation of replicas of historical and cultural heritage elements. The advantage 
of this technique is that it allows the details and dimensions of the original to be 
faithfully reproduced with high resolution, as well as to use similar or compatible 
materials. On the other hand, it is quite a costly technique as it needs complex 
machinery like robotic arms and high expertise to be handled. 
5 First Steps in Preserving Heritage Using 3D Techniques 
Acciona is a Spanish company that started in 2012 to work with 3D printing 
techniques at the Innovation Division. The ﬁrst large-scale 3D printer that was used 
by Acciona was a D-shape 3D printer with a printable volume of 2 × 2 ×2m . 
In 2016, Acciona ﬁnished the ﬁrst pedestrian 3D-printed bridge in the world, 
manufactured, assembled, and installed in Alcobendas (Madrid, Spain) based on 
D-shape 3D printing technology. 
Having reached this milestone, Acciona entered the ﬁeld of historical and cultural 
heritage preservation with one of the group’s most pioneering and innovative 
companies, Acciona Cultura, which is a leading company in developing and 
applying immersive narratives and interactive technologies, to design and produce 
iconic museums, exhibitions, events, and cultural and brand experiences around the 
world. 
During 2017 and 2018, Acciona began to create its ﬁrst 3D-printed replicas 
of heritage elements and to experiment with Reality Capture and additive and 
subtractive manufacturing techniques. This led him to carry out several projects 
that helped him to reﬁne these techniques and become true pioneers in the use of 
these technologies. The most important projects developed during this period were a 
Replica of “Oso y Madroño” sculpture, emblem of the city of Madrid and a Replica 
of “La Dama Oferente”, which is quite a well-known historical Spanish sculpture. 
5.1 Replica of “Oso y el Madroño” Sculpture 
The sculpture of the “El Oso y el Madroño” was originally created in 1967 by 
sculptor Antonio Navarro Santafé and is located in the Spanish city of Madrid. It 
represents the heraldic coat of arms of the city of Madrid and was placed in the 
Puerta del Sol, the central square of the city, on May 10, 1967.12 
12 Estatua Del Oso Y El Madroño (2024).

3D Heritage: Preserving Historical and Cultural Heritage Through Reality... 385
Fig. 1 Process of creation of the Replica of the Statue “El Oso y el Madroño” 
The statue is made of stone and bronze, weighs approximately 20 tons and is 4 m 
high and represents a bear that is resting its hands on the trunk of a strawberry tree 
and directing its jaws towards one of its fruits. 
In November 2017, the International Fair was held in the city of Guadalajara 
(Mexico), in which one of the main pavilions was the Madrid Pavilion. At this fair, 
Acciona Cultura designed the pavilion that represented the city of Madrid, so in 
order to occupy a privileged place in the center of it, it was decided to make a 
replica of the sculpture of “El Oso y el Madroño”. 
To this end, and with the collaboration of the company Leica, which provided 
a laser scanner, the digital model of the sculpture was made using Reality Capture 
technology. The software used to perform the meshing of the point cloud obtained 
was Autodesk Remake. 
Once the digital model of the sculpture was obtained, it was printed using the 
D-shape 3D printer that Acciona had in its facilities using a micro-concrete as main 
material. The size of the replica was the same as that of the original sculpture, 
as it was smaller than the printing space of the 3D printer. Once the printing was 
complete, the part was cured in the curing chamber and then painted to simulate the 
original color (Fig. 1). 
When the replica was completed, it was shipped to Guadalajara (Mexico) to be 
exhibited in the Madrid Pavilion. Once presented there, it was the center of attention 
of the fair and was visited by numerous visitors, as well as prominent politicians 
from the city of Madrid. 
After the International Fair and in view of the great reception that the replica of 
the statue had had, Acciona and the Madrid City Council donated the sculpture to 
the city of Guadalajara, and it was installed on Avenida de Chapultepec Sur, in a 
section located between Progreso and España streets, one of the main roads of the 
city, which was renamed “Paseo de Madrid”. 
The replica of the sculpture of the “El Oso y el Madroño” served as the basis for 
uniting the two cities on both sides of the Atlantic, certifying this collaboration 
through the signing of a memorandum between the mayor of Madrid and the 
president of the municipality of Guadalajara.

386 J. D. Garcia-Espinel et al.
5.2 Replica of “Dama Oferente del Cerro de los Santos” 
Sculpture 
In 2018, as Acciona was a patron of the National Archaeological Museum, the ﬁrst 
contacts were made with it in order to explore the possibility of being able to make 
replicas of historical elements using the techniques of Reality Capture and additive 
and subtracting manufacturing. 
In order to explore the feasibility of developing these capabilities for Acciona 
Cultura, it was decided to make a replica of the Iberian sculpture from the second– 
third century BC called “Dama Oferente del Cerro de los Santos”, which represents 
an aristocratic woman in the religious rites of the Iberian people, who inhabited the 
east and south of the Iberian Peninsula (Spain). 
It is a 1.35 m tall female ﬁgure made of limestone that was found before 1870 
in the sanctuary of the Iberian culture located on the Cerro de los Santos, in 
Montealegre del Castillo (Albacete, Spain). A large number of votive offerings and 
stone sculptures of men and women in offering postures were found at the same 
site. The chronology of the site is understood from the fourth century BC. to Roman 
times. 
The ﬁgure shows a rich dress, which denotes belonging to a high social level. 
She is shown richly attired in three overlapping robes. The lower one, with very ﬁne 
folds, touches the ground and frames the shod feet. On top he wears a ﬁne tunic with 
embroidery on the chest. Finally, the upper tunic is a cloak whose edges fall hieratic 
under the hands, highlighting the offering. 
To make the digital 3D model of the sculpture, the photogrammetry technique 
was used due to the good lighting conditions in the museum where the statue was 
located. More than 80 photographs of the original statue were taken and through 
Autodesk Recap Pro software, the mesh and subsequent 3D model of the ﬁgure 
were generated. 
In this case, as the ﬁgure has a high degree of detail and needs to use a 
manufacturing methodology that achieves maximum resolution to achieve this, it 
was decided to use the additive manufacturing technique to generate the envelope 
of the sculpture and then mill the piece to obtain its details. In this case, it was used 
geopolymer material to simulate the original texture of the statue. 
Once the piece was manufactured on Acciona’s 3D printer, it was taken to the 
facilities of a collaborator who had a robotic arm with a milling head that he used to 
engrave tombstones and sculpt funerary statues. 
From the original 3D model that had been obtained by photogrammetry, the 
original piece was milled, obtaining all the details of the original sculpture. The 
work could be completed in its entirety in 2 weeks. 
Once the piece was ﬁnished, it was taken back to Acciona’s workshop where it 
was painted to simulate the original color of the sculpture located in the National 
Archaeological Museum. Once the resulting piece was examined by the technicians, 
it was destroyed, as had been previously agreed with the museum.

3D Heritage: Preserving Historical and Cultural Heritage Through Reality... 387
Fig. 2 Process of creation of the sculpture “Dama Oferente del Cerro de los Santos” 
The result obtained from this test was very satisfactory and allowed Acciona to 
learn how to combine additive and subtractive manufacturing techniques to obtain 
replicas of heritage elements with high resolution (Fig. 2). 
6 Collaboration Between Acciona and Spanish National 
Archeology Museum (MAN) 
6.1 The Collaboration 
In February 2018, an agreement was signed between the Spanish National Archae-
ological Museum (MAN) and Acciona to carry out two projects aimed at demon-
strating Acciona’s technological capabilities in large-scale 3D printing and Reality 
Capture and Acciona’s commitment to the preservation of historical and cultural 
heritage. This agreement was sponsored by Acciona Cultura, as this company was 
building at that time the most advanced museum contents of the world, such as 
the Boris Yeltsin Presidential Center (Yekaterimburg, 2015), the National Museum 
of Qatar (Doha, 2019), or more recently the Grand Egyptian Museum (El Cairo, 
2022).13 Manuel Fernández Torres, Head of Museums and Expos of Acciona 
Cultura, was one of the main sponsors of this collaboration and participated actively 
in this initiative. 
The core team involved in this collaboration was Acciona’s Advanced and Digital 
Innovation Hub (AADIH), led by José Daniel García Espinel, director of AADIH 
at Acciona’s Innovation Division. Luis Rodolfo Clemente Ortega and Raúl Boldú 
Toro, both managers of 3D Printing and Mixed Reality Skill Centers of AADIH, 
actively worked on this collaboration. Special mention should also be given to 
Telmo Pérez Luaces, Director of Innovation at Acciona, who pushed this initiative 
forward.
13 Acciona Cultura. Projects (n.d.) https://cultura.acciona.com/projects. 

388 J. D. Garcia-Espinel et al.
The agreement signed with the MAN included two initiatives with the following 
objectives:
 Digitalization Project: capturing or digitizing the MAN collection of medieval 
pieces, consisting of the 3D reproduction of 30 of the most important pieces in 
the collection which were showcased for MAN visitors in a large touch screen 
monitor in the exhibition hall. The goals for Acciona related to this initiative 
were: 
– Acquire experience in the scanning of pieces of art and museography with 
high level of detail requested in several museum projects. 
– Demonstrate Acciona’s commitment to the preservation of historical and 
cultural heritage. 
– Position Acciona Cultura as a benchmark in new technologies applied to the 
restoration of historical and cultural heritage.
 3D Printing Project: large-scale 3D printing of an historical and cultural heritage 
property and scanning the geometry of a prestigious and large architectural 
element included in the MAN collection in order to obtain a digital 3D replica of 
it. The element to reproduce was the “Arco de San Pedro de las Dueñas (León)”, 
one of the most prestigious elements of the medieval collection of the museum. 
The goals for Acciona related to this initiative were: 
– Develop the Reality Capture technique to increase the degree of resolution of 
3D printing technology. 
– Achieve high-quality surface ﬁnishes and texturing of 3D scanned pieces. 
6.2 Digitalization Project: Creation of 30 Digital Replicas 
of the Medieval Collection 
The ﬁrst step that was taken for the creation of the 30 digital replicas of the MAN’s 
medieval collection was the selection of the scanning technique. Initially, the use 
of the photogrammetry technique was proposed, as it had been used in the replica 
of the sculpture of the “Dama Oferente del Cerro de los Santos”, but it had to 
be discarded because many of the objects in the collection were metallic and the 
shine on the lighting objects made it impossible to obtain a quality 3D model by 
photogrammetry. 
For this reason, it was decided to use a high-precision handheld scanner (0.1 mm) 
that used a sweep of unstructured blue LED light beams. This scanner had the ability 
to capture 1,000,000 points per second for volume and 7.5 images per second for 
textures that aligned with the geometry automatically in real time. In this way, it 
was possible to generate 3D models in high deﬁnition and with a very rich color. 
The process of scanning the elements was as follows:

3D Heritage: Preserving Historical and Cultural Heritage Through Reality... 389
 Scanning of each element: The scan was carried out with the multi-section 
technique, obtaining a dense point cloud in each pass that contained geometry 
and the color of the texture. The time it took for each element ranged from 
10 min for the simplest (small and matte textured) to several hours for the 
more complicated (larger with glass and reﬂective metal elements). The scanning 
operations of the elements were always supervised by specialized personnel from 
the MAN who were in charge of handling the pieces and minimizing the time in 
which the pieces were out of the museum’s display cases.
 Post-processing of point clouds: This stage of the process involved aligning 
the different scanned parts as well as manually cleaning up the “noise” of the 
point clouds. To do this, different mathematical algorithms were used to ensure 
the precise alignment of the point clouds with the ﬁnal geometry. This process 
is carried out with the help of software provided by the manufacturer of the 
precision scanner. The post-processing of the scanned elements ranged from 
30 min for the smallest and simplest to several days for the largest and most 
complex.
 Mesh generation: This process was performed using the meshing function over 
the point cloud that the manufacturer’s software had. The process required 
computing power on the computers running the software, which had to have very 
powerful NVIDIA GPU graphics cards. In this way, the duration of the meshing 
generation lasted from a few minutes to several hours, depending on the size of 
the point cloud.
 Mesh optimization: Once the mesh was obtained, it was optimized, reducing the 
meshing to 1,000,000 polygons to be processed with the modeling software. 
Subsequently, those points that required meshing reﬁnement were manually 
modiﬁed. In some parts, this operation lasted several days.
 Textures: After the mesh had been optimized and the errors had been corrected, 
the textures obtained by the scanner through the taking of photographs during 
the scanning process were applied to it. To do this, the original textures were 
processed with speciﬁc texture processing software, creating the texture maps 
through the Physically Based Rendering (PBR) technique. These texture maps 
were imported into the texture processing software and the necessary corrections 
and masks were applied to work with different materials. In this way, many of 
the details of the polychromes of the scanned elements that were not reﬂected in 
the point cloud were captured on the ﬁnal 3D model (Fig. 3). 
Once we reached the end of the process, everything was completed, and the result 
was the ﬁnal digital model of the scanned element in high resolution and with a 
high degree of detail which was projected in the room of medieval elements of the 
National Archaeological Museum on a large-format touch screen. In this way, 30 
of the most important pieces of the museum’s medieval collection were digitally 
preserved, allowing the thousands of visitors to observe the details of many of them 
by enlarging the images on the touch screen. All the scanned elements were also

390 J. D. Garcia-Espinel et al.

Fig. 4 Digital application for visualizing the 30 digitized 3D elements in the MAN 
uploaded to the Sketch Fab web page of the MAN where all the 3D models created 
were shared openly with the external public.14 
But the most important thing is that having created a high-detail digital replica 
of these elements, in the hypothetical case that any of the pieces suffered some 
damage, we could have documented, with high precision in the digital model, the 
characteristics of geometry and texture of the original piece, which would allow us 
to faithfully restore it or even make a duplicate of it in case the piece disappeared 
completely (Fig. 4). 
6.3 Replica of the “Arco de San Pedro de las Dueñas” (Leon) 
The arch of San Pedro de Dueñas is one of the jewels treasured by the National 
Archaeological Museum in its room dedicated to Romanesque Art. The sculptural
14 3D models by Museo Arqueológico Nacional (@man) (n.d.). 

3D Heritage: Preserving Historical and Cultural Heritage Through Reality... 391
work of the capitals is of a high quality and belongs to the school of capitals of the 
ﬁrst period of the Collegiate Church of San Isidoro de León. The “Arco de Dueñas” 
arrived at the National Archaeological Museum in 1945 from the hands of an antique 
dealer. 
The history of this monastery begins in the year 973 when Doña Sancha 
Salomona and her sister ordered it to be built in the place of Villapedro, which would 
later be sold to the majordomo of Ramiro III, who placed it under the dependence 
of the Monastery of San Tirso de Sahagun (León). The abbey church was begun in 
1109, following the style of the Collegiate Church of San Isidoro de León, although 
later it would also be inﬂuenced by the remarkable church of San Tirso de Sahagún. 
The Monastery of San Pedro de Dueñas is located on the southeastern border of the 
province of León (Spain).15 
Due to the extraordinary historical relevance of this architectural jewel of Spanish 
Romanesque art, it was decided to select it for the creation of its 3D digital models 
and the subsequent reproduction of it using large-scale 3D printing techniques. This 
medieval element consisted of four columns with richly carved capitals, an arch 
above the columns, and two sets of ashlar walls on either side of the columns. As a 
whole, it had dimensions of 221 cm high and a width of 3.34 m, weighing several 
tons. 
First of all, the digital model of the “Arco de Dueñas” was made, for which, 
due to the dimensions of the element to be scanned, two scanning techniques 
were combined. At the beginning, a ﬁrst raw digital model of the arch, columns, 
and masonry walls was obtained using a Leica BLK360 scanner, which allowed 
scanning at a speed of 680,000 points per second with an accuracy of 4 mm. 
Thereafter, the high-precision handheld scanner (0.1 mm accuracy) was used to scan 
the elements of the arch with greater detail. The ﬁrst model was used for 3D printing 
trials and the second model, more accurate, was used for the ﬁnal element and the 
3D printing process of elements of the arch with high precision. The whole 3D 
scanning process took around 2 weeks (Fig. 5). 
After the digital model of the “Arco de Dueñas” was created, at the facilities 
of the company Acciona in Torrejón de Ardoz (Madrid) where the company’s 3D 
printing workshop was located, several printing tests were carried out in order to 
Fig. 5 Manufacturing process of the “Arco de Dueñas”. (From digital model to physical replica)
15 Arco San Pedro de Dueñas (2024). 

392 J. D. Garcia-Espinel et al.
adjust the type of material to be used. Finally, it was decided to use a micro-concrete 
that closely resembled the original texture of the arch stone and had a color that 
could later be treated to simulate the aging of the ashlars. 
During the preliminary tests carried out, it was possible to verify that Acciona’s 
large-scale 3D printer could not achieve a sufﬁcient degree of detail for the 
realization of the capitals of the four pillars, so it was decided to print them with 
a 3D printing technique by Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM) that allowed us to 
obtain a high degree of detail of the parts using a robust manufacturing material, 
similar to the micro-concrete of the rest of the arch. 
Finally, it was decided to manufacture the “Arco de Dueñas” in several sections. 
On the one hand, the columns on both sides were manufactured using Acciona’s 
large-scale 3D printing technology, along with the ashlar walls that accompanied 
them, and on the other hand, the upper arch, which was later mounted on the four 
columns. The capitals were printed without detail so that the four capitals could be 
assembled later. The printing process took 3 weeks. 
Once the set of pieces was assembled, the material was textured and colored to 
simulate the ﬁnish of the original arch. This was carried out by Acciona Cultura 
specialists in museography who had previously worked in the most important 
museums created by the company. Subsequently, the capitals, which were the 
elements of the arch with a greater degree of detail, were incorporated and textured 
together with the arch as a whole. These tasks were carried out within a week. 
Once the “Arco de Dueñas” was ﬁnished, it was agreed with the technicians of 
the National Archaeological Museum to place it in the gardens that are located at 
the entrance of the museum, next to Serrano Street at Madrid (Spain). To this end, 
the Arch at night was transported from Torrejón de Ardoz and installed in its ﬁnal 
location. 
On April 8, 2019, the “Arco de Dueñas” was inaugurated by Mr. Andrés 
Carretero, director of the National Archaeological Museum and by Mr. Juan Ignacio 
Entrecanales, executive vice president of Acciona, and presented to the media in a 
ceremony presided over by Mrs. Carmen Jiménez Sanz, deputy director general 
of State Museums. The event was attended by Mr. Jose María López-Galiacho 
González, CEO of Acciona Cultura, and Arantza Ezpeleta, general director of 
Technology and Innovation at Acciona (Fig. 6).16 
The realization of the arch of the Monastery of Dueñas using the most advanced 
techniques of Reality Capture and large-scale 3D printing represented a new mile-
stone in the collaboration between technology and innovation for the preservation 
of our most precious assets of historical and cultural heritage. And it came in 
addition to other similar actions that we have seen in this chapter that have taken 
place over the last few years to preserve the city of Palmyra, devastated by ISIS,
16 Reproducen a Escala Real En 3D En Hormigón El Arco Románico De San Pedro De Las Dueñas 
(León) (n.d.). 

3D Heritage: Preserving Historical and Cultural Heritage Through Reality... 393
Fig. 6 Inauguration of the 3D-printed replica of the “Arco de Dueñas” at the MAN 
or the Yungang Caves in China and that undoubtedly show the commitment of 
technological advances and innovation to the preservation of our history. 
7 Conclusions 
Captured Reality technologies, as well as additive and subtractive manufacturing, 
have become key elements for the preservation of the historical and cultural heritage 
of humanity. 
With the creation of the ﬁrst digital replicas made by Cyark on Mount Rushmore 
in South Dakota (USA) in 2010, followed by the physical replicas made in 
subtractive manufacture of the Triumphal Arch of Palmyra by the Institute of Digital 
Archaeology in 2017, two milestones were reached that conﬁrmed the potential of 
these techniques to achieve full-scale replicas that preserved architectural elements 
of our history to ensure that they could reach the highest level of detail for future 
generations. 
Subsequently, with the work carried out by Acciona’s innovation team in collab-
oration with Acciona Cultura, a specialist in museography and cultural projects, and 
Spanish National Archeology Museum (MAN), demonstrated that a new milestone 
was reached, by carrying out for the ﬁrst time in history the physical replication of 
an element of historical and cultural heritage using Reality Capture technology and 
large-scale 3D printing. 
The physical replica of the Arch of the Monastery of Dueñas, together with 
the digital replicas of 30 pieces from the medieval collection of the National 
Archaeological Museum, demonstrated that it was possible to preserve our history 
not only by protecting the physical elements that show us the legacy of our ancestors, 
but also by generating digital 3D models of them that, in the event of any disaster, 
they can guarantee that future generations will be able to enjoy them by being able 
to replicate them physically or digitally through the techniques of Captured Reality 
and additive manufacturing.

Part V 
The Historic Urban T erritory as a Focus 
for Digital Experiences

Segovia, Heritage and City. From 
the Special Plan for Historic Areas 
to the Smart Digital Project: New 
Strategies for Heritage Planning 
and Preservation 
Miguel-Ángel Chaves-Martín 
1 Introduction 
The Special Plan for Historic Areas of Segovia (PEAHIS) was ﬁnally approved, 
after more than 10 years of work and uncertainty, in the municipal session of 6 
September 2019. A century of interventions, debates, proposals, projects, urban 
planning and heritage conservation that had ﬁnally led the city of Segovia to its 
declaration as a World Heritage City in 1985 was left behind. Since then, new 
conservation and urban planning policies have ﬁnally led to the ﬁnal document for 
the management and control of the architecture and urban planning of the city of 
Segovia. The result has been a necessarily interdisciplinary project full of values 
and also of controversies and contradictions, of successes and errors, which over 
more than 10 years has conditioned the conservation, management and image of the 
city and its cultural assets. 
The new Plan was oriented towards the conservation, restoration, rehabilitation 
and revitalisation of the historic areas and their unique elements, organising and 
protecting the city’s historic centre from an urban and cultural point of view. But 
a complex that extends beyond the initial historic areas to encompass the double 
reality that has characterised and singularised the urban form since its origin: the 
double settlement on the rock (walled enclosure) and in the surrounding valleys 
(historic suburbs) next to the fertile plains of the two rivers (Eresma and Clamores) 
that surround it and the new growth from them. Awareness of the uniqueness of 
the settlement and of the heritage assets and historical elements that characterise it 
will be the basis of a plan that places the emphasis not only on the conservation 
and maintenance of the urban and architectural structure and its heritage value, but

398 M.-Á. Chaves-Martín
also on the silhouette and contours of the urban landscape and its environmental 
characteristics, as well as on the cultural values that encourage its revitalisation. 
Since the declaration of Segovia as a World Heritage City in 1985 by the 
UNESCO, its conservation has become a strategy for the sustainable reconciliation 
of urban growth and quality of life. The whole city came to be considered 
urban cultural heritage insofar as its existence and cultural value were recognised, 
maintained and consolidated over time despite the considerable transformations 
suffered, and reactivated with renewed impetus in recent years, to which the 
approval and implementation of the Special Plan for Historic Areas of Segovia made 
a substantial contribution. 
Now, 4 years after its implementation, the new Management Plan for the city of 
Segovia is at an advanced stage of drafting, as a support tool for the planning of 
strategies that combine the protection, conservation and management of this space, 
both converging in the announced and delayed Smart Digital Segovia project that, 
from the central administration (National Plan for Smart Cities of Spain), began to 
be developed in 2018. Implementing a central Smart City core that, starting from an 
updated graphic base, georeferencing and geolocation, develops a management and 
information processing system that allows its digitisation and public availability of 
most of the information of the local administration, structured in nine major lines 
of action among which Smart Urban Planning (Architecture and Urban Planning) 
stands out in a convergence with the other Plans that highlight the importance and 
need for new digital tools and techniques focused on heritage conservation and 
management. 
2 Background: Heritage and City as a Historical Process 
In the middle of the twelfth century, Abdalá al Idrisi stated that “Segovia is not a city 
but is made up of many nearby villages”. This description of the city clearly tells us 
about the two nuclei that characterise it: the walled city, high up on the rock, like an 
acropolis which, from the end of the eleventh century, began to be repopulated, and 
the suburbs, more populated neighbourhoods outside the walls, scattered around it 
along the aqueduct and the courses of the river Eresma and the Clamores stream. The 
result is a unique urban settlement in which nature and monuments are integrated 
into a landscape of singular beauty. 
In a quick tour of its history we start, based on small primitive settlements, from 
the powerful presence of a Roman enclave which, in the absence of excavations 
that would allow us to better understand its urban structure, bequeathed us the 
incomparable Aqueduct, the symbol of the city. After centuries of wars and 
abandonment on the border between the Christian territories and those occupied by 
Islam, repopulation began with Alfonso VI in 1088 and the city gradually took shape 
as it grew on the rock. On this relatively small walled enclosure, like an acropolis 
between the two valleys, the population settled, especially the nobles, grouped 
around the parishes and palaces; the castle and the wall were built, conﬁrming

Segovia, Heritage and City. From the Special Plan for Historic Areas ... 399
Fig. 1 Segovia. Historic urban landscape. View of the historic city from the surrounding country-
side and wooded environment with the mountains in the background 
the military and warlike character of Segovia. Meanwhile, the suburbs, the whole 
area outside the city walls, were the “food” of the city, with much more intense 
economic, industrial and commercial activity. Within them, the Aqueduct became a 
fundamental piece in understanding their structure and development, as it became 
the backbone in the shadow of which the different neighbourhoods that it supplied 
with water along its route grew up. 
There was a proliferation of Romanesque churches and houses, late examples of 
Gothic architecture, large monasteries and convents, and ﬁnally, in the early years of 
the sixteenth century, an imposing cathedral in the highest central point of the walled 
city. These were years of economic splendour supported by the powerful cloth 
industry, which saw the ﬂourishing of palaces and great houses in both Gothic style 
and the new Renaissance language. The sixteenth century saw the peak of the city’s 
splendour and the beginning of its decadence, which dragged on throughout the 
Baroque period, with renovation work still being carried out, especially in convents 
and churches, adapting them to the new tastes (Fig. 1). 
The crisis worsened from the mid-eighteenth century and throughout the nine-
teenth century. Unlike other cities, Segovia hardly grew at all. For this reason, just 
as important as the process of expansion was the process of interior reform, which 
took place mainly in the walled enclosure, although sometimes it was also carried 
out in the suburbs. This process basically took place through two mechanisms: 
the increase in the width of the streets with the modiﬁcation of alignments to 
improve accessibility, and the creation of squares and open spaces in the places 
occupied by convents and churches, as a direct consequence of the process of 
disentailment of ecclesiastical property begun in 1835. Nevertheless, the lack of 
municipal ﬁnancial resources put the brakes on the implementation of these plans 
on numerous occasions, preventing the numerous planned demolitions. 
The loss of the monumental heritage was the most dramatic consequence of this 
situation, and all the criticisms and adverse comments that are now made about that

400 M.-Á. Chaves-Martín
nineteenth-century mentality are derived from it. Segovia presented an aged and 
neglected image, with an increasing number of dilapidated buildings, with old and 
winding streets crossed or modiﬁed in some sections by new, wider roads, as a result 
of the alignment plans, with problems of sewerage, lighting, hygiene and sanitation, 
and a heritage that was still neglected, with only four monumental declarations at 
the end of the 1920s: the Aqueduct, declared in 1884, with enormous controversy 
between the institutions, which debated between its heritage value and its lost utility; 
the tower of the church of San Esteban, declared in 1896 to protect it, precisely, 
from deterioration that in the end was reduced to rubble and reconstruction; the 
Monastery of El Parral in 1914; and the Church of La V eracruz in 1919. On the other 
side of the scale, the demolition of the gates of the wall in 1886 (San Juan) and 1888 
(San Martín), the controversial and interminable restoration of the Alcázar after its 
ﬁre in 1862, the disastrous restoration of the also burnt convent of Corpus Christi in 
1903, the demolition of the old convent of San Agustín in 1915, the disappearance 
of the churches of San Pablo and San Facundo, and so many other interventions 
that were ignored by the public, and so many other interventions that sometimes 
ignored the past in favour of the ideals of modernity and progress, and at other 
times sought unjustiﬁed (if not invented) antiquity rather than authenticity, as some 
of the examples given above attest, and of which relevant protagonists of the new 
times, still little recognised by the Segovian elites, such as Le Corbusier himself, 
also left their mark. 
The situation Segovia had reached during the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, 
with a major economic, industrial and commercial crisis carried over from the 
previous century, had not given rise to experimentation with new proposals for 
contemporary architecture. In fact, the few that could be materialised by architects 
such as Manuel Pagola, Casto Fernández Shaw or Jesús Carrasco Muñoz were often 
overshadowed by the maintenance of a tradition, sometimes misunderstood, which 
continued to defend the sgrafﬁto on the façades of buildings as wall cladding and 
eclecticism or style architecture as a formal proposal. 
The industrial city, with its new needs and harsh debates, only tangentially 
touched the city of Segovia. There was not an excessive working-class population 
for which to provide a housing solution by analysing the minimum housing. Nor 
was there an industry to drive it forward and require this always surplus labour, for 
small, traditional factories that did not require technological proposals and studies 
of habitability and rationalisation of spaces and functions. Although this did not 
prevent the destruction from happening, either on paper, in alignment projects that 
were difﬁcult to materialise due to lack of economic resources, or in execution, 
demolishing some of the ramshackle mansions, churches and disentailed convents, 
to lay out a garden, a square or a street wide and straight enough for a tramway to 
run along it, which, in the end, would never be built either. Progress and heritage 
did not go well together, and intellectuals and professionals in the ﬁeld of culture 
fought for the safeguarding of a remarkable and sometimes deteriorated heritage 
complex from different positions and attitudes. Their efforts focused above all on

Segovia, Heritage and City. From the Special Plan for Historic Areas ... 401
maintaining the values and beauties, still intact, of a past amidst the pressures and 
desires of progress and modernity as it was then understood. 1 
From the end of the 1920s and during the ﬁrst years of the Republic, heritage, 
conservation and restoration of monuments in Spain had undergone a notable 
advance, which led to a new and modern administration of cultural assets, with the 
creation of the post of area conservator architect, as the ﬁrst professional ﬁgure in 
charge of the protection of Spanish monuments. Of the seven zones into which the 
country was organised, Segovia was included in the fourth, under the responsibility 
of the architect Emilio Moya, who had trained in the restoration of monuments in 
Italy, as a pensioner of the Spanish Academy in Rome. His work both in the city and 
in the province of Segovia, under the protection of the new ideas defended by Torres 
Balbás and López Otero at the Athens Conference of 1931 on the Conservation of 
Monuments of Art and History, as well as the massive declaration of monuments 
throughout Spain by the decree of 3 June 1931, and the Law of the Spanish Artistic 
Treasure of 1933, were episodes as relevant as they were ignored once the Civil War 
was over.2 It was then that the Marquis of Lozoya and his inseparable collaborator in 
Segovia, the architect Cabello Dodero, began, as if starting practically from scratch, 
ignoring much of what had been applied years before, their work to safeguard 
heritage. 
3 Declarations of Monuments and Urban Planning in the 
Second Half of the Twentieth Century 
As we have stated in previous studies (Chaves, 2019, pp. 446–454), all those who 
have approached the ﬁgure of Juan de Contreras y López de Ayala, Marquis of 
Lozoya, from his role in the conservation of Segovia’s monumental heritage, have 
highlighted two great successes that marked his entire career. On the one hand, just 
after the end of the Civil War and at the head of the Directorate General of Fine 
Arts, keeping the National Artistic Treasure Law of 1933 in force was not only a 
brave gesture when it came to maintaining a good law with republican links, but, 
above all, the wisdom of conserving it, understanding its value in the organisation 
and conservation of Spanish heritage, demonstrated by the fact that it remained in 
force until 1985. On the other hand, and very especially linked to his native city, of 
which he would never tire of afﬁrming “in Segovia the most exciting work of art is 
the city itself, carved by the centuries and by history in a situation of exceptional 
beauty” (Marqués de Lozoya, 1973, p. 21), his great success was in the conservation 
of the city of Segovia (p. 21), his great success would be the declaration of the city 
as a National Monument of Historic-Artistic Interest on 12 July 1941, including
1 A detailed analysis of this whole process can be found in (Chaves, 1998 and 2019). 
2 The most complete study on the situation of heritage in Spain during the 1920s and 1930s in 
(Esteban Chapapría, 2007). 

402 M.-Á. Chaves-Martín
not only the historic walled enclosure, but also the surroundings of the suburbs in 
partial complexes near the Aqueduct, and which was continued in the Declaration 
of Picturesque Landscape in 1947 for the city’s tree-lined streets and avenues. 
In all these cases, the personality and ﬁgure of Juan de Contreras was key to 
understanding the process of constructing the image of the city of Segovia. Despite 
the evident transformations that were taking place, Lozoya ﬁxed his gaze and his 
interest in highlighting the historical value of a heritage that had stood still in 
time, paying special attention to certain monuments and to an urban image that was 
always conditioned by a past, a lineage and a tradition that he wanted to perpetuate, 
achieving a leading role in the defence of the historical and monumental heritage 
that characterised the image and the historical urban landscape of Segovia. 
On 5 July of that same year 1941, the president of the Advisory Board of the 
Monumental City of Segovia sent the mayor of the city the “draft regulations of 
the Ordenanzas Monumentales de la Ciudad de Segovia approved by this Advisory 
Board; and one hundred and twenty-two ﬁles of the Monumental Inventory, a list of 
which is also attached”. As the report of the Historic Areas Plan itself points out, this 
is the ﬁrst general inventory of the capital, which not only includes the main urban 
landmarks but also their adjoining buildings that enhance their character within the 
city (PEAHIS, 2019, Memoria Vinculante , p. 14). 
The Monumental Declaration of 1941 also led to the approval of the “Ordenanzas 
Monumentales de la Ciudad de Segovia, para el cumplimiento del Decreto de 12 
de julio de 1941” ( Monumental Ordinances of the City of Segovia, for compliance 
with the Decree of 12 July 1941 ), and in particular “for a better adaptation and 
speciﬁcation of the protection derived from it to each speciﬁc building of the 
urban fabric of Segovia”. In March 1944, the Regulations for compliance with 
the Monumental Ordinances were approved, and in 1952, the Plan General de 
Ordenanción Urbana. The developmentalism of Franco’s Spain in the 1960s was 
to bring about important urban planning changes under the new Plan General de 
Ordenación Urbana of 1964: 
• New developments: alignment and widening of streets, some of which became 
wide avenues, and rearrangement of squares and public spaces. 
• Need for facilities: linked to the technological and developmentalist spirit of the 
time, new buildings were erected on sites resulting from historic demolitions, 
such as the Telefónica building on the ruins of the Palace of Enrique IV , the new 
Hospital 18 de Julio on the site of the Convent of San Agustín, the building of 
the Women’s Section in the Convent of La Merced and the Teaching University 
in the surroundings of the Romanesque church of San Juan de los Caballeros, 
among others. 
• A strong promotion of social housing, both public and private initiatives in the 
extension areas of the city and in the refurbished areas of its historic centre. 
This loss of heritage values took a radical turn in the 1970s. The UNESCO 
Convention for the Protection of World Heritage in Paris in 1972, the Italian Charter 
of Restoration of 1973, and the Amsterdam Charter of 1975 on the protection of 
European architectural heritage, together with the new urban planning policies in

Segovia, Heritage and City. From the Special Plan for Historic Areas ... 403
historic cities initiated by the plans of Bologna (1975) and Ferrara (1976), marked 
a turning point in relation to the previous criteria for heritage protection. The 
protection of all the elements and interventions from any period was then proposed, 
while also including, within the protection of the monument, the surroundings made 
up of streets, squares and gardens. The monument is no longer just an asset to be 
protected, but to be reactivated through new uses and rehabilitation projects that, in 
coherence with its values, are adapted to modern needs and functions. This technical 
vision, together with the change in sensitivity of the period of democratic transition, 
will mark the evolution of heritage. 
Urban planning in the city of Segovia reached a new milestone in 1984 with 
the approval of the new General Urban Development Plan. It even contemplated the 
drafting of a Special Protection Plan, as well as the creation of a belt of undeveloped 
land for special landscape protection. The following year, Segovia was declared 
a World Heritage City by UNESCO. In the 1990s, the ﬁrst Special Plans were 
developed in different areas of the historic city and its suburbs (neighbourhoods 
outside the city walls), followed by the new General Plan of 2008 and the so-
called Areas of Integral Rehabilitation (ARI) and Areas of Rehabilitation of the 
Historic Centre (ARCH) in the same years, all of them preceding this new Plan, 
aimed at the conservation, restoration, rehabilitation and revitalisation of the historic 
areas and their unique elements, both of the walled enclosure and of the historic 
suburbs and the picturesque landscape that surrounds it. A landscape full of values 
and singularities where the city, the countryside, the woodland and the mountains 
converge. 
4 Special Plan for Historic Areas of Segovia (PEAHIS). New 
Forms of Planning and Management of Heritage, 
Architecture and Urban Planning 
The Special Plan for Historic Areas of Segovia (PEAHIS) started in 2009 and was 
ﬁnally approved in the municipal session of 6 September 2019. The result is a 
necessarily interdisciplinary project full of values and of controversies and con-
tradictions, of successes and errors, which over more than 10 years has conditioned 
the conservation, management and image of the city and its cultural assets. 
The new Plan is aimed at the conservation, restoration, rehabilitation and revital-
isation of the historic areas and their unique elements, organising and protecting the 
city’s historic centre from an urban and cultural point of view. But a complex that 
extends beyond the initial historic areas to encompass the double reality that has 
characterised and singularised the urban form since its origin: the double settlement 
on the rock (walled enclosure) and in the surrounding valleys (historic suburbs) 
next to the fertile plains of the two rivers (Eresma and Clamores) that surround it 
and the new growth from them. Awareness of the uniqueness of the settlement and 
of the heritage assets and historical elements that characterise it will be the basis of

404 M.-Á. Chaves-Martín
a plan that places the emphasis not only on the conservation and maintenance of the 
urban and architectural structure and its heritage value, but also on the silhouette 
and contours of the urban landscape and its environmental characteristics, as well 
as on the cultural values that encourage its revitalisation. 
We are, therefore, faced with an urban and heritage plan whose fundamental 
objective, as expressed in its informative report, is the protection of the Historic 
Areas of Segovia through urban planning, insofar as they are historic urban 
landscape, and its determinations are oriented towards the conservation, restoration, 
rehabilitation and revitalisation of these areas and their integral elements. The 2009 
UNESCO Forum stated in this regard that: 
The concept of historic urban landscape addresses the wider territorial and landscape 
context and therefore goes well beyond historic centres or ensembles. It reﬂects and has led 
to the shaping of a modern society and consequently is of great value for the understanding 
of our present way of life. It is crucial to understand the historic urban landscape 
before undertaking any contemporary architectural project. The drive for modernisation 
is legitimate, but it is crucial to ﬁrst reﬂect its impact on the identity of the city and the 
lifestyles of communities. (FORUM, 2009,p .4 ) 
This brief deﬁnition highlights both the ambition of an idea and the ambiguity 
with which it is formulated. In a context of a constantly evolving meaning and scope 
of the concept of cultural heritage, the historic urban landscape is proposed as a 
broader reality than the hitherto named historic centres and urban ensembles, which 
must, therefore, be reinterpreted (Martínez & Tort, 2012). Without abandoning 
the heritage logic, the aim is to offer something more, a new reading capable of 
incorporating the geographical context, a regional frame of reference, which implies 
a wider landscape and territorial context. By saying landscape and territory, it is 
intended as an approach to modern society and a better understanding of our current 
way of life. Landscape seems to mean, therefore, the possibility of a broader vision 
of the anthropic space to which historic centres and ensembles belong, a vision 
that values its natural, cultural and social dimensions and not only its heritage 
dimensions. The new concept aims to relate the material and immaterial components 
of the urban, with the uses and customs of the inhabitants of each place, where, over 
the course of history, certain distinctive features have been created (Fig. 2). 
In this way, the Special Plan for Historic Areas of Segovia afﬁrms its interest in 
responding to the primary objective of preserving the quality of the environment 
in which people live, improving the productive and sustainable use of urban 
spaces, without losing sight of their dynamic character, and promoting social and 
functional diversity, as stated in the project report. The objectives of urban heritage 
conservation and those of social and economic development are thus integrated, 
with an approach based on a balanced and sustainable relationship between the 
urban environment and the natural environment, between the needs of present and 
future generations and the heritage of the past sustained by all its cultural values. 
The deﬁnition of Historic Urban Landscape established by UNESCO in 2011 ﬁts 
perfectly with the physical reality of Segovia by identifying it as one: 
An urban area resulting from a historical layering of cultural and natural values and 
attributes, which transcends the notion of “ensemble” or “historic centre” to encompass

Segovia, Heritage and City. From the Special Plan for Historic Areas ... 405
Fig. 2 PEAHIS. Special plan for historic areas of Segovia. Full deﬁnitive document on the website 
of Segovia City Council (September 2019) 
the overall urban context and its geographical setting. This general context includes other 
features of the site, principally its topography, geomorphology, hydrology and natural 
features; its built environment, both historic and contemporary; its infrastructure, both above 
and below ground; its open spaces and gardens, the conﬁguration of land uses and their 
spatial organisation; visual perceptions and relationships; and all other elements of the 
urban fabric. It also includes social and cultural uses and values, economic processes and 
the intangible aspects of heritage as it relates to diversity and identity. (PEAHIS, 2019,p . 
9) 
This objective is linked to the conception that landscape and its inhabitants are 
part of the same reality, combining the right to landscape with the right to landscape. 
The latter extends its enjoyment and defence to all, recognising the landscape as the 
common heritage of society as a whole, especially, if possible, in landscapes that 
have already achieved recognition in various declarations and protection through 
different ﬁgures, as is the case with the landscape of the city of Segovia. 
Preserving the environment at the cost of worsening the quality of life of the 
inhabitants is not a sustainable solution, since the worsening of quality will lead to 
a loss of interest by the citizens themselves, leading to a “devitalisation” that ends 
up deteriorating the physical reality of the heritage as well, in a degenerative spiral 
that causes the loss of what was intended to be preserved. For this reason, policies 
that merely repress behavioural and regulatory policies, with a purely normative 
scope, are not the best breeding ground for improving the quality of life of citizens 
and for the protection and revitalisation of cultural heritage. This means that it 
is necessary to bring together an arsenal of tools of diverse scope (legal, urban 
planning, landscape, architectural, facilities, etc.) that can correct or alleviate the 
processes of degradation that begin with the loss of vitality of historic areas. Thus, 
the Special Plan for Historic Areas of Segovia proposes a set of strategies governed 
by the principles of sustainability, prevention, caution and revitalisation, all aimed

406 M.-Á. Chaves-Martín
at improving the quality of life of the inhabitants, so that the protection of cultural 
heritage is effective through its revitalisation and use. 
In this sense, the Special Plan for Historic Areas of Segovia takes into consider-
ation that “the defence of the natural and cultural heritage implies the integration 
of strategies for the conservation, management and planning of historic urban 
areas in the processes of local development and urban planning, and that the 
application of a landscape approach contributes decisively to maintaining urban 
identity”. Therefore, from an integral vision of the historic areas of Segovia, the 
Plan establishes three models for the protection of cultural heritage, with the aim of 
carrying out integrated urban and heritage strategies (Bandarin & V an Oers, 2014): 
• Model of intervention in heritage, whose fundamental instruments are the formu-
lation of the Catalogue and the Technical Suitability Report of the Interventions 
in the assets. Architectural Catalogue. Catalogue of Cultural Assets. Catalogue 
of Singular Elements and Elements of Interest. Catalogue of Public Spaces. 
• Spatial model, through the formulation of urban planning, whose basic instru-
ment is the Ordinance and Building Protection Plan, as well as the Schematic 
Elevations, the Urban Planning Management Areas and the Speciﬁc Planning 
Areas. 
• Heritage management model, whose fundamental instrument is the future formu-
lation of the Management Plan for the World Heritage Site, with the creation of 
the management body that will enable the follow-up, monitoring and evaluation 
of the policies developed on the property and of a technical body that will report 
on certain aspects of the Plan. 
The analysis of the landscape is approached from qualitative or descriptive and 
quantitative parameters, about the valuation of the different units in relation to a 
series of relatively objective criteria. Studies of rural landscape and urban landscape, 
the former being considered as a combination of natural and agrarian elements in 
different “doses” (areas where human pressure is not excessively evident and areas 
where anthropic activity over time has left its mark: pastures, crops, settlements, 
roads, etc.). It is essential to consider this rural landscape surrounding the urban 
area, not only as a formal and aesthetic component but also as a changing and 
dynamic reality that undergoes major changes and transformations, generally of a 
negative nature and induced, fundamentally, by irresponsible human activity. Only 
in this way can urban and territorial planning be sensitive to the possible depletion 
of such a major cultural resource as the landscape, guaranteeing its protection. 
The knowledge and preservation of this rural landscape and its response to human 
actions is important because its consequences affect us directly, either by altering 
the ecological balance of our environment, or by the social and economic effects 
that landscape change brings with it. Changes in the conﬁguration of the landscape 
also entail changes in the visual features of the territory, thus causing an alteration 
in visual quality. Until recently this situation was not considered, but nowadays 
landscape has come to occupy a privileged place, at least in developed societies, 
due to a greater public awareness of the visual quality of its surroundings. Landscape

has been recognised as a valuable resource, closely linked to the quality of life, the

The conservation of all this urban heritage, tangible and intangible, thus becomes

Continuing the Strategic Plan of the city of Segovia 2006–2016, the City Council

Modeling and Monitoring the Rosenwald 
Ideal: Digital Documentation 
and Preservation at the T ankersley 
Rosenwald School, Alabama 
Danielle S. Willkens, Botao Li, and Junshan Liu 
1 Introduction 
Designed to combat systemic racism in the Jim Crow South, Rosenwald Schools 
were critical to mobilizing education for African Americans and empowering the 
generations who led the civil rights movement. By the time of the closure of 
the Rosenwald Fund, there had been 5357 schools, shops, and teacher’s homes 
constructed in 883 counties and 15 states (Anderson, 2010; Ascoli, 2006; Bergdoll 
&G r a y , 2017;B i r d , 2023; Deutsch, 2011; Feiler & Lewis, 2021; Johnson-Jones, 
2019; Mansell & Binkley, 1997). Between July 1, 1921, and July 1, 1929, the fund 
was so productive that four classrooms were built every working day. By 1928, 
approximately one-third of the nation’s African American children in rural areas 
were educated in Rosenwald schools, and one in ﬁve rural schools were built by the 
Rosenwald Fund (Hoffschwelle, 2012). 
Despite their widespread inﬂuence, many Rosenwald schools fell into disuse 
and disrepair following the landmark 1954 Supreme Court ruling for Brown v. 
Board of Education that overturned the 1896 Plessy v. Ferguson case that allowed 
schools to maintain “separate by equal” policies. Few integrated schools used the 
Rosenwald structures due to the rural locations, and movements away from trade-
based elementary education meant that many of these schools closed in the 1960s. 
Decommissioned, many of the structures collapsed due to deferred maintenance 
or their materials were salvaged for other, local projects. Only in the late 1990s 
and early 2000s did interest increase in preserving the few remaining structures: 
a 2012 study by the National Trust for Historic Preservation estimated that only 
10–12% of the nation’s Rosenwald Schools endured. There is currently a national
