study of assets underway, sponsored by 116 H.R. 3250 Julius Rosenwald and the 
Rosenwald Schools Act of, 2020, and put into action on January 13, 2021, as Public 
Law No: 116–336. Within this is a resource study of 13 structures associated with 
Rosenwald; although there are two Rosenwald schools, Tankersley is not explicitly 
included in the study. There is a rich archive associated with the Rosenwald fund, 
as evidenced by program reports, the community school plans, and maps (Fig. 1); 
yet, a contemporary account of surviving resources had, until the recent federal law, 
been entirely left to individuals and philanthropic initiatives, a consistent policy 
within the record of historic preservation in the United States (Stubbs & Makaš, 
2011). Even with federal sponsorship, necessary funding, research accessibility, and 
information dissemination are still very slow. For example, the Rosenwald archives 
at the Franklin Library Special Collections and Archives at Fisk University are 
still closed to the public, and the digitization project for the Rosenwald database 
continues to be delayed (http://rosenwald.ﬁsk.edu). 
Of the 5357, buildings noted in the 1931 map, 4978 were schools, and approx-
imately 500 survive (Feiler, 2021). Feiler’s ambitious project photographed 105 
schools in all 15 program states. He discovered that of the surviving schools, about 
half had been restored and received new life as community centers, church facilities, 
homes, and daycare ofﬁces. Feiler captured the interior of the Tankersley School, 
noting its unrestored condition and light ephemerally, yet errantly, streaming from a 
hole in the roof.

Modeling and Monitoring the Rosenwald Ideal: Digital Documentation... 415
Fig. 2 The east façade of the Tankersley Rosenwald School in Hope Hull, Alabama. Willkens 
photograph, February 2023 
Following the standards of the Department of the Interior’s National Register 
criteria, Rosenwald Schools are historically signiﬁcant due to their afﬁliations 
with education, ethnic heritage for African Americans, and Social/Cultural history. 
Rosenwald Schools were, however, not just valuable to Black students but also 
to demonstrating integrated partnerships between both public and private entities. 
To secure Rosenwald funds, the ﬁnancial model required using both community 
and state funds for construction. Although Rosenwald Schools did not challenge 
segregation, it did force white-run district and state boards to provide funding to 
Black schools that were systemically underfunded and overcrowded (Aaronson 
& Mazumder, 2011). Furthermore, the school plans were developed by architect 
Robert R. Taylor (1868–1942) and later Samuel Leonard (commonly known as 
S.L.) Smith (1875–1956) became not only established standards for school plans but 
models for white school districts (Dresslar, 1920; Smith, 1924, 1936). The revised 
edition of Community School Plans ( 1931) noted that the Rosenwald Fund, with 
headquarters at George Peabody College, Nashville, would provide “plans, without 
cost, to all southern states for both colored and white schools ...  this service has 
been given since 1920 and has stimulated wholesome developments in education for 
both groups.” 
Built in 1922, and dedicated in the spring of 1923, the Tankersley Rosenwald 
School is one of two surviving Rosenwald projects in Montgomery County, 
Alabama (Fig. 2). Rosenwald Schools were pioneered in Alabama, and the state 
once housed 389; 14 were in the capital county of Montgomery (Ransom, 2021).

416 D. S. Willkens et al.
The Tankersley project cost $5300, with $1500 from the local African American 
community, $2800 from public educational funds, and $1000 from the Rosenwald 
School Building Fund. The site now consists of 3.15 acres but was once part 
of a 15-acre complex: school, playground, two water pumps, two privies, a 
basketball court, baseball diamond, pecan grove, demonstration garden, and timber 
forest (Tankersley Rosenwald School, 2008). This was a spacious arrangement 
considering the Rosenwald Building Fund required only a 2-acre site (Hoffschwelle, 
2012). The school was active until 1967 and was purchased by the current owners, 
the Montgomery County Farmer’s Service and Welfare Association, in 1994. 
Much like the original building initiative, the current effort to save the Tanker-
sley Rosenwald School through documentation, preservation, and rehabilitation is 
collaborative. The interdisciplinary project team consists of practiced professionals 
and educators, with expertise in architecture, architectural history, construction 
technology, historic preservation and adaptive reuse, public history, and reality 
capture (RC): (alphabetical order) Gorham Bird, Richard Burt, Elijah Gaddis, 
Keith Hébert, Junshan Liu, Hunter McGonagall, and Danielle Willkens. Additional, 
critical support comes from Auburn School of Architecture students as well as 
Georgia Tech PhD candidate in architecture, Botao Li. The authors led the digital 
documentation, supporting the essential stabilization and weatherization for the 
structure, exploring preservation planning and adaptive reuse strategies alongside 
alumni and community members, and completing a Historic Structures Report 
(HSR). 
Using LiDAR, aerial and terrestrial photogrammetry as well as immersive 360 ◦ 
photography in iterative captures, the Tankersley Rosenwald School project aims 
to fully document and study the structure from the lenses of historic educational 
architecture, African American heritage, and environmental performance, as well 
as heritage building information modeling (HBIM) and predictive modeling to 
advance conservation and adaptive reuse efforts at a site plagued with intense heat 
and abundant humidity. As interpretive immersion technologies advance through 
digital archives, collections, and databases, so do options for layered, interactive 
models that can advance the potential of HBIM. These tools can augment the 
study the past and assist in the design of sensitive adaptations that ensure the 
viability and integrity of historic structures, especially in systemically underserved 
communities and regions. Furthermore, this study provides an in-depth analysis 
of a disappearing building typology in the rural South of the United States: 
the Rosenwald School. Incorporating innovative interpretative methodologies for 
documentation and public outreach, this chapter will explore methods for capturing 
and aligning data between ﬁeld work, design analysis, and the rich Rosenwald 
archive in the Library of Congress. In the last 2 years, the site has transformed from 
abandoned and structurally compromised to a building that has been secured and 
stabilized, poised for restoration and adaptive use to be reinstated as a community 
resource (Fig. 3).

Modeling and Monitoring the Rosenwald Ideal: Digital Documentation... 417
Fig. 3 View from a drone of the protective blue roof now installed on the Tankersley Rosenwald 
School, September 2023. Willkens photograph 
2 Rosenwald Schools as Practical Innovation 
In the 1910s, literacy and school enrollment rates for African Americans in southern, 
rural areas were comparable to those of a third-world nation (Bond, 1936; Aaronson 
& Mazumder, 2011). Building on a successful record of soliciting funding from 
white industrialists for Tuskegee Institute since 1884, Booker T. Washington (1856– 
1915) broadened his attentions to other educational endeavors to cultivate younger 
students and establish a vast cohort for his instructional ambitions. The ﬁrst schools, 
sponsored by Henry H. Rogers (1840–1909) of Standard Oil between 1904 and 
1909, were built for $700 a structure and intended to bridge the institutional gap for 
students in rural communities (Mansell & Binkley, 1997). After Rogers’s death, 
Washington sought the support of Julius Rosenwald (1862–1932). The son of a 
German Jewish immigrant, Rosenwald was an early investor in the mail-order 
company of Richard Sears. After meeting Washington at a philanthropic event for 
Tuskegee in Chicago in 1911, Rosenwald became interested in using his newfound 
wealth from the rapid expansion of the Sears, Roebuck and Co. to fund rural schools 
in the south through a cooperative investment initiative. 
The overall designs and ethos of the Rosenwald Schools extolled practicality 
through efﬁciency and innovation. The schools used passive design strategies to 
keep them comfortable in the hot and humid southern climates, and they were 
intended to be demonstration tools for agricultural and industrial operations, as well 
as proper hygiene and sanitation practices. Instead of retroﬁtting older structures 
and salvaging materials or furniture, the program necessitated the construction of 
new, purpose-built schools with an elevated architectural character and features

418 D. S. Willkens et al.
catered to enhancing student learning while simultaneously providing necessary 
space for communities to gather, learn, and coordinate efforts in self-determination 
and advancement. 
2.1 Alabama Foundations 
The ﬁrst six Rosenwald Schools were in Alabama, fast expanding to Georgia 
and Tennessee. Between 1913 and 1915, the initiative built 80 schools and at 
the time of Washington’s death on November 14, 1915, there were another 12 
under construction. Recognizing a sizable gap in resources and the accessibility 
of information, Tuskegee’s sponsored literature was comprehensive, providing 
information on site selection, building materials, shop drawings for furnishings, 
landscape and planting plans, equipment lists, and fundraising ideas that ranged 
from basket suppers to concerts, evening socials, and special rally days (The Negro 
Rural School and Its Relation to the Community, 1915). The speciﬁcity of the 
content ensured not only transparent budgets but also the expectations for the 
operations and arrangements of the schools. 
As identiﬁed by the Alabama Historical Council, Rosenwald schools in the state 
fall into three categories:
 Subtype 1: school buildings constructed by various communities under the 
supervision of Tuskegee Institute but not according to standardized plans or 
speciﬁcations;
 Subtype 2: school buildings constructed from 1915 to 1920 under the supervision 
of Tuskegee Institute according to plans and speciﬁcations of R.R. Taylor, 
Director of Mechanical Industries, and W.A. Hazel, Division of Architecture, 
Tuskegee Institute;
 Subtype 3: schools which were built from 1920 to 1937 under the supervision 
of the Rosenwald Southern Ofﬁce in Nashville according to designs and the 
speciﬁcations prepared by Samuel L. Smith (Mansell & Binkley, 1997). 
In 1995, the Cahaba Trace Commission received a grant from the Alabama 
Historical Commission to assemble a National Register Multiple Property Nom-
ination Form (MPDF) for Alabama’s Rosenwald School Building Fund Program 
and Associated Buildings, 1913–1937. This nomination was listed in the National 
Register on October 10, 1997, and formed the basis for the individual nomination 
for the Tankersley Rosenwald School, one of the few remaining sites in the state. 
Building momentum from this team’s documentation project and the overall grow-
ing visibility of Rosenwald School advocacy, the Alabama Historical Commission 
received an Underrepresented Communities Grant from the National Park Service 
in April 2022, for a Multiple Property Documentation Form (MPDF) for historic 
African American schools. This work will span from fall 2022 to summer 2024.

Modeling and Monitoring the Rosenwald Ideal: Digital Documentation... 419
2.2 T ankersley Rosenwald School Site History 
Located in Hope Hull, Alabama, in Montgomery County, the Tankersley Rosenwald 
School is a plan no. 20, subtype #3, adapted for three teachers. In addition 
to its relatively good integrity, the Tankersley Rosenwald School represents a 
unique condition within the Rosenwald typology since the community had already 
established, through grassroots leadership and the Negro Community Trustees 
Board, a school within the Pythian Masonic Hall in 1917 (Mustafa, 2001; Tankersley 
Rosenwald School, 2008). Due to austerity measures from the Great War, there had 
been a temporary moratorium on constructing new schools. However, in the early 
1920s, the community recognized the opportunity for a purpose-built school to meet 
growing needs. The community purchased ﬁve acres from Dr. William Tankersley 
(1874–1955) and then bought ten more from an adjacent site to construct the two-
teacher school for grades 1–6. 
Like many Rosenwald Schools, the site was named after a local champion: in this 
case, a white educator-turned-doctor who supported the educational initiative. Born 
in Montgomery County, Tankersley taught in the region between 1895 and the early 
1900s before returning to college for his medical degree from Transylvania Medical 
School (now the University of Kentucky), and he practiced in the Montgomery area 
until the early 1950s. 
The Tankersley Rosenwald School operated from 1923 until 1967. It was placed 
on the Alabama Register of Landmarks and Heritage in 2001, and the Tankersley 
Rosenwald School retains its integrity through many of the original design features, 
including its east-west orientation, its original room arrangement with the partition 
of paneled doors, its banks of tall windows (some windows have been removed 
for protection) and even its blackboards. Its exterior still displays its simpliﬁed 
Bungalow/Craftsman design elements through weatherboard siding, paneled doors, 
angular timber support brackets, and its wide, overhanging eaves with exposed rafter 
ends. The building’s standing sheet metal (tin) roof was replaced with an asphalt 
shingle roof in 1997. The foundation was stabilized, and the building’s exterior was 
painted white, replacing the original gray color in 2007. 
Since then, signiﬁcant water intrusion has impacted the structural integrity of 
the building. Following its nomination to the National Register of Historic Places 
in 2008, the Tankersley Rosenwald School has undergone signiﬁcant alteration due 
primarily to storm damage and lack of funding for repairs and restoration. Pho-
tographs from the original nomination forms reveal that the building lost the shed 
roofs above the entry doors, along with their supporting timber brackets. The most 
immediate threat to the building’s survival and architectural and structural integrity 
is the signiﬁcant collapse of the roof, rafters, and ﬂoor in one of the building’s 
classrooms. This breach of the roof happened several years ago, according to its 
owners. 
In 2010, the site received $40,000 from the National Trust for Historic Preserva-
tion and Lowe’s Charitable and Educational Foundation to restore the building and 
rehabilitate the site into a community center. Although expected to reach completion

420 D. S. Willkens et al.
in 2011, the site remained in stasis for another decade. Consequently, in 2021, 
the site was nominated and accepted into the Alabama Historical Commission’s 
Places in Peril due to neglected and deferred maintenance. Although granted a 
Lowe’s Charitable and Educational Fund Grant of $40,000 in 2008, administered 
through the National Trust for Historic Preservation, the building continued to fall 
into disrepair, and as the integrity of the foundation and roof continued to decline, 
the damage to the interior of the building and threat of collapse rapidly increased 
in the last few years. The Tankersley Rosenwald School is representative of a 
broader category of places in peril in Alabama. Montgomery County alone has 
lost over 85% of its original Rosenwald Schools. The research team believes the 
recent designation of the Tankersley School as among Alabama’s Place in Peril is a 
welcome recognition of the community’s valuation, and a spur to greater protection 
and funding for schools like Tankersley. This school, while maintaining much of its 
integrity, is in peril of rapid structural deterioration. 
In 2022, Auburn University, with Georgia Institute of Technology’s School 
of Architecture, partnered with the site owners for a successful application for 
$500,000 from the National Park Service’s African American Civil Rights Grant 
program for the “Tankersley Rosenwald School: Stabilization and Exterior Reha-
bilitation” project (P22AP01992-00). The funds are supporting the protection of 
original building fabric and materials during the construction of Phase 1, including 
the existing clapboard siding, interior beadboard wall paneling, original pine 
ﬂooring, and the original trim and millwork. Due to the structural deterioration of 
the roof, the original wooden-paneled ceiling has partially collapsed. To address 
the structural issues, some original structural framing members will require repairs 
and bracing. This project intends to halt the decay of the building by addressing 
the water intrusion so that future phases of work can prioritize interior restoration 
and rehabilitation. Within many preservation projects, this process is known as 
“mothballing” to prevent further damage as project partners secure future funding. 
2.3 Rosenwald Plan Types 
Despite the organization and depth of the construction and guidance materials 
available in the 1910s, the Rosenwald program soon proved too burdensome for 
Tuskegee Institute to operate independently, even with support from the state’s 
General Education Board. Without construction supervision, some schools cut 
corners, and others were built on sites that were either undesirable or too remote. 
Some structures were built with such poor materials and construction craft that 
they had to be reconstructed. Noted issues included poor foundations, inadequate 
window sashes or windowpanes, cheap hardware, insufﬁcient plastering, thin 
weatherboarding, and defective ﬂoors and roofs. Above all else, many of the 
structures were plagued with poor maintenance. 
The increase in construction efﬁciency in the 1920s was largely due to a 
reorganization of the Rosenwald Fund following the 1919–1920 audit by Fletcher

Modeling and Monitoring the Rosenwald Ideal: Digital Documentation... 421
Dresslar (1858–1930). Although the National Park Service’s resources on Rosen-
wald Schools call Dresslar an architect, he did not complete a degree in the 
ﬁeld or apprentice with an architect. He did, however, closely study schoolhouse 
design, particularly in rural areas, through his work in education and hygiene. 
Dresslar’s student and protégé, S.L. Smith, was also transformative in shaping the 
Rosenwald School initiative, even though he lacked formal architectural training. 
Given Washington’s interests in self-reliance and initial guidance from leading 
African American architect Taylor, it is interesting that the Rosenwald program 
eventually came within the purview of two white educators who were not from 
the south. Dresslar and Smith did, however, consult with architects such as Walter 
R. McCornack (1877–1961) for their revised and updated edition of Community 
School Plans (1931). Nonetheless, the architects of the Rosenwald initiative shared 
educational ties: Taylor was the ﬁrst African American architecture student at the 
Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) and McCornack later served as the 
dean of the School of Architecture and Regional and City Planning at MIT from 
1939 to 1945. 
Like most Rosenwald Schools built after 1920, the Tankersley School is oriented 
east-west, with the main entry on the east side of the building and the classroom 
spaces on the west. As an adapted ﬂoor plan no. 20, subtype #3, the Tankersley 
School is largely symmetrical in plan. It has two classrooms with teachers along 
the northern sides of the classrooms (to the right side of the image in Fig. 4). 
The classrooms have a folding partition, allowing these spaces to be combined 
as needed. Each classroom has small, built-in storage areas for school supplies 
and cloakrooms. Although Smith discouraged the use of corridors to enhance 
the efﬁciency of interior plans, the Tankersley School transformed the vestibules 
ﬂanking the Industrial Room into connective corridors, mediating the exterior and 
points of entry to the various interior rooms (Fig. 5). The smaller rooms on the 
northeast and southeast corners of the building could be used as classrooms for 
smaller tutorials, accommodating students beyond grades 1–6 who occupied the 
school’s primary cohort. Still, other documents reference a kitchen and library. It is 
unlikely that these smaller rooms were used as a kitchen since there is no heating 
source, with the two brick chimneys serving the larger classrooms and Industrial 
Room (Mustafa, 2001). 
The classrooms of the Tankersley School followed the standard in 1920, with 
teaching spaces of 22-feet by 30-feet, allowing for 45 single desks in ﬁve rows with 
nine to each row (Community School Plans, 1931). The folding partitions separating 
the two large classrooms are still intact, as are two batteries (e.g., groupings) of 
ﬁve tall and narrow double-hung 9/9 windows, reaching directly beneath the eaves 
to prevent as much afternoon glare as possible. Located on the western side of 
the building, these followed guidance privileging right-handed students since the 
directional light would not cast shadows across their page as they wrote. Providing 
access to the forest on the western side of the site, the school altered the standard 
plan from batteries of six windows to ﬁve since there were two doors on the western 
façade leading directly to the exterior (Fig. 6). The stairs and shed roofs above these 
thresholds are now missing.

424 D. S. Willkens et al.
Teachers would stand at the north sides of the large classrooms, with the northern 
room in a more ideal conﬁguration since the blackboard would be directly behind 
the teacher and not at the back of the room. The northern and southern façades of the 
building have only two apertures on each side: one for the supplementary rooms and 
a square, louvered attic vent beneath the gable. The timber brackets supporting the 
gable ends are no longer installed, but are stored within the building for restoration 
or, as needed, to be used as models for in-kind reproductions. 
The foundations, ﬂoors, and roof of the building have been compromised due to 
deferred maintenance. Many of the original brick piers show displacement and need 
repointing. There is evidence of the use of Portland Cement in some of the piers, 
causing crumbling and some evidence of friability in the brickwork. Movement 
in the piers and water inﬁltration have impacted the tongue and grove ﬂoors, and 
the original metal roof was replaced with asphalt shingles. Storms and humidity 
caused roof damage, leading to weakened areas and full punctures in the envelope. 
Subsequently, water inﬁltration damaged the building’s structure and interior ﬂoors, 
necessitating temporary stabilization measured to prevent the collapse of the entire 
roof in the large span of the double classroom space. Original school guidance 
from 1915 speciﬁed singles with a creosote stain, and subsequent issues of the 
Community School Plans do not specify rooﬁng materials. The horizontal hatching 
on the drawings, however, indicates the use of shingles. Hence, it is possible that 
the original standing seam metal roof of the Tankersley Rosenwald School was 
an adaptation. There are plans to restore this appearance during the building’s 
rehabilitation. 
The interior of the Tankersley Rosenwald School is remarkably intact (Figs. 7, 8 
and 9). Blackboards, beadboard walls, and the ‘breeze windows’ survive. These are 
interior 6-pane transom windows with a center horizontal pivot. They allow light to 
pass through the interior rooms and, when open, air to passively ﬁlter through the 
spaces. The built-in storage cabinets retain their original partitions and hardware, 
and some hooks are still visible in the cloakrooms. In interior paint scheme also 
follows the Rosenwald guidance: color within the lower portions of the walls and 
trim to enhance the framing elements and the use of buff or white upper walls and 
ceilings to reﬂect light. Although now boarded for security, many of the original 
windows are retained in situ, and others have been stored within the building, 
awaiting restoration. Evidence of the original window shades is not present, and 
the original doors are in poor condition and will need to be reproduced. 
3 Documentation Methodologies 
Since 2021, the project team has been documenting the site to not only record 
the historic structure, named an Alabama Place in Peril that same year due to 
deferred maintenance and structural concerns, but also to produce and enact a

Fig. 8 The combined classrooms of the Tankersley Rosenwald School, looking north with 
temporary structural bracing to support the rafters. Willkens photograph, February 2023

Fig. 9 Interior photographs of the Tankersley Rosenwald School: The storage area of the northern 
classroom (left) and the folding partition separating the two classroom spaces (right), looking 
south. Willkens photographs, February 2023 
feasible preservation plan to ensure the long-term survival of the building. From 
their inception, Rosenwald Schools were formative community centers used for 
not only youth education but also celebratory events and performances, meeting 
spaces, and resources for lifelong learning through seminars and libraries that were 
open to surrounding community members. The goal is to restore this function of 
the Tankersley School, providing a place for meetings, local events, and critical 
civic and public health initiatives, such as voter registration and polling, as well as 
vaccination clinics. 
As part of the documentation and advocacy project for the site, the team has 
been conducting iterative ﬁeld work using both analog and digital surveys, archival 
research, and history harvesting through an ongoing oral history project led by 
Auburn Depart of History faculty and co-directors of the Public History Program, 
Drs. Gaddis and Hébert. 
Despite the number of Rosenwald Schools constructed, their corresponding 
archival record is thin due to the purposeful omission of school records for African 
American communities within white-run local boards and state Departments of 
Education (Hoffschwelle, 2006; Leggs, 2007). This is why the documentation and 
preservation of the building are critical to telling the story of Rosenwald Schools: 
these are living artifacts.

Modeling and Monitoring the Rosenwald Ideal: Digital Documentation... 427
3.1 Traditional Surveys and Archival Resources 
As an in-depth complement to the 2008 National Register listing, now with some 
outdated condition assessments, the Historic Singular Report (HSR) will further 
identify and describe the aesthetic and technical aspects of the building that deﬁne 
its character and the paths needed for future preservation, restoration, and possible 
rehabilitation. 
The major elements of the HSR include an executive summary of ﬁndings with a 
special focus on updates from the National Register listing, an expanded background 
history and architectural description of the building and site, and a digitized 
and collated project archive of collected historic and contemporary photographs, 
architectural drawings, and written descriptions. Many of the drawings include new 
materials about the site, reﬂective of ongoing research: a historic site plan that 
captures the area during the school’s major period of signiﬁcance, c. 1922–1967, 
and a set of as-built measured drawings following the Secretary of the Interior’s 
Standards and Guidelines for Architectural and Engineering Documentation, for 
submission to the Historic American Building’s survey. Currently, the HABS 
records at the Library of Congress contain only one Rosenwald School (HABS 
KY-288 Cadentown Rosenwald School) with a measured drawing set, despite the 
number of schools constructed and the wealth of construction documentation for 
the educational initiative. 
As part of the preservation planning for the site, the HSR includes identi-
fying possible areas for archaeological studies, post-1967 interventions and an 
inventory of removed or deteriorated building fabric, and an updated condition 
assessment, with particular attention to structure, enclosure, and decoration. The 
report addresses major health and safety issues in the building, such as the 
identiﬁcation and treatment needed for hazardous material abatement (i.e., lead 
paint) and itemizing project needs and recommendations, with the categories of 
urgent, necessary, desirable, ongoing monitoring, and future needs. The HSR also 
includes preservation planning: exploring future uses, opportunities, and funding 
considerations. 
An HSR on the Tankersley School is essential to any forward movement at the 
site. However, this traditional reporting method also needs to be complemented 
with in-depth digital documentation to capture the current condition of the building, 
assess structural issues, build a comprehensive heritage Building Information Model 
(HBIM), and develop a historically and environmentally responsive design strategy 
for the rehabilitation of the site. 
3.2 Digital Documentation 
Reality Capture techniques, such as Terrestrial Laser Scanning (TLS), photogram-
metry, and Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UA Vs), have been used to create accurate

428 D. S. Willkens et al.
and detailed representations of heritage sites (Carvajal-Ramirez et al., 2019; 
Martinez-Carricondo et al., 2020; Youn et al., 2021). These methods enable 
the generation of high-resolution data, which is crucial for understanding the 
current condition of historic buildings and informing preservation efforts (Adami 
et al., 2018). Heritage Building Information Modeling (HBIM) is an extension of 
Building Information Modeling (BIM) that has been speciﬁcally developed for the 
documentation and management of historic structures (Liu et al., 2023). HBIM 
integrates geometric, spatial, and semantic information into a single digital model, 
providing a comprehensive and accessible platform for the analysis, management, 
and preservation of heritage sites (Bagnolo et al., 2022). Various studies have 
demonstrated the potential of these technologies in different contexts. 
Recent developments in digital technology introduced new tools for capturing 
and documenting cultural heritage sites, such as Matterport technology (Matterport, 
2022). This innovative approach creates immersive virtual tours, capturing high-
resolution imagery and spatial data of heritage buildings (Woodward & Heesom, 
2021; Liu et al., 2022, 2023; Liu & Willkens, 2021). The use of Matterport technol-
ogy in combination with other RC techniques and HBIM has not been extensively 
explored, presenting an opportunity for further investigation and innovation in 
heritage documentation. 
To document the Tankersley School, the project team utilized TLS, aerial pho-
togrammetry, and immersive 360◦ photography. A FARO Focus S-350 scanner was 
used to capture high-resolution TLS scans of the interior, exterior, and crawlspace 
of the Tankersley Rosenwald School. The TLS scanning took approximately 6 h 
to capture 51 scans. Scanning was performed using a medium resolution setting 
(12 million–28 million points captured by each scan) with a ﬁeld view of 360 ◦ 
horizontally and 270 ◦ vertically. Panoramic photographs were also captured to 
colorize the points. Each scan lasted about 8 min on average, including setting up 
the scan station, scanning, and capturing panoramic photographs. Field notes were 
taken to track scan locations for post-processing. The TLS survey provided detailed, 
accurate, and comprehensive point cloud data, which formed the basis for the HBIM 
model (Murphy et al., 2013). This data captured the architectural and structural 
features of the building, including walls, windows, doors, and roof structure, as 
well as the building’s relationship to its surrounding context. A Matterport Pro2 3D 
camera was utilized to create immersive virtual tours of the Tankersley Rosenwald 
School. This process was completed in approximately an hour with 39 total setups. 
This method allowed for the efﬁcient capturing of high-resolution imagery and 
the creation of a detailed, navigable 3D environment. The virtual tour served as 
a valuable resource for documenting the existing conditions of the school and 
informing the development of the HBIM model (Fig. 10). The iterative aerial 
photogrammetry methods will be outlined in a subsequent section. 
The captured data from the various RC techniques were processed using 
specialized software programs. Agisoft Metashape was employed for processing 
aerial and terrestrial photogrammetry data, while FARO SCENE software was 
utilized for processing TLS data. The 51 TLS scans captured a total of over

Modeling and Monitoring the Rosenwald Ideal: Digital Documentation... 429
Fig. 10 Matterport virtual tour of the Rosenwald School, allowing iterative inspection and 
analysis within compromised portions of the building, such as the trusses that need sistering in 
the main classroom space 
840 million points. The mean registration error is less than 1/6 of an inch (3.9 mm), 
which is sufﬁcient for HBIM development in this case (Barrile & Fotia, 2022). 
The immersive virtual tour captured by Matterport provided an additional source 
of high-resolution imagery, enhancing the accuracy and detail of RC data of the 
building. By incorporating the Matterport data with TLS and photogrammetry data, 
a comprehensive and detailed representation of the Tankersley Rosenwald School 
was achieved (Fig. 11). 
Using Autodesk Revit, the team developed an HBIM model based that incorpo-
rated the captured RC datasets with geometric, spatial, and semantic information 
(Fig. 12). This provided a comprehensive representation of the building and its 
features. The TLS and photogrammetric (both aerial and terrestrial) point clouds 
serve as the primary data source for developing the Revit HBIM model. At the same 
time, the immersive virtual tour captured by Matterport technology provides highly 
detailed imagery, enabling the precise identiﬁcation and visualization of building 
components. This combination of data sources facilitates the creation of a detailed 
and accurate HBIM model. This is essential to a remote and compromised structure, 
such as the Tankersley School, since it is not possible to visit the site on a regular 
basis and repetitive, contact invasive inspections can be destructive. The user-
friendly visualization interface provided by the Matterport virtual tour also allows 
the team to work alongside stakeholders. This enhanced visualization improves 
communication, ensuring that everyone involved in the project clearly understands 
the building’s current state and preservation requirements. Furthermore, the immer-
sive virtual tour has the potential to be integrated into the HBIM model as a visual

430 D. S. Willkens et al.
Fig. 11 TLS imagery of the Rosenwald School 
reference, complementing the point cloud data. This integration streamlines the 
model validation process and offers a comprehensive understanding of the site. As 
a result, the HBIM model becomes a more powerful tool for conservation planning, 
structural analysis, and stakeholder engagement. 
4 Iterative Site Studies 
Although there can be a prescriptive workﬂow, there is no “routine” reality capture 
since there are myriad, unexpected conditions. For example, there can be physical 
challenges to a site and changes in weather, vegetation, or lighting conditions 
that can dramatically impact digital documentation. This also means that the more 
times a researcher or team undertakes digital documentation, the nimbler they can 
be navigating challenges and learning curves. Although the environmental issues 
impacting digital documentation could be perceived as detrimental, the transient 
conditions associated with reality capture can constructively add a 4D aspect to site 
documentation that is otherwise difﬁcult to record in analog surveys: the passage 
of time. Digital documentation can offer researchers the opportunity for iterative 
digital documentation to productively monitor elements, such as environmental 
conditions, rain inﬁltration, structural movement, and rates of change or decay 
within building assemblies. Such studies underscore the didactic, computational, 
and visualization possibilities associated with using reality capture in architectural 
history and historic preservation.

4.1 Predictive Deterioration Modeling 
For the study of the Tankersley Rosenwald School’s roof, the team used four 
datasets of aerial images, captured in April 2021, December 2022, February 2023, 
and September 2023. These sets were captured with a DJI Mavic Pro 2 and Mavic 
3 Enterprise to monitor roof damage and track deterioration. However, it is not 
sufﬁcient to simply extract quantitative results from images only since the 2D 
images can be distorted by the camera angle, camera height, shadows, and stability 
of drone, which can impact human labor judgment. Furthermore, the 2D images 
do not contain measurement information. Therefore, 2D aerial image datasets were 
processed by photogrammetric techniques to reconstruct 3D point cloud models of 
the building and extract the resulting quantitative analysis. 
For this project, the CloudCompare technique was utilized to assist point cloud 
model analysis and extract quantitative roof damage results (Fig. 13). The general 
workﬂow of CloudCompare consists of data collection, photogrammetry process-
ing, targeted element segmentation (e.g., manually isolating elements and cleaning 
noise), the alignment of two-point clouds, and calculating differences. After aligning 
two targeted point clouds through root-mean-square deviation (RMSD), the algo-

432 D. S. Willkens et al.
Fig. 13 CloudComapre image of the Tankersley roof, highlighting differences between May 2022 
and February 2023 
rithm can calculate the cloud-to-cloud distance of analogous points, reﬂecting any 
geometric differences between the two point clouds. It is worth noting that both 
planned and manual ﬂight patterns were used for the image captures, and the ﬂights 
were executed by different members of the research team, all FAA Certiﬁed Remote 
Pilots. Despite their experience, some portions of the point clouds are incomplete 
within the datasets due to different weather conditions and the changing nature of 
surrounding trees. Furthermore, as of September 2023, the roof is protected by a 
blue tarp, preventing water inﬁltration and preparing the area for anticipated repairs. 
Since this tarp distorts the aerial photogrammetry data, the dataset collected from 
September 2023 was not used for cloud analysis. 
Although the CloudCompare could be affected by incomplete data and surround-
ing trees, the results still demonstrate high-quality proof of geometric deformation, 
and the imagery between May and December 2022 accurately predict the collapse 
and deﬂection of elements in the northwest corner of the roof as reﬂected in the 
February 2023 capture. 
The predictive model interprets deterioration progress from an environmental 
perspective, such as weather and surrounding plants. Since the building was 
abandoned for a period, the roof damage was caused by a lack of maintenance and 
natural forces. Natural forces can be divided into catastrophic events and subtle 
factors. Catastrophic events, such as earthquakes and ﬂoods, can cause immediate 
damage, which usually has a huge impact. Subtle factors include typical rainfall 
and wind. These usually have minor impacts, but the effects can accumulate after 
repeated instances on the building, especially when maintenance is mismanaged 
or delayed. From a geological perspective, there are no detected catastrophic 
events near the site; therefore, the deterioration can be explained from a long-term, 
repetitive actions.

Modeling and Monitoring the Rosenwald Ideal: Digital Documentation... 433
The incentive for a predictive model stems from the question, “Why does the 
damaged roof only exist at the northwest corner when the building is made of all 
the same materials and has not had major interventions?” A successful predictive 
model can predict future deterioration, and inform timely preservation and assist in 
a comprehensive assessment of the relationship of built heritage to its surrounding 
features. 
The gabled roof is made of plywood panels covered by building paper and asphalt 
shingles, supported by wooden rafters and beams. Originally, the structure would 
have been tar-covered boards covered by a tin roof. To investigate water penetration 
in the current roof conﬁguration, the emphasis focuses on rainwater, humidity, wind 
speed, and shadow study to elaborate damage progress. For this site, the surrounding 
landscape is also key (Figs. 14, 15 and 16). 
The western side of the building consists of evergreen trees, whereas the planting 
plans for the southern and eastern sides are deciduous. Therefore, the shadows of 
the surrounding trees have a different impact on the roof, depending on the time 
and season. The point clouds processed by drone photogrammetry captured the 
surrounding trees at different times of the year. Within the Revit HBIM, the trees 
were adjusted by location, size, and height to execute a shadow analysis. For this 
shadow study, deciduous trees were removed during the winter season since the 
branches only cause limited shadows (Fig. 17). 
Fig. 14 Local weather data for the Tankersley site emphasizes the high humidity

434 D. S. Willkens et al.
Fig. 15 Of note were signiﬁcant rain events in August 2022, causing a signiﬁcant collapse on the 
northwest portion of the roof 
Fig. 16 Following the heavy rains, the site experienced the lowest wind speeds of the year. This, 
paired with the high humidity and shade from neighboring trees, meant that the roof did not have 
the opportunity to dry, and the wooden members absorbed water and then failed 
Certain essential dates were selected for shadow study, based on the principle 
of the Earth revolving around the sun: Summer Solstice (SS) with the highest sun 
in the sky and the longest day of the year, Winter Solstice (WS) with the lowest 
sun and the shortest day of the year, and Autumnal/Vernal Equinox (A/VE). The 
resulting shadow study highlighted that due to the plant type and orientation of the

Modeling and Monitoring the Rosenwald Ideal: Digital Documentation... 435
Fig. 17 A shadow study of the building, showing the location and impact of coniferous trees, 
casting shadows on the structure, especially the northwest corner, across all seasons

436 D. S. Willkens et al.
building by these natural elements, the northwest corner roof is in shadow more 
than any other parts of the building. Studying local weather patterns also informs 
the predictive model. Assessing the humidity, wind, and rainfall information for 
Montgomery, Alabama, the summer is the most humid season with the least wind. 
Therefore, moisture can be easily trapped in the northwest corner roof with little 
opportunity to dry within the shaded conditions. The winter season has the most 
rainwater but the lowest temperatures, making penetrating rainwater hard to dry. 
From an environmental perspective, the shadow studies, rainfall, humidity, and 
wind information all veriﬁed that the northwest corner was more likely to suffer 
from deterioration and damage. This kind of analysis can inform future maintenance 
works, and possibly the need for tree removal within the historic footprint of the site 
to ensure the structure’s longevity. Based on this model, the northwest corner should 
become a focal area for regular maintenance and inspection to avoid penetrating 
dampness that reduces material durability and structural stability. As a non-contact 
invasive method captured with several short visits to the site, this procedure for data 
capture to construct predictive models should also be used at other heritage sites to 
anticipate challenges and proactively initiate preservation work. 
4.2 Sustainable Rehabilitations for Passive Reinvention 
As noted in the National Trust’s guidance for Rosenwald Schools, these structures 
are not well suited as museums. From their inception, they were designed and built 
with programmatic and spatial ﬂexibility: rooms could change shape and size based 
on the needed use, and the form of education delivery (e.g., lecture or Socratic 
method) could easily switch to a performance space or one for hands-on learning 
and fabrication. In today’s educational pedagogy, Rosenwald Schools are exemplars 
of experiential education. These buildings were designed with passive strategies 
in mind, not as ‘green’ models but as efﬁcient structures making the most of the 
available resources. The buildings carefully considered ventilation, brightness, and 
glare within the student experience, as well as heat dispersion. 
5 Conclusions 
The Tankersley Rosenwald School is a rare survivor within an ambitious building 
program and educational initiative that shaped the South and generations of 
students. Yet, these schools have only recently received the preservation attention 
and some of the funding needed to ensure their endurance. If Rosenwald Schools 
exist only in books and community bulletins, the United States has lost a signiﬁcant 
build record of resilience in the face of segregation and systemic educational 
oppression. Therefore, the documentation, restoration, and rehabilitation plans for 
the Tankersley Rosenwald School aspire to be models for other locations, leveraging

Modeling and Monitoring the Rosenwald Ideal: Digital Documentation... 437
university-sponsored service-learning opportunities to expand physical and digital 
access to the site while reinstituting a community staple.

Immersive Art and Urban Heritage: 
An Interdisciplinary Study 
of Socio-Environmental Justice 
in Houston and Amsterdam 
Asma Mehan and Sina Mostafavi 
1 Introduction 
The intricate conﬂuence of urban studies, enriched by the interplay of immersive 
art and design, critical mapping, urban heritage, and socio-environmental justice, is 
more than a mere theoretical endeavor (Fraser & Howard, 2017). This symbiosis, 
as viewed through a multidimensional prism, offers invaluable insights into the 
historical evolution, persistent power dynamics, and aspirations of inclusivity within 
urban contexts (Mehan et al., 2023; Boodaghi et al. 2022; Mehan, 2020; Harvey, 
2013; Augé, 1995; Mitchell, 1996; Lefebvre, 1996). 
A pivotal element to this inquiry is the methodological approach harnessed. 
Eschewing traditional qualitative methods, the chapter adopts a mixed-method 
strategy, juxtaposing quantitative GIS-based spatial analyses with qualitative ethno-
graphic observations (Mehan, 2023a). This composite approach not only facilitates 
a nuanced understanding of spatial patterns but also the socio-cultural narratives that 
underpin them (Kruijer et al., 2024). Moreover, participatory workshops with local 
communities have been instituted, providing a grassroots perspective, and fostering 
a more democratic and inclusive approach to urban understanding. By integrating 
these varied methodologies, the research moves beyond mere spatial representation, 
enabling a richer, more holistic understanding of urban dynamics (Mehan 2024a, b).

440 A. Mehan and S. Mostafavi
At the heart of this discourse lies critical mapping, transcending simple car-
tography to encapsulate a multidimensional analysis, and reﬂection of urban 
ecosystems (Mehan & Mostafavi, 2023a; Bazazzadeh et al., 2021; Harvey, 2013). 
This approach, further buoyed by technological advancements in art and culture, 
as expounded by Rutten ( 2018), offers a dynamic tool for understanding and 
inﬂuencing urban transformations. 
The grounding of this study in the concrete urban terrains of Amsterdam and 
Houston adds tangible depth to the discourse (Manovich, 2016). These cities, each 
with its rich historical context and distinct socio-political context, serve as fertile 
grounds to underscore the transformative potential of immersive art and design 
(Mehan & Mostafavi, 2023b). This potential is further ampliﬁed by the exploration 
of the “embodied experience,” whereby immersive art becomes an active conduit, 
engendering a deeper emotive connection between the observer, space, and history 
(Schäfer & van Es, 2017; Milovanovic et al., 2017;B i r d , 2008). 
Central to this chapter is the meticulous deconstruction of the collaborative 
interdisciplinary project unveiled at the V enice Biennale 2023, led by authors. 
Beyond its innovative approach, the project is underscored by clear aims. Primarily, 
it seeks to unravel the socio-political complexities that give rise to urban commons, 
focusing on the nuances of liminal spaces (Mehan, 2022, 2015; Thomassen, 2009). 
Additionally, the project aspires to foster a more inclusive urban dialogue by 
leveraging the “phygital” nexus, bridging the tangible with the digital (Mostafavi 
& Mehan, 2023; DeMers, 2017). Marrying architectural humanities and robotics, 
the project aims to establish pioneering paradigms for co-designing urban spaces, 
navigating the delicate balance between public and private spheres (Mostafavi, 
2021; Williams et al., 2020). 
Woven into the broader narrative of this book—digital interventions in cultural 
heritage—the chapter offers an in-depth exploration of immersive art’s role within 
pulsating urban spaces (Foth et al., 2015). Bridging critical mapping and socio-
environmental justice, we delve deeper into urban heritage, painting a comprehen-
sive tableau of the challenges and possibilities inherent in the urban landscapes of 
North America and Europe. 
2 Immersive Art, Urban Heritage, and the Co-production 
of Liminal Spaces in Houston and Amsterdam 
Liminal spaces, with their transformative capacities, offer a tantalizing canvas 
within urban studies. They not only represent physical boundaries but also signify 
deep-rooted socio-cultural transitions and contests. Within the contemporary urban 
framework, these spaces emerge as sites of both tension and collaboration. They 
question established urban norms while also paving the way for innovative spatial 
interactions (Low, 2017).

Immersive Art and Urban Heritage: An Interdisciplinary Study of. . . 441
Understanding the co-production of such spaces in urban centers such as Houston 
and Amsterdam demand a more profound contemplation of their inherent dualities. 
Derived from the Latin word l ¯ımen, liminality primarily pertains to thresholds 
(Bachelard, 1994; Zimmerman, 2008). As Bigger ( 2009) highlights, Turner’s 
perspective elucidates the “In-Between” or “Inside-Out” nature of these transitional 
zones, often straddling multiple realms and resisting straightforward categorizations 
(Turner, 1969). 
Historically, liminal spaces have been pivotal in ritualistic contexts, symbolizing 
processes of transition, transformation, and reintegration (Douglas, 1966). Turner’s 
tripartite model, encompassing separation, the liminal phase, and re-assimilation, 
offers a comprehensive understanding of these dynamic spaces. The concept of 
“Communitas,” as described by Turner, resonates deeply within urban studies. Such 
collective experiences often transpire in urban liminal zones, transcending societal 
hierarchies and fostering unique communal bonds (Park, Burgess & McKenzie, 
1925; Turner & Turner, 1978). 
Contemporary urban environments, increasingly complex and multifaceted, 
witness the emergence and evolution of liminal spaces that intersect the physical 
and digital domains (Mehan, 2023b, c). As postulated by Horvath, Thomassen, 
and Wydra ( 2015), such spaces blur the dichotomies of public and private. Augé’s 
(1995) notion of non-places further deepens this discourse, spotlighting spaces 
bereft of anthropological meaning yet brimming with potential for socio-cultural 
exchanges. Echoing Lefebvre’s spatial triad, Shields ( 1999) accentuates the inter-
play of perceived, conceived, and lived spaces in urban settings. 
However, urban liminality isn’t merely an academic concept; it possesses deep 
political undertones. As Turner ( 1967) articulates, these spaces grapple with issues 
of power, belonging, and heritage. In an age where the decolonization of urban 
spaces is gathering momentum, liminal areas stand out as potential arenas for 
challenging and rewriting hegemonic narratives (Mehan, 2023d;R o y , 2016). 
Focusing on Houston and Amsterdam, this chapter intricately maps the co-
production of speciﬁc liminal spaces, positioning them against broader urban 
dynamics. Highlighting the resistance and potentiality of these sites, the chapter 
also probes into their role in negotiating power structures (Ratto & Boler, 2014; 
Massey, 2005). 
The research accentuates a harmonious fusion of technology and design, as 
portrayed in Fig. 1. Through the synthesis of volumetric 3D printing, spatial 
lattice structures, and a tetrahedron-based material system, the study unveils a 
transformative spatial conﬁguration (Mostafavi et al., 2023). With elements such 
as circular design, artisanal craftsmanship, robotics, and augmented reality at its 
core, the installation stands as a testament to the symbiotic relationship between 
immersive art and urban heritage. The intricate mesh of physical and digital 
dynamics, reminiscent of the liminal spaces, becomes palpable in this immersive 
framework (Castells, 2010; Carpo, 2017).

3 Interdisciplinary Collaboration in Urban Research: 
Immersive Art, Urban Heritage, and Socio-Environmental 
Justice in Houston and Amsterdam 
Central to the study of urban environments is their heritage—the architectural, 
cultural, and socio-historical legacies that shape a city’s identity. This project 
takes a pioneering leap by combining immersive art, urban heritage, and socio-
environmental justice to present a comprehensive narrative of urban spaces in both 
Houston and Amsterdam (Checker, 2005). Through interdisciplinary collaboration 
and pedagogical innovation, this research is a testament to the intricate intertwining 
of art, design, heritage, and justice in urban landscapes (Mehan, 2023e; Hudson-
Smith et al., 2009). Merging micro-scale materialization techniques with macro-
scale critical urban studies, it delves into the intricate narratives, heritage nuances, 
and socio-environmental imbalances inherent in urban spaces (Soja, 2010). This 
endeavor ﬂourishes through collaborations with thought students and faculty from 
Texas Tech University and a diverse array of global industry partners. 
Incorporating elements like computation-based design, immersive technologies, 
and socio-environmental justice frameworks, this project, in partnership with Texas 
Tech University and global industry contributors, illustrates the potential of an 
interdisciplinary approach (Mostafavi et al. 2024). Our methodological design 
pushes the boundaries of urban studies, diving deep into the historical, cultural, and 
socio-political nuances of both cities, while also projecting visions for sustainable, 
inclusive urban futures (Fig. 2).

Immersive Art and Urban Heritage: An Interdisciplinary Study of. . . 443
Fig. 2 Interdisciplinary collaboration illustrated in the implementation of the FabriCity XR 
Project in Amsterdam and Houston’s contexts. (Source: TTU HCOA Joint Graduate Studios 
(UCD+DFC) Led by Authors) 
3.1 Computation-Based Design and F abrication in the Context 
of Heritage 
Incorporating urban heritage, this immersive installation seamlessly blends digital 
design and fabrication techniques to reconstruct and represent historical architec-
tural forms and patterns (Kolarevic, 2003). The interplay between design compu-
tation and fabrication allows a beautiful transition from ancient urban blueprints to 
modern tangible reinterpretations (Mehan & Stuckemeyer, 2023a, b). The Digital 
Computation Fabrication studio channels this spirit, creating AR-assisted assembly 
systems based on heritage-inspired lattice networks (Mehan & Abdul Razak, 2022). 
This synergy enables a dynamic exploration of historical urban structures while also 
offering glimpses into potential future architectural directions.

444 A. Mehan and S. Mostafavi
3.2 Urban Heritage, Community, and Spatial Justice 
Heritage is more than just relics of the past; it’s a living testament to a city’s 
socio-cultural journey and its evolving relationship with its inhabitants (Lowenthal, 
1985). While Houston and Amsterdam each have distinct historical narratives, both 
cities echo themes of community interactions, spatial justice, and socio-political 
evolutions (Mehan & Casey, 2023; Heilbron, 2023). The importance of spatial 
justice and inclusivity becomes paramount when delving into these narratives (Soja, 
2010). By adopting an interdisciplinary pedagogical approach, this segment of the 
project emphasizes the importance of democratizing urban spaces, ensuring heritage 
isn’t a closed book but an open dialogue, resonating with both experts and the 
general populace. 
3.3 Extended Reality and Urban Heritage 
In an era characterized by rapid digital transformation, the FabriCity XR project is a 
prime example of how technology can complement traditional historical scholarship 
(Hudson-Smith et al., 2009). By leveraging XR technologies and gamiﬁcation, users 
are not mere spectators but active participants in the urban historical narrative. The 
role of AR in curating these experiences cannot be overstated; it enables a visceral 
connection with the past, rooting historical narratives in the present, and paving the 
way for a future where urban heritage is actively engaged with, rather than passively 
observed. The “phygital” approach stands as a bridge across time, fostering a deeper 
connection between citizens and their urban surroundings. 
Through its meticulous combination of various disciplines, this project exempli-
ﬁes the future of urban research. By weaving together immersive art, urban heritage, 
and socio-environmental justice narratives, it paints a holistic picture of Houston and 
Amsterdam. The interdisciplinary methodology champions a future where cities are 
not just understood in their physicality but are also deeply felt, engaged with, and 
reimagined through a conﬂuence of art, technology, and justice. 
4 Urban Heritage as a Catalyst for Socio-Environmental 
Justice in Houston and Amsterdam 
Amid the overwhelming cascade of modern urban development, urban heritage 
stands resolutely as an essential anchor, helping us navigate the past, understand 
the present, and shape the future (Tappert et al., 2024;V a r ı ¸ s Husar et al., 2023). 
In cities like Amsterdam and Houston, the vestiges of urban heritage, whether 
in tangible structures or intangible traditions, play a signiﬁcant role in addressing 
socio-environmental challenges.

Immersive Art and Urban Heritage: An Interdisciplinary Study of. . . 445
Amsterdam, often termed the “V enice of the North,” is emblematic of urban 
heritage preservation and evolution. The city’s historical fabric is palpable in its 
iconic waterways, the canal belt, which has even been recognized as a UNESCO 
World Heritage site. These winding canals, bordered by picturesque narrow houses 
with gabled facades, stand as enduring symbols of Amsterdam’s Golden Age, 
during which the city thrived as a major trade hub. As a testament to their cultural 
signiﬁcance, many of these houses have been converted into museums, galleries, 
and institutions that further reinforce Amsterdam’s commitment to safeguarding its 
urban heritage. 
These centuries-old structures aren’t merely architectural marvels; they narrate 
stories of Amsterdam’s dynamic socio-economic transformations. The histori-
cal city center, with its labyrinth of alleyways and courtyards, chronicles tales 
of merchants, artists, and immigrants who have, over centuries, contributed to 
Amsterdam’s cosmopolitan character. The city’s architectural heritage, from the 
Renaissance to Baroque and onward, captures epochs of prosperity, cultural efﬂo-
rescence, and periods of economic downturns and recoveries. 
The neighborhood of Bijlmermeer, a stark contrast to the traditional image 
of Amsterdam, is a testimony to the city’s post-war architectural experiments. 
Designed as a modernist utopia, the area’s high-rise apartment blocks were intended 
to address housing shortages. However, Bijlmermeer’s evolution took unexpected 
turns. As many Surinamese immigrants settled in the region, it became a melting pot 
of cultures. While often criticized for its urban planning shortcomings, Bijlmermeer 
encapsulates a critical phase of Amsterdam’s heritage: a time when the city grappled 
with rapid modernization and demographic shifts. This intersection of architectural 
vision and socio-cultural dynamics accentuates the pivotal role of urban heritage in 
shaping socio-environmental justice conversations (Nell & Rath, 2009). 
Markenplein, another emblematic zone, is not just a space surrounded by canals 
but is also imbued with profound historical narratives. Adjacent areas like the 
Jordaan or the Jewish Quarter echo with tales of resistance, especially during World 
War II. One cannot walk these cobblestoned streets without feeling the weight of 
Anne Frank’s diary, which chronicles a Jewish girl’s life in hiding during the Nazi 
occupation. Such poignant heritage sites, while reminding us of somber periods, 
also champion resilience, inclusivity, and the human spirit’s indomitable will. 
In essence, Amsterdam’s urban heritage is a tapestry woven with architectural 
wonders, socio-economic metamorphoses, immigrant stories, and poignant histori-
cal episodes. Through this lens, the city doesn’t just showcase its past but also offers 
invaluable lessons for shaping a more inclusive and equitable future (see Figs. 3 
and 4). 
Houston, on the other hand, is a quintessential example of twentieth-century 
American urban sprawl. While relatively younger than Amsterdam, it too has 
rich layers of history etched in its urban fabric. The city’s origins in the oil 
industry, juxtaposed with its rich tapestry of diverse communities, reﬂect a unique 
convergence of industrial heritage and multicultural narratives. For instance, the 
predominantly African American neighborhood of Fourth Ward is a testament to 
the city’s tumultuous racial history, giving voice to the challenges of redlining and

446 A. Mehan and S. Mostafavi
Fig. 3 Contextual and historical analyses of Buffalo Bayou and Galena Park neighborhoods 
in Houston from the social and environmental justice perspectives. (Source: TTU HCOA Joint 
Studios (UCD +DFC) Led by Authors) 
Fig. 4 Contextual and historical analyses of Bijlmermeer and Markenplein neighborhoods in 
Amsterdam from the social and environmental justice perspectives. (Source: TTU HCOA Joint 
Studios (UCD +DFC) Led by Authors) 
urban displacement. The Freedmen’s Town Historic District, with its brick streets 
and preserved homes, represents both the oppression faced by its inhabitants and 
their resilience in creating a community of signiﬁcance. Such sites don’t just speak 
of the past but of ongoing struggles for environmental justice and spatial equity, 
especially in the face of modern gentriﬁcation pressures (Shelton, 2017; Pellow, 
2000) (see Figs. 3 and 4). 
Two such neighborhoods, Buffalo Bayou and Galena Park, serve as microcosms 
that epitomize Houston’s urban tapestry. A contextual and historical analysis of 
these regions, focusing on social and environmental justice perspectives, uncovers 
layers of history that have shaped their present and inﬂuence their future. 
Buffalo Bayou, often regarded as the mother bayou of Houston, has been central 
to the city’s history since its inception. As a crucial waterway, it enabled commerce, 
transportation, and development, laying the foundation for Houston’s growth. Over 
time, the Bayou transformed from a pure trading route to a recreational and natural 
space, enhancing the city’s environmental and cultural vitality. 
However, a deeper historical analysis reveals a more nuanced narrative. Buffalo 
Bayou’s shores have witnessed disparities in urban development and access. While 
parts of the bayou boast of green spaces, public artworks, and recreational facilities,

Immersive Art and Urban Heritage: An Interdisciplinary Study of. . . 447
other stretches have been marginalized, bearing the brunt of industrial activities and 
environmental degradation. 
From a social justice perspective, the bayou’s history is a testament to evolving 
land use practices and their implications for marginalized communities. Periodic 
ﬂooding events, coupled with inconsistent urban planning, have disproportionately 
affected vulnerable populations along its banks, emphasizing the need for a balanced 
approach to preservation and development. Adjacent to Buffalo Bayou and the 
Houston Ship Channel lies Galena Park, an industrial enclave that offers a stark 
contrast in terms of heritage and environmental dynamics. Historically, Galena Park 
evolved as an industrial hub, with the establishment of reﬁneries, warehouses, and 
rail infrastructure. 
The city’s industrial heritage, while economically signiﬁcant, brought forth 
challenges from an environmental justice perspective. Residents, primarily from 
lower-income backgrounds, have long grappled with issues of air and water 
pollution emanating from nearby industries. The chronic exposure to pollutants 
and associated health risks underscores the region’s environmental justice concerns 
(Bullard & Wright, 1986). 
Moreover, the neighborhood’s socio-cultural fabric paints a picture of resilience 
amid adversity. Despite facing environmental challenges, the community has been 
active in advocacy and environmental activism, seeking accountability from indus-
tries and striving for a healthier living environment (Pulido, 2000). 
Galena Park stands as a poignant reminder of the complexities of urban heritage, 
where economic aspirations, environmental challenges, and the relentless spirit of 
communities converge. 
In examining Buffalo Bayou and Galena Park, we unravel the multifaceted 
heritage of Houston. These neighborhoods, while distinct in their historical trajec-
tories, underscore the city’s broader themes of environmental justice, socio-cultural 
evolution, and the interplay between heritage and urban planning. As we peer into 
their past, we’re compelled to reﬂect upon their future, championing strategies that 
honor their legacy while fostering inclusivity, sustainability, and resilience. 
Moreover, as both cities grapple with the challenges of climate change, their 
urban heritage offers valuable insights. Amsterdam’s intricate water management 
systems, born from its historic relationship with water, present sustainable urban 
solutions relevant today. Simultaneously, Houston’s historical wrestle with ﬂooding, 
especially in its bayou regions, exempliﬁes the socio-environmental repercussions 
of unchecked urbanization and the need for ecologically attuned urban planning 
(Bedient & Blackburn, 2007). 
Heritage, as represented in these cities, isn’t static. It is dynamic, evolving, and 
is a dialogue between the past, present, and future. Urban designers, planners, and 
policymakers can harness this rich heritage to create more equitable and sustainable 
urban futures. Engaging with these heritages also educates and empowers local 
communities, allowing them to reclaim their narratives, participate in decision-
making processes, and inﬂuence the trajectory of their cities. 
The multiscale approach employed in this research underscores the intricate 
layers of urban heritage. At a macro level, the overarching architectural styles,

448 A. Mehan and S. Mostafavi
Fig. 5 Macro maps of selected parcels in Houston and Amsterdam (Fig. 4) provide a 2D 
representation, while isometric exploded mapping illustrates the multi-layered analysis from 
social and environmental justice viewpoints in both cities. (Source: TTU HCOA Joint Studios 
(UCD+DFC) Led by Authors) 
city planning philosophies, and urban growth patterns reﬂect the broader societal 
values and priorities of epochs gone by (Marcuse, 2017). On a more micro scale, 
individual landmarks, public squares, and even street names become repositories of 
local histories, personal memories, and community identities (see Fig. 5). 
The incorporation of Augmented Reality (AR) in this research further ampliﬁes 
the prominence of urban heritage. By weaving together, the physicality of built 
environments with the ethereality of historical narratives, AR provides an immersive 
journey into urban heritage (Mostafavi et al., 2023). Users, while walking through 
the streets of Amsterdam or Houston, can transcend time, delving into historical 
events, cultural shifts, and architectural transitions. This fusion of the modern digital 
realm with the age-old tales of urban heritage fosters a more profound appreciation 
and understanding of cities and their socio-environmental trajectories (Bulkeley & 
Betsill, 2005)( s e eF i g . 6). 
In addressing socio-environmental justice, one cannot ignore the silent, yet 
powerful narratives embedded in the bricks, streets, and stories of a city. As 
demonstrated in Houston and Amsterdam, urban heritage is more than just a 
retrospective appreciation of a city’s past—it’s a catalyst, a roadmap, and a call to 
action for present and future urban challenges. In essence, this research reiterates 
the inextricable bond between urban heritage and socio-environmental justice. 
Urban heritage, far from being mere remnants of the past, emerges as an active 
participant in contemporary urban discourses (DeV erteuil, 2011; Harvey, 2009;

Immersive Art and Urban Heritage: An Interdisciplinary Study of. . . 449
Fig. 6 Snapshots of web-based extended reality interactive environment on smart devices. 
(Source: TTU HCOA Joint Studios (UCD +DFC) Led by Authors)

450 A. Mehan and S. Mostafavi
Schlosberg, 2013). As cities globally grapple with the dual challenges of preserving 
heritage and ensuring justice, the tales of Amsterdam and Houston offer valuable 
insights, lessons, and inspiration (Soja, 2010; Swyngedouw, 2004; Holiﬁeld et al., 
2018). It is within the folds of these tales that we ﬁnd hope, wisdom, and guidance 
for envisioning cities that are both historically reverent and forward-looking. 
5 Discussion and Implications 
The convergence of immersive art and design, critical mapping, urban heritage, and 
socio-environmental justice not only broadens the horizons of urban studies but also 
accentuates the intricate layers of urban fabric. This fusion reafﬁrms the thesis that, 
in the contemporary urban discourse, interdisciplinary collaboration is pivotal and 
foundational rather than just supplementary. 
The interactions among these domains necessitate a profound reevaluation of 
urban planning paradigms and public art policies. Traditional urban strategies, once 
ﬁrmly grounded in the realm of technical engineering and infrastructural modalities, 
now need to realign their compass to engage with the richness of art, emotional 
resonance, historical signiﬁcance, and the ﬂuctuating socio-political ethos. Such 
a paradigm shift echoes in the tapestries of cities, where immersive art, deeply 
interwoven with urban heritage, can actively disrupt the conventional passivity 
of urban narratives. This disruption, rooted in the real-world intricacies of urban 
landscapes, holds the potential to galvanize community engagement, fostering more 
grassroots, decentralized, and heritage-aware urban renewal efforts. 
Critical mapping, particularly as witnessed within the urban contours of Ams-
terdam and Houston, offers more than just cartographic insights. These critical 
mappings, when meticulously examined, serve as a canvas where tales of resilience, 
socio-political upheavals, inclusivity drives, and the intricate dance between public 
and private realms unfold (Kozlowski et al., 2020). Engaging with these stories 
offers a transformative lens through which cities can be imagined and reimagined— 
cities that are not merely structures but are pulsating, living entities that breathe their 
past while eyeing the future. 
The project presented at V enice Biennale 2023 embodies the dual-edged sword 
of technological integration within urban spaces. As technology molds urbanity, 
it brings forth an array of challenges. It’s imperative to acknowledge that while 
technology might democratize urban solutions, it can concurrently disenfranchise a 
segment devoid of technological literacy. This dichotomy extends to issues of digital 
privacy, equitable access to technology, and the dilemmas posed by digital heritage 
preservation. 
From a socio-political lens, the kaleidoscope of urban dynamics emphasizes a 
pressing need for policies that are deeply rooted in inclusivity. This sentiment, 
though vocalized often, clashes against the stark reality of contemporary urban gov-
ernance, which is frequently entrenched in bureaucratic labyrinths. Breaking free

Immersive Art and Urban Heritage: An Interdisciplinary Study of. . . 451
from these constraints requires an invigorated thrust towards blending innovative 
techniques with interdisciplinary insights. 
6 Concluding Remarks 
In the traverse of this chapter, a deliberate navigation between the realms of 
immersive art, urban heritage, and socio-environmental justice emerges, offering 
a panoramic view of the ever-evolving domain of urban studies. The urban matrices 
of Amsterdam and Houston, emblematic in their complexity, serve as potent 
illustrations of the pervasive nature of the themes discussed. These metropolises, 
acting as insightful microcosms, foreground the intricate interplays and challenges 
intrinsic to the broader canvas of urban heritage in a contemporary setting. 
The burgeoning digital epoch, exempliﬁed by pioneering endeavors like the 
V enice Biennale 2023 project, sketches an urban trajectory rife with both immense 
possibilities and inherent challenges. Cities, rather than being mere static constructs, 
are revealed as ﬂuid entities, perpetually evolving and recalibrating in the face of 
shifting socio-political, technological, and environmental paradigms. 
However, as the architectural fabric of our city inches closer to a profound digital 
transformation, the indispensability of meticulous evaluation becomes palpable. 
The oncoming digital tide sweeping across urban landscapes globally mandates 
strategies rooted in the trinity of ethical considerations, inclusivity paradigms, and 
sustainability frameworks. 
While Amsterdam and Houston provide insightful case studies, the extrapolation 
of ﬁndings to cities with distinct socio-cultural and political dynamics requires 
caution. The pace at which technology evolves might outstrip the recommendations 
and observations made within this chapter, necessitating periodic reassessments. 
Immersive art, by nature, is open to a spectrum of interpretations, and hence 
the derived implications might vary based on individual perceptions and cultural 
backgrounds. 
There is an urgent call for policymakers, urban planners, and artists to fos-
ter deeper interdisciplinary collaborations, ensuring that the synthesis of varied 
perspectives leads to more holistic urban solutions. Recognizing the potential of 
disenfranchisement, city administrations should proactively invest in community-
based technological training programs, ensuring equitable access and participation 
in the emerging digital urban narrative. Special emphasis should be placed on 
blending technological advancements with traditional conservation techniques to 
ensure that urban heritage sites retain their historical integrity while embracing 
the future. As digital tools become pervasive, developing ethical frameworks and 
guidelines will be paramount, ensuring that technological interventions respect 
privacy, cultural sensitivities, and local values. 
In summation, the intricate tapestry woven in this chapter underscores a pivotal 
assertion: the trajectory of urban studies, both contemporary and prospective, hinges 
upon an integrated melding of diverse disciplines, cutting-edge tools, and forward-

452 A. Mehan and S. Mostafavi
thinking methodologies. This interdisciplinary fusion stands as a luminary, guiding 
stakeholders through the labyrinthine challenges of urbanity, and illuminating 
potential routes towards a more harmonious, inclusive, and vibrant urban horizon. 
Thus, the chapter beckons scholars, policymakers, and practitioners to undertake 
a profound and critical immersion into the multi-hued narratives of urbanity, 
cultivating a foundation for a more just and effervescent urban future.
