Asma Mehan is a researcher, educator, and architect working at the intersection of architectural 
humanities and critical urban studies. She is currently an assistant professor at Texas Tech 
University College of Architecture, and the director of the Architectural Humanities and Urbanism 
Lab (AHU_Lab). She is the author of Tehran: From Sacred to Radical (2022) and Kuala Lumpur: 
Community, Infrastructure, and Urban Inclusivity (2020). She has authored over 50 articles and 
essays in scholarly books and professional journals in multiple languages, such as English, Persian, 
and Italian, on critical urban studies, architecture, urban planning, housing, and heritage studies.

456 A. Mehan and S. Mostafavi
Sina Mostafavi is a practicing architect, researcher, and educator with computational design and 
architectural robotics expertise. He is an associate professor at Texas Tech University College of 
Architecture, where he is the director of the Hi-DARS lab. Sina is the founder of the award-winning 
SETUP architecture studio. Mostafavi’s research focuses on innovative applications of emerging 
materials and technologies, empowered by hybrid human–machine intelligence, for integrated 
design, inclusive automation, and circular production. He holds a doctoral degree from TU Delft, 
where he has been a senior researcher and manager at the robotic building lab of Hyperbody 
Research Group at BK-City.

Digital Citizenship in the Interactive 
Dissemination and Perception of Cultural 
Heritage: The Museum Case 
Thomas Heskia, Ivana Scharf, and Verónica Donoso 
1 Introduction 
In the wake of digital media advancements, the discourse surrounding digitizing 
cultural heritage prompts a fundamental question: how will the digitized heritage be 
accessed by its audience—essentially its “heirs”—both today and in the future? The 
trajectory of digitalization is pivotal, for it can either lead to the monopolization of 
knowledge, surveillance, and the establishment of post-democratic and neoliberal 
structures, or it can foster a culture of commons and participation, supporting 
prosperity and the common good (Stalder, 2016; Lätzel, 2019). At the heart of this 
dilemma lies the key query: how do we ensure equitable access and foster a digital 
environment that promotes civic engagement and counters potential imbalances? 
The solution lies in the meticulous development of digital literacy, or, in a broader 
context, digital citizenship. 
Digital literacy (Gilster, 1997, Zhang, 2021, in the context of culture Stahl & 
Walter, 2019, p. 454) accentuates the social aspect of digitalization, spotlighting 
individuals’ capacity to navigate electronic channels and engage in meaningful 
interactions. Digital literacy relevant for museums, heritage sites, and the like 
encompasses a spectrum of competencies, which can—as exempliﬁed in the digital 
strategy of the Württembergisches Landesmuseum—be grouped as follows:

457

458 T. Heskia et al.
1. ICT Competence: Proﬁciency in handling current hardware and software. 
2. General Media Literacy: Critical analysis and creation of media content. 
3. Information Literacy: Skill in locating, evaluating, and effectively using infor-
mation. 
4. Communication and Collaborative Work: Proﬁciency in effective communication 
and teamwork. 
5. Establishment of a Clear Online Identity and Digital Reputation: Including strict 
adherence to all data protection guidelines.
These competencies have to be brought together to create the digital competent 
museum, that is, an entity that incorporates digital data, sources, and publications 
while generating new content to achieve its objectives (Landesmuseum Württem-
berg, 2022). 
Digitalization now involves transferring knowledge from the analog world into 
the stream of digital data. This process is already underway, evident in the increased 
digitization of cultural heritage or the creation of digital twins of whole museums. 
Within this environment, analog components as museum objects, archaeological 
artifacts, historical buildings, as well as contemporary premises do not merely fade 
away in the face of digitization; instead, they are reevaluated and typically even 
enhanced. Digital offerings, however sophisticated they are, will never replace the 
lived experience of visiting museums or heritage sites. 
Numerous initiatives are striving to standardize the structure of digital collections 
(Knaus, 2019), both in commercial and non-commercial sectors (e.g., museum 
digital1 ). With the rise of text-based and up-to-date AI systems, structural dif-
ferences in primary data are becoming less signiﬁcant; the crucial factor is that 
high-quality content is publicly accessible. In addition to digitizing their collections, 
museums also contribute other secondary data to the digital information stream. 
This includes publications, websites, digital documentation of analog exhibitions, 
or entirely digital exhibitions. Given this context, any digital strategy implemented 
by museums and heritage sites (Gries, 2019) is a learning process that now also 
interacts with the learning capabilities of AI systems. It represents a journey toward 
digital maturity (Finnis & Kennedy, 2020) and digital sovereignty (Floridi, 2020), 
which is evolutionary for museums and World Heritage sites and aims to evolve 
continuously. 
In conventional approaches to digital literacy in museums, the critical perspective 
is primarily taken from the content provider’s standpoint—in this case, researchers 
and curators rather than that of museum and heritage site audience. While the 
general focus has increasingly shifted toward visitor orientation, surprisingly little 
attention has been given to the question of how the audience decodes, absorbs, and 
processes cultural content in their broader life context. In essence, there is a desire 
for an open-minded, critical audience, yet relatively little has been done to address 
the processing within the broader societal context, a sphere that is less controllable
1 https://de.about.museum-digital.org (last accessed 30.09.2023). 

Digital Citizenship in the Interactive Dissemination and Perception. . . 459
by the museum. This tendency could stem from curators, researchers, and museum 
directors viewing themselves as holding interpretative authority. Being critical is 
regarded as an inherent part of the production process rather than a task for the 
audience. 
2 Citizenship in the Digital Realm 
However, it is becoming increasingly evident that sheer proﬁciency in navigating 
digital possibilities is not sufﬁcient, especially in a time when the digital landscape 
is inundated with misinformation, surveillance, abuse, and distorted echo chambers 
being a threat for democracy—neither from the producer’s nor the consumer’s side. 
We must particularly note that especially cultural and historical content—that is, 
the very core of what museum and heritage professionals engage with—is prone to 
distortion and misuse in political discourse, where it may be selectively manipulated 
for one-sided arguments. As digital dissemination of information is by no means 
neutral, it should be aligned with the shared values—in our context with the values 
of a democratic, liberal, tolerant, transparent, and social or simply “open” society 
(Popper, 2020). For this, we aim to introduce “digital citizenship” as a form of value-
based engagement with digital production, communication, and consumption into 
the museum discussion. It emphasizes not just proﬁciency in the use of digital tools 
but active participation, critical thinking, and ethical conduct in the digital sphere 
on both sides of the communication channel. 
“Citizenship” is already a complex and multifaceted concept, spanning legal, 
political, social, and cultural dimensions. At its core, it signiﬁes the status of 
being a member within a speciﬁc political community, entailing a balance of rights 
and responsibilities. Political scientist T.H. Marshall ( 1950) provided a seminal 
deﬁnition delineating social citizenship as a status encompassing civil, political, 
and social rights. Civil rights relate to individual freedom, political rights involve 
participation in political processes, and social rights encompass the entitlement to a 
baseline of economic welfare and security. Citizens, as the holders of these rights, 
are also accountable for their responsible utilization. Citizenship is essentially 
about the ability and willingness of individuals to contribute constructively and 
responsibly to the community (Cohen & Ghosh, 2019; Bellamy, 2008). 
In the digital age, the concept of citizenship extends to the realm of digital 
citizenship, where scholars leverage the broader understanding of citizenship to 
navigate the challenges and opportunities presented by technology (Ribble & Bailey, 
2007) characterize digital citizenship as the norms of appropriate, responsible 
behavior with regard to technology use. This underscores the signiﬁcance of ethical 
and responsible engagement with digital tools and platforms in our contemporary 
society. Overall, the concept of citizenship evolves with societal changes, and 
in the digital context, it involves understanding and navigating the rights and 
responsibilities associated with technology use in contemporary society.

460 T. Heskia et al.
Numerous efforts have been undertaken to gain a deeper and more precise 
understanding of the multitude of concepts related to digital technologies and 
the skills/competencies necessary for individuals to become adept and responsible 
users. Many of these terms have originated from various disciplines and emphasize 
different aspects, for instance, ICT literacy, information literacy, digital skills, or 
practical user training in the workplace. An important point to consider is that, 
in relation to the increasing digitization of society, a range of issues has become 
apparent, and societal problems have also manifested in the digital sphere. The 
Council of Europe addressed these developments in a comprehensive discussion 
back in 2017 (Council of Europe, 2017). This discussion revolved around the 
idea of citizens being reduced to consumers, a trend that was evident in reduced 
political engagement and growing mistrust in politics. Additionally, factors such 
as the dispersion of unifying cultural frameworks, individualization, migration, 
and the transfer of state power to international entities have contributed to these 
challenges (Council of Europe, 2017, p. 8). Since then, particularly during the 
Corona pandemic, phenomena such as increased misinformation and anti-science 
became part of the discussion. Even though, contrary to general perception, anti-
science sentiment has not increased (Wissenschaft im Dialog, 2020), it became 
evident that it has a destabilizing effect on society and has gained a signiﬁcant 
platform, particularly through digital channels. 
It was thus just natural to extend the idea of citizenship to the digital sphere and to 
formulate a distinct concept of digital citizenship. This concept must revolve around 
how the digital citizen can navigate the often-ambiguous aspects of technology, 
algorithms, artiﬁcial intelligence, participation, freedom of speech, and privacy. 
Power imbalances, inﬂuenced by wealth disparity and corporate control of online 
platforms, also affect digital citizenship, giving rise to worries about manipulation 
and surveillance (Council of Europe, 2017, p. 9; Carmi & Yates, 2021, Ciofﬁ et al., 
2022). It is imperative to tackle these imbalances to guarantee the robust evolution 
of digital citizenship. 
The Council of Europe arrived at the following comprehensive deﬁnition: 
Digital Citizenship refers to the ability to engage positively, critically, and com-
petently in the digital environment, drawing on the skills of effective communication 
and creation, to practice forms of social participation that are respectful of human 
rights and dignity through the responsible use of technology (Council of Europe, 
2017). 
This comprehensive deﬁnition encapsulates the essence of digital citizenship, 
emphasizing positive and critical engagement, competency, effective communica-
tion, and the responsible use of technology to safeguard human rights and dignity. 
It provides a framework for navigating the complexities of the digital age and 
underscores the crucial role of responsible digital citizenship in building a more 
inclusive and equitable digital society. 
Digital citizenship involves adept and positive engagement with digital technolo-
gies, encompassing a spectrum of activities, such as creating, working, sharing, 
socializing, investigating, playing, communicating, and learning. The citizenship 
aspect entails active and responsible participation in communities at various levels

Digital Citizenship in the Interactive Dissemination and Perception. . . 461
across political, economic, social, cultural, and intercultural dimensions. As empha-
sized by the Council of Europe, being a digital citizen necessitates lifelong learning 
in formal, informal, and non-formal settings, along with a continual defense of 
human dignity (Council of Europe, 2017). 
It is erroneous to assume that critical skills automatically develop with the 
availability of technical means. Hence, it is imperative to approach the concept of 
citizenship, comprehend its normative nature, and apply it in the digital realm. In 
the context of heritage and museums, this implies the ability to comprehensively 
interpret digitally prepared and enhanced cultural heritage and critically distinguish 
between documented reality, hypothetical reconstruction, historizing ﬁction, alter-
nate history, and new realities. Ultimately, it involves understanding the constantly 
expanding cultural heritage as a digital artifact. 
Digital citizenship is a comprehensive concept that involves not only cultivating 
critical skills but also fostering values and behaviors: Beyond digital literacy— 
our sole starting point—it requires critical thinking, creativity, communication, and 
collaboration to generate meaningful digital content using complex technological 
tools. Values play a pivotal role in shaping digital citizenship, promoting responsible 
and ethical actions, understanding rights and responsibilities, and considering legal 
aspects, such as intellectual property. Furthermore, digital citizens are mindful of 
security and privacy concerns, ensuring the safeguarding of personal information 
and online interactions. The behavioral aspect encompasses equal and open access, 
ensuring that virtual environments do not jeopardize physical, psychological, and 
social well-being. 
Drawing from the 20 Competencies of Democratic Culture (CDCs), the Council 
of Europe in a slightly different structure identiﬁes a total of 10 different domains of 
digital citizenship divided into 3 sections (Council of Europe, 2022, pp. 13–14).
 Section 1—Being online 
– Domain 1 Access and Inclusion focuses on combating digital exclusion, 
emphasizing skills for future citizens to participate in open digital spaces with 
inclusivity. 
– Domain 2 Learning and Creativity discusses citizens’ ongoing learning 
in digital environments, emphasizing creativity development for conﬁdent 
navigation in technology-rich societies. 
– Domain 3 Media and Information Literacy centers on interpreting digital 
media with critical thinking, highlighting the importance of education for 
meaningful community participation beyond technical skills.
 Section 2—Well-being online 
– Domain 4 Ethics and Empathy focuses on online ethical behavior and 
interaction, emphasizing skills like recognizing and understanding others’ 
feelings and perspectives, with empathy being crucial for positive online 
engagement. 
– Domain 5 Health and Well-being highlights the need for attitudes, skills, val-
ues, and knowledge beyond basic digital competence to navigate challenges

462 T. Heskia et al.
in both virtual and real spaces. In a digitally rich world, awareness of issues 
like online addiction, ergonomics, and excessive device use is vital for overall 
health and well-being. 
– Domain 6 e-Presence and Communications centers on developing personal 
and interpersonal qualities for positive online presence and interactions. It 
includes competences in online communication, managing data, and ensuring 
coherent and consistent online identity and interactions.
 Section 3—Rights online 
– Domain 7 Active Participation involves competences needed for citizens to 
responsibly navigate digital environments, making informed decisions while 
actively engaging in democratic cultures. 
– Domain 8 highlights the Rights and Responsibilities of digital citizens, 
including privacy, security, access, and freedom of expression. Emphasizes 
the need for ethical behavior and empathy to ensure a safe and responsible 
digital environment for all. 
– Domain 9 Privacy and Security encompasses personal protection of online 
information (privacy) and self-awareness of online actions (security). Involves 
competences such as information management, online safety measures, and 
using security tools to prevent potential risks. 
– Domain 10 Consumer Awareness recognizes the digital citizen as a consumer 
in online spaces. Emphasizes the need to understand the commercial reality 
of the digital world, particularly in social media and virtual social spaces, to 
maintain autonomy and make informed choices. 
This extensive enumeration already illustrates the various areas of life penetrated by 
the digital. It shows that responsible and respectful handling online not only impacts 
a positive digital life but also has effects on physical health and mental well-being 
in the analog world. 
3 Inquiring into Citizenship into the Realm of Museums 
and Heritage Sites: Methodological Approach 
Museums and heritage sites perceive themselves not only as the custodians of 
society’s cultural memory but also as signiﬁcant contributors to the ongoing scien-
tiﬁc and societal discourse. Through their curated knowledge, research initiatives, 
and intensive communication, they aim to make a valuable contribution to civil 
society, showcasing their relevance and ultimately reafﬁrming their existence as 
predominantly public institutions (Graf & Rodekamp, 2016; Simon, 2010). As 
previously noted, museums are expanding into the digital sphere. Consequently, 
they face the question of how to address the digital citizen and contribute to digital 
citizenship using their resources.

Digital Citizenship in the Interactive Dissemination and Perception. . . 463
As a method to delve deeper into this question, we chose the social science 
approach of a focus group, in which a small group of specialists and stakeholders 
bring forth various aspects in a moderated discussion that will be captured and 
evaluated afterward. The goal is to understand the participants’ system of relevance 
(Krueger & Casey, 2019). Using a call through the online platform museum hub, 
we assembled a group of ten participants intended to represent the social ﬁeld 
of German museums. This included six museum staff members engaged with 
digitization (including one director), one representative from academic museum 
research, one representative from a museum association, and one interested museum 
visitor. A representative from a commercial service provider supplying museums 
with digital services canceled at the last minute. The museum representatives came 
from four diverse German museum institutions, including one regional universal 
museum, one archeological museum, one immersive cultural history museum, and 
one exhibition space (“Kunsthalle”). The focus group took place on September 20, 
2022. The group was facilitated by Verónica Donoso assisted by Thomas Heskia. 
Ivana Scharf acted as an observer. During the three-hour session, participants delved 
into four key topics, guided by the previously outlined concept of digital citizenship. 
In this setting, the authors aimed to explore the potential of museums and 
heritage sites as spaces where digital citizenship can be nurtured and practiced. The 
discussion revolved around the following questions: 
1. Why is digital citizenship important for museums, heritage sites, and cultural 
organizations in general? 
2. How can museums ensure that they nurture and promote digital citizenship? 
3. How well are the participating institutions at boosting digital citizenship? 
4. What does it need to developing a digital citizenship strategy for a 
museum/heritage site/cultural organization? 
Question 1 Why Is Digital Citizenship Important for Museums, Heritage Sites, 
and Cultural Organizations in General? 
Participants of the focus group referred to several aspects which they consider 
valuable about digital citizenship. They highlighted various aspects of digitizing 
museum work and its signiﬁcance for digital citizenship. Foremost, it is the 
democratization of cultural heritage that is propelled by digitization. It serves 
society as a whole, fostering a culture of participation, prosperity, and shared 
knowledge. 
Through this process, individuals who would typically lack access to cultural 
heritage gain the opportunity to participate and engage in humanistic values. This is 
initially an option because whether and how citizens engage with cultural heritage 
depends not only on the fundamental offering but also on various primarily social 
factors as well as the mode of presentation. Many pioneering digital offers appeared 
unidimensional, incomplete, and non-satisfying at ﬁrst glance. At least museums 
started to bring their vast collections online, such as the digital collection of the 
Vienna Kunsthistorisches Museum (Museum of Art History) 2 and to interconnect
2 https://www.khm.at/entdecken/digitales-museum/ (last accessed 30.09.2023). 

464 T. Heskia et al.
digitized objects with current exhibitions, such as the Badisches Landesmuseum 
(Baden State Museum). 3 Even if direct participation does not occur, digitization 
of cultural heritage as open data gradually ensures its dissemination anyway. 
When digitized materials or inherently digital artifacts are available online, they 
are accessed by text-based AI systems, making them valuable contributors to the 
digital data pool. This also holds true for their nuanced, critical analysis, research 
ﬁndings, information materials, and teaching resources, all of which serve as 
original contributions from museums to the digital landscape. 
Through their publicly accessible digital collections, museums and heritage sites 
can extend their purpose far beyond their static and localized presence into a global 
digital space. Museums can literally transform their visitors into critical and open-
minded global citizens. On the one side by connecting people from all corners of 
the world with their speciﬁc collections—even with the objects for which there is 
no space for display. This works especially well with special interest groups. Even 
for the most unique preferences (i.e., coins from the early imperial era), global 
communities of relevant size can be found, an effect that has also been referred 
to in the commercial context as the “long tail” (Anderson, 2008). Simultaneously, 
they can link local visitors to the broader global heritage. Many museum collections 
have been built with objects from other regions and places. The digitization of 
these cultural objects can bring the possibility to get in touch with the cultures 
and the people from where these objects come from. Opening this dialogue is 
important to co-create new narratives around the objects and new meanings of 
the objects themselves. This dialogue would not be possible if objects were not 
digitized and made accessible to audiences beyond the physical museum visitors. 
In this sense, as one participant pointed out, digital citizenship is an opportunity to 
show different perspectives on the collection. And this perspective is not always one 
that is comfortable for the museum as it used to be. 
Excursion 1 The New Openness of Museums 
The newly found public awareness is driving the ongoing transformation of 
museums. Objects with doubtful provenance can no longer be hidden within 
museum walls—sometimes literally concealed deep in museum depots. Museums 
are embracing a whole new level of transparency. People from the very communities 
where these objects originated now have convenient access to them. This principle 
applies equally to items in ethnographic museums as well as to artworks obtained in 
contexts of war. Objects acquired by European colonial authorities—through private 
adventurers, in the course of ofﬁcial expeditions or by local administrations—were 
often recorded as purchases or donations. From today’s perspective, even when they 
do not involve violent looting, it must be said that the acquisitions often involve 
unfair practices, which rightfully trigger claims for restitution being the cultural 
heritage of someone else (Meijer-van Mensch & Brunotte, 2022). The transactions 
that occurred in the post–World War II era need to be reevaluated in terms of
3 https://www.landesmuseum.de/digital (last accessed 30.09.2023). 

Digital Citizenship in the Interactive Dissemination and Perception. . . 465
their fairness and voluntariness. Not to mention genuine looted art that can still 
be found even in Western collections. These are often smaller objects, which still 
remain undiscovered in the depots, for example, antiquarian books as part of entire 
collections that have gone to historical libraries in tens of thousands (Hall & Köstner, 
2016). Digital museums and also other heritage institutions, such as libraries, are 
facing mounting pressure from a global audience to meticulously examine the 
provenance of their objects and harmonize the historical values inscribed in their 
collections with the principles of a modern, postcolonial, and democratic world. 
What effect does this now have on a democratic digital museum? To make a 
meaningful contribution to global digital citizenship, one must critically examine 
the values historically inscribed in their collections. Once this introspection occurs, 
engaging in constructive dialogue with origin communities becomes possible, unen-
cumbered by geographical and, in recent years, pandemic-related barriers. German 
museums, such as the Grassi Museum für V ölkerkunde in Leipzig, have initiated 
digital contact with the peoples from whom speciﬁc artifacts—including, among 
others, human remains—originate. This outreach has, at times, led to tangible 
and analog repatriation efforts, often accompanied by jointly conducted return 
ceremonies.4 It can be concluded that a museum can only positively impact global 
citizenship, even in the digital realm, when it aligns itself with the contemporary 
values of a postcolonial society. While signiﬁcant progress has been made, many 
museums still grapple with the burden of their historical legacy. 
This example of how museums engage with origin communities is just one 
instance of how digitization has the potential to create new networks that lead to 
real-world connections. Interest groups for whom a physical visit is not currently 
feasible can be easily brought into contact. These new networks can serve as a 
foundation for bolstering civic values and may foster increased civic engagement. 
By reaching out to and actively involving new audiences, museums can become 
more relevant to the broader public, emphasizing the signiﬁcance of dialogue and 
participation in shaping a museum’s impact on society. 
Question 2 What Is Urgent: How Can Museums Ensure that They Nurture 
and Promote Digital Citizenship? 
In addressing the urgent needs within their institutions, participants emphasized 
the critical necessity for capacity building and training opportunities. Recognizing 
the importance of a comprehensive understanding of available possibilities, they 
underscored the centrality of training as a focal point. It becomes evident that 
lifelong learning is vital for both museum staff and volunteers, as well as it is for the 
population that forms the audience. However, the focus extends beyond technical 
capabilities, emphasizing the cultivation of awareness regarding the pivotal role 
cultural institutions play in harnessing and advancing societal beneﬁts—especially 
in and through digital channels. Persuading colleagues of the signiﬁcance of delving 
deeper into technology and data is imperative, emphasizing the crucial importance
4 https://grassi-voelkerkunde.skd.museum/forschung/dekolonisierung-restitution-und-
repatriierung/faq/ (last accessed 30.09.2023). 

466 T. Heskia et al.
of digital literacy and citizenship. Engaging in labs or internships proves invaluable 
for grasping best practices in this evolving digital landscape. The ability to adapt 
to constant changes and embrace uncertainty in processes is crucial, alongside the 
openness to share perspectives and ideas about ongoing transformations. Equally 
important is ensuring that visitors and the museum’s audience can effectively 
engage with these new digital opportunities. Therefore, it is not only essential to 
open collections to new audiences to increase accessibility, but also crucial to reﬂect 
on the implications of this transformation. 
In our increasingly digital and interconnected society, a museum’s relevance 
hinges on its digital presence and positive perception. Establishing a robust digital 
footprint becomes paramount, enabling museums to reach individuals who might 
not otherwise step through their physical doors. Digital interactions through social 
media have become commonplace, necessitating museums to actively engage with 
audiences in these online spaces. However, museums must progress beyond passive 
offerings, extending outreach efforts to communities previously untouched by their 
exhibits. Digital outreach serves as a tool, allowing museums to become potential 
focal points for societal integration. While achieving widespread societal integration 
on a global scale might seem ambitious given the growing societal divides, museums 
can still reach a substantial number of people within their spheres of inﬂuence. 
Excursion 2 From Outreach to Crowd-Sourcing 
The evolving landscape of dialogue transcends the physical conﬁnes of museums 
and heritage sites, necessitating innovative strategies to engage with the museum’s 
audience beyond its traditional visitors. The potential to be found in the digital 
space is not sufﬁcient; rather, the museum itself must go out actively to engage 
with societal groups that may not independently ﬁnd their way to the museum. 
The digital revolution has opened up entirely new possibilities here, and in the 
meantime, a distinct ﬁeld of Digital Outreach has been developed. The function of 
outreach has evolved as well: it is not anymore to be seen merely as a marketing 
tool to simply attract new visitors. In its further stage of development, Outreach 
serves as an outward service to society, which, in turn, leads to a transformation of 
the organization itself. Including this, Scharf et al. provide an extensive deﬁnition 
of museum outreach: 
Outreach is a systematic process in which the cultural institution strategically plans, 
implements, and evaluates cross-departmental measures to engage societal groups who, 
for various reasons, do not proactively access cultural offerings. This process brings 
about a change in the institution’s attitude, diversity of personnel, program design, and 
communication. The goal is to achieve a more diverse audience that reﬂects society. (Scharf 
et al., 2018) 
At its highest level, outreach can be seen as a society-oriented development 
approach. It might even be the essential pathway for the museum to effect 
meaningful changes in the external world. To achieve this, it is important that 
outreach is not understood unidirectionally but rather that active participation of 
the population is aimed for (Simon, 2010). Outreach becomes a means to promote

Digital Citizenship in the Interactive Dissemination and Perception. . . 467
citizenship, both digitally and analogously. Subsequently, it requires citizenship to 
unfold its full potential. 
Participation can be elevated to an entirely new level through new technologies. 
Digitality ensures that initiatives like crowdsourcing and citizen science open up 
new possibilities of interaction to further enrich the digital citizenship experience 
for their audiences. From 2014 to 2022, “Coding DaVinci” was a Hackaton for 
open cultural data that aimed to create innovative projects to release the innova-
tion potential of cultural heritage. 5 Europeana’s Transcribathon, as an initiative 
encouraging the public to transcribe handwritten texts from libraries and museums, 
is another example for this approach. 6 It provides an accessible platform for 
individuals to share knowledge and participate in civic engagement, fostering a 
sense of community involvement. People can learn to decipher old handwritings and 
in turn contribute their transcripts which are then counterchecked by the community. 
Digital citizenship holds signiﬁcance not only for museum visitors but also 
for museum professionals and collaborators. The role of curators is undergoing 
a signiﬁcant transformation, embracing new ways for connecting with people. 
V olunteers and other external interest groups, integral to many museums, represent 
a vital civic component that can be further empowered through digital initiatives 
(Van Hoven & Wellman, 2016). This evolution underscores the importance of digital 
engagement for museum staff and collaborators, fostering collaborative efforts and 
enriching the museum experience for all involved. The most recent developments 
lead to co-curation or citizen curation, which can take the form of a digitally 
supported co-creation of museum content together with the audience.7 
In conclusion, museums play a pivotal role in fostering digital citizenship that 
extends beyond their traditional boundaries. It is crucial to think innovatively, 
envisioning new potential audiences and functions for museums to contribute 
meaningfully at community and societal levels. Integrating digital elements into 
museums not only enhances their internal dynamics but also facilitates diverse 
collaborative projects. By providing digital collaboration platforms, museums open 
up opportunities for “unusual” and distant audiences to share their perspectives, 
enriching the signiﬁcance of objects, collections, and repositories. Digital citizen-
ship becomes the key for the participatory museum (Simon, 2010). 
Question 3 What Is Actually Being Done to Boost Digital Citizenship? 
There is a high diversity in the scope and extent of relevant activities in the 
institutions. Some participants of the focus group admitted to not being engaged 
in digital citizenship initiatives yet and being rather behind in terms of digital 
literacy and other aspects of digitization. Other participants indicated that their 
museums have already developed or are starting to launch some smaller projects 
in this area and referred to the steps their organizations are taking to embrace the
5 https://codingdavinci.de (last accessed 30.09.2023). 
6 https://europeana.transcribathon.eu/education-de/ (last accessed 30.09.2023). 
7 https://curatorialresearch.com/curatorial-education/citizen-curators-how-we-created-a-
curatorial-community/ (last accessed 30.09.2023). 

468 T. Heskia et al.
digital. However, it was also admitted that the concept of digital citizenship is still 
largely unknown and, therefore, appropriate accompanying measures for civic value 
are lacking. 
Embarking on the journey of digitizing objects or collections appears as a 
logical initial stride into the digital realm. Yet, a noteworthy contention arises—Big 
Data collections are frequently tailored to experts, leaving non-expert audiences, 
especially the general public, somewhat excluded. This exclusion is exacerbated 
by the fact that data often resides within internal databases, lacking permeable 
open data architectures and web interfaces. Established software solutions like 
TMS (The Museum System) originally run on local servers and, like many old 
database systems, suffer from the challenge that secure migration to web-based 
environments is relatively complex. However, server- and workstation-independent 
cloud-based solutions like TMS Cataloguer are still geared toward those who 
manage collections, for example, by offering features for digitally mapping loan 
trafﬁc.8 Consequently, despite the considerable efforts invested in digitization, it 
may not necessarily yield added value for digital citizenship. Rather, it serves as 
a foundation upon which further development and expansion must be built. The 
challenge lies not just in the digitization process itself but in ensuring that the digital 
realm becomes an inclusive space accessible to diverse audiences. It is believed that 
the potential for fostering digital citizenship at museums still needs to be explored 
and that, although digitizing collections can help, this alone is not enough. 
Expanding the museum’s inﬂuence beyond conventional visitors and cultivating 
an environment conducive to democratic behavior emerges as a crucial facet of 
digital citizenship, an aspect presently overlooked and undervalued in museum 
contexts. Once visitors are within the museum’s conﬁnes, the integration of 
digital elements should extend inward. This means that digitization doesn’t merely 
establish connections with the external world but penetrates within, allowing 
visitors to engage with the museum or heritage site on-site in alignment with their 
digital habits. This begins with the provision of complimentary Wi-Fi to guests, 
encouraging their social media activities and fostering a context-driven digital 
connection (Adam, 2017). Furthermore, the creation of inviting analog spaces, such 
as courtyards on museum premises, proven to attract diverse audiences, particularly 
the younger, can contribute to promoting digital interconnectedness. 
It has become commonplace for objects in museums to be photographed, 
adhering to conservation considerations and generally shared while respecting the 
museum’s rights. The question arises regarding the value of recurrent photos of 
museum highlights, such as the Mona Lisa or Klimt’s Kiss, for which the Belvedere 
Museum in Vienna has even set up a dedicated poster copy for selﬁes. This is where 
additional and more nuanced information, potentially offered by the museum and 
ideally shared digitally, becomes crucial. Emphasizing open architectures is also 
essential, enabling visitors to directly connect with their own digital devices and
8 https://museumswissenschaft.de/the-museum-system-ein-global-verwendetes-
sammlungsmanagementsystem/ (last accessed 30.09.2023). 

Digital Citizenship in the Interactive Dissemination and Perception. . . 469
operate within their familiar digital environment. In practical terms, this means 
moving away from traditional audio guides, where each visitor is directed on a 
narrowly deﬁned path using museum-provided devices and headphones. Instead, 
the focus shifts toward integrating with visitors’ devices. Given the ubiquity of 
smartphones and headphones, even among seniors, the future direction involves 
offering majority app-driven or web-based guides accessible through personal 
devices. There are now numerous proprietary museum apps, exempliﬁed beautifully 
by the Museum Barberini in Potsdam 9 and information easily accessible through 
VR codes. In seamlessly integrating into the information ﬂow of digital citizens, 
the museum becomes a valuable disseminator of its content. This approach allows 
the museum to align itself with the digital landscape, reaching and sharing its 
valuable content with a broader audience. Simultaneously, efforts are made to 
provide inclusive options for the minority who are not digitally connected. 
Participants ﬁnally reﬂected on different ideas and initiatives through which 
museums could further contribute to digital literacy and citizenship.
 Museums have the potential to transform into hubs of alternative learning, 
providing high school students with opportunities to cultivate digital skills, like 
coding, ﬁlming, or editing. Learning such skills based on individual interests 
can be especially helpful for students who face difﬁculties in regular classroom 
instruction or even school dropouts.
 Envisioned are intergenerational collaborative projects, fostering encounters 
where individuals from diverse age groups convene to interact, offer assistance, 
and share a wealth of knowledge and skills. This collaborative effort might 
involve younger individuals instructing the elderly in the use of social media 
or digital content digitization. In turn, the older generation can bridge the gap by 
imparting museum-derived knowledge to younger audiences who may typically 
show less interest and engagement.
 Photography exhibitions have the potential to cultivate various relevant literacies, 
including visual, media, and information literacy. Pertinent discussion points 
within this context can explore varying levels of reality. Questions arise regarding 
the extent to which already the presence of a camera inherently modiﬁes 
reality, the principles of artistic composition and design, and the commencement 
of manipulation and fake. Is it during the capture or in the post-production 
stage? Such distinctions hold signiﬁcance, especially as the proliferation of AI 
introduces yet another realm of possibilities for editing and generation.
9 https://app.museum-barberini.de (last accessed 30.09.2023). 

470 T. Heskia et al.
4 Intermediate Summary: The Added Value 
Considering the idea of digital citizenship within museums and heritage institutions 
leads to a full range of added values. 
Firstly, it leads to a signiﬁcant emphasis on increased interaction and collab-
oration opportunities within museums and heritage sites. These institutions are 
envisioned not just as repositories of artifacts or historical places but as dynamic 
real and virtual spaces where individuals can meet, interact, and actively partake in 
the cultivation of democratic behavior. 
Secondly, the push toward increased accessibility and inclusion is evident, 
primarily through the digitization of objects and collections. This transformative 
process allows museums to extend their offerings, encompassing aspects, such 
as culture, heritage, history, and art, beyond the conﬁnes of traditional visitors. 
Simultaneously, the digitization of objects unlocks new pathways for analysis, 
distribution, remixing, reuse, and co-creation of new meanings and narratives 
around these materials. 
Lastly, the integration of the above-described digital initiatives within the 
museum environment serves as a catalyst for the enhancement of digital literacy 
and other essential skills. Engaging with these tools presents participants with 
valuable opportunities to elevate their digital proﬁciency and acquire other relevant 
literacies, such as visual literacy, contributing to a multifaceted and enriching 
museum experience. 
Question 4: What Does It Need to Develop a Digital Citizenship Strategy for 
a Museum/Heritage Site/Cultural Organization? 
The group ultimately reﬂected on how to strategically approach the challenge of 
digital citizenship to develop a clear and worked-out action plan. The goal of such 
a strategy is to establish a framework for guiding digital citizenship initiatives in 
museums, promoting positive engagement with digital technologies both on-site 
(e.g., through digital collections) and online. This includes encouraging active and 
responsible participation locally and globally. Additionally, the initiative aims to 
support the development of digital skills among museum staff, visitors, and the 
general public. 
Participants discussed various requirements and challenges to enhance the active 
contribution of museums to digital citizenship. Human resources and capacity 
building emerged as critical factors, emphasizing the need for staff and volunteers 
equipped with adequate digital skills, knowledge of digital literacy, and an under-
standing of citizenship issues. Continuous professional development, upskilling, and 
reskilling opportunities were underscored as essential components of this effort. 
Lifelong learning, a shifted mindset, and a clear understanding of museums’ roles in 
fostering both conventional and digital citizenship were deemed crucial. This needs 
to be ensured through effective “digital” leadership. The management literature has 
not yet formed a uniﬁed picture regarding the prerequisites for digital leadership. 
However, it certainly encompasses digital consciousness, a deep understanding of

Digital Citizenship in the Interactive Dissemination and Perception. . . 471
digital processes, and a high degree of agility (Kreutzer et al., 2017; Creusen et al., 
2017; Wagner, 2017; Franco, 2020). 
A deeper understanding of the museum’s audience and non-visitors, both 
intended and unintended, was highlighted as necessary. The advent of digitization 
introduces new audiences with distinct needs and preferences that may differ from 
traditional visitors. Technical infrastructure emerged as a requirement at various 
levels, tailored to speciﬁc museum projects. This could involve VR sets, interactive 
screens, or specialized equipment for digitizing diverse objects or collections. 
Backstage, adequate access to social media platforms and production equipment 
was emphasized. 
Networking opportunities with professionals and organizations interested in 
advancing digital citizenship in museums were deemed vital. The exchange of 
good practices and experiences was identiﬁed as essential for fostering digital 
citizenship. Efﬁcient outreach strategies, especially for engaging new and diverse 
audiences beyond the expected visitors, including hard-to-reach demographics like 
adolescents, were considered. The role of digital tools in this outreach was also 
discussed. 
Finally, participants stressed the need for increased ﬁnancial resources to mate-
rialize these initiatives. Establishing a robust Digital Citizenship strategic plan 
requires a thorough assessment of the current state within the organization, consid-
ering strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats. Formulating a clear vision, 
identifying speciﬁc focus areas, and articulating strategic goals, such as ensuring 
widespread digital access to cultural heritage data and the inclusion of relevant target 
groups, were seen as imperative. 
In the pursuit of fostering digital citizenship and advancing digitization, it is 
imperative to acknowledge and confront the inherent obstacles and challenges. 
Participants in discussions have underscored the signiﬁcance of considering various 
risks within this context. 
One notable challenge arises in the process of digitizing objects and entire 
collections for public accessibility. This task is often complicated by compliance 
with European Union and local laws, encompassing areas, such as copyright, intel-
lectual property rights (IPR), General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), license 
management, and adherence to the public domain, among others. Furthermore, 
the appeal of digital collections and projects poses a unique challenge. While 
digitization enhances accessibility, artistic considerations introduce limitations. 
Issues like perspective or texture problems in virtual spaces necessitate a delicate 
balance between accessibility and artistic quality. 
Effective outreach in the digital realm is another complex undertaking. The 
challenge lies in understanding museum audiences comprehensively and devising 
strategies that genuinely engage them. It goes beyond mere dissemination, requiring 
a strategic and personalized approach to connect with diverse audience segments 
(Scharf et al., 2018). Outreach achieves its greatest impact when it leads to 
comprehensive participation. When participation shifts to the digital realm, a 
series of new challenges arises. These include, among others, an unpredictable 
breadth of involvement, constraints on digitization coupled with process dominance,

472 T. Heskia et al.
often reduced depth of participation, challenges related to anonymity, participants’ 
doubts about self-efﬁcacy, lack of commitment, and limitations due to asynchrony 
(Sommer, 2022). Finally, it is important to note that while the concept of Digital 
Citizenship serves as a tool to bridge the digital divide, simultaneously, this very 
divide has the potential to undermine these efforts. Ensuring the accessibility of 
initiatives, both in actuality and in perception, is crucial for individuals with varying 
levels of digital afﬁnity and literacy to fully engage in these endeavors. 
To make tangible strides toward digital citizenship, an essential component is 
the development of a structured implementation plan that delineates necessary 
steps, establishes timelines, and involves diverse employee groups across depart-
ments. Establishing mechanisms for execution and assessment is imperative for 
systematically monitoring progress. Adequate budget and resources, encompassing 
material, ﬁnancial, and human resources, must be allocated for successful strategy 
implementation. A critical element is the development of a risk assessment plan to 
identify potential risks and formulate mitigation strategies, ensuring the successful 
realization of the digital citizenship strategy. 
5 Key Findings and Conclusion 
The consensus among participants highlighted the substantial potential of digital 
citizenship within museums. This potential lies in its ability to encourage visitors 
and the public to actively and positively engage with a spectrum of digital 
technologies, both on-site and online, including digital hands-on stations, virtual 
reality and other immersive applications, interactive games, and co-creation tools. 
The envisioned outcomes include fostering local and global participation, as well as 
contributing to the development of digital skills for museum staff, visitors, and the 
wider public. 
While some participants acknowledged their current disengagement with digital 
citizenship initiatives, revealing a perceived lag in digital literacy and other aspects 
of digitization, others reported active involvement or initiation of projects in this 
domain. These proactive institutions outlined speciﬁc steps, such as digitizing 
collections, utilizing online surveys and analytics tools, monitoring website trafﬁc, 
and investing in a robust social media presence, showcasing their commitment to 
embracing the digital landscape. 
There was agreement among the participants that digital citizenship can have 
a great potential at museums to encourage museums’ visitors and the public to 
positively engage with digital technologies. This encompasses activities, such as 
creating, working, sharing, socializing, investigating, playing, communicating, and 
learning on site, for example, through digital collections and online. The sole option 
is not enough; hence, it is imperative to actively encourage both visitors and the 
public to participate responsibly and engage on both local and global scales. This 
involvement is crucial in fostering the development of digital skills among museum 
staff, visitors, and the broader public.

Digital Citizenship in the Interactive Dissemination and Perception. . . 473
To promote digital citizenship, heritage sites, and museums need to enhance 
interaction and collaboration, becoming hybrid spaces where democratic behavior 
is practiced. Achieving this involves improving accessibility and inclusion, starting 
with digitization and the training of the staff’s digital skills (Barnes et al., 2018). 
However, it is the sharing of data that leads to new possibilities for dissemination, 
research, remixing, and collective creation of new meanings and narratives. Engag-
ing with digital tools allows participants to enhance their digital skills and other 
relevant competencies, such as visual and writing abilities. With the advent of text 
and image-based AI systems, the next challenge is once again on the horizon.
